For where there is no sincere and faithful leadership, each person seeks his own interests at the expense of others, and each one reckons himself wiser and better than the others.

I say that when a person loses the leadership of the Holy Spirit, the law of selfishness, injustice and rebellion comes upon him within, and he enters into countless conflicts between soul and body and between mind, emotion and senses; the body rebels against the soul to ride the whole of a person's life and lead it into fleshly lusts, with servility and humiliation before temporal pleasures.

C. Entering a state of extreme despair, in which no one will accept responsibility, so that each man takes hold of his brother and says to him: “Thou hast clothing,” a sign of accepting him as ruler, because handing over the garment to another is a symbol of a person handing over his body to the leadership of another. But because of the ruin that has come upon the country, with everyone unable to act, each one says: “Make me not a ruler of the people” [7], explaining it by saying: “I will not be an healer (a binder of wounds); for in my house is neither bread nor clothing” [7]. Thus all became hungry and naked, so who would accept the rulership? Who can bind the wounds of such a people while he himself finds no food or clothing? This is the natural fruit of one who seeks a human savior, supposing him able to rescue him and lead his life without resorting to the unique divine Savior. The psalmist says: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Ps 146:3).

D. The loss of shame and of the fear of God, for they came to have an uncovered face that is not ashamed to commit evil: “They declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not” [9]. The gravity reached the point that Jerusalem sank into repeated stumblings, not out of weakness or ignorance but deliberately, to provoke the Lord [9]. Evils are committed in word and deed without shame or modesty. This is the picture of the world in the modern age, as many young people feel that the deviations they practice, in all their forms, are a natural right of man.

He says: “The shew of their countenance doth witness against them” [9], for merely looking at their faces reveals the marks of sin and their deprivation of the work of grace in them, and as the Scripture says: “In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil” (1 Jn 3:10).

Even if the wicked are visible and have become the majority, there is a holy few belonging to the Lord, whom God will not overlook; they are not lost and no harm befalls them. Therefore the prophet says: “Say ye to the righteous, that it shall be well with him: for they shall eat the fruit of their doings” [10]. In the midst of severe distress the Lord keeps His righteous ones, and turns everything that comes upon them into their good and their glory. Joseph the righteous suffered much, and his labors were the very way of his glory; and we see him say to his brothers: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Gen 50:20).

God does not destroy the righteous with the wicked (Gen 18:25), but keeps His righteous ones in the time of trial; He hides them in His pavilion in the day of evil and covers them with the covert of His tabernacle (Ps 27:5); He knows them, for He has graven them upon the palms of His hands (Isa 49:16).

St. Justin comments on the prophet's words: “Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves. Say ye to the righteous, that it shall be well with him: for they shall eat the fruit of their doings” [9-10]: [Truly your hand is raised to commit evil, for you killed Christ and do not repent; rather, you still hate and kill, as far as you are able, those who believe in Him as God, the Father of all, and you curse us without cause, and you do so to those who stand on our side. But all of us pray for you and for all men, as our Christ, the Lord of all, taught us, when He commanded us to pray even for our enemies, and to love those who hate us and bless those who curse us.] And St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [They bound Jesus and brought Him to the hall of the high priest. Do you wish to know that this also was written and spoken of Him? Isaiah says: “Woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves, saying: Let us bind the righteous, because he is troublesome to us.”]

They supposed that they were doing evil to the righteous, but they were doing it to themselves, and so they reap the fruit of their work, not as divine punishment for vengeance but as the natural fruit of their conduct and their life. “Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him” [11]. “Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (2 Cor 9:6).

E. The love of authority rather than the care of love: True leaders are like fathers who embrace all as their children and give their lives laid down for the people; but when the grace of God is removed, leaders, even religious ones, turn into domineering rulers who have no concern except to defend their positions and their authority with various justifications, under the cover of defending the truth, the dignity of leading positions and the ability to cut off evil. These turn from self-giving fathers into little children ruled by the “ego,” or into something like women (a symbol of bodily weakness) who seek control, for it says: “As for my people, children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, they which lead thee cause thee to err, and destroy the way of thy paths” [12].

Some scholars see that this was fulfilled literally, since some boys took the kingship in Judah and some women played grave roles in the management of affairs. As for the symbolic side, the guides here, especially the priests and prophets, were overcome by the spirit of recklessness and the love of domination, and so they turned away from true love and faithful care. In their hypocrisy these say to the wicked, Thou art righteous (Prov 24:24). And as the wise man says: “The place of judgment, that wickedness was there; and the place of righteousness, that iniquity was there” (Eccl 3:16).

In the midst of this corruption, especially on the part of the leaders, God intervenes for the simple ones among His people, and stands up to judge them as the vinedressers who ate the vineyard instead of caring for it, rebuking them thus: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks? Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: but ye feed not the flock” (Ezek 34:2-3). They seize the rights of the poor, as Jezebel seized the field of Naboth the Jezreelite (1 Kgs 21); they beat the people to pieces and grind the faces of the poor [15].

entries.section: 3. The removal of the means of luxury together with haughtiness:

paragraphs.text: 16 Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet: 17 Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts. 18 In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon, 19 The chains, and the bracelets, and the mufflers, 20 The bonnets, and the ornaments of the legs, and the headbands, and the tablets, and the earrings, 21 The rings, and nose jewels, 22 The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins, 23 The glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails. 24 And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty. 25 Thy men shall fall by the sword, and thy mighty in the war. 26 And her gates shall lament and mourn; and she being desolate shall sit upon the ground.

After speaking of the judgment of the corrupt leaders, he began to speak of the haughty daughters of Zion, who perhaps were behind the corruption of these leaders. The daughters of Zion had forgotten their belonging to Zion and to the Lord, and walked like pagan women in arrogance, with luxury and frivolity.

St. John Chrysostom says: [These words were not directed to them alone but to every woman who imitates them. Paul also stands as an accuser when he tells Timothy that the adornment of women should not be “with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” (1 Tim 2:9). For the wearing of gold is harmful in every place, especially when (the woman) enters the Church and passes before the poor. Do you wish to be an object of accusation? Wear the appearance of cruelty and inhumanity.]

St. John Chrysostom sees that our life is a time for spiritual striving, not for luxury in dress and haughtiness in walking. It is fitting for us now to strive as in a spiritual battle, not caring for outward appearances but for obtaining victory and triumph, for the time of open glory will surely come.

Once again the same saint asks us to fix our eyes on our Christ, so that we care for the inner adornment that befits Him and do not seek outward things. [You have Christ as your Bridegroom, O virgin, so why do you seek to attract human lovers?!]
The prophet presents to us some features of the wantonness that marked the daughters of Zion:

A. Haughtiness: “Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks...” [16]. Pride took control of them, so they became haughty and walk with stretched forth necks, after they had forgotten their fathers and mothers whose necks were bowed under the yoke of bondage in Egypt.
“Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Prov 16:18-19).

B. Wanton eyes [6]: They were occupied with hunting the hearts of men and capturing them, as a natural fruit of the emptiness of the inner heart, so with their eyes they set nets of death, for the wise man says: “And I find more bitter than death the woman, whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands: whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her” (Eccl 7:26).
The word “wanton” in the original means that they beautify their eyes with a black powder, since the people of the East were fond of wide eyes surrounded by a black circle.

C. Wantonness in walking: “Walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” [16], a sign of the corruption of the inner heart. They walk in conceit and pride and put “anklets” on their feet, or bells on their shoes, to draw attention to themselves.
What will the Lord do to these arrogant daughters who walk in frivolity and luxury?

entries.section: 3. The removal of the means of luxury together with haughtiness:

paragraphs.text: A. “The Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts” [17]. Baldness or a bald patch is, for a girl, a sign of extreme ugliness, for God gave woman her hair as a crown of glory for her, that she may live honored and beloved in the Lord, admired, loved and honored by her husband, so that she shares family life with him on an equal footing, being the body that the head cannot do without. But when she departs from the natural law with a spirit of pride and frivolity, she loses even her natural beauty and honor and becomes like one struck with baldness.

The uncovering of her secret parts is a figure for the exposure of the corruption of her nature, or a reference to her nakedness, with no one to spread his skirt over her, cover her life and give her his name that she may take shelter in it and be joined to him.

This is the state of the human soul fallen through pride, for it loses God's gifts to it, and the corruption of its nature is exposed, so that it becomes without beauty, strength or honor; the most trivial sins mock it, and mere imagination and daydreams make sport of it.

B. The removal of all the outward show of wealth and adornment: the tinkling ornaments about the feet, the cauls, the round tires like the moon, the earrings, the bracelets, the mufflers, the bonnets, the chains, the headbands, the tablets (veils, shawls), the earrings (amulets), the glasses (transparent garments for bodily allurement), the fine linen (costly undergarments), the hoods and the vails.

Thus He takes from her the outward adornment and the undergarments, that she may be in nakedness and ugliness... perhaps she will return to God and ask that He Himself cover her, and so the Lord Himself becomes her covering garment (Gal 3:27; Col 3:10).
God allows this discipline for the daughters of Zion that they may find in the Savior the secret of their adornment and glory.
Here he points to what befalls the daughters of Zion during the captivity, for he says:

entries.section: 3. The removal of the means of luxury together with haughtiness:

paragraphs.text: “And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink” [24]; after they were occupied with perfume and fragrant scents, spending much on them, they were taken captive by the enemy and carried to a foreign land, where they are absorbed in work without rest, so that the smell of sweat becomes offensive. This is what actually happened; as for the spiritual side, the proud soul loses its deceptive outward adornment, and the stench of its nature, its poverty and its nakedness are exposed, that it may perhaps feel the need of One who saves it and satisfies it. And as it was said to the angel (bishop) of the church of the Laodiceans: “Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked: I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see” (Rev 3:17-18).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of the sanctification of the sense of smell in us, so that the fragrance of the Holy Spirit in us may not turn away from us and the stench of our own nature remain with us, saying: [Let us be healed also with respect to smell..., and instead of dust being poured upon us in place of fragrant scents, let us smell the fragrance of the anointing that was poured upon us, which we received spiritually, and which fashioned us (anew) and changed us, so that a sweet fragrance comes forth from us.]

The prophet says: “Instead of a girdle a rent” [24]; after the daughters of Zion had girded themselves with decorated golden girdles set with precious stones, they were bound with ropes to be drawn into captivity as humiliated women. A painful picture that reveals the fruit of sin!
“And instead of well set hair baldness”; as a sign of humiliation the hair of noblewomen is cut, to make them appear ugly.

“Instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty” [24]... Thus sackcloth became their clothing instead of splendid garments, and a brand appeared on their foreheads or hands as a sign of slavery... for slaves of both sexes were stamped with a particular mark by burning, so that the master might know who belonged to him.

entries.section: 3. The removal of the means of luxury together with haughtiness:

paragraphs.text: In brief, he expressed the complete shattering of their life because of their reliance on outward appearances and on the human arm. Therefore he says: “Thy men shall fall by the sword, and thy mighty in the war. And her gates shall lament and mourn; and she being desolate shall sit upon the ground” [25-26]. The men died, the women were taken captive, and the great city became as though empty!
“And in that day seven women shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let us be called by thy name, to take away our reproach.” [1].

These seven women are all the nations, among them the Jews, for all felt an extreme emptiness invading the depths because of the corruption of human nature. These nations gather as a bride seeking her Bridegroom; she wants His name that He may take away the reproach of her corruption, and then she eats her own bread and wears her own apparel. Her Christ is more important than all her needs; in Him she finds all satisfaction, covering from nakedness and protection from all shame.

This is from the symbolic, spiritual side. As for the literal side, the prophet Isaiah prophesied what would befall Judah, as it would be exposed to fierce wars in which a great number of men would be killed, so that every woman would long to find a man for herself under whose name she might take shelter, whatever it cost her. She is ready to share him with six other women, which is something a woman by her nature cannot bear; she even asks her husband not to be obliged to provide anything, but she eats and drinks from her own labor, which is contrary to nature itself... All this is because she wants to bear children by him, so that her reproach may be taken away (Gen 30:23; 1 Sam 1:11).
2 In that day shall the branch of the LORD be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and comely for them that are escaped of Israel.

Now, if humanity with all its peoples (the seven women) has discovered its need for the Savior, here the prophet announces to it His coming, saying: “In that day shall the branch of the LORD be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and comely for them that are escaped of Israel” [2].

“That day” means the fullness of time (Gal 4:4), in which the Only-Begotten Son of God became incarnate, who was called “the Branch of the LORD,” or “the Branch” (Jer 23:5; 33:15; Zech 3:8; 6:12). He is the Branch of the LORD and a Branch of righteousness for David, for He is the One born before all ages, eternally, of the very essence of the Father, and by His Incarnation He was born of the seed of David.

By His entry into the world He declared the divine splendor and the surpassing glory upon the simple strangers who believe, as well as upon those of the Jews who are saved. As Simeon the elder said: “A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.”

This Branch sprouted by His Incarnation, and dwelt in our midst to reflect the divine splendor upon our nature, so He says to His Church: “Thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezek 16:14).
The word “branch” also corresponds to “Nazareth,” so the Evangelist says: “That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene” (Mt 2:23).

3 And it shall come to pass, that he that is left in Zion, and he that remaineth in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, even every one that is written among the living in Jerusalem: 4 When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning, who is it that enjoys the Branch of the LORD?

“He that is left in Zion, and he that remaineth in Jerusalem” [3]. These are the few who accepted faith in the Lord Christ from among the community of the Jews; they remained in the spiritual Zion, in the Church, the new Jerusalem.

From the literal side it refers to the remnant that remained from the captivity, but from the spiritual side it is the holy few, the little flock whose heart does not leave Zion and whose spirit does not depart from the Jerusalem above. Many of the prophets spoke of this remnant (Zech 13:9), and it has been found in every age: in the days of Elijah the prophet the Lord declared that He had seven thousand men who had not bowed the knee to Baal; during the captivity Daniel was found with the three young men among the holy few, and also Esther and Mordecai; and after the captivity we also hear of this holy few (Mal 3:6; 4:2); and the Lord Christ Himself speaks of the little flock to whom it is the Father's good pleasure to give the Kingdom (Lk 12).
In brief, every faithful soul that lifts its heart to the Jerusalem above sees the Church, holy in the Lord, and rejoices and is glad because of her.

Isaiah's heart was bound to Jerusalem, the capital of his country and the city of God which contains His holy temple, and he entered into bitterness because of the corruption that had come upon it. Now, as he announces the coming of “the Branch of the LORD,” he sees a new Jerusalem inhabited by saints in the holy Lord, who enjoy eternal life. He says: “Shall be called holy, even every one that is written among the living in Jerusalem” [3].

The Church, the icon of heaven, is the pledge of the Jerusalem above, into which nothing defiled or unclean may enter, nor anyone who makes a lie, but only he who has washed his robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 7:14).

As members of the holy Church, the new Jerusalem, we have enjoyed the anointing of the Spirit of the Holy God, that we may fulfill the evangelical commandment: “But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation” (1 Pet 1:15).

Who sanctifies our life? The Lord Himself, for the prophet says: “When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughter of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning” [4]. He washed our defilements in the waters of Baptism by the merits of His blood, and He still washes all our weaknesses with His blood that flowed from His pierced side mingled with water. If our hands have been stained with blood through our sins, He offers His blood as an atonement for us, to present us as a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle, but holy in everything.

This washing or purging is accomplished “by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning.” The spirit of judgment was accomplished by His being lifted up on the Cross, bearing the price of our sins in His body, fulfilling divine justice on our behalf in Himself. As for the spirit of burning, it means what the Law had previously announced in the Book of Leviticus concerning the “burnt offering,” where the sacrifice is burned completely as a sign of perfect love... So the sacrifice of Christ in our name is the “burnt offering” that was offered as a sign of our perfect love in Him toward the Father. Perhaps by the spirit of burning he also meant the fiery Holy Spirit who descended upon the Church to sanctify her and wash every member in her.
* In the last days, when the fullness of the time of freedom came, the Word Himself washed the filth of the daughter of Zion, for He washed the feet of the disciples with His own hands (Jn 13:5).
St. Irenaeus * The excellent spiritual bath (of Baptism) removes the corruption of the soul.

St. Clement of Alexandria St. Clement of Alexandria comments on the saying “purged the blood of Jerusalem” by saying: [Here is the blood of the crime and the killing of the prophets]; for whoever denied Christ shared with his fathers in the killing of the prophets, but whoever received Him has been purified and sanctified in his depths.

entries.section: 4. Christ's dwelling in the midst of His Church:

paragraphs.text: 5 And the LORD will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night: for upon all the glory shall be a defence.

The Church is washed by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, that is, through the unique burnt sacrifice that the Lord Christ offered and by the work of the Holy Spirit in the waters of Baptism, and so she asks for the dwelling of her slain Bridegroom in her midst; He covers her by day like a cloud that shades them and leads her by night as a pillar of smoke and a pillar of fire that lights the way for her. Thus the Church recalls in her memory the tabernacle of meeting in the midst of the wilderness, where God met with His people, but it is a new tabernacle on a level different from the tabernacle of the Old Covenant, in that:

A. “Upon every dwelling place” [5]: the divine presence or divine indwelling is no longer limited to a tent or a temple, but He dwells in His Church, which extends everywhere, in the east and in the west; He dwells in the hearts of the priests and the people, and His doors are open to all peoples and nations wherever they are.

B. “And upon her assemblies”: this expression points to God's work in the Church as one assembly, or one community, in which each member enjoys the gift of the divine indwelling not as an isolated individual but as a living member of the community, joined with the rest of the members through Christ the Head; he has his personal relationship with God, which increases his union with his brethren.
C. “Will create... a cloud and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire”: the Lord Christ is the secret of the protection and illumination of His Church.

D. His saying: “For upon all the glory shall be a defence” means that the glory of the king's daughter is within (Ps 45), hidden in her. Outwardly she shares with her Christ His sufferings, His crucifixion, His death and His burial, so that what was said of her Bridegroom is said of her: “He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isa 53:2); and inwardly she shares with Him the glory of His Resurrection.

The soul that realizes the value of the inner glory of its Christ and the joy of His Kingdom within it covers it because it is precious... For we are accustomed to hide what is precious and keep it, while what is worthless needs no covering or keeping. The Church, in her preoccupation with her glorified Christ, says: “He shall lie all night betwixt my breasts” (Song 1:13)... She wants Him in her depths, hidden in her heart!

entries.section: 5. The Church of Christ as a tabernacle and a refuge:

paragraphs.text: 6 And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain.
The Lord dwells in His Church and makes of her a tabernacle that shields the suffering, wounded souls from the heat of the day, and shelters them from storms and rains (Isa 4:6).

St. John Chrysostom sees that this tabernacle is the great cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1), saying: [The remembrance of the saints raises up and restores the soul that has been weighed down with woes, so that it becomes like a cloud that protects it from the very hot and burning rays (of the sun).]

“Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill: and he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes” [1-2].

This song proclaims the story of divine love, in which God loved man and still loves him and cares for him, and God continues in His love while man meets love with barrenness. This story was fulfilled with our first parents Adam and Eve, and also with the people of God at the beginning of their existence, for Moses the prophet says: “For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance. He found him in a desert land, and in the waste howling wilderness; he compassed him about, he watched him, he kept him as the apple of his eye” (Deut 32:9-10). God brought His people out of bondage not merely to give them the land flowing with milk and honey, but to establish the Church of the New Testament that fills the whole earth and enjoys the inner Kingdom of God, as the psalmist says: “Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land” (Ps 80:8-9).
It is clear that the “vineyard” here refers to the whole people: the kingdom of Israel and Judah; so what did the Lord present to His beloved people?

A. He set them on “a very fruitful hill” [1], for He brought them into Canaan, which flows with milk and honey; so the drought that comes and the famines that occur are not due to the nature of the land or the circumstances of the region, but are the fruit of the sins of the people.

God established the Church of the New Testament on a fruitful hill, for He lifted her heart as if to heaven, that her children might enjoy the richness of the heavenly life, so that they are satisfied and lack nothing.

B. “He fenced it (made a hedge around it)” [2]: this hedge is the Law with which the Lord surrounded His people anciently, so that they would not mingle with the surrounding pagan nations and take over their abominations from them. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The Law is a hedge, made for safety (Isa 8:20)]. St. Ambrose sees that the wall is “the divine providence that keeps the vineyard from the attack of the spiritual beast.” And St. Jerome sees that it is the guarding of the angels.

C. “And gathered out the stones thereof” [2]: the stones refer to pagan worship, where the idols were of stone, which the Lord removed from the midst of His people, or removed His people from them, so that all might live a godly life. The stones also refer to the nature of hardness and violence which our Lord Jesus wants to remove from every heart by the work of His Holy Spirit. In the words of Ezekiel the prophet: “I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh” (Ezek 11:9). This new heart and new spirit (Ezek 36:26) is realized by our receiving the new spiritual birth in the waters of holy Baptism. St. Cyprian says: [It is Baptism in which the old man dies and the new man is born, as the Apostle declares, affirming that He saved us by the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5).]

D. “Planted it with the choicest vine (a chosen vine)” [2], that is, He planted it as a vine of the best kinds of vines, as a chosen people that received a covenant with God, that it might bear “truth” in it, as the Lord says: “Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?” (Jer 2:21).

As for the Church of the New Testament, “the Truth” Himself came, the Word of God incarnate, to present Himself as a vine who carries us in Him as living branches that bring forth much fruit (Jn 15:5).

E. “And built a tower in the midst of it” [2], in which the owner of the vineyard or the watchman dwells to guard the vineyard from the attacks of thieves and wild beasts. Some scholars see that the tower is the company of the prophets and priests and all the spiritual and civil leaders who ought to have watched over the flock and kept it from the little foxes that spoil the vines.

In the New Testament the tower is the altar of the Lord that is set up within the soul, on which the believer offers his prayers, his fasts, his gifts and his whole life as a burnt offering to the Lord, through his union with the sacrificed Christ. Through this spiritual tower the Church of Christ is kept strong and effective in every heart, where the believers enjoy fellowship and union with the Lord Himself.

F. “And also made a winepress therein” [2], for pressing the grapes and making the wine of love that is offered for spiritual joy. What is this winepress but the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, who trod the winepress alone, and of the nations there was none with Him (Isa 63:3). He offered His blood, poured out, as the wine of love that gladdens every believing heart.

St. Ambrose says: [He dug a winepress, because the mysteries of the sufferings of Christ appear like new wine... and the crowd supposed that the disciples were drunk when they received the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:13). He dug the vat of a winepress so that the inner fruit might be poured out in it.]

St. Irenaeus says: [God planted the vineyard of the human race when He first created Adam and chose the fathers, then He committed it into the hands of the vinedressers when He established the Mosaic dispensation, and He fenced it by presenting teachings concerning their worship of Him, and built a tower by choosing Jerusalem, and dug a winepress when He prepared a vessel for the prophetic Spirit. And so He sent prophets before the Babylonian captivity, and then more prophets (during the captivity and after it), seeking the fruits...]
What did the vineyard give to its owner?

“And he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes” [2]. The Lord expected to gather love in return for love, and repentance and remorse in return for the forgiveness of His sins, but He found hardened hearts that bring forth no fruits worthy of repentance. All have gone astray and become corrupt and come short of the glory of God, so it was fitting for the Word of God to come down to us as a new vine, who alone plants us in Him so that we bring forth much fruit (Jn 15:5).

* When He says: “I am the true vine” (Jn 15:1), He distinguishes Himself without doubt from that one to whom He addressed the words: “How then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?” (Jer 2:21), for how could a true vine, from which it is expected to bring forth grapes, have brought forth thorns?!
* I expected it to bring forth fruit, and I found sin.
St. Augustine * I longed for it (the vine) to give wine, and it brought forth thorns. Behold, you see the crown with which I am adorned.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem

entries.section: 2. A judgment between God and His people:

paragraphs.text: 3 And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. 4 What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? 5 And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down: 6 And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. 7 For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for truth, but behold bloodshed; for justice, but behold a cry.

entries.section: 2. A judgment between God and His people:

paragraphs.text: Nothing is harder than for a being to enter into a judgment with a son who is beloved to him, but before the hardness of man's heart and his ingratitude He asked to stand before His people for a dialogue, asking: “What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?!” [4]. And the wonder is that He left the judgment to the other party, to His opponents, so that they might judge themselves by themselves. This is God's way in dealing with us: He exposes our souls before us, and uncovers our weaknesses before our eyes, and leaves us to judge ourselves by ourselves, not because He wants to win or to punish, but because He seeks our return to Him and our entering into relations of love and affection with Him.

What more could God have done with us than He did?! He created us out of nothing, and set us in His image and likeness, and gave us the earth with what is on it and under it and above it, and offered the stars for our benefit, and when our nature became corrupt He sent us His Law and His prophets, and finally He came Himself to write the song of His love in blood in His body on the Cross!
Since the vineyard found nothing with which to answer the Vinedresser, wonderful in His love, the Vinedresser began to announce His disciplines so that the vineyard might be moved, which are:

entries.section: 2. A judgment between God and His people:

paragraphs.text: A. “I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up” [5]. If the angel of the Lord encamps round about them that fear Him (Ps 34:7), and the Lord Himself is a wall of fire round about His people (Zech 2:5), then God in His love gives up the opponents and removes from them the heavenly guard, that they may realize their weakness and feel that they are without hedge or wall, so that wild beasts enter among them to graze as in a desert or a bare wilderness, perhaps that they may return to God and seek Him as a refuge for themselves.

If the grace of God is removed from a person, he becomes without a hedge, and his soul opens to the love of the world, so that its herds of unclean swine enter and go out without hindrance, and his heart becomes trodden down by unclean lusts and his thoughts wander in abominations, and his senses descend into evil desire.

As St. Clement of Alexandria says: [These things (the removal of the hedge and the permission for enemies to enter) are accomplished by divine permission to turn them to good and edification. For [divine providence is an art of discipline.]

entries.section: 2. A judgment between God and His people:

paragraphs.text: B. “I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged” [6]. When the Lord departs from His vineyard, that is, the human soul, it comes to be in emptiness and is counted a waste. The Lord weeps over it as He wept over Jerusalem, saying: “Behold, your house is left unto you desolate” (Mt 23:38).

When the vineyard bears fruit, the vinedresser prunes and digs it so that it may bring forth greater fruit, but if it brings forth wild grapes he does not stretch out his hand to it. If the pruning and digging point to the Lord's tender disciplines toward His children, then as we walk with Him in the way, He stretches out His hand to us as His children, caring for us and tending us and also disciplining us so that we increase in the fruit of the Spirit. So not pruning and not digging point to the absence of discipline, and this is the harshest kind of punishment... total neglect and being unworthy even of discipline. As St. John Chrysostom says: [When the physician stops giving the bitter medicine or using the scalpel, this means that the patient's condition is completely hopeless.

C. “But there shall come up briers and thorns” [6]. This is the fruit of man's withdrawing from God and separating from Him, for he brings forth from himself thorns and briers. The Apostle says: “And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient” (Rom 2:28).
What is this thorn but man's losing his peace, to carry within him troubles and cares that he cannot face by himself alone?!

D. “I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it” [6]. Rain in the Old Testament points to the gift of the Holy Spirit, for the man who is ungrateful to the Lord and seeks separation from Him loses the indwelling of the Spirit in him, and his heart turns into a wilderness that bears no fruit of the Spirit. Therefore instead of bringing forth “truth” he brings forth “bloodshed,” and instead of “justice” he brings forth “a cry” [7].

entries.section: 2. A judgment between God and His people:

paragraphs.text: The Lord seeks to find in us His garden, fruitful by the Spirit, where the soul speaks to Him, saying: “Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits” [16]. But the soul's deprivation of the spiritual rain turns the delightful garden into a dreadful place in which there is nothing but bloodshed and continual crying!

St. John Chrysostom sees that rain in the Holy Bible points to teaching. Thus when a person denies God he deprives himself of enjoying the Lord's teaching in his depths; he reads the word of God and perhaps studies it, but he does not enjoy its efficacy and sweetness in his depths. This is what St. Augustine declared in his first homily on the Gospel according to our teacher Matthew the Evangelist, saying: [He was like a little bird in a nest, who in the pride of his heart wanted to fly by himself, studying the Holy Bible in a spirit of criticism, and fell to the ground, and the passers-by almost crushed him under their feet, had it not been for the grace of God which snatched him up and returned him to the nest of faith until he had two wings with which he can fly.
St. Augustine sees that the rain here points to the preaching that passed from the vineyard (the Jewish people) to the Gentiles.
He says: “For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for truth, but behold bloodshed; for justice, but behold a cry” [7].

God gave every possibility to the whole community: to the priests and Levites as to the people, to the rich as to the poor, to the learned as to the unlearned, that this vineyard might bring forth “truth” and “justice,” and “the Truth” came incarnate from the tribe of Judah, but they shed His blood, and instead of justice there was the cry: “Crucify Him, crucify Him.”

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: 8 Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth! 9 In mine ears said the LORD of hosts, Of a truth many houses shall be desolate, even great and fair, without inhabitant. 10 Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah. 11 Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them! 12 And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands. 13 Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst. 14 Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it. 15 And the mean man shall be brought down, and the mighty man shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be humbled: 16 But the LORD of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and God that is holy shall be sanctified in righteousness. 17 Then shall the lambs feed after their manner, and the waste places of the fat ones shall strangers eat. 18 Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope: 19 That say, Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it! 20 Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter! 21 Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight! 22 Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink: 23 Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!

After the Lord disclosed His love for His vineyard and His surpassing care for it, and how the vineyard deprived itself of the sweet spiritual fruit or the gladdening wine, and made thorns that were woven into a crown upon the head of the Lord Christ, He began to review the most important sins of the people and their evil fruit, which brought bitter woes instead of enjoying the blessings of the Lord and the fellowship of His glories.

A. “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!” [8]. By this he means that they were absorbed in buying houses and fields by every means, in selfishness, until one did not leave a place for his brother, especially the poor and needy. A very small few owned the agricultural land and the houses in order to exploit the common people, and this contrary to the Law, which required that the lands remain distributed equally (Num 33:54) and that in the year of Jubilee everyone's property return to him (Lev 25).

The land in Canaan is a free gift presented to the whole people so that all might live in prosperity, enjoying what it pours forth of milk and honey, as though it were the property of the Lord who gives it to them. But by these actions they committed the sin of greed and also of pride, with disobedience and the breaking of the Law. Therefore the blessing was removed and the curse came, so the houses become desolate because of death or captivity; in a moment 185,000 died in the war. Moreover, the fields do not bear fruit as usual, for ten acres of vineyard yield one bath (about 27.5 kilograms) instead of about 500 baths; and an homer (283.5 kilograms) of seed yields an ephah [a tenth of a homer (Ezek 45:11)], that is, the harvest amounts to a tenth of the seed that was cast into the ground.

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: B. “Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!” [11]. If the first woe fell on them because of greed and injustice, the second is because of excessive frivolity. They came to be drunk in the early morning instead of rising for work, and they also stay until a late hour of the night, that is, they are drunk by day and by night. Thus they break the divine commandments: “Man goeth forth unto his work and to his labour until the evening” (Ps 104:23). Their life turned from the spiritual joy mixed with the seriousness of life and worship into a frivolity mixed with laxity; they use all the instruments of music [12] while being occupied with holding feasts to excite their feelings and senses to evil, ignoring the godly life in the Lord. As Amos the prophet says: “That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David; that drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed” (Amos 6:6-7).

* See how God blames luxury also; for He does not condemn them here for a greed they committed but merely for extravagance. Behold, you eat to excess while Christ has not what is necessary. You eat various cakes while Christ has not dry bread. You drink Thasian wine and do not give Christ a cup of cold water, though He is thirsty. You lie on a soft embroidered bed while He perishes from cold.

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom As for the work of frivolity, it is the captivity of the inner man away from the knowledge of the truth, to live a captive of ignorance, hungering and thirsting inwardly, with nothing to satisfy or quench him. The prophet says: “Therefore my people are gone into captivity, because they have no knowledge: and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude dried up with thirst” [13]. The wise man says: “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Prov 13:21).

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: Through frivolity a person loses his inner awareness and descends to the abyss, which opens its doors wide to swallow without limit. In this a person loses his splendor and his joy [14], and falls into humiliation [15].

This is the bitter fruit gathered by those who walk in the wide gate, the gate of continual frivolity to satisfy temporal lusts. But what is more serious is their eternal destruction, for he says: “Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it” [14]. He portrays the abyss, Sheol, like an opening of the earth to swallow the wicked, as happened with Korah and his company... It opens to ask for more, swallowing them into the depths so that they remain in darkness forever.

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: This is what happens to those occupied with a life of luxury and frivolity; but as for God, the LORD of hosts, He is exalted and sanctified by His condemnation of sin in justice and righteousness [16].

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: Perhaps some will ask: What is the state of the faithful little remnant of the Lord? The prophet answers: “Then shall the lambs feed after their manner, and the waste places of the fat ones shall strangers eat” [17]. The sheep, the little flock, graze wherever the Good Shepherd, Jesus Christ, leads them, for He keeps them from injustice and persecution. These eat in quiet and safety without anyone disturbing them (Ex 34:14). When the Church of the Old Testament is laid waste by the Jews' refusal of faith in the Lord Christ, the Gentiles (the strangers) inherit the promises, the covenants, the Law, the prophecies and so on...

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: C. “Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope!” [18]. This third woe falls on those who seek sin with intense desire and diligence; they strive for it of their own choice and push themselves to it or pull it forcefully toward them. Danger comes upon these, for they fall into the cords of vanity and are tied to the cart of sin so as to become attached to it.
They draw sin as with a rope, and since it is extremely heavy it collapses upon their heads and shatters them.

Some of the Fathers see that the wicked descend from sin to sin as if they were making a long rope that draws them toward evil in bondage... Every fall leads to another fall and every descent causes a further descent, so that instead of the wicked man thinking of ascending, he collapses more and more.
* Truly, every man weaves a rope for himself with his sins: “Woe unto them that draw iniquity as with a long rope” [18 LXX].
Who makes a long rope? He who adds sin to sin.
How is sin added to sin? When we cover a sin that was committed with another sin.
* When (the wicked) threaten to kill the righteous, they only bind themselves with chains, with a strong, rough rope of their own making.
* Blessed are those who in work and conduct sing the songs of ascents (degrees), and woe to those who draw sin like a long rope (and so descend with it).

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Besides the gravity of sin in that it draws a person into a chain of sins, making him like a ball with which sins play, the second danger is that it stirs up a spirit of contempt and mockery instead of the person's desire to be freed from it, so the wicked repeat: “Let him make speed, and hasten his work, that we may see it: and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw nigh and come, that we may know it!” [19]. They doubt the possibility of God's judgment, so they suppose that they are able to face Him with proofs and arguments. In contempt they repeat “the Holy One of Israel,” the title that the prophets used for their hope in the coming of the Messiah, the Savior... as though they were throwing this hope to the wind.

In every age there are wicked people who make light of God's long-suffering and mock His promises and His love, as well as His disciplines, thinking they are mere words or illusions that will not be fulfilled:
“Behold, they say unto me, Where is the word of the LORD? let it come now” (Jer 17:15).
“The days are prolonged, and every vision faileth” (Ezek 12:22).

“There shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, and saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (2 Pet 3:4).

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: D. “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!” [20]. The fourth woe falls on those who confuse truth with falsehood, good with evil, light with darkness, sweetness with bitterness, knowledge with ignorance. These give sin a coating of virtue, as when they justify anger by defending the truth, or condemning others under the cover of the desire for reform, and so on...

St. Clement of Alexandria sees that this woe is a threat against liars and the proud. God is the Truth, and the devil is the liar and the father of liars; whoever knows the will of God knows the truth and walks in goodness, but whoever ignores the divine will leaves the circle of truth to live in falsehood, and in this he loses his ability to discern and perceive the good, or the light, or the true knowledge of heavenly and divine things.

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: E. The claim of wisdom and understanding together with contempt for the opinions and counsel of others: “Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!” [21].

* He who is occupied with his own self and does not seek the counsel of others bears the mark of folly. It is said: “Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him” (Prov 26:12).

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom F. The mighty who corrupt their powers: “Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink” [22]. When leaders are occupied with feasts, luxury and drunkenness, they lose their true role; thus we often corrupt our own powers by our departure from our serious goal and our immersion in the pleasures of this world.

entries.section: 3. A detailed presentation of the sins of Israel:

paragraphs.text: G. Taking bribes: “Which justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!” [23].

24 Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. 25 Therefore is the anger of the LORD kindled against his people, and he hath stretched forth his hand against them, and hath smitten them: and the hills did tremble, and their carcases were torn in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

Because of the sins that the people committed, the anger of the Lord was kindled like a flame of fire that burns the stubble, to make them like dust [24]. He allowed them to be disciplined with great firmness until the hills trembled and their carcases lay in the streets. Here he means what befell the people of God during the violent Assyrian invasion.
In the midst of this flame he says: “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still” [25]; He is still full of love, awaiting man's return to Him!

26 And he will lift up an ensign to the nations from far, and will hiss unto them from the end of the earth: and, behold, they shall come with speed swiftly: 27 None shall be weary nor stumble among them; none shall slumber nor sleep; neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken: 28 Whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind: 29 Their roaring shall be like a lion, they shall roar like young lions: yea, they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry it away safe, and none shall deliver it. 30 And in that day they shall roar against them like the roaring of the sea: and if one look unto the land, behold darkness and sorrow, and the light is darkened in the heavens thereof.

The prophet presents to us a terrible description of the army of Assyria in its invasion of the people of God. This description reveals the invasion of the human soul by the enemy of good, with violence, ferocity and perseverance, and at the same time it rebukes the slack believers; for the wicked, for the sake of temporal spoil, do not tire until they achieve their goal, while the children of God are slack in obtaining fellowship in eternal glory.

A. “None shall be weary” [27]. In spite of the length of the distance they cover and the difficulties that face them, they feel no weariness because of their strong desire to enjoy the spoil... while we believers often grow slack in our spiritual striving under the pretext of exhaustion or weariness.

B. “Nor stumble” [27] in spite of the roughness of the road; perhaps because God called them to discipline His people, He made the road easy for them. It was more fitting for us not to fear the roughness of the road, for as long as we are in the hand of our Christ, “the Way,” we never stumble.

C. “None shall slumber nor sleep” [27] for the sake of the temporal and evil goal set before them. Is it not fitting for us believers neither to slumber nor sleep, but to remain awake in spirit until we achieve the aim of our mission?!

D. “Neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken” [27], that is, earnest and braced for work. The Lord commanded us: “Let your loins be girded about” (Lk 12:35), that we may fulfill the Lord's service with strength.

E. “Whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs shall be counted like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind” [28]. They are ready with their weapons and equipment, so as to fight with strength and for a long time and with lightning speed, and thus achieve the goal. It is fitting for believers to prepare against the battle of the devil with the spiritual weapons of faith of which the Apostle Paul spoke at greater length (Eph 6).

F. “Their roaring shall be like a lion, they shall roar like young lions: yea, they shall roar, and lay hold of the prey, and shall carry it away safe, and none shall deliver it” [29]. They bear the image of their master the devil, who walks about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet 5:8). It was fitting for believers to be sober and vigilant, resisting this enemy, stedfast in the faith (1 Pet 5:8-9), which is able to shatter the enemy.
The Lamb, the Lord of glory Jesus, came forward as a lion from the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5), so that the devil may not defeat us, but we resist him by the Lord and shatter his powers.

G. “And in that day they shall roar against them like the roaring of the sea” [30], as the army falls upon them with the voices of the soldiers like the roaring of the sea that cannot be resisted, sweeping and swallowing all that is before it... as though they had no hope of escape from Assyria.

H. Finally the people lose all hope, for “if one look unto the land, behold darkness and sorrow, and the light is darkened in the heavens thereof” [30]. In the time of distress they lift up their eyes, perhaps to find a way of salvation, but darkness settles over their thoughts, and the clouds of smoke rising from the fires destroy every hope they have. They rejected God, “the true Light,” so darkness reigned in their depths. Therefore the psalmist cries: “In thy light shall we see light” (Ps 36:9).

entries.section: 1. The prophet's vision in the temple:

paragraphs.text: 1 In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. 2 Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. 3 And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. 4 And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke.
“In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple” [1].

The prophet enjoyed this vision in the year of the death of King Uzziah, perhaps after he had announced his earlier prophecies, which carried a threat to the people, and the people met them with aversion and contempt; therefore this vision was revealed to him that he might proclaim it to the people, affirming that he bears a divine message and presents the word of God. Perhaps this vision took place before the prophecies, and the prophet announced it afterward to assure the people that what he utters is not from himself, as St. Paul did when he wished to confirm his apostleship by speaking of the vision that he saw at the beginning of his ministry (2 Cor 12).

The vision appeared in the year of the death of King Uzziah, who reigned over Judah at the age of 16 for 52 years and did that which was right in the sight of the Lord, and he prospered in all his works: in wars, in building and rebuilding cities, and so on... But when his name was greatly lifted up he fell into pride and wanted to burn incense to the Lord on the altar of incense, so the Lord struck him with leprosy while he was in the temple, and the priests thrust him out, and he was a leper until the day of his death, isolated in a house far from the king's palace.

Perhaps Isaiah had been following with joy the success of Uzziah along with the uprightness of his heart and his growth in the Spirit, but he was very grieved at his fall in his last days, and his dying thus isolated from the people of God, expelled from His holy temple, representing the vanity of temporal glory.

The prophet looked at the people in the year of Uzziah's death and saw them cast down like sheep without a shepherd, especially since the king had withdrawn from the people for a time before his death because of his leprosy. Isaiah realized that the people needed heavenly care, because the arm of man is unable to satisfy the needs of the people, and as the psalmist says: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation; their spirit goeth forth, they return to their dust” (Ps 146:3).

In the midst of this bitterness the Lord declared this vision to Isaiah for his comfort: the vision most likely took place in the temple at a time when the prophet was alone for private worship, crying out to God to take over the care of His people. The Lord appeared to him sitting on a throne high and lifted up to assure him that He is the heavenly Shepherd of His people, whose thoughts are higher than the thoughts of men and His ways than their ways. He sits on high in order to carry His Church with Him, sharing His heavenly glories. He saw His train filling the temple, for He dwelt in His Church, awaiting every soul that comes to Him to enjoy union with Him. He saw the Lord Christ in His glory (Jn 12:41), filling heaven and earth with His divinity and His care.

St. John Chrysostom sees that Isaiah and the other prophets did not see the essence of the divinity as it is, but God appeared to them through His condescension, as much as they could bear the vision, because of His love for His creation; even for the heavenly ones and the bearers of His throne, each of them sees Him according to his capacity, but the essence in itself, that is, in its absolute perfection, cannot be comprehended.

* The Seraphim cry out, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth... The heavenly powers are seized by awe without ceasing, so they turn their faces and spread their wings like a wall, to shield them from the unbearable radiance that comes from God, and yet what they see is only a reduced image of the reality...

While the Seraphim are not even strong enough to behold God, who is revealed to them only as a condescension on His part according to their weakness, we see people who dare to picture in their minds the very nature that the Seraphim are unable to comprehend. They claim that they are able to look upon it clearly and without limit!
Tremble, O heavens, and be astonished, O earth.

* Truly God, even for these orders, is incomprehensible and cannot be approached. For this reason He condescends to appear in the way recorded in the vision. God, whom no place contains and who does not sit on a throne... out of His love for us appears seated on a throne, surrounded by the heavenly powers.

* These (visions of the prophets) are revelations, all of them examples of His condescension, and not visions of His essence by its disclosure. For if they had beheld His very essence they would not have seen Him under different forms, since He is simple, without form or members or defined manners; His nature does not sit or stand or walk...

entries.section: 1. The prophet's vision in the temple:

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom “Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory” [2-3].

Perhaps what comforts the soul of the servant is that his heart is lifted up to see the angelic service, and he realizes that all the troubles and weaknesses of the Church will one day end, so that she may share with the heavenly ones in praise forever. And that the Church here, as the icon of heaven, enjoys the pledge of the heavenly service. In one Coptic homily the Church is defined as: [a place of comfort; she is the assembly of the angels and the place of the Cherubim and the Seraphim]. It is said that St. Pachomius the Egyptian used to see the Church filled with angels.

The Seraphim are the servants of the divine throne; they bear the Lord with joy and exultation, and praise Him without ceasing. It is as though the work of every servant or prophet in the Church is to draw every soul to the Lord as a throne for Him to dwell in, and to establish His Kingdom within it, so that it becomes like the fiery heavenly Seraph. Each Seraph has 6 wings: with two he covers his face, a sign of his being marked by the fear of God, since he cannot comprehend all the divine splendor; with two he covers his feet, a sign of modesty, if this expression is right; and with two he flies, soaring in the heavenly places. Thus it befits us to be like the Seraph, enjoying the fear of God in modesty with constant growth and continual ascent toward the heavenly places.

As for the seraphic hymn, “the Thrice-Holy,” it appears in the writings of Origen; and perhaps the date of its use in Alexandria goes back to an earlier time. It is said in Church tradition that Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who took care of the body of the Lord after it was taken down from the Cross, heard this hymn as they were putting the spices on the body of the Lord before His burial.

entries.section: 1. The prophet's vision in the temple:

paragraphs.text: The Seraphim say: “The whole earth is full of his glory” [3]; not only does it fill the heavens but the whole earth. He dwelt on the earth to raise up heaven from the earth. And as St. Clement of Alexandria says, the earth becomes heaven for the true believer. Although our body in its origin is dust, the Word of God received our human nature to sanctify it, so our body became glorified in Him, and we no longer despise it, because it shares with the soul its worship of God, its striving and its crown.
The following is noted in this hymn:

A. The word “Lord” came in the plural, Adonai, and not the singular, Adon. Perhaps for this reason, together with the repetition of the word “holy” three times, St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, saw it as proclaiming the glory of the Trinity, while the Apostle Paul attributes it to the Holy Spirit (Acts 28:25-26), and St. John to the Son (Jn 12:41), while ancient Jewish tradition attributes it to the Father.
* By means of (the Seraphim) the mystery of the Trinity was clearly proclaimed, when they uttered that wonderful cry “Holy,” as it carries beauty together with awe for each Hypostasis of the Trinity.

St. Gregory of Nyssa B. God is called “LORD of hosts,” which is the title of God in His battle against evil or against the powers of darkness, and it has a teaching meaning. It does not appear in the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, Job, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, but appears rarely in Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and the Psalms; it is used abundantly in the books of the prophets: in Jeremiah it is used about 80 times, in Haggai 14 times, in Zechariah 50 times, and in Malachi more than 24 times. The first to use it was Hannah, the mother of Samuel, in the song of victory which she uttered when she felt that God was the secret of her victory in her inner battle.
C. This hymn is used in the Divine Liturgy as a sign of the believers' fellowship with the heavenly ones in worship on a heavenly level, in a spirit of unity and harmony together:
* May we gather together in our consciences in agreement and cry to Him earnestly as with one mouth, that we may share in His great and glorious promises.

St. Clement of Rome * That you may realize with what awe and fear they utter that name as they glorify Him and praise Him; but you call upon Him in your prayers and petitions with great laxity, although you ought to be filled with awe and be in vigilance with reverence.

St. John Chrysostom * The new things go in harmony with the old, and the old with the new. Behold the Seraphim say to one another: Holy, holy, holy, LORD of hosts. The two Testaments go in one melody, and have one voice...

entries.section: 1. The prophet's vision in the temple:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine “And the posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke” [4].

The foundations of the house of the Lord shook before the cries of the Seraphim glorifying the Holy God, and the house was filled with thick cloud, a sign of the dwelling of the glory of God in it. And when the Lord Christ entered Jerusalem, the city was also moved (Mt 21:10). We need the Lord to declare His dwelling in us, to establish His Kingdom within us, that we may share with the Seraphim their eternal hymn, so that the depths of our souls are shaken with Isaiah the prophet, and the glory of the Lord is declared in us, and our depths are sanctified, so that we are counted witnesses of truth for His Gospel.

5 Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. 6 Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: 7 And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.

When we stand in the presence of the Holy God, His glory is declared to us and we discover our uncleanness, as happened with Isaiah the prophet: “Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts” [5].

The Apostle Paul confesses that he is the first of sinners (1 Tim 1:15), not because he thinks about his sins and tries to count them, but as the fruit of his enlightenment by the Spirit of the Holy God, who exposes our depths, so that we discover that we are nothing before the glory of God, and that we are utterly sinners before His holiness. Therefore when Abraham, the father of the fathers, began to speak with God, he said: “Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes” (Gen 17:27).

Perhaps Isaiah wanted to share with the Seraphim in their praises to God, and so he realized that he was of unclean lips, and as he looked at the company of the Seraphim in their exultations, he realized that he dwelt among a people of unclean lips.

* With daily sighs the saints grieve over the weakness of their nature, and while they search into the change of their thoughts, their will and the depths of their inner consciences, they cry out in supplication, saying: “Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified”... And so they realize the weakness of man's righteousness and its imperfection, together with the constant need of God's mercies. Therefore he whose evils and sins God removed with the coal of “His living word” on the altar, after his wonderful vision of God and of the heavenly Seraphim and his enjoyment of the revelation of the divine mysteries, says: “Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips.”

Father Theonas * Behold, you see how all the saints truly confess, not on behalf of the people but rather about themselves, that they are sinners, yet they never despair of their salvation, but look to complete justification by the grace and mercy of the Lord.

Father Theonas His sense of the uncleanness of his lips and the uncleanness of the lips of his people did not crush his spirit, but filled him with hope in God, whom he had enjoyed seeing in the vision as the “LORD of hosts,” able to raise up from humanity spiritual soldiers for Himself. This was fulfilled for him, as he said: “Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar: and he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged” [6-7].

It is said in the Fraction of the Liturgy of St. Cyril: [As You purified the lips of Your servant Isaiah the prophet when one of the Seraphim took a coal with the tongs from the altar and laid it in his mouth, and said to him: Lo, this hath touched thy lips, it taketh away thine iniquities and purgeth thee from all thy sins; so also we, the weak sinners, Your servants who seek Your mercy, graciously purify our souls, our bodies and our hearts, and give us this true coal, which gives life to the soul, the body and the spirit, which is the holy Body and the precious Blood of Your Christ.]

And in another prayer of the Fraction the priest says: [For I have come forward to touch Your Body and Blood out of my longing in Your love; so do not burn me with them, O You who formed me, but burn up all the thorns that choke my soul.]
St. Mary bore the Word of God incarnate in her, the burning coal, who sanctifies humanity with His precious blood.

entries.section: 3. The mission of Isaiah the prophet:

paragraphs.text: 8 Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me. 9 And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. 10 Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed. 11 Then said I, Lord, how long? And he answered, Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land be utterly desolate, 12 And the LORD have removed men far away, and there be a great forsaking in the midst of the land. 13 And if a tenth remain in it, it shall return and become a waste; but as the terebinth and the oak, which, when they are cut down, have a stock, so its stock shall be a holy seed.

When Isaiah the prophet saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and His train filling the temple, and the Seraphim praising Him, and his lips had been cleansed by the divine coal, he longed for the heavenly life and the angelic praise, but at the same time he longed to see his people enjoying this heavenly life, as though he were saying with the Apostle Paul: “Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you” (Phil 1:24). This is also what the prophet declares by saying: “Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me” [8].

This is the fifth scene of the same vision, in which he was called to the prophetic work, on behalf of the Kingdom of the Lord; these scenes are: 1. The scene of the Lord in His glory [1]. 2. The scene of the Seraphim praising Him [3]. 3. The shaking of the posts of the door and the filling of the house with smoke [4]. 4. The sanctification of the prophet's lips [5-7]. 5. The call of Isaiah by the voice of God Himself [8 ff.].

The call came from God Almighty Himself, and since Isaiah believed in God's saving power and His sanctifying work, he came forward for the work, realizing that where he is weak he is strong in the Lord. When we realize that we are nothing, let us believe in God, all in all, who is able by His Holy Spirit to work through us.

Here we must point out that while the speaker is one: “Whom shall I send?” we find Him using the plural form: “Who will go for us?” to affirm that He is the one God, the Trinity, or the God of three Hypostases.

entries.section: 3. The mission of Isaiah the prophet:

paragraphs.text: The Holy God, the Three Hypostases, accepted Isaiah's offer, and said to him: “Go” [9]. God did not want to send Isaiah to receive honor or glory, but to enter into bitterness with a people who reject the truth... For service is not Church positions or honors, but it is spiritual striving for the washing of the feet of others and urging them to accept the truth, and this through the holy altar that sanctifies the inner lips and gives the effective word of God in the life of the servant and those served.

The Lord put His words in the prophet's mouth: “Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not” [9]. The Lord put in Isaiah's mouth many prophecies about the Lord Christ and His saving work; and they were fulfilled at the coming of the Lord Christ: they heard and saw but did not believe in Him, because their inner insight had been struck with blindness; this is the opposite of the disciples to whom the Lord said: “Blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear” (Mt 13:11-16).
St. John Chrysostom says of this people: [They see how He casts out demons and they say: He has a devil; they see those raised from the dead and do not worship Him, but think of killing Him.]

We have already studied this prophecy in our explanation of the Gospel according to Matthew the Evangelist, chapter 13, so I will be content here with St. Augustine's comment on the question: Why are the Jews blamed for their unbelief, since God blinded their eyes?

[They were not able to believe because Isaiah prophesied this, and he prophesied because God had told him beforehand what their state would be.
