But if you ask: What is the cause of their inability to believe? I answer at once: They were unwilling. God saw their corrupt will, and therefore told the prophet beforehand, because the future is not hidden from Him... God blinded them and hardened them merely by leaving them and withdrawing His help from them.]

St. Irenaeus answers the same question, saying: [They are struck with blindness because of their unbelief in God, for they look toward Him and do not see Him, because to them He is as though He did not exist; just as the sun, His creature, afflicts those of weak sight so that they cannot see its light. But to those who believe in Him and follow Him, He gives a fuller and greater enlightenment to their minds.]

entries.section: 3. The mission of Isaiah the prophet:

paragraphs.text: This is the interpretation of the prophet's words: “Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed” [10]. It is noted here that God does not ascribe the people to Himself, but calls them “this people,” and this usually happens when God declares His wrath against them and counts them unworthy to belong to Him because of the fatness of their hearts, the heaviness of their ears and the blindness of their eyes, that is, because of violence (hardness), disobedience and spiritual ignorance.

This prophecy points to the Jews' denial of the Lord Christ at His coming, as it also points to the denial of the words of prophecy in the days of Isaiah, so that they fall under captivity and ruin comes upon them at the hands of Sennacherib the Assyrian.

entries.section: 3. The mission of Isaiah the prophet:

paragraphs.text: The prophet Isaiah grieved when he realized the weight of the responsibility laid upon him and the troubles and sufferings awaiting him, as he also grieved when he realized what would befall the people of destruction, so that the cities become waste without inhabitant and the houses without man and the land be desolate and waste [11], and he cried: “How long, O Lord GOD?” [11]. Was he asking: How long will this people remain in hardness?! Or was he asking: How long shall I proclaim prophecies so bitter and harsh?!

entries.section: 3. The mission of Isaiah the prophet:

paragraphs.text: The Lord disclosed to him the state of the people after their breaking before Sennacherib, and declared that even if a tenth remains in the land [13], He will return and raise up the people through this remnant and make of them a holy seed. In this he prophesies concerning the captivity and what happens after the captivity. At the same time it is regarded as a prophecy concerning the captivity of the Jews in their denial of faith in the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world, but in the last days a remnant remains that returns to faith in Him. The Apostle Paul says: “That hardness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles be come in. And so all Israel shall be saved” (Rom 11:25-26).

entries.section: 1. The alliance of Rezin and Pekah against Ahaz:

paragraphs.text: 1 And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.

At the beginning of Ahaz's reign, Rezin king of Syria allied himself with Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, against Judah [1]. The first attacked from the direction of Transjordan, while the second rushed in with his armies from the north, and Ahaz was defeated. They went up to Jerusalem, the capital, to besiege it, but they were not able to storm it. The cause of the battle was the political disagreement between Ahaz and the other two kings; Ahaz saw fit to ally himself with Assyria, while the two kings saw fit to ally themselves with Egypt.

Ahaz found himself in a predicament, so he asked for the help of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, who hastened toward Damascus, where he killed Rezin (2 Kgs 16:9), and he did the same also to Samaria (2 Kgs 15:29).
2 And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.

When Ahaz learned that Syria had settled in Ephraim (the northern kingdom, or Israel) in order to ally with it against him, “his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind” [2]. Ahaz and his people realized that they were unable to face Syria and Israel, but the true cause of their fear was their lack of faith in God as a support for them, able to fortify them and grant them victory. They lost their inner peace by isolating themselves from God, the source of victory and peace.

3 Then said the LORD unto Isaiah, “Go forth to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field; 4 And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah. 5 Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee, saying, 6 Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal: 7 Thus saith the Lord GOD, It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass. 8 For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people. 9 And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah's son. If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established.”

Ahaz was greatly troubled, because he had left out of his calculations the element of faith, or “the divine presence.” He did not call for repentance and a return to God, nor did he go to the temple to lay the matter before God, nor did he send to the prophet to consult him. Rather, he used human means, resorting to Assyria for his protection, and going out to the end of the conduit of the upper pool [3], west of Jerusalem at the head of the valley of the son of Hinnom, to examine with the men of state the sources of water, in order to divert them to the city so that it might benefit from them during the expected siege, and to deprive the enemy of them (2 Chr 22:3-4; Isa 22:9-11), as he was also busy fortifying the city as far as he could.

With all this, God intervened, not for the sake of Ahaz, but for the sake of the very few holy ones of His people, and for the sake of David His servant and the city dear to Him. He asked Isaiah to go out to meet Ahaz, together with Shear-jashub (= the remnant shall return), as a sign and a wonder in Israel (Isa 8:8), assuring him: “Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah” [4].

The prophet and his son met the king at the pool so that God might declare to the king that salvation would not be accomplished by human planning and temporal means, but by the transcendent work of God and His care for His children. The prophet met the king at the pool to assure him that God wants to speak with mankind wherever they are: He meets Levi at the place of tax collection, Zacchaeus at the sycamore tree, the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, and so on... He seeks us and goes to us wherever we are, longing for our salvation more than we ourselves long for it.
God asked Ahaz not to fear and not to let his heart grow faint, for these reasons:

a. That the two enemies, “Pekah and Rezin,” are nothing but two smoking firebrands [4]. In this way the children of God find resistance and alliances of enemies against them, but all this is no more than a smoking firebrand that clouds the air and offends the nose for a while, without a blazing fire to burn. The enemy of good is strong and mighty in appearance, but he becomes very small and utterly weak before us if we hide in Christ, the Conqueror of the devil and of all his powers.
St. John Chrysostom says to Theodore the Fallen:

[If Satan has this power to cast you down to the ground from a lofty height and exalted virtue, to the farthest limits of evil, how much more is God able to raise you up to your former confidence, and to make you not only as you were, but happier than before.]

b. The failure of the enemies' plot: The two kings made a hidden, satanic plot, but God, who knows all hidden things, declared it so that King Ahaz might take precautions, despite his wickedness and his foolishness. The Lord says, “It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass” [7]. The enemy may succeed at first, reckoning that he is achieving his evil aims, but the Lord scatters the proud in the imagination of their hearts (Lk 1:51).

c. Syria will not be able to expand as it thought, but will keep to its borders: “For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin” [8]. So however much Rezin may fight, he will return to Damascus, and his kingdom will not expand at the expense of Judah as he supposes. As for Ephraim, within a period of 65 years it will be broken, that it be not reckoned a people [8]; some see that this refers to a period of 5-6 years, that is 11 years, since the captivity of Israel was accomplished 11 years after the word of the prophet Isaiah (2 Kgs 17:3, 6). Yet some scholars see that the prophet is referring here to the ruin of Israel by Esarhaddon, who brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the children of Israel, to put an end to the nation of Israel completely (2 Kgs 17:24).

The prophet concluded his speech by saying, “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established” [9]. For unless they believe the divine promise and trust in it, relying on the arm of the Lord, they will not stand firm in these harsh and difficult circumstances. Faith is the shield (1 Thess 5:8) that protects us from the blows of the enemy.
This statement appears in the Septuagint as: “If ye will not believe, neither shall ye understand.” St. Augustine commented on it at length; among his words are these:
[You cannot obtain understanding unless faith dawns in the heart, which says with the prophet: “If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not understand.”]
[Faith is sought, but understanding is found, for the prophet says: “Unless ye believe, ye shall not understand.”]
[According to the teaching of the Catholic Church, it is fitting for the mind to be nourished first by simple faith, so that it may be able to understand the heavenly, eternal things.]

[You (he is addressing the heretics) have not been taught in the Kingdom of Heaven, that is, the true, catholic Church of Christ; otherwise you would have drawn from the treasury of the Holy Scriptures what is old and also what is new. The Lord Himself says: “Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” (Mt 13:52).]

St. Augustine sees that through faith the Lord Christ accompanies a person, walking with him all the way, as He did with the two disciples of Emmaus who besought Him to stay with them, and when He sat at meat with them, “their eyes were opened, and they knew him” (Lk 24:31).

St. Clement of Alexandria comments on the same statement, saying: “This means that if you do not believe what the Law prophesied and receive the teaching of the Law, you will not understand the Old Testament, which He (the Lord Christ) interpreted by His coming.”

entries.section: 4. Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign:

paragraphs.text: 10 Moreover the LORD spake again unto Ahaz, saying, 11 “Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.” 12 But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD.” 13 And he said, “Hear ye, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?”

entries.section: 4. Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign:

paragraphs.text: God offered Ahaz every possibility of salvation, but his heart had become utterly hardened, and he trusted in Assyria and not in God. Even so, God in His love and kindness returned to speak with him through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above” [11]. It is as though He were saying to him: Why do you seek help from Assyria, a stranger? I am your God, ready to confirm my promises to you with a sign from the earth or from heaven, for I am the God of heaven and earth. Ask what you wish and I will give it to you. Ask that an earthquake or a splitting of the earth occur, as happened with Korah and his company, or ask for lightnings or thunders or rains or a sign in the sun, as happened with Joshua when the sun stood still. For although I do not like to give signs for show, yet out of my love for the house of David, and so that you may believe in me, I will give you the desire of your heart. But Ahaz had set his gaze on Assyria, rejecting any help from God, and so he refused to ask for a sign from Him, justifying that with a Scripture text, “neither will I tempt the LORD” [12] (Deut 6:16). He did not say this out of trust in God, but out of a desire not to deal with Him.

This passage is read at the Morning Hour on the Friday of the second week of the Great Fast, when the readings focus on “the temptation of the Lord Christ.” It is as though the Spirit of the Lord is affirming that in every age there are wicked people who wish to cover their wickedness with Scripture texts; even Satan himself used the same approach in his dialogue with the Lord Christ at the temptation. How dangerous is the misuse of the word of God!

entries.section: 4. Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign:

paragraphs.text: Ahaz was deceitful in his answer even to the Lord, so the prophet rebuked him, saying: “Hear ye, O house of David; Is it a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also?” [13]. The people were wearied by the injustices of Ahaz and his household, and now they are like those who weary God by their lack of faith in Him, relying on Assyria and not on the Lord.

14 But the Lord himself shall give you a sign; “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. 15 Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. 16 For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings.”

Ahaz refused to ask God for a sign that he might be assured that He would save him from Syria and Israel, and behold, the Lord presents Himself as a sign, not to Ahaz alone but to all mankind, that we may be assured that He saves it, not from human arms but from all the powers of wicked darkness, lifting it above temporal events and carrying it with Him into the Father's embrace. At the same time He assures Ahaz that the house of David will not fall completely, but that the Son of David, “the wondrous sign,” will come, who is able to raise up the fallen tabernacle of David.

The sign that the Lord wants to give every believer is that He gives Himself, “Immanuel.” We do not deepen the request or raise it on high; rather, like Ahaz, we are afraid to ask, although He waits to give us Himself; He comes down to us to raise us to Himself, so that He may be our good portion that will not be taken from us. For this reason St. Irenaeus says: [What Isaiah said, “Lift up on high and deepen below,” means to point to the One who descended and ascended (Eph 4:10).] Let us ask for this wondrous sign, Immanuel, who came down to us to lift us up to His heavens.

Truly it is a unique sign, and as St. John Chrysostom says: [Since what was about to happen was strange, such that many could not believe it even when it was accomplished, He sent first, before everything, prophets to proclaim this truth.]
And with the same meaning the martyr Justin says: [The things that seemed unreasonable, and even impossible, to men, God proclaimed by the spirit of prophecy...]

a. “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” [14]. As the martyr Justin says in his Dialogue with Trypho (66): [It is clear to all that no one in the race of Abraham was born of a virgin, or was said to be, except our Christ.]

The virginity of St. Mary is a Gospel truth that hides our faith in Christ Jesus her Son. For the Word of God, at His incarnation, did not care about the kind of place in which He would lie, or the clothes with which He would be swaddled, or the food on which He would feed, but He specified precisely the “virgin” who would become His mother.

The Hebrew word used for virgin is “Alma,” and not “virginity,” nor “Isha.” For “Alma” means a young virgin who may be betrothed, whereas “virginity” means an unbetrothed virgin, while Isha means a married woman. It is as though the word “Alma” corresponds exactly to the state of St. Mary, being a virgin and at the same time betrothed to St. Joseph, who was for her a defender and faithful witness to her chastity, whose presence removes every doubt or suspicion about her.
The prophet Ezekiel spoke (Ezek 44:1-2) about the virginity of St. Mary:
* Ezekiel testified and showed us this, saying:
I saw a gate toward the east, the Lord the Savior entered it, and it remained well closed as it was.

The Sunday Absalia Adam: the virginity of St. Mary is a proof of our faith in the Lord Christ, that He is not of the seed of man, that He is not of this world, but is the incarnate Son of God, who came to us from on high. She bore “Immanuel,” which means “God with us”; He came down to us incarnate in the virgin womb, to take on our nature and become one with us, dwelling in our midst, sanctifying all that is ours.
* Those who proclaimed that He is Immanuel, born of the Virgin (Isa 7:14), proclaimed also the union of the Word of God with the work of His hands.
When the Word became flesh, and the Son of God became the son of man, the Pure One opened with purity and the pure womb, giving mankind renewal in God.
St. Irenaeus * The Lord Christ opened the womb of the holy Church, that silent womb, without blemish, full of fruit, where the people of God are born.

St. Ambrose * Your divine birth, O Lord, has given all mankind a birth... Humanity bore You according to the flesh, and You bore it according to the Spirit... Glory to You, who became a child that You might make all things new.
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * We affirm that the only-begotten Son became man... so that, being born of a woman according to the flesh, He might renew the human race in Himself.
St. Cyril the Great b. “Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good” [15].

Here the prophet affirms the humanity of the Lord Christ; for though He is not of the seed of man, He truly became the Son of Man, sharing with us our food and our conduct and resembling us in everything except sin alone (Heb 2:7).

Butter and honey are the food of little boys, for He did not reach manhood all at once, but passed through the stage of boyhood, during which He knows to refuse evil and choose the good, a sign of the maturity of His soul and mind. We see Him at twelve years of age sitting in the midst of the teachers, hearing them and questioning them, until they were astonished at His teaching (Lk 2:46-47).

This was fulfilled with regard to our Lord Jesus Christ, born alone of the Virgin; but with regard to what took place in the days of Ahaz, God announced the birth of a son to Isaiah, of whom it was said: “For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings” [16]. This was fulfilled with all precision, for the king of Assyria attacked Damascus a short time after this prophecy was announced and Rezin was killed (2 Kgs 16:9), and Hoshea the son of Elah killed Pekah the son of Remaliah and reigned in his place (2 Kgs 15:30), and 200,000 captives were quickly returned (Shear-jashub = the remnant shall return), and that not by might nor by power but by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Kgs 18:8-15).

entries.section: 6. Assyria, the ally, becomes an enemy:

paragraphs.text: 17 “The LORD shall bring upon thee, and upon thy people, and upon thy father's house, days that have not come, from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah; even the king of Assyria. 18 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. 19 And they shall come, and shall rest all of them in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns, and upon all bushes. 20 In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard. 21 And it shall come to pass in that day, that a man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep; 22 And it shall come to pass, for the abundance of milk that they shall give he shall eat butter: for butter and honey shall every one eat that is left in the land. 23 And it shall come to pass in that day, that every place shall be, where there were a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings, it shall even be for briers and thorns. 24 With arrows and with bows shall men come thither; because all the land shall become briers and thorns. 25 And on all hills that shall be digged with the mattock, there shall not come thither the fear of briers and thorns: but it shall be for the sending forth of oxen, and for the treading of lesser cattle.”

Since Ahaz leaned on Assyria as his ally without returning to the Lord, God allows Assyria to turn into an enemy against Judah, and Judah passes through a bitterness it had not passed through since the kingdom was divided into two kingdoms, “Israel and Judah” [17]. At the same time it sees difficult days from the side of Egypt, so that Judah becomes like something between two millstones, not in the sense that Assyria and Egypt agree against it, but that the two struggle against each other and Judah becomes the scapegoat for both, with the battles and conflicts taking place in its land.

entries.section: 6. Assyria, the ally, becomes an enemy:

paragraphs.text: “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly (the armies of Egypt) that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee (the armies of Assyria) that is in the land of Assyria. And they shall come, and shall rest all of them in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns, and upon all bushes (that is, the armies will cover all the regions of Judah)” [18-19].

entries.section: 6. Assyria, the ally, becomes an enemy:

paragraphs.text: The Lord goes on to depict the destruction that Assyria will bring about with a hired razor that shaves the hair of the head, the hair of the feet, and the beard [20]. It is as though the enemy stretches out his hand, as with a razor, to wipe away everything that belongs to the king and his household and the great ones (the head), and what belongs to the common people (the feet), and also the priests (the beard). Thus Assyria turns into a destroying and shattering razor! Shaving the beard was a sign of humiliation, since captives were compelled to submit to it involuntarily.

entries.section: 6. Assyria, the ally, becomes an enemy:

paragraphs.text: Once again He gives a picture of the destruction of Judah, which was famous for raising sheep, so that every man owned many head; but after the destruction, a man of means has a young cow and two sheep [21], and the good vineyards turn into land of briers and thorns [23], since there are no working hands because of the war...

entries.section: 1. The victory of Assyria over Syria and Israel:

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover the LORD said unto me, “Take thee a great roll, and write in it with a man's pen concerning Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 2 And that I take unto me faithful witnesses to record, Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah.” 3 And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, “Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz. 4 For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria.”

In the previous chapter the Lord spoke with Ahaz, who was trembling before Syria and Israel; now He speaks with the people, affirming the ruin of the two kingdoms that had allied together against Judah. By divine command Isaiah took a great tablet and wrote on it in clear letters “Maher-shalal-hash-baz,” which means “Hasten to the spoil, hurry to the plunder.” The prophet Isaiah placed the tablet in a visible place in the temple so that everyone might read it, and two priests witnessed to it, Uriah and Zechariah. Uriah was a high priest in the days of Ahaz, his spiritual counselor and his partner in pagan worship. He had built an altar like the altar of the Syrians that Hezekiah saw in Damascus, so that the king might offer sacrifices upon it (2 Kgs 16:10-16).

The two priests signed the tablet, or sealed it with their two seals, as trustworthy witnesses, for in the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established (2 Cor 13:1); they bore witness that what he wrote was written before the event occurred.

entries.section: 1. The victory of Assyria over Syria and Israel:

paragraphs.text: The prophet Isaiah declares that when his son Maher-shalal-hash-baz is about one year old, the prophecy against Syria and Israel will be fulfilled, saying: “Before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother, the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria” [4]. This was accomplished by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29; 16:9; 1 Chr 5:26).

entries.section: 2. A warning to the people of Judah:

paragraphs.text: 5 The LORD spake also unto me again, saying, 6 “Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son; 7 Now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory: and he shall come up over all his channels, and go over all his banks: 8 And he shall pass through Judah; he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel.”

After God had declared His salvation of the city of Jerusalem by shattering Syria and Israel, who had allied against it, He began to recount the sins of the people of Judah and the chastenings that would come upon them. Although He defends them, He does not defend their sins, nor does He cover them up, but He asks for repentance from them and a return to Him.

entries.section: 2. A warning to the people of Judah:

paragraphs.text: He says: “Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah's son” [6]. “Shiloah” is a watercourse whose name means “Sent,” and which is called “Siloam” in the New Testament. This channel was cut in the rock; it is several thousand feet long and lies southwest of Jerusalem. The waters flow in it quietly, the city depends on it, and it was a symbol of the house of David. What does it mean that the people refused the waters of this channel? They compared it with the rivers of Damascus, Abana and Pharpar, and so they rejected it and despised it. This points to their disdain for what God had given them, “the kingdom of Judah,” as they looked to what others had, “human arms.” They lost their faith in God, the giver of victory, and feared Rezin and the son of Remaliah, strangers and enemies of Judah, taking refuge in anyone who would rescue them from the two.
The waters of Shiloah point to the power of the quiet and meek Spirit, the source of sanctification and the fountain of righteousness.
Also “Shiloah” means “Sent,” pointing to the Lord Christ, whom the Father sent for our salvation, and whom the Jews rejected, refusing the work of His Holy Spirit.

entries.section: 2. A warning to the people of Judah:

paragraphs.text: They rejected the quiet watercourse and sought overwhelming, mighty waters, so the Lord chastens them by bringing up upon them “the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory” [7]. If Judah leans on Assyria, he will indeed come and save it, but afterward he turns and pours over it like the river Euphrates that they admired and desired, overflowing Judah and drowning it [7]. Tiglath-pileser the Assyrian rescued Judah, but Sennacherib the Assyrian attacked Judah with force and reached the neck, and besieged the head, Jerusalem, which was about to fall had God not intervened: “He shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck; and the stretching out of his wings (the two branches of the Euphrates) shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel” [8].

Thus God allows chastening, and trials come like a sweeping flood until they reach our necks, but He keeps the head (our faith in the Lord Christ, our Head) above the floods of trials, so that our faith does not fail and we perish (Lk 22:32), because we are the land of Immanuel, the possession of the Lord.

St. Augustine comments on the words of the Lord Christ, “Be ye therefore wise as serpents” (Mt 10:16), saying: [We must imitate the wisdom of the serpent, which puts its head between its coils when danger surrounds it, so that the blows fall on the body and not on the head, knowing that it will not perish as long as its head is safe. So it is fitting for us to keep our faith in the Lord Christ, our Head, unharmed, whatever afflictions come upon us, and then we will not perish.]

entries.section: 2. A warning to the people of Judah:

paragraphs.text: However much the enemy of good tries to stretch out his wings within us [8], no harm will touch us as long as our whole land is the land of Immanuel, that is, as long as our life is hidden under the shadow of the Lord's wings, as long as we carry within us the Kingdom of Christ!

9 Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and give ear, all ye of far countries: gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces; gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces. 10 Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us.

While the prophet is speaking about the events of his own time, behold, the Lord lifts his eyes and the eyes of the believers toward the saving work of Christ. God in His love is gentle with the people of Judah, so He saves them from the alliance of Syria and Israel against them, and at the same time, since the people sin by taking refuge in Assyria, Assyria itself becomes their opponent. This is what God permitted, but He did not permit the complete destruction of Judah, because from it comes the Lord Christ, the Lion that comes out of the tribe of Judah. He permits the Assyrian invasion to overflow as far as the neck of Judah, but it does not touch the head, for the Word of God becomes incarnate from the tribe of Judah, from St. Mary, and Immanuel dwells among us, who makes of our hearts a land, or a kingdom, for Himself... This is what moved the prophet to pass suddenly from the problem of Judah in the prophet's time, or shortly after it, to speak of the powers allied against Immanuel, saying:

“Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and make, all ye of far countries. Gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces. Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand: for God is with us” [9-10].

The matter did not stop with Assyria, which collapsed when 185,000 of its men died in the battle, but the prophet announces the fall of all the powers of the world that oppose the truth: Assyria, followed by Babylon, then Persia and Media and the Roman Empire (Isa 54:17; Mic 4:13). And all the more he meant the spiritual powers of darkness that oppose the Kingdom of Christ. The prophet announces that the raging of the enemies, their alliance and their wicked counsels against the Church are directed against Immanuel who dwells in her midst; therefore the powers of darkness collapse, and the true Church enjoys victory.

This prophetic voice cries out against all who oppose Christ, proclaiming what the Lord Himself said to Saul: “Why persecutest thou me...? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Acts 9:4-5). Let the enemy do all he can in opposing the believers; he only shatters himself.

11 For the LORD spake thus to me with a strong hand, and instructed me that I should not walk in the way of this people, saying, 12 “Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy; neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. 13 Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. 14 And he shall be for a sanctuary, and for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. 15 And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken.”

It seems that some did not believe the words of the prophet and reckoned them a political conspiracy or national treason and opposition to the king and the authorities, so that Judah should not take refuge in Assyria and perish at the hands of the Syrians and Israel. The Lord took hold of Isaiah, as it were by the hand, to strengthen him [11]. Some see that Isaiah himself, as a man, sometimes inclined to the opinion of the king and his counselors and the people, but God insisted on making the way clear to him even though it was contrary to the opinion of the community; it is as though He took him by the hand to lead him into the narrow, rejected way. Perhaps the Lord took him by the hand to strengthen him because of the false accusations made against him, and so that he would not cease his prophetic work because of what these people stirred up, but He wants him to strengthen the faithful hands by their sanctification to the Lord. It is as though the Lord holds the hands of Isaiah so that the latter in turn may hold the hands of the faithful and place them in the hands of the holy God. Therefore He says: “Neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread” [12-13]. Every faithful soul in the service of the Lord is opposed, but the Lord Himself supports it, not only that it may work but that it may support others and encourage them to work in the Spirit of God, looking not at the opposition but at the support of the Lord of hosts for them.

How wonderful are these words: “Fear not... sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.” The evil powers have united and allied in arrogance and pride, but the children of God unite together in the Lord, they unite under the leadership of the holy Lord of hosts in love and sanctification. These do not lean on human arms and do not want an alliance between light and darkness, but believe in overcoming and victory through sanctification, or fellowship with the holy God.

It is not Isaiah alone who is opposed, nor the faithful believers alone, but “Immanuel” Himself becomes an object of opposition and a stone of stumbling to many: “And he shall be for a sanctuary, and for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken” [14-15].

He is a “sanctuary,” or a “holy stone,” for the believers who take refuge in Him and hold fast to Him for their protection and salvation; He is the “foundation stone” and the “cornerstone” that joins the believers from the Jews with the believers from the Gentiles like two walls that meet together in Him. At the same time He is a stone of stumbling and offence to unbelievers.

* Whenever (Christ) is presented in Holy Scripture as a stone, He is a stone of stumbling to unbelievers and a foundation stone to believers (Isa 8:14; 28:16; Dan 2:34, 45; Mt 21:44; Lk 20:17; Acts 5:11; Rom 9:33, etc.).
St. Augustine The Lord Christ came to His own and His own received Him not, therefore He says “a rock of offence to my house”; what increases His wounds is that the rejection is from His own house.
St. Peter quoted this prophecy (1 Pet 2:8), declaring its fulfillment in the person of the Lord Christ.

16 “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples. 17 And I will wait upon the LORD, that hideth his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him. 18 Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the LORD of hosts, which dwelleth in mount Zion.”

Although the Lord Christ's own, or the people of His house, rejected Him so that He became a stone of stumbling to them, there was found a holy remnant that received Him, such as the disciples and the apostles and the Marys and the house of Lazarus, and so on... This remnant is reckoned a holy leaven which the Spirit of God uses to leaven the dough in the whole world.
What happened with the Lord Christ took place with Isaiah in a faint image, since he was a type of Christ, for he too had faithful disciples.

“Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples” [16]. The holy few received the words of the prophet Isaiah as true prophecies and a divine word, reckoning his words a declaration of the mind of God and His holy will. These the prophet called his disciples and also “the children whom the LORD hath given me” [8]. These must seal or bind up what they heard, for these prophecies must be kept safe until the times of the New Testament, when they are revealed to simple children (Mt 11:25). Sealing them also means the obligation not to add to them or take away from them.

What Isaiah mentioned seemed in his time an impossible matter that had to be resisted; for this reason he and his disciples had to arm themselves with patience for the Lord [17]. They lived in an oppressive atmosphere: the Lord was hiding His face from His people [17], as though they were not His people and He did not know them, delivering them over to their rejected and ruined minds, a matter that grieved the heart of Isaiah and his disciples; and at the same time the people looked at them as strangers and oddities, full of folly. So by his saying, “Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the LORD of hosts” [18], he means that Isaiah and his disciples were like signs and wonders to the people, since they differed from everyone in their faith, their conduct and their thoughts toward the Lord.

Isaiah's disciples were reckoned as his children, and in this he bears a type of the Lord Christ, who longs to bind the believers in Him with a unique bond, like the bond of a father with his children.

* He is a brother and friend and bridegroom: “Henceforth I call you not servants... but I have called you friends” (Jn 15:15). And Paul says: “I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor 11:2); “that he might be the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom 8:29). We are no longer only His brothers but have become His children, for He says: “Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me” [18]; not only this, but we have become His members and His body.
* Here (Heb 2:13; Isa 8:18) (Christ) shows Himself a father as He showed Himself earlier a brother.
St. John Chrysostom * [He is speaking with those seeking baptism.]

* The angels share your joy, and Christ Himself, the Great High Priest... presents you all to the Father, saying: “Behold I and the children which God hath given me,” that He may keep you all the object of the delight of His gaze.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem As the prophet Isaiah presents his disciples to God as witnesses of the truth, a type of the person of the Lord Christ, who presents His believers to the Father as members of His body and sons of the truth, the delight of the Father, so it is fitting for us also to care for everyone, especially the members of the family, that we may present them to God as His beloved. And as St. John Chrysostom says: [Let us think seriously about our wives and our children and our servants, realizing that by this we establish for ourselves a good (easy) order, and our dealings with them become gentle and tender.]

19 And when they shall say unto you, “Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter,” “Should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” 20 To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. 21 And they shall pass through it, hardly bestead and hungry: and it shall come to pass, that when they shall be hungry, they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and look upward. 22 And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness.

The people felt as though God had hidden His face from them, so they began to demand that the officials, perhaps including some of Isaiah's disciples, resort to those who have familiar spirits and to soothsayers, to seek counsel and to learn about future matters. The prophet calls them those “that peep and that mutter” [19], because they speak in a low voice, as though from another world, to perfect the playing of their part.

What does resorting to divination mean? It is a person's loss of every refuge or help, as happened with King Saul. He felt that he was isolated from God and from His prophets, and even the people had withdrawn from him, so he resorted to the dead, asking them through the woman who practiced divination.

It was fitting for the people of Judah, leaders and people, to resort to God and consult His prophets and hear the word of God that gives light in the midst of the darkness [20], and so receive good counsel and knowledge of the will of God and help and grace; but when they resort to divination in all its forms and to asking the dead, this means that they lifted their eyes upward and found heaven angry [21], and looked toward the earth and behold, thick darkness had settled upon it.

In brief, the people of Judah fell into two grave sins: resorting to human alliances instead of relying on God, and returning to divination and the dead instead of enjoying the living word of God that gives enlightenment and strength.
This painful picture proclaims an important truth: the need for a divine Savior!

entries.section: 1. A light that shone in the darkness:

paragraphs.text: 1 But there shall be no gloom for her that was in anguish. As in the former time he humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, so in the latter he honors the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the nations. 2 The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined. 3 Thou hast multiplied the nation, thou hast magnified the joy for it: they joy before thee according to the joy in harvest, and as men rejoice when they divide the spoil. 4 For the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, thou hast broken as in the day of Midian. 5 For every weapon of the armed man in the battle, and every garment rolled in blood, shall be for burning, fuel of fire.
The end of the previous chapter was extremely dark, so this chapter begins with the word “But”... for God does not leave His people like this, but wants to shine upon them with His light.

“But there shall be no gloom for her that was in anguish. As in the former time he humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, so in the latter he honors the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined” [1-2]. This prophecy was fulfilled by the appearing of the Lord Christ and His preaching in Galilee of the nations. The Evangelist says: “That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles; The people which sat in darkness saw great light” (Mt 4:14-16). This region was marked by lowliness, so Nathanael says: “Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (Jn 1:46). Perhaps this is because this spot (Galilee of the nations) lies on the border of the nations, so it was exposed to invasions, and because of its mixing with the neighboring pagan nations it took on many pagan customs and remained for long periods in spiritual decay; therefore the prophet put it: “The people that sat in darkness.”

The region of Galilee was a district comprising twenty cities which Solomon gave to Hiram king of Tyre. The Jews in it were few in number; most of its inhabitants were Phoenicians, Greeks and Arabs, therefore it was called “Galilee of the nations.” The Lord Christ, the Teacher of mankind and the Sun of Righteousness, came to it to shine upon those who sit in darkness. As for the district of Capernaum, whose name means “Comforter,” it is considered one of the most important districts of Galilee; it was a Roman fortress in which there was a garrison of Roman commanders.
* He dwelt in Galilee so that those who sit in darkness might see a great light.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Let those who sit in the darkness of ignorance see the great light of perfect knowledge; the old things are passed away, behold, all things are become new (2 Cor 5:17); the letter has ended and the Spirit has advanced, the shadows have fled and the truth has come to them.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus * By faith they come out of the darkness and death of sin into light and life.

St. Augustine * The light of the Logos, who is life, shines in the darkness of our souls; He comes to where the rulers of this darkness are, who oppose the human race to subject it to darkness. These rulers do not stand firm in their power when the light shines upon them, which came to make human beings children of light.
Origen God does not allow the darkness to last, but shines with His light... So what happens?

entries.section: 1. A light that shone in the darkness:

paragraphs.text: a. “Thou hast multiplied the nation” [3]; although it fell under discipline with severe blows, it grows and multiplies by the mercy and grace of God.

b. “Thou hast magnified the joy” [3]. The nation rejoices as on the day of harvest or the day of enjoying the spoil, as though the secret of its joy were the abundant harvest and the triumph or victory over the enemy of good.

Joy is the mark of the Church of the New Testament, rejoicing in the Gospel life in the midst of sufferings. She rejoices over her continual harvest of many souls for the sake of the Kingdom of God, and enjoys the spoil of victory over the enemy of good. Her life is continual rejoicing over the souls that repent and enjoy salvation and over her unceasing victories.

entries.section: 1. A light that shone in the darkness:

paragraphs.text: c. Enjoying glorious freedom: “For the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, thou hast broken as in the day of Midian” [4]. She is freed from the heavy yoke and the staff and the rod of forced labor, as a symbol of freedom and salvation from the slavery of the devil through the Cross, so that the devil and his powers no longer have authority over the believer who enjoys the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

6 For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. 7 Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this.

The secret of the nation's enjoyment of continual growth and lasting joy together with glorious freedom is the coming of the Messiah as Savior, Conqueror and Victor on behalf of mankind against the enemies. The Son of God came incarnate to bear the yoke of the Cross in our name, and so He gives us every possibility of salvation. For the prophet says: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, for the increase of his government, and of peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this” [6-7].

Believing mankind was awaiting the divine Incarnation, in which the Son of God, who is the Creator, the Giver of life and its glory, comes to raise our dead and corrupted nature to the goodness in which it was created, by re-creating it and renewing it continually, so that He gives it continuity of life together with joy and freedom.

a. “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given,” that is, He becomes man, so that the Son of God becomes the Son of Man and is reckoned a child, bearing our human nature truly in the perfection of its form, without separation from His divinity and without mingling or confusion or alteration. He shares our human life except for sin and remains as He is, “the Son of God”... The Apostle says: “Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Heb 3:14).
* He became man in the body of our salvation, so that He might have something to offer on our behalf as salvation for us all.

St. Athanasius the Apostolic * Who is this who wants us to share in His flesh and blood? Surely He is the Son of God! How did He become a partner with us except through flesh? And how did He break the bonds of death except by His bodily death? For Christ's endurance of death put death to death.

St. Ambrose b. “And the government shall be upon his shoulder,” for He reigned from a tree, as the Psalmist says, the tree of the Cross which He carried on His shoulder as the throne of His divine love.
* The government shall be upon his shoulder, for He entered His Kingdom by carrying the Cross.
Origen * This means the power of the Cross, because He used His shoulders when He was crucified, by carrying the Cross.

The martyr Justin c. “His name shall be called Wonderful,” because He is beyond comprehension; He was given a name which is above every name, that at his name every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth (Phil 2:9-11).
The disciples and apostles realized the power of the name “Jesus”; by it they preached, and by it they healed the sick, cast out demons and raised the dead.

The writings of Origen reveal the early Church's esteem for the name of Jesus as a secret of power to which the believer holds fast in order to live as a conqueror and victor over sin and Satan and all the powers of darkness. Among his words: [By His name demons are often driven out of people, especially if it is repeated in a sound manner and with full confidence. Great is the name of Jesus, which has its effectiveness even if the wicked sometimes use it. The name of Jesus heals those who suffer in mind, and drives out the spirits of darkness, and grants healing to the sick.] He also declares that His titles reveal His manifold and abounding grace, for he says: [Although Christ is one in His essence, He has many titles that point to His authority and His works; it is understood that He is grace, righteousness, peace, life, truth, the Word...]

d. “Counsellor,” as He is “the wisdom of God” (1 Cor 1:24), in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (1 Cor 2:3). The Septuagint reads “the Messenger of the great counsel”... What is this great counsel for which the Father sent Him? The revelation of the divine mystery to mankind, and the disclosure of the Father, whom no one knows except the Son and he to whom the Son will reveal Him.

* The Son of God was called thus (the Messenger of the great counsel) because of the things He taught, especially because He revealed the Father to mankind, for He says: “I have manifested thy name unto the men” (Jn 17:6)... He declared His name by words and deeds.

St. John Chrysostom * There is no knowledge without faith, and no faith without knowledge... The Son is the true Teacher about the Father; we believe in the Son in order to know the Father, with whom also is the Son. Again, in order to know the Father we must believe in the Son, for He is the Son of the Father. The knowledge of the Father and the Son, in the manner of the true Gnostic, is the attainment of the truth by means of the truth... Truly, few are those who believe and know.
St. Clement of Alexandria * The divine Word was sent as a physician to sinners, and as a teacher of the divine mysteries to those who are pure and without sin.

Origen e. “The mighty God”: true God of true God, one with the Father in essence, who alone is able to renew our nature as the Creator, and the Intercessor who alone is able to atone for the sins of the whole world.

f. “The everlasting Father”: He attaches the title “Mighty God” to “Everlasting Father,” to declare that the power of the Lord Christ, the true God, is not in displaying might and greatness but rather in offering a unique fatherhood of love toward mankind, through which we enjoy the power of Christ in us. He is the almighty Creator who gives Himself to His believers as members of His body and as His children, so that they bear His capacities within them. In other words, in Christ Jesus the incomprehensible power of God is revealed together with His surpassing practical love, so that we may say with the Apostle: “I can do all things through Christ Jesus who strengtheneth me.”

g. “The Prince of Peace”: He is the King of Peace (1 Thess 5:23), who offers us His blood for our reconciliation with the Father, so that we carry inner peace with Him (Rom 5:1), peace with God and with ourselves and with our brethren, shattering the wall of enmity, inward and outward.

He is the Son of David, “Prince and King,” not on the level of earth and time, but to reign eternally upon the throne of His father David (Lk 1:32-33) on the level of the inner heart and eternity; neither His kingdom nor His peace has any limits [7].

He reigns with truth and righteousness, as He hides us in Himself so that we become walkers in the truth, bearing His righteousness. The cause of this is that “the zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this”; He is zealous over mankind as the heavenly Bridegroom united with His bride.

In brief, the prophet Isaiah declares this wondrous, mighty Child, who does not save Ahaz from the opposition of his enemies, but establishes a new kingdom whose foundation is the throne of David, a kingdom of true peace that extends to the peoples and nations, and of whose peace there is no end [7], as He gives us Himself, the mystery of eternal peace.
* Behold, the Son of God has been given to us.
A little later he says: “And of peace there shall be no end” [7].
The Romans have limits (an end), but the kingdom of the Son of God is without limits.
Persia and Media have limits, but the Son has no limits.
He says after that: “Upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom...”; the holy Virgin is of the seed of David.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem

8 The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel. 9 And all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart, 10 “The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars.” 11 Therefore the LORD shall set up the adversaries of Rezin against him, and join his enemies together; 12 The Syrians before, and the Philistines behind; and they shall devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

The Word of God, in His unlimited love, condescends to become man in order to give light to those who sit in darkness, shining upon them with His divine light, granting them the light of knowledge, offering them His life as the mystery of joy and rejoicing and continual victory; but man, on the contrary, exalts himself in pride, reckoning in himself that he is able by his human arm to accomplish salvation. This is what happened in the days of the prophet Isaiah and what happens through the ages; the house of Jacob exalted themselves, rejecting his prophetic counsel, and also in the days of the Lord Christ when they denied faith in Him... Yet with all this, the hand of God remains stretched out in love, awaiting man's return to Him.
In this passage there are three poetic verses in Hebrew that end with the phrase: “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still” [12, 17, 20] [also (Isa 10:4)].

Some see that this outstretched divine hand is a sign of God's calling to man to draw near to Him and meet with Him and be united with Him. It is also a sign of God's protection of him, as though He were assuring him that however great the obstacles, the hand of the Almighty is stretched out to save him from every evil and rescue him from bitterness and distress. It is also a sign of the divine discipline springing from love, He stretches out His hand to press upon man so that he returns to himself and seeks God as his helper. These three signs were fulfilled through the Incarnation of the Word, in which He calls us to sonship to God, offers us free salvation, and bears the wages of sin in His body to draw us to Himself. The divine hand is a symbol of the divine Word, who came down to us to declare the love of the Father and to reconcile us with Him by His blood as the price of our sins and transgressions.

God, in His love, allowed distress for the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim), but instead of repenting they exalted themselves all the more. This is what the prophet revealed by saying: “That say in the pride and stoutness of heart, The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars” [10]. Some see that the prophet is speaking here about the earthquake that occurred in the days of Uzziah, which seems to have been widespread (Amos 1:1; Zech 14:5); because of it most of the houses of Samaria and Ephraim fell and there were many victims, and they began to mock the judgment of God, declaring that although He had permitted the destruction of their houses made of brick and the fall of the sycamore trees, they would erect palaces made of hewn stones and plant cedar trees that an earthquake could neither demolish nor remove. It is as though in this they repeat what man did when he set out to build the tower of Babel so that its top might reach to heaven (Gen 11:3-4).

The prophet Isaiah answers this by announcing a more severe chastening from God: since they did not tremble at the earthquake, He will allow the enemy “Rezin,” king of Syria, to rage, and He also stirs up his enemies (perhaps he meant Assyria, which attacked Israel and afterward turned against Judah). He allows the nations to rage against Israel to devour them completely, as a beast devours sheep and swallows them: “And they shall devour Israel with open mouth” [12]; yet the mercies of God remain awaiting their return, as he continues his speech: “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still” [12].

13 For the people turneth not unto him that smiteth them, neither do they seek the LORD of hosts. 14 Therefore the LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day. 15 The ancient and honourable, he is the head; and the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail. 16 For the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are destroyed. 17 Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men, neither shall have mercy on their fatherless and widows: for every one is an hypocrite and an evildoer, and every mouth speaketh folly. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still. 18 For wickedness burneth as the fire: it shall devour the briers and thorns, and shall kindle in the thickets of the forest, and they shall mount up like the lifting up of smoke. 19 Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts is the land burned up, and the people shall be as the fuel of the fire: no man shall spare his brother. 20 And he shall snatch on the right hand, and be hungry; and he shall eat on the left hand, and they shall not be satisfied: they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm: 21 Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: and they together shall be against Judah. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.
The people remain hard of heart, therefore: “The LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush (halfa grass or straw), in one day” [14].
a. He removes the leaders of the people, whatever their rank (the head, the branch).
b. He removes the false prophets (the tail, the rush).
c. The destruction of the guides because they cause them to err [16].

d. He takes no pleasure in the young men because of their youth, nor in the orphans or the widows, although He is “a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows” (Ps 68:5)... for all together shared in evil, with stubbornness and arrogance and folly [17]. The Assyrian kings were extremely cruel: Tiglath-pileser showed no mercy to the young, or to the widows or orphans in Ephraim.
e. The whole people turn into something like a forest burning with the fire of divine wrath [19], not because God takes vengeance for Himself, but because their wickedness is a destroying fire [18].

f. The nation turns into a state of chaos whose law is violence and injustice and insatiability, ruled by bloody, destructive civil wars: “No man shall spare his brother. He shall snatch on the right hand, and be hungry; and he shall eat on the left hand, and they shall not be satisfied: they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm (that is, his neighbor or relative)” [19-20]... This is a hideous picture of a society whose law is war, violence and selfishness with greed. One consumes the other (Gal 5:15), and as the prophet Haggai says: “Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes” (Hag 1:6), a sign that their life is empty of the blessing of the Lord and His grace.

g. The infighting does not stop at individuals but creeps into the tribes themselves, so that one tribe allies with another against a third, and so on: “Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: and they together shall be against Judah” [21].
“For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still” [21].

entries.section: 1. The first woe against the leaders:

paragraphs.text: 1 Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and to the scribes that write grievousness which they have prescribed; 2 To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless! 3 And what will ye do in the day of visitation, when the desolation shall come from far? To whom will ye flee for help? And where will ye leave your glory? 4 They shall either bow down among the prisoners, or fall under the slain. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

Some see the woe directed here against the leaders as a continuation of what was said in the previous chapter about the pride of Israel, and they prove this by the fact that it also ends with the phrase that was repeated before: "For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still" (Isa 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4). On this view the discourse is directed against the leaders of the ten tribes (Israel). However, the rest of the discourse is addressed to Jerusalem, the capital of Judah, and for this reason some scholars hold that what is said here applies to the leaders of both kingdoms, since they were alike in evil.

God exposes the unjust conduct of the leaders, which centers on judging falsely and ruling with injustice [1]. They keep the weak from enjoying their stolen rights, and they rob the poor of their right, especially the fatherless and the widows [2]. As the Wise Man says: "So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power" (Eccl 4:1).
Now, since Isaiah perceives the justice of God, especially in His defense of the weak, he asks these leaders:

entries.section: 1. The first woe against the leaders:

paragraphs.text: "And what will ye do in the day of visitation, when the desolation shall come from far? To whom will ye flee for help? And where will ye leave your glory? They shall either bow down among the prisoners, or fall under the slain" [3-4]. Punishment is certainly coming, especially upon the religious and civil leaders; this is a settled matter and a truth that cannot be ignored. As he said before: "Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him" (Isa 3:11). They will find no help, because what helps us in judgment is our mercy and compassion toward others. Their glories vanish because these were bound to time and not to God. Therefore some of them fall as captives, to bow down in humiliation among the prisoners, and some are killed when Assyria attacks them, and so fall under the bodies of others. They trampled the right of the weak, and so others tread them under their feet.

entries.section: 1. The first woe against the leaders:

paragraphs.text: Yet for all this God still stretches out the hand of His love to save them from their evil: "For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still" [4].

5 "Woe to Assyria, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation. 6 I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. 7 Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few. 8 For he saith, Are not my princes altogether kings? 9 Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus? 10 As my hand hath found the kingdoms of the idols, and their graven images did excel them of Jerusalem and of Samaria; 11 Shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols?" 12 Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. 13 For he saith, "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the kings like a valiant man: 14 And my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped." 15 Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up him that is not wood. 16 Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire. 17 And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; 18 And shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body: and it shall be as when a sick man melts away. 19 And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, that a child may write them.

The prophet has already spoken of Assyria's military power, its might and its victory even over the people of God. He has also affirmed that what befell the people came by divine permission for discipline. But Assyria exalted itself against God and reckoned that by this victory it had conquered the God of this people and humbled Him... Therefore the Lord turns back and disciplines Assyria itself, so haughty and arrogant.

The prophet Isaiah was accustomed to speak boldly and frankly. While he calls Assyria the rod of God's anger, and the staff in their hand the indignation of the Lord [5], because Assyria is an instrument for carrying out the Lord's discipline, we find him calling the people of God "an hypocritical nation" and "the people of my wrath" [6], because this people carried the outward form of worship while corruption crept into their inner life. This is what led him to call the people by hateful names and to declare that God delivers them over to Assyria for plunder and spoil, so that Assyria may tread them under foot and they become trodden down like the mire of the streets... Whoever makes light of the holy life in the Lord hands his life over to corruption and ruin, and collapses, so that the enemy of good mocks him and treads him under his feet.

Assyria did not realize this truth, that it was merely an instrument of discipline [7]; rather, in pride it said: "Are not my princes altogether kings?" [8]. That is, the governors whom the king of Assyria appoints under his command are all kings, so what then is his own position? He is the king of kings!

He also said: "Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?" [9]. Scholars hold that the speaker here is Sennacherib the Assyrian, boasting of his victories together with those of Sargon before him, as victories won on behalf of Assyria as a whole, which show the futility of resisting the Assyrian advance.
Perhaps by Calno is meant "Calneh," mentioned with Hamath and Gath in (Amos 6:2), which is thought to be Kullani or the modern Kulanhu, six miles from Arpad, near Aleppo.

Carchemish: the eastern capital of the Hittites, west of the Euphrates at a ford in the river and north of where it meets the Sajur. Its location was excellent for trade, and it was very rich. Ashurnasirpal of Assyria (885-860 B.C.) exacted a very large tribute from it, and Sargon captured it in 717 B.C., and with its fall the Hittite empire fell. The Romans called it Circesium; on its site now stands Jarablus.

Arpad: a city in Aram about 13 miles north of Hamath, now on the site called "Tell Arpad." The Assyrians captured it in the ninth century before Christ, but it rebelled against them, and they returned and captured it several times, boasting of their victory over it.

Thus the greatest cities of the Hittites or the Arameans did not stand before Assyria; will the cities of Judah and Israel stand before it? Assyria reckoned that it had conquered the gods of the nations and the idols that protect them, so that the God of Israel or of Judah would not stand before it either [10-11], supposing that He is on the same level as these idols.

God allowed it this much, but He turns back and disciplines Assyria for its scorn of Him: "Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the kings like a valiant man: and my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped" [13-14].

Thus Assyria supposed that by its own strength and wisdom it had done mighty works: it ruled kings and removed peoples, destroyed, killed and grew rich. In its campaigns it looked upon the peoples as the nest of a bird, with no strength or power, and plundered the abandoned eggs in it... No one was found to stand before it or to utter a word.
Assyria did not realize that it was an axe or a saw that God used for discipline, and so the instrument exalted itself over the one who wields it. Therefore God disciplines it in this way:
A. He sends leanness among "his fat ones," that is, the mighty heroes of his army [16].

B. He kindles under "his glory," that is, his army, a burning like the burning of a fire [16], and it consumes it until it becomes ashes. God becomes "the light of Israel" into a fire that devours Assyria, and the Holy One a flame that crushes the enemy [17]. In other words, God, who is light for the believers and the mystery of sanctification of their life, becomes a devouring fire and a flame for the wicked who resist Him.

C. He destroys his army so that a small number remains (the trees of the forest), whose names a child can write [19]. This is as regards number; as regards strength, they lose their spiritual and bodily energy and become like a consumptive who melts away [18].

20 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. 21 The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God. 22 For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness. 23 For the Lord GOD of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land.

The prophets often spoke of the "remnant" that will be saved. By it they meant the very few who remain faithful to the Lord amid the collapse of the religious leaders and the corruption of the judges, the rulers and the people as well. This remnant, which escapes the corruption of the community and its abominations, is saved from the great tribulation in the time of bitter trial (Rev 3:10). This remnant that escapes the oppression of Assyria does not rejoice in its return to Jerusalem, but in something greater: it rejoices in its meeting with the mighty God Himself [21].

The Apostle Paul quoted the saying of the prophet Isaiah [(Isa 22-23) LXX], saying: "Isaiah also crieth concerning Israel, Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved: for he is finishing the matter and judging in righteousness, because the Lord will make a decreed matter upon the earth" (Rom 9:27-28).

This saying occurs in Isaiah [(Isa 22-23) LXX] and carried a prophecy about the captives, since they were very many in comparison with the very few who escape from captivity... and that God allowed this, and even decreed this discipline for the sake of righteousness. The Apostle applied this prophecy more broadly to the Messianic age, when a very great number of the Jews are held captive in unbelief, refusing to believe in the Messiah, while few are saved by accepting the Messiah the Savior; and God allowed this for the sake of righteousness, to open the door to the Gentiles.

St. John Chrysostom comments: [He means that I do not care about the multitude (the huge number), and I am not swayed by the race (the Jews), but I save those who come forward as worthy of salvation. He did not mention "the sand of the sea" for no reason, but to remind them of the ancient promise (Gen 22:17; 32:12), which they had made themselves unworthy of. Why then are you troubled if the promise is not fulfilled (for all), since all the prophets showed that not everyone is saved? Then the Apostle also shows the way of salvation... "For he is finishing the matter and judging (quickly) in righteousness, because the Lord will make a decreed matter (quickly) upon the earth" (Rom 9:28)... This matter is faith, which carries salvation in few words: "That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved" (Rom 10:9). Behold, you see that the Lord is completing a short word upon the earth, and the wonder is that this short word carries not salvation only but righteousness as well.] He also says: [Lest you think that God cares only for the huge number, he says: "Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved."] And St. Augustine says: [This is the remnant of that nation which believes in Christ.]

entries.section: 4. Be not afraid, O my people:

paragraphs.text: 24 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, "O my people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian: he shall smite thee with a rod, and shall lift up his staff against thee, after the manner of Egypt. 25 For yet a very little while, and the indignation shall cease, and mine anger in their destruction." 26 And the LORD of hosts shall stir up a scourge for him according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb: and as his rod was upon the sea, so shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt. 27 And it shall come to pass in that day, that his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the fatness.

Some scholars hold that the prophecy here points to the following event: when Hezekiah the son of Ahaz and his successor refused to pay tribute, Sennacherib the Assyrian attacked Judah with a strong army and besieged Jerusalem, and was on the point of taking the city, but God ordered its deliverance. The army was slain and Sennacherib fled, where his sons killed him.

The prophecy here pointed to an important matter, namely that God is the One who works in all generations. God does not cease to command His people not to fear, for He is the Father who is committed to our life, our salvation, our growth and our peace, and He works in every age with an uplifted arm for the salvation of His believers.
