If the exodus of the children of Israel, or their deliverance from slavery, is counted an extraordinary thing that reveals God's care for His believers, then in the days of Hezekiah He repeats their exodus or deliverance on a mightier level, amid the bitterness that all were suffering.

entries.section: 4. Be not afraid, O my people:

paragraphs.text: God asks His people not to fear Assyria, for it will be destroyed, as God raises up a scourge against it [26]. He strikes it with His angel with a deadly blow (2 Chr 32:21), as He struck Oreb, the prince of Midian, before (Judg 7:25; Ps 83:11), and as He struck Pharaoh and his hosts in the Red Sea through the rod of Moses [26]. Thus God destroys Assyria to remove this yoke from the shoulder of His people [27] and from their neck because of the fatness (the oil), for the sake of the holy anointing which King David received, and his sons after him.

The second matter is that the Anointed One, the mighty Messiah, grants rest to the whole earth, and peace, through His blessed reign... This is the main line of the whole book, indeed of the Holy Bible in both Testaments.

28 He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages: 29 They are gone over the passage: they have taken up their lodging at Geba; Ramah is afraid; Gibeah of Saul is fled. 30 Lift up thy voice, O daughter of Gallim: hearken, O Laishah: poor Anathoth! 31 Madmenah is removed; the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee. 32 As yet shall he remain at Nob that day: he shall shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.

Before speaking of the fall of Assyria, the prophet spoke of the Assyrian invasion of Judah, to make clear its mighty military ability and the speed of its advance toward Jerusalem the capital, with the weakness of Judah's resistance, indeed its absence, and how Judah was terrified and trembled [28-32]. The prophet gave a poetic description that reveals the bitterness of the cities of Judah, but Assyria halts at Nob (a city of the priests lying north of Jerusalem), perhaps to rest the army and prepare to confront Jerusalem. Sennacherib stood there to raise his hand and stretch it out in threat against Jerusalem [32], and so appeared as a lofty, arrogant tree. He threatened to crush Jerusalem and did not realize that God had allowed his own crushing, and that He would strip from him the branches with which he exalts himself.
In this prophecy God does not mean Sennacherib alone, but every evil movement that resists the Church of God or any of His children.

33 Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled. 34 And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one.

God proclaims the complete destruction of Assyria, for He lops its branches and even pulls up its roots, so that its loftiness collapses and its glory comes down to the dust [33-34]. This is the fruit of pride!

entries.section: 1. The appearance of the son of Jesse:

paragraphs.text: 1 And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots. In chapter nine he spoke of the Savior as the wonderful Child that is born: "For unto us a child is born... and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father" (Isa 9:6). Here, however, he affirms His humanity, as the King who is the son of Jesse: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots" [1]. He did not say the son of David, although by the Law He is the son of David, but he wished to present Him in a very humble form, as a rod and a branch of Jesse, who lived and died of little account. And the wonder is that the offspring of King David became so weak that Joseph and St. Mary came to be extremely poor.

While the inspired text in the previous chapter speaks of Assyria, who represents the enemy of the Church, as lofty and strong branches (Isa 10:33), the Messiah appears as a humble rod or branch. He wanted to crush pride, the destroyer of mankind, by His humility. As the Church says of Him on Good Friday: "He showed through weakness (the Cross) what is greater than power."
* This is Christ, who was conceived by the power of God through the Virgin of the seed of Jacob, the father of Judah and the father of the Jews, of the seed of Jesse...
St. Justin Martyr

entries.section: 2. The Savior and the Spirit of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: "And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord." [2].

When the Lord Christ came representing humanity, the Holy Spirit rested upon Him, who is not a stranger to Him, for He is His Spirit. The resting of the Holy Spirit upon Christ differs from His resting upon us; for Him it is a hypostatic indwelling, one with Him in the same essence with the Father, an indwelling without limit. For us, however, it is a free gift and a grace granted to us in Christ Jesus as far as our nature can bear, that He may work its continual renewal. Therefore it was said of the Lord Christ that "it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell" (Col 1:19; 2:9), and out of His fulness, which fills all, all believers receive grace for grace (Jn 1:16).

The Word of God is wisdom itself, and understanding and might... So the resting of the Holy Spirit is not a temporal indwelling but an eternal union among the three hypostases. In the divine Incarnation our Lord Jesus accepted the appearance of the Holy Spirit resting upon Him, in order to give to us in Him, as members of His body, the gift of the Holy Spirit, the Giver of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge and the fear of the Lord.

Perhaps some will ask: why did the Holy Spirit rest upon the Lord Christ at His baptism? We answer: the Holy Spirit is the One who formed the humanity of the Lord Christ from the moment of the Annunciation of the divine Incarnation. And since the divinity of the Lord never parted from His humanity, His humanity was never apart from the Holy Spirit, nor in need of the Spirit's renewal for it, for it never fell into sin, nor did the old man have any place in it. Rather the Lord asked to be baptized "to fulfil all righteousness," that is, to present to us a new righteousness that we carry within us through His holy body. The resting of the Spirit upon Him was in truth for the sake of the humanity that is sanctified in Him, and so receives His Holy Spirit.

St. Gregory of Nyssa says in this: [Today (Jesus) was baptized by John, to show the one who had been defiled, and to make the Spirit descend from above, and so lift man to heaven, and raise up the fallen one who had descended and had come into shame. Christ set right all evils, taking on the whole of humanity that He might save humanity, and become an example for each one of us. Therefore He sanctifies the firstfruits and the fruits of every work He does, that He may leave to His servants a good zeal, without doubt, to follow in His steps.]
St. Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of the work of the Holy Spirit in our life as the fountain of our goodness, saying:
[He is called the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ... and He Himself is the Lord.
The Spirit of prophecy, of truth and of freedom, the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, goodness and the fear of God.
He is the maker of all these things, He fills all by His essence and contains all things; He fills the world in His essence and yet the world cannot comprehend His power.
Good and upright, royal by nature and not by adoption.

He sanctifies and is not sanctified, He measures and is not measured, He gives participation and does not need participation, He fills and is not filled, He contains and is not contained, He bestows inheritance and glorifies... with the Father and the Son.
He is the finger of God, fire like God (the Father)...
The creating Spirit who creates anew by Baptism and the Resurrection.

He is the Spirit who knows all things, who gives where He wills, who guides, speaks, sends, sets apart and is grieved, who reveals, enlightens and gives life, or rather who is Himself the light and the life.

He creates temples and deifies (gives participation with God), He gives perfection even before baptism [as in the case of Cornelius (Acts 10:9)], and you seek Him after baptism as a gift... He works in us the divine work, He is divided into tongues of fire, distributing the gifts, He appoints apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers.
He is understood in many ways, He is clear, and He pricks the hearts...].

"And his delight shall be in the fear of the Lord: and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither decide after the hearing of his ears: but with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and rule with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the hypocrite." [3-4].

A. The Lord Christ presents to us a living picture of dealing with others: that it should not rest on bare outward appearances, and that our senses should not be the judge, especially smell, sight and hearing.

He says, "His delight His breath shall be in the fear of the Lord" [3]. The sense of smell is the quickest sense in man's life, and it must be absorbed, together with the rest of the senses, by the fear of God. Here we must distinguish three kinds of fear: the fear of slaves, the fear of hired servants, and the fear of sons. Slaves fear their masters lest they kill them, hired servants fear their employers lest they deprive them of wages or reward, but sons fear lest they wound the feelings of their fathers. This exalted fear, which the Spirit of the Lord gives us that we may revere God, is not fear of punishment or of losing the reward, but because we are sons who do not want to wound the feelings of His love.

B. "He shall not judge after the sight of his eyes" [3], but according to inner works, as the One who searches the hearts and knows the thoughts and intentions. The Lord Christ takes a stand opposed to what happened in the days of Isaiah, when the judges judged according to faces. This plague of "partiality" often strikes those who bear leadership responsibilities, and the Lord stood firmly against this pestilence, rebuking the religious leaders who were struck with partiality and hypocrisy, such as the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the scribes, while He gently called the children to Him and was merciful to sinners and tax collectors.
C. Rejection of human slanders: "neither decide after the hearing of his ears" [3].
D. His care for the poor, the wretched and the oppressed [4].

E. "And he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth" [4]. The Lord of glory came to smite with His word (the rod of His mouth), or with the sword of His mouth (Rev 2:16; 19:6), the two-edged sword of the Word (Heb 4:3), everyone who clung to the love of earthly things and became earth. His aim is to shatter in us the love of temporal things, in order to lift all our powers toward heavenly things.

He came to slay hypocrisy and pretense by His Holy Spirit (the breath of His lips), so that believers may live by the Holy Spirit working within them, without being occupied with deceptive appearances.

F. "And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins" [5]. The rich in the East wore a girdle embroidered with threads of gold as an ornament, a sign of greatness and splendor, and to gather up the loose robe. The poor, especially slaves, wore a cheap girdle that helps a person move quickly in serving his master and guests; the girdle was also used on journeys to gather up the garments, and soldiers used it... In any case, our Lord Jesus Christ came into the world as a spiritual King girded with righteousness and faithfulness, a sign of His wealth and beauty as the Holy One who gives the holy life, and He came as a servant girding Himself to wash human feet, so as to cleanse everyone who comes to Him.
Righteousness is often likened to a garment or a girdle, for by the righteousness of Christ we are covered and set in motion for work and striving (Job 29:14; Ps 109:18-19; Eph 6:13-17; Rev 19:8).

entries.section: 4. The marks of the Messianic age:

paragraphs.text: 5 And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins. 6 The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them. 7 And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. 8 And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den. 9 They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

After speaking of the work of the Lord Christ, he went on to speak of the Messianic age, presenting to us a living picture of it, the most striking feature of which is that believing humanity is marked by being united together in one body, bearing the nature of love and peace, so that every rebellion or violence, every love of bloodshed and killing, or of sabotage and destruction, disappears from their life.
He portrays this age, saying:

entries.section: 4. The marks of the Messianic age:

paragraphs.text: "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb" [6]; there is no greater contrast than this: the shedder of blood dwells with the gentle lamb, unable to defend itself. The one with the heart of a wolf, who loves to prey, lives with the person as gentle as a lamb; both bear a new nature whose constitution is love and harmony. The one who was a wolf no longer threatens the lamb, nor does the lamb fear the one who was formerly of the class of wolves, for all have become one flock bearing the new creation that is in Christ Jesus.

"And the leopard shall lie down with the kid" [6]. The first is an animal that lies in wait for its prey to attack it treacherously, and the second plays carelessly and so provokes the leopard to pounce on it... But the nature of violence and predation has been removed from the leopard, so that it lies down with the kid.

entries.section: 4. The marks of the Messianic age:

paragraphs.text: "And the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them" [7]. A strange, mixed flock under strange leadership. Who can imagine a little boy leading a calf, accompanied by a young lion and a fatling! This little boy points to the spiritual leaders of the Church, who by a spirit of simplicity are able, by the Spirit of the Lord, to make of believers who come from different nations and peoples, and who bear varied gifts, a gentle flock that submits to the spirit of the Gospel as to a little child.
Truly gentle leaders, like the child, who know no love of domination, know how to turn lion cubs into flocks, and this by the work of the Spirit of the Lord.

"And the cow and the bear shall feed" [7]. St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the cow points to the Jews, because it is one of the animals under the yoke and is clean according to the Law, while the bear points to the Gentiles and the pagan peoples, since it is a beast of prey (violent) and unclean according to the Law. It is as though it is one of the marks of the Messianic age that members of Jewish origin come together with others of Gentile origin in one "flock," under the leadership of the one good Shepherd.

Although the bear is marked by predation, it is slow in movement, so that the milch cow counts as a precious and easy prey which it is able to devour without its escaping, unlike the young bull. Yet despite this temptation we find a strange reconciliation and friendship between them, as between their young, for it is said: "their young ones shall lie down together" [7]. This is what actually happened, for the generations that followed in the Church of the New Testament bore no distinction between those of Jewish and those of Gentile origin.
"And the lion shall eat straw like the ox" [7], for it lost its savage nature and its nature changed, so that it became like a tame animal that seeks not flesh but straw.

entries.section: 4. The marks of the Messianic age:

paragraphs.text: "And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp" [8]; the sucking child is no longer alarmed, because the poison of the asp has been made void.
"And the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den" [8]. The weaned child puts his hand into the mouth of the viper and is not harmed at all.

entries.section: 4. The marks of the Messianic age:

paragraphs.text: In brief, the work of the Lord Christ is to change fierce human nature through His servants, who are marked by a spirit of gentleness, so that the whole Church, servants and those served, bears a spirit of love and unity. Thus corruption does not strike the Church, the holy mountain of the Lord, "for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord" [9], not a purely philosophical, rationalistic knowledge, but the knowledge of encounter and union and the practical experience of the new life in the Lord. This spiritual knowledge fills the life of believers as a natural matter, realized by the Incarnation of the Word of the Lord, who came to make the truth known to us, and by the work of His Holy Spirit, so that knowledge came to fill the earth "as the waters cover the sea" [9]. The Lord of glory Himself says: "It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God" (Jn 6:45; Isa 54:13; Jer 31:34; Mic 4:2; Heb 8:10; 10:16).

St. Macarius the Great speaks to us of this practical spiritual knowledge, saying: [When (the soul) is united with the Comforter Spirit in an indescribable intimacy, and is wholly mingled with the Spirit, it is counted worthy to become itself spirit; by being mingled with Him it then becomes wholly light, wholly eye, wholly spirit, wholly joy, wholly rest, wholly gladness, wholly love, wholly compassion, wholly goodness and tender mercies.]

10 And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious. 11 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. 12 And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. 13 The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim. 14 But they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines toward the west; they shall spoil them of the east together: they shall lay their hand upon Edom and Moab; and the children of Ammon shall obey them. 15 And the Lord shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make men go over dryshod. 16 And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria; like as it was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt.

A. The Lord Christ came to establish His Kingdom from all the nations and peoples, giving peace to the true believers: "And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious" [10]. The Apostle Paul quoted this prophecy when he spoke of the Gentiles glorifying God for His mercy upon them (Rom 15:6, 12), showing that his phrase "in that day" was fulfilled by the coming of the Messiah, who gathered the Gentiles into His Kingdom. The Lord of glory Jesus became an "ensign" around which the children of God that were scattered abroad are gathered together in one (Jn 11:52), so that they became one flock under one Shepherd. The Lord became an ensign proclaiming divine love in its deepest form, by being lifted up on the Cross, spreading out His hands to gather the whole world into His embrace (Jn 12:32), preaching the joy of the Gospel of salvation, which restored to man his first dignity and his victory over the powers of darkness, opening to them the gates of Paradise.

He says, "to it shall the Gentiles seek"; He is the desire of the nations, the Greeks sought Him (Jn 12:20-21); and the centurion Cornelius the Gentile sent to Peter to hear about the Lord Christ (Acts 10).

"And his rest shall be glorious"; the Jesuit translation has "his dwelling place shall be glory"; perhaps he means that His Cross, which was a shame, became glory through His Resurrection, for His empty tomb became holy to the believers, in which they perceive the truth of their Christ, the Giver of life and resurrection.

B. The Lord Christ gathers into His Church the remnant that accepted salvation, which came from scattered places (Acts 2; Jas 1:1; 1 Pet 1:1); therefore the prophet says: "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros (Upper Egypt), and from Cush, and from Elam (a kingdom east of the Tigris and northeast of the Persian Gulf), and from Shinar (the plain of Babylon), and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea" [11]. This prophecy was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost, and also during the ministry of the Apostles and through the generations, and it will be fulfilled again more widely in the last days, when the Jews accept faith in the Lord Christ, as the Apostle Paul says (Rom 11:11-27). On that day those who accept the faith, coming from the Jews, join the Church that had already gathered the Gentiles, and all become members of one body: "And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth" [12].

Some interpreters try to reckon this a glory for the nation of Israel in a literal way, but here is a proclamation of the glory of the Church, which gathers from the Gentiles and the Jews together, collecting all from the ends of the world to its ends without distinction of race... for all become one Church bearing the ensign of their one Christ.

C. The union that took place between Israel (Ephraim) and Judah at their return from the captivity, after conflicts and even enmity between them had been entrenched for long centuries, presents a picture of the union between the Gentiles and the Jews [13].

In ancient times the Philistines, the people of the East, Edom, Ammon, Moab and Egypt were opposed to the people, so God gave His people the possibility of victory over them [14-16]. In the New Testament, however, the victory is not by military triumphs but by these nations accepting living faith, so that they become instruments of building and not of resistance and destruction. God, who earlier turned the sea for the salvation of His people, when He brought them across it after opening a way for them to pass through, likewise dries up all resistance in the hearts of the Gentiles, so that the way of the Messianic Kingdom is opened.

In other words, He who brought His people up from Egypt, taking them through the midst of the waters of the Red Sea, is the One who brings them across from Assyria after the captivity [16], and He is the One who brings the Gentiles across into His Kingdom despite all the obstacles and difficulties that stand before them.

entries.section: 1. God's mercies in the midst of His wrath:

paragraphs.text: "And in that day thou shalt say, O Lord, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me." [1].

The new song uttered by everyone who enjoys the saving work of the Lord Christ begins with the words: "And in that day thou shalt say." Which day is this? It is the day of the Cross, or the great Day of Atonement, on which we praise the Lord who turned wrath into salvation, comfort and glory. The divine wrath against the sin we commit took form in the crucifixion of the Lord Christ, the incarnate Word of God, to lift us from wrath to glory. The wonderful comforts of God appeared when He freed us, not from the Babylonian captivity, but from the captivity of the devil and his hosts and his evil works, that righteousness might reign in us.

Thus we offer praise and thanksgiving to God, not like the Pharisee who stood in the temple boasting over others, but like the thief on the right, driven outside the camp for his sins, who finds in his company the Lord Christ crucified for his sake, opening to him the gates of Paradise. So God's wrath against us turns into surpassing heavenly and divine comforts. On that day He Himself became our peace (Eph 2:14), and in Him God reconciled the world unto Himself (2 Cor 5:19).

entries.section: 2. Yahweh, the secret of our salvation, strength and joy:

paragraphs.text: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation." "Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation." [2-3].

The Coptic Church took a portion of this hymn to chant it to the crucified Lord on Covenant Thursday and Good Friday, namely: "My strength and my song (my hymn) is the Lord, and He is become my salvation. God is the secret of our strength, our praise and our salvation! In the midst of her sharing in her Bridegroom's sufferings the Church praises and sings; and her song or hymn is Christ Himself, who is everything to her.

Through the crucified Christ we have come to know the joyful sound (Ps 89:15); the shout of victory over the devil and his evil works! The shout of salvation by which we pass from the left to the right and enjoy the fellowship of the joyful heavenly Kingdom.

By the Cross a fountain of blood and water burst forth from the pierced side that we might be sanctified and cleansed, but also that we might drink and rejoice, for we have found the fountain of our eternal salvation.

Here he calls God "Yah Yahweh" (the Lord Jehovah); "Yah" is an abbreviation of the name "Yahweh," as though the hymn repeats this divine title "Yahweh" to affirm that He is the eternal God who does not change, on whom the believer leans, finding in Him his strength, his joy and his salvation forever, so that he is always at peace without fear. As St. Augustine says: [If you wish your joy to be steadfast and lasting, cling to the eternal God, to Him in whom no change occurs, but who continues steadfast in one state forever.]

entries.section: 3. Witness to the works of God:

paragraphs.text: 4 And in that day shall ye say, "Praise the Lord, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted. 5 Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth. 6 Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion: for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee."

Some see the preceding phrases [1-3] as representing a hymn independent of the phrases that follow [4-6], which represent a second hymn. In any case, if the first announces the springing up of praise and thanksgiving in the soul through the enjoyment of the Lord's salvation, the second completes it, announcing the obligation to bear witness to God the Savior before the nations. For what we experience through our union with God our Savior stirs in us a longing that others enjoy the same salvation. "And in that day shall ye say, Praise the Lord, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted. Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth. Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion: for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee" [4-6].
How do we preach the Lord?

A. By evangelism: "declare his doings among the people," as the Lord says to His disciples: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature" (Mk 16:5). Every believer is bound to bear witness to his Savior, for we see the psalmist David, declaring his repentance in the fiftieth Psalm, saying: "Grant me the joy of thy salvation, and I will teach sinners thy ways."

B. By holy joy: "Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth." There is no greater witness to the Savior than others' touching our inner joy in the Lord, which passes through all events and troubles. The psalmist says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the nations, The Lord hath done great things for us" (Ps 26:2).
The voice of inner rejoicing bears witness to the dwelling of the Holy One in us!

Holy joy proclaims the joyful Kingdom of God within us. It is told in the life of St. Apollo the priest in Thebes, on the borders of Hermopolis (Ashmunein), that his face was always cheerful, thereby drawing many to the ascetic life as a life joyful within and satisfying the heart with the Lord Himself. He often repeated the saying: [Why do we strive with sullen faces?! Are we not heirs of eternal life? Leave gloom and sullenness to the pagans and wailing to the sinners (the wicked); but for the righteous and the saints it is fitting that they rejoice and smile, because they enjoy spiritual things.]
"The oracle concerning Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see:" [1].
The prophet wished to affirm that he is the writer of the prophecy, and enjoyed it concerning Babylon. His affirmation that he is the one who saw it is for two reasons:
A. Although Isaiah prophesied concerning Judah and Jerusalem, he speaks here of the fate of the neighboring nations, affirming that the God of the saints is the very God of all nations.
B. Babylon was of no account at that time, so it was hard for the hearer or reader to believe what is said of it in these prophecies.

The word "oracle" came in Hebrew as massâh, and it was translated in the Targum, the Vulgate and the Syriac version with the meaning of "load" or "burden," perhaps because the prophet himself, by reason of his tenderness, felt a heavy and bitter burden over the troubles and divine disciplines that would come upon these nations. Even if these disciplines were deserved and would in the end turn to good, the prophet, as a man of God, does not stand gloating but grieving. In this spirit the early Church lived, disciplining, but in love and gentleness, not closing the door of repentance before sinners, even those who denied the faith. They counted men like Novatian heretics because of their harshness toward sinners. As St. Ambrose says in his reply to him: [By this they have passed sentence on the corruption of their teaching, for by denying the authority to loose they have denied their authority to bind also... What more shall I say of their increasing arrogance? For their will is contrary to the will of the Spirit of the Lord, who inclines to mercy and not to harshness... They do what He does not will. For He is the Judge and has the right to punish, yet we find Him by His mercy pardoning...! We must know that God is a God of mercy, inclined to pardon and not to harshness. Therefore it was said: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice" (Hos 6:6); how then will God accept your offerings, you who deny mercy, when it has been said of God that He does not will the death of the sinner so much as that he return (Ezek 18:32)?]
Some scholars think that what is said about Babylon in the two chapters (13, 14) is not the work of the prophet Isaiah, and their arguments for this are:
A. That Babylon was bound in friendship with Judah (Isa 39), so how could he proclaim a harsh prophecy against it?!
B. Babylon was subject to Assyria in weakness.
C. It appears from the discourse that Israel was in captivity to Babylon at the time the prophecy was proclaimed.

The answer to this is that the prophet was speaking of the future by the spirit of prophecy, pointing to the discipline of Israel by Assyria, then the position of Babylon afterwards when Assyria was shattered and Babylon became a great kingdom, and the captivity of the people and then their return, and finally the coming of the Savior Immanuel in the fullness of time. The prophet speaks of the future as a present he is living, and this is a natural thing the prophets were accustomed to, to affirm that what they proclaim will be fulfilled exactly. Nor do we ignore that the prophet who gave precise details about the person of the Lord Christ, His life, His saving work and the marks of His age, can prophesy the rise of the Babylonian state and the captivity of the people by it, which took place about 100 years after the proclamation of the prophecy. The prophet Jeremiah later, during the Babylonian era, echoed the very cries of Isaiah.

Finally, the prophet's speaking of the return from the captivity (Isa 11) and his threatening of the Babylonian captivity (Isa 39) indicates that the matter of the Babylonian captivity was not far from the mind of the prophet Isaiah.

entries.section: 2. A call to the nations to fight Babylon:

paragraphs.text: 2 Lift ye up a banner upon the bare mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the tyrants. 3 I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness. 4 The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle. 5 They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.

The greatness of Babylon had not yet appeared, but the prophet sees it coming, its capital a city of tyrants, and so he begins his prophecy about it with the Lord's inciting the nations to throng together against Babylon, to storm its gates and humble its pride, saying:

"Lift ye up a banner upon the bare mountain" [2]. Thus God issues a command to make war on Babylon, calling the nations to raise the banner of war on a mountain empty of every tree or plant so that the whole army can see it. It was the custom in ancient times for some soldiers to gather wood and kindle it by night on the mountain as a sign of the beginning of war; so their being on a mountain without trees helps the army quickly notice the beginning of the war.
"Exalt the voice unto them" [2], that is, sound the trumpets to rouse the armies.

"Shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the tyrants (the nobles)" [2], that is, they wave their hands to encourage resolve for storming the city of the free nobles with courage and boldness.

What is Babylon but the arrogant soul, which we must storm, not with banners of war, nor with the sound of trumpets, nor with the waving of human hands, but by raising the banner of love that belongs to our crucified Christ, so that it says: "His banner over me was love" (Song 2:4). Let us blow the trumpet of the Gospel, joyful to souls, and let us stretch out the hand of practical love to support the weak soul that pride has humbled... Thus we storm the soul by the Spirit of the Lord working in us, and draw it to the account of His heavenly Kingdom through spiritual warfare made effective by divine grace and not by human work.

entries.section: 2. A call to the nations to fight Babylon:

paragraphs.text: The discourse here is greater than a call to Persia and Media to storm the great empire of Babylon; it is a call that touches the eternal salvation of the soul. Therefore he goes on to say: "I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness. The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle. They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the land" [3-5].
In this text we note:

First: who are these sanctified ones and mighty ones belonging to God who are used in this battle? Some see them as the military leaders of Persia and Media, who were called to a holy battle, not because they were saints in their life or faith, but because God called them, without their knowing, to accomplish His holy purposes, and gave them power to work and used them to accomplish things that were not in their thoughts. They were counted God's mighty ones in spite of their unbelief in Him, just as Cyrus the pagan was called the anointed of the Lord, whose right hand God held, to tread down nations before him, and so on... (Isa 45:1).
Such is the wonderful goodness of God, who turns the energies and works even of the wicked to the account of the growth of His Kingdom and the building up of souls.

If God called the pagan stormers of Babylon His sanctified ones and His mighty ones, what then is the state of His children, the "spiritual soldiers," who are truly the saints of the Lord, since they are set apart for holy spiritual work, who fight against the devil and all his evil works for the sanctification of their own depths and the sanctification of others by winning them with divine love; He also calls them "His mighty ones" because they carry His strength and work by His Holy Spirit; and He also counts them "them that rejoice in my highness," since they accomplish the glory of the great name of God.
The holy Fathers see Baptism as an entrance into spiritual soldiery, where the candidate for baptism is sealed with the seal of the Spirit and is counted a spiritual soldier for the Lord's kingdom.

* Each one of you comes and presents himself before God in the presence of countless armies of angels, and the Holy Spirit sets a mark on your souls. By this you enroll yourselves in the army of the great King.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem * As the seal is stamped on soldiers, so the Holy Spirit is stamped on believers.
St. John Chrysostom * He who receives the bath of regeneration is like a young soldier who has been given a place among the combatants but has not yet proved his worthiness for soldiering.

St. Gregory of Nyssa Second: what is the voice of the multitude standing on the mountains like a great people, "a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle" (Isa 43:4), but the voice of the Church gathered together in a spirit of love and unity on the holy mountains, enjoying the life on high, dwelling on the summits of the blessed commandments and not at the foot, gathered from the kingdoms of many nations as an army with banners (Song 6:10)... They are many churches with differing cultures, but through one faith and one mind they live as a heavenly spiritual army... This is the mark of the true Church: a heavenly Church! Therefore the Apostle Paul says: "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Cor 3:18).
* How many have attacked the Church, and those who attacked it have perished, while she has soared into heaven.
* The Church is your hope, your salvation and your refuge. She is higher than heaven and wider than the world.

entries.section: 2. A call to the nations to fight Babylon:

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land" [5]. The Church is gathered from a far country, for most of her members were pagans bound to the world, strangers to the house of God, but they became the heaven of the Lord and His sanctuary, destroying temporal thoughts or the love of earthly things, to carry others to the experience of the heavenly life. It is as though the destruction of the earth means the shattering of the closing of the heart upon temporal things so that it opens to heaven. As St. Clement of Alexandria says, the earth becomes heaven for the believer (the gnostic).
This is from the symbolic side; but from the literal side, God called the nations of Persia and Media and others to use them to destroy the whole land of great Babylon.

6 Howl ye; for the day of the Lord is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty. 7 Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every man's heart shall melt: 8 And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames. 9 Behold, the day of the Lord cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it. 10 For the stars of heaven and the mighty ones thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine. 11 And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the tyrants. 12 I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir. 13 Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, in the wrath of the Lord of hosts, and in the day of his fierce anger. 14 And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land. 15 Every one that is found shall be thrust through; and every one that is joined unto them shall fall by the sword. 16 Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled, and their wives ravished. 17 Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it. 18 Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eyes shall not spare children. 19 And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. 20 It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there. 21 But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and owls shall fill their houses, and ostriches shall dwell there, and wild goats shall dance there. 22 And jackals shall cry in their palaces, and wolves in the temples of pleasure: and her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged.

The prophet portrays for us the dreadful day of Babylon's destruction at the hands of Persia and Media as the day of the Lord, on which He declares His wrath against Babylon, which resisted Him and His children.

This was fulfilled at the hands of Cyrus, who was not cruel, but his army was violent, savage and barbarous; therefore the soldiers destroyed Babylon not so much to plunder its treasures as from a desire to shed blood.

Some see that what is stated here was indeed fulfilled in the days of Cyrus but only in part, though it will be fulfilled more fully in the last days, as the Book of Revelation (Rev 17) speaks of the judgment of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, Babylon the great, the mother of harlots.

I say that this prophecy announces what is accomplished with respect to the kingdom of the devil, not only in the last days but in the heart of every person who accepts faith in the Lord Christ as King, who establishes a new Jerusalem in him in place of the harlot Babylon, that is, establishes His holy city in place of the kingdom of the devil.

A. The prophet says: "Howl ye; for the day of the Lord is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty. Therefore shall all hands be faint" [6], so that they have no strength to carry weapons. The kingdom of Babylon had become mistress of the whole world; God had been long-suffering toward it for tens of years, while the Babylonians went on in the pride of their hearts and their arrogance against the Lord Himself; therefore when they fall under His wrath their violent weapon-bearing hands grow faint, and they become very weak and an object of mockery.

This is the picture of the enemy of good as St. John Chrysostom disclosed it in his letter to his friend Theodore the fallen, explaining to him that the devil appears extremely violent and possessed of power and might, but when we carry our Christ he grows weak and collapses. And in an article on: "The power of man to resist Satan he says: [Satan is wicked, and I concede that, but he is wicked toward himself and not toward us so long as we are watchful, for such is the nature of evil, it is destructive only to those who cling to it alone"].

B. "And every man's heart shall melt: and they shall be afraid" [7-8]. Thus a state of trembling and fear seizes all, men and women, young and old and children; all become shattered, none supports his brother, but each one breaks himself as he breaks those around him!

The secret of their trembling is their being deprived of the fear of God. He who fears God fears neither man nor events but is filled with joy and peace; therefore it was said: "The head of wisdom is the fear of God." St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian says: [Let the fear of God be in your heart, beloved, like the weapon in the hand of the soldier.]

C. "They shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth" [8], for they carried within them the fruit of evil, which they bring forth in bitterness upon bitterness. And the wonder is that the Holy Bible likens the pains of the wicked to the pains of labor, and also the pains of the believers (Jn 16:20); the former groan in despair and in trembling because they bring forth wind (Isa 26:18), while the latter rejoice in the midst of outward sorrow because they bring a man into the world (Jn 16:20).
D. "Your faces shall be as flames" [8], red with shame because of their utter brokenness and their cowardice, as their faces sometimes grow pale [8], turning yellow with fear.

E. "To lay the land desolate, with none to walk upon it" [9], as a symbol of what befalls the body (the earth) in the loss of all true vitality. He who resists the Lord for the sake of the lusts of the body loses even his body and his inner soul is laid waste, for it was said: "Therefore I will shake the heavens (the soul), and the earth (the body) shall remove out of her place, in the wrath" [13]. Perhaps here he also points to nature's rebellion against the one who disobeys its Creator. It is as though nature itself disobeys the one who disobeys the Lord!

F. Darkness comes upon them: "For the stars of heaven and the mighty ones thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine" [10]. This points to the darkness of ignorance that comes upon the man who resists God, for he does not see the light of the heavenly bodies, all of them, including the sun and the moon. He does not see the Sun of righteousness, that is, faith in Christ, who is able to give him wisdom and knowledge; nor does he see the light of the moon, that is, the Church life enlightened by the Lord, as the moon bearing the reflections of the light of the sun; nor does he enjoy the light of the other stars, or fellowship with the saints who shine as luminous stars.

G. The men die in the war, and since the women of Babylon were accustomed to a licentious life, they seek a man to fulfill their evil lusts, and it is hard for them to find one: "I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir (perhaps a region in the southeast of Arabia or a place on the west coast of India)" [12]. This also points to the scarcity of laborers because of the war, with the return of the captives and the liberation of the nations from the Babylonian authority.

H. The loss of leadership and shepherding: "And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land" [14]. He means that on the day of Babylon's defeat the army loses its leadership, and the hired soldiers, or those conscripted from the nations, flee each to his own country.

This is the state of the soul far from God, for it loses its inner leadership, so that man lives as one chased, or as sheep with no shepherd to gather them... He carries within him bitter conflicts and a scattering of thought, with a shattering of inner energies.

I. Slaughter of all without distinction between soldier or civilian, man, woman or child [15]. Here he depicts what the Medes do against Babylon, for the Medes do not destroy it to acquire wealth [17] but to destroy all of Babylon's energies, so they pay no regard to a small youth or to a child in his mother's womb [18]; they ruin all its resources, so that it becomes like Sodom and Gomorrah, which were burned with fire from heaven.

J. Babylon becomes an everlasting wilderness; no Arab shepherding his flock dwells in it, nor do shepherds lie down in it for fear of the beasts of prey that inhabit it (Isa 30:20-21). It becomes a ruin in which owls dwell in what remains of the houses, and there are in it ostriches, wild goats, jackals and wolves.

Father Serenus says: [We must not take all these names haphazardly, but they point to the ferocity (of the demons) and their madness under the symbol of predatory beasts, as being harmful and dangerous... and more evil than they.]
It is a picture of the soul that surrenders to the enemy of good, so that he uses it for the account of the kingdom of darkness, fills it with evil and turns it into a factory of corruption:
"But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there" [21]... Violence dwells in it, and ferocity, and the love of shedding innocent blood without cause.

"And owls shall fill their houses" [21], where most Easterners take their voices as an ill omen... It is as though nothing is heard within the wicked man but the voices of despair and pessimism, which reveal an inner emptiness.

"And ostriches shall dwell there" [21], that is, it is full of uncleanness (Lev 11:16; Deut 14:15), its voice like wailing (Mic 1:8); heavenly joy does not enter it, its nature is dry, it does not love its eggs (Lam 4:3); it buries its head in the sand when it sees a hunter approaching it, and it used to be thought that it does this because it supposes that thereby the hunter does not see it, but it has recently been shown that it does this because it is too cowardly to see itself fall victim to the hunters.
"And wild goats shall dance there" [21]. Perhaps it means the ibex, found only in desolate places. So the demons dance and sport in the wicked soul, since they find a place for themselves in it.

"And jackals (an animal larger than a fox and smaller than a wolf) shall cry in their palaces, and wolves in the temples of pleasure" [22]... that is, the palaces and temples are turned from places of pleasure into a refuge for fierce beasts.

All this came upon Babylon, "the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency" [19], the golden city (Isa 14:4), rich in its treasures (Jer 51:13), the glory of all the earth (Jer 51:41), likened to the head of gold in the statue mentioned in the Book of Daniel. The prophecies were fulfilled in it literally as they were stated, for history records that Cyrus tore down a large part of the walls and buildings of Babylon, and after 20 years Darius pulled down the rest of the walls and removed its bronze gates and crucified three thousand of its notables. It is said that the length of the wall of Babylon was 60 miles, 15 miles on each side, its height 300 feet and its thickness 80 feet, so that six chariots could drive side by side on the wall. Its depth in the ground was 35 feet so that the enemy could not dig a way for himself beneath it, and 250 towers for watching and guarding stood upon the wall, and it had 100 huge, shining bronze gates.

Babylon was indeed turned to ruin, and Alexander the Great tried to restore its glory but died before carrying out his projects. Its stones were used in building Baghdad, repairing canals and erecting many public facilities.

Finally, the prophet affirmed that what he says is quickly fulfilled: "And her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged" [22]. The star of Babylon began to shine in 606 B.C., and it fell into the hands of Persia and Media in 536 B.C., while the prophecy came in the eighth century B.C.
Babylon has remained a symbol of every proud, rebellious soul, as the Book of Revelation has it, where it was said: "For in one hour is thy judgment come" (Rev 18:10).

1 For the LORD will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land: and the strangers shall be joined with them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob. 2 And the people shall take them, and bring them to their place: and the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of the LORD for servants and handmaids: and they shall take them captives, whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors. 3 And it shall come to pass in the day that the LORD shall give thee rest from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve. The God who permitted His people to be humiliated during the Babylonian captivity is Himself the merciful God who chose them as His own people [1]. He had already brought them out of Egypt, freed them from Pharaoh, and brought them to the Promised Land with a high arm; and now He accomplishes another exodus, freeing them from captivity and returning them to their land, not empty-handed and not in weakness but in strength, drawing strangers to them to become sojourners who share their faith and worship. He also gives His people strength, so that they take captive those who had taken them captive, and rule over those who had oppressed them; thus the people find rest from toil and bondage [4].

St. John Cassian sees that what happened long ago to this people is a type of what happens to the believer who receives “the word of the Lord,” which is able to go before him and free him from the tyranny of “evil lusts” and their domination over his body, lusts that hold him captive as in the bars of vice and cut him off from hidden knowledge.

We need God's constant work with us, to bring us out, not from the bondage of Pharaoh nor from the captivity of the Babylonians, but to set us free through the Cross, by His Holy Spirit, from the captivity of sin, leading us from darkness to light, that we may live in the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

This wonderful picture of God's love for His believers is proclaimed with power in the rite of Baptism, where a person takes off the garments of bondage and captivity and confesses that he renounces Satan and all his hosts and rejects his inward slavery, receiving the holy oil so as to bear the splendor of the Spirit within him... He goes down into Baptism to enjoy membership in the body of Christ, and so becomes able to live the new life that overcomes death and darkness, to praise God, saying: “In thy light, O Lord, shall we see light” (Ps 36:9).

* God anoints your faces and seals them with the sign of the Cross. In this way God restrains all the madness of the evil one, so that the devil does not dare to look upon such a sight, for blindness strikes his eyes as he gazes at your faces, and he is like one who looks at the rays of the sun and leaps away in flight...
Know once more that it is God Himself who anoints you through the hand of the priest, and not a man. Listen to the words of Paul, who says: “It is God who establishes you in Christ, who anointed us.”
After he anoints all your members with this oil, you become safe, able to silence the serpent, and no harm will come to you.

* In the fullness of the darkness of night the priest takes off your garment, as one leading you into heaven itself through the rite, and anoints your whole body with the olive oil of the Spirit, so that your members may be strong, not overcome by the arrows that the enemy directs against you.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: 4 That thou shalt take up this proverb against the king of Babylon, and say, “How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased! 5 The LORD hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers. 6 He who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke, he that ruled the nations in anger, is persecuted, and none hindereth. 7 The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet: they break forth into singing. 8 Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us. 9 Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. 10 All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us? 11 Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee. 12 How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! 13 For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: 14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High. 15 Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit. 16 They that see thee shall narrowly look upon thee, and consider thee, saying, Is this the man that made the earth to tremble, that did shake kingdoms; 17 That made the world as a wilderness, and destroyed the cities thereof; that opened not the house of his prisoners? 18 All the kings of the nations, even all of them, lie in glory, every one in his own house. 19 But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet. 20 Thou shalt not be joined with them in burial, because thou hast destroyed thy land, and slain thy people: the seed of evildoers shall never be renowned. 21 Prepare slaughter for his children for the iniquity of their fathers; that they do not rise, nor possess the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities.”
The prophet speaks in the name of the people freed from the dominion of Babylon, and taunts its king, describing him thus:

a. “The oppressor” [4]. If Babylon was called the city of gold because of its excessive wealth, this wealth was achieved through the injustice and arrogance of its king; this injustice will not last, and this arrogance must be broken: “How hath the oppressor ceased! the golden city ceased! The LORD hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers” [4-5].

In every age there is someone who oppresses with arrogance, resisting the truth and persecuting the devout of the Lord; but injustice comes to an end and the humiliated are raised up. This is what happened in the days of St. John Chrysostom, when Eutropius opposed the Church and abolished her right to protect those who took refuge in her. Because of his misconduct and abuse of power the army rose against him and demanded his execution, so he fled to the cathedral that was near the palace, went to the altar and clung to the pillar. The people thought that Chrysostom would take vengeance on him for himself and for the Church, but the saint refused, declaring his mercy and love even toward enemies... The matter ended with his fleeing from the church and being killed by the sword at Chalcedon. In his second homily on Eutropius Ἄτροπος there is that which reveals the weakness of all injustice before the children of God.

[Let him who will, drive me out; let him who will, stone me and hate me; for the plots of enemies against me are the supports for obtaining the crown of victory, and the abundance of my rewards depends on the number of my wounds.

Therefore I do not fear the conspiracies of enemies; I fear one thing only, and that is sin. If no one can force me to sin, then let the whole world rise up in war against me, for such a war makes me all the more glorified.
I want to teach you a lesson, which is that you should not fear the deceptions of those in power, but fear the power of sin. No one will harm you unless you harm yourself.

If you do not sin, tens of thousands of swords threaten you, but God snatches you from them so that they do not come near you. But if you commit evil, then even if you are inside Paradise you will be driven out of it].

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: b. “He who smote the people in wrath with a continual stroke, he that ruled the nations in anger” [6]. He did not stop striking, therefore the Lord broke his rod; and he did not hold back from persecuting the peoples, stifling the breath of men and restricting their freedom, so he deserved to fall into humiliation. As it was said: “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head” (Obad 15).

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: Because of these traits, when Babylon fell the earth was at rest and broke forth into singing [7], and it was said to Jacob: “And it shall come to pass in the day that the LORD shall give thee rest from thy sorrow, and from thy fear, and from the hard bondage wherein thou wast made to serve” [3]. This rest was fulfilled in part by the return of the people from captivity, but “there remaineth a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9), which is entrance into the new life in Christ Jesus, as He is “our true Sabbath” and “our eternal rest.”

Those of the millennial way of thinking try to interpret this rest as an enjoyment of the thousand-year reign, where they seek a temporal rest on earth under the rule of Christ in a material way; but he who has tasted the rest of Christ and the consolations of the Holy Spirit truly realizes how he has received a surpassing rest in this world, which is the pledge of the heavenly rest.

* All men saw that God had betrothed our nature, and Satan saw it and retreated. He saw the pledge and was terrified and withdrew; he saw the garments of the Apostles and fled (Acts 19:11). O the power of the Holy Spirit...!
Consider what the Spirit did. He found the earth full of demons and made it heaven.
St. John Chrysostom. The Fathers realized that the enjoyment of Baptism is an entrance into rest and a taste of the life of Paradise:
* Behold, you are now in the courtyard of the palace; you will soon be led to the King.
* Soon Paradise will be opened to each one of you.

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem. At the fall of Babylon the fir tree (the king) rejoiced, and also the cedars of Lebanon (the leaders), saying: “Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us” [8], meaning that since you lay down in the grave there is no longer a hand to harm us; for enemies were accustomed to cut down trees in wars to oppose the countries they seized, and to use them as fuel or for building, as Nebuchadnezzar did... In any case, wars waste natural resources.

The Lord Christ lay down on the Cross in the body, but the one whose strength was shattered and whose abilities were crucified was the devil... So through the Cross we have become free from the bondage of the enemy, able to tread his power under our feet. St. John Chrysostom says: [Do not fear Satan, even though he is a spirit without a body, for nothing is weaker than he].

The mockery of the king of Babylon did not stop with the kings; rather the prophet portrays him going down into Sheol, where the kings and great men of the earth receive him (perhaps those whom he had persecuted), rising from their thrones in Sheol, not to honor him but to mock and ridicule him, so that he may sit upon their thrones as he did while on earth. They say to him with contempt:

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: “Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?” [10]; we thought you an immortal god, as you claimed, and we never imagined that you would die in humiliation like us!

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: “Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee” [11]. You used to lie on silk and perfume yourself with the costliest perfumes; how then have you gone down to Sheol as your bedchamber, to lie on decay and be covered with worms?

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High” [14].

You have imitated the devil your master, who was a great and distinguished star among the heavenly beings, “Lucifer, son of the morning”; he exalted himself against God his Creator, and thought that he could rise to the level of God Himself and even become greater than He, so he fell and became darkness instead of light, since he cut himself off from God, the source of light. You wanted to sit upon the mount of Zion (Ps 48:2), the holy mountain of God; you counted yourself like God in greatness and exalted yourself above the clouds!

This is the secret of the destruction of the king of Babylon: his fall into pride and his exalting himself not only against the kings around him but even against God Himself, so that he became an instrument of Satan, bearing his mark, “pride.” This was the sin of our first parents when they were in Paradise; it was also the sin of the king of Tyre, who became a symbol of Satan (Ezek 28:12-16); and it is also the mark of the Antichrist, the man of sin, of whom it is said: “Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God” (2 Thess 2:3-4).
St. John Cassian says:

[Pride of heart alone was enough to cast down from heaven to earth a being of such great power, adorned with such mighty qualities; the fall of (the devil), who was so great, obliges us to realize what caution we must observe, we who are surrounded on every side by the weakness of the flesh...

He was puffed up and thought that he had no need of divine help to continue in the purity that he had, and he thought within himself that he was like God. Thus he considered that he needed no one, relying on the power of his own will, by which he could supply himself with all that is necessary for achieving virtue and for the continuance of perfect blessedness. This thought alone was the cause of his first fall].

“Thus God the Creator, the Physician of all, knowing that pride is the cause and head of all evils, takes care to heal opposite by opposite, so that what was lost through pride is restored through humility”... One says: “I will be like the most High” [14], but the Other: “Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant... he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil 2:6-8). One says: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God,” while the Other says: “Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart” (Mt 11:28). One says: “My rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek 29:3) LXX, and the Other: “I do nothing of myself, but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works” (Jn 5:30; 14:10)].

St. Ephrem the Syrian says: [In the humble man the spirit of wisdom rests], [when you appear in the eyes of your brethren like pure gold, count yourself as a vessel that is not needed, and you will escape the pride that is hated by God and men], [The proud man is like a tall and splendid tree with no fruit in it... and the envious man is like a fruit beautiful on the outside and spoiled within].

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: Thus pride brings man down to Sheol, so the prophet says to the king of Babylon: “Thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit” [15]. You have fallen from the summit of the mountain of your dreams, and come down from the cloud of your imagination, to live in Sheol with the devil your master.

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: Where is your might, you who made the earth to tremble and shook kingdoms [16] by your violence? You turned the world into a wilderness and destroyed the cities in order to take their inhabitants captive [17]!

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: Where are your glory and your honor? For all the kings of the earth lie in glory, even those whom you humiliated and tortured, for they died in their houses, prayers were offered for them, and some of their bodies were embalmed, “But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch” (there are some plants that are very poisonous and some that harm the skin, so that when a branch of them falls in the wilderness no one dares to approach it), “and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit” (that is, worthless; no one thinks of you, just as no one thinks of the garments of the slain of war during the battle), “as a carcase trodden under feet” (which a man treads beneath his feet)” [19].
This prophecy points to the slaughter of Belshazzar on the night the Medes entered Babylon, when no one concerned himself with the king's body amid the ruin that befell the city.

entries.section: 2. Taunt against the king of Babylon:

paragraphs.text: Thus the king of Babylon lost everything; even his people and his sons were killed [20-21] because of the pride of his heart; he lost the royal city and the royal offspring.

22 “For I will rise up against them, saith the LORD of hosts, and cut off from Babylon the name, and remnant, and son, and nephew, saith the LORD. 23 I will also make it a possession for the hedgehog, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts.”

Because of pride God takes away from Babylon its name, and leaves in it neither remnant nor offspring (Jer 51:62), that it may be an example before the whole world. It becomes a ruin (Isa 13), inhabited by the hedgehog and pools of water [23].

Some scholars see that the hedgehog here (“qippod” in Hebrew) does not mean the animal known as the hedgehog with its long spines, but a bird of the kind that take shelter in deserted places; their argument is that the hedgehog does not take shelter in pools of water. But those who hold that the translation of “qippod” means the hedgehog animal say that the ruin comes upon the land so that one part of it becomes pools of water and the other a shelter for the hedgehog. In any case, the great royal city is turned into a dwelling either for animals or for birds that live in the wilderness, and it is counted unclean, full of abominations, in need of sweeping with the besom of destruction, that is, complete extermination, to be rid of its abominations, lest it corrupt those around it.

24 The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, “Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand: 25 That I will break the Assyrian in my land, and upon my mountains tread him under foot: then shall his yoke depart from off them, and his burden depart from off their shoulders. 26 This is the purpose that is purposed upon the whole earth: and this is the hand that is stretched out upon all the nations. 27 For the LORD of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it? and his hand is stretched out, and who shall turn it back?”

The prophet mentions what will befall Assyria and Philistia so that the hearers may be assured of the truth of the prophecy concerning Babylon, which will be fulfilled about 200 years after its announcement.

Assyria transgressed the land of Judah without justification and blasphemed against God; therefore God permits it to enter the land of Judah and its mountains, as the land of God and His mountains, and there He shatters it, in the holy places that it violated [24-25], so that Assyria becomes an example before all the nations that think of attacking [26].

God reveals His plan in disciplining the wicked, which is that He leaves them to carry out their evil will in complete freedom, so that they reap the fruit of their evil as corruption and destruction, as though sin carries its punishment within itself, just as the holy life in the Lord carries its glory within it. Therefore it was said: “The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand” [24].

28 In the year that king Ahaz died was this burden. 29 Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent. 30 And the firstborn of the poor shall feed, and the needy shall lie down in safety: and I will kill thy root with famine, and he shall slay thy remnant. 31 Howl, O gate; cry, O city; thou, whole Palestina, art dissolved: for there shall come from the north a smoke, and none shall be alone in his appointed times. 32 What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation? That the LORD hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it.

“In the year that king Ahaz died was this burden. Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent” [28-20].

Philistia at that time was made up of several principalities, therefore he addresses it saying: “whole Palestina.” He asks it not to rejoice because the rod that smote it has been broken. Some see that this rod is Tiglath-pileser, who took possession of Philistine cities and who died a year or two before Ahaz; he would be succeeded by Shalmaneser, Sargon and Sennacherib, who were worse than he.

The majority of scholars see that the broken rod is Uzziah, who smote the Philistines harshly, so they rejoiced at his death (2 Chr 26:6); and that the root of the serpent is the house of David, from which comes King Hezekiah, who struck them a blow harsher than that of Uzziah his forefather (2 Kgs 18:8), and enslaved them.

As for the flying serpent, it is like the bronze serpent that Moses lifted up in the wilderness, a type of the person of the crucified Lord Christ, who bore the poison of our sins in His body in order to destroy it by His life-giving death. Thus the prophet moves from the deliverance of the people of God from human enemies to their eternal deliverance from the devil, the enemy of good, and that through the Cross.

The prophet declares that Philistia faces a harsh famine [30] and a devastating war, so that their cities turn into smoke, while in the end the Lord protects His people and has compassion on its poor [32].

God, in His goodness, does not prevent evil and does not compel the wicked to repent, but in the end He fulfills the plan of His salvation for His believers who trust in Him, turning all things to their edification.

entries.section: 1. The swiftness of the prophecy's fulfillment:

paragraphs.text: “The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste and destroyed; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste and destroyed” [1].

The Moabites came from the offspring of Lot, so they are related to Israel. They dwelt east of the Dead Sea, and their land was divided into the land of Moab and the plains of Moab, which were in the Jordan valley opposite Jericho. The sons of Reuben allowed the Moabites to dwell in their cities, and learned from them the worship of the god Chemosh. There were also at times good relations between Moab and Israel: Naomi sojourned there and returned with Ruth, and when Saul opposed David, David deposited his parents with the king of Moab. Yet the Moabites bore a spirit of enmity toward Israel and Judah, and often allied themselves with the neighboring peoples against them.

The prophet Isaiah prophesies the destruction of the great cities of Moab, and this prophecy was fulfilled literally and exactly within three years of its announcement (Isa 16:14); the destruction came at the hands of the king of Assyria, suddenly and in an unexpected way.

“Ar”: a Semitic name meaning “city”; this city lay about 14 miles south of the river Arnon (Num 21:15; 22:36), and was also called Aroer (Deut 2:36). The Greeks called it Areopolis after the god of war “Ares,” and the Jews called it “Rabbath Moab”; it is Khirbet al-Rabba.
“Kir”: a Semitic name meaning “wall” or “walled city,” about eleven miles east of the southern part of the Dead Sea; its site today is the city of Karak in Jordan.

The two cities Ar and Kir were destroyed in one night, not in one day or one daytime. For when the Sun of righteousness is absent from the human soul, which is like a great walled city, the darkness of evil and ignorance comes upon it, and it loses all that it labored for through long years, and ruin befalls it. Therefore St. Paul says: “Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober. For they that sleep sleep in the night; and they that be drunken are drunken in the night” (1 Thess 5:5-6).

* Who is like that manifest one who watches and prays in secret, surrounded by a halo of hidden light amid the outer darkness? But the wicked man walks as a son of darkness; he stands in the brightness of day, and although the light clothes him from without, darkness enfolds him from within.
Beloved, let us not be deceived into thinking that we are watchful, for he who does not watch in righteousness, his watching is not counted to him!

St. Ephrem the Syrian * When man leaves (the love of) the dark world he becomes clean and pure by the work of the Spirit and by his clinging to true purity... so the soul shines forth with light and itself becomes light, according to the promise of the Lord (Mt 13:43).
