St. Gregory of Nyssa

entries.section: 2. The shattering of the great cities:

paragraphs.text: 2 He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off. 3 In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly. 4 And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; her soul shall tremble within her. 5 My heart shall cry out for Moab; her fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, like an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction.
The prophet Isaiah portrays what befell the great cities of Moab besides Ar and Kir, saying:

“They go up to the house (Bajith) and Dibon, to the high places, to weep” [2]. When ruin came upon Moab, many took refuge in the pagan gods, crying out with tears and wailing, hoping that they might be able to rescue them, but in vain, as the prophets and priests of Baal did in the days of the prophet Elijah.

They took refuge in “the house”; some see that Bajith means “a temple,” or “house” (bayit), that is, “the house of the god Chemosh or the temple of the god,” or bat, meaning “daughter,” that is, “the daughter of the city” or its inhabitants.

“Dibon”: a Moabite name meaning “high places” or “leanness” or “dissolution.” It is a city three miles north of the river Arnon, northwest of Aroer, called in Arabic “Dhiban”; there stood the high place of the Moabite god Chemosh.

Some translate “Bajith and Dibon” as “the house of Dibon” or “the daughter of Dibon,” as though the Moabites had fled to the temple of the god Chemosh, or his house, in Dibon, weeping and lamenting over the ruin that had come upon them.
“Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba” [2].

“Nebo” was laid waste, near the great mountain Nebo, east of the Jordan at the southern end of the Dead Sea; it is the mountain on which Moses the prophet went up to look from afar at the Promised Land, and his soul rejoiced, longing to cross over to the land of the living and enjoy the heavenly Canaan, and he died there (Deut 34). Nebo was fortified by the great mountain, a center of defense for the Moabites, but it was lost and laid waste and became a cause of wailing. In the very place where Moses rejoiced, the Moabites wailed; what rejoices the heart of the believer breaks the soul of the unbelieving denier!

They also wailed over “Medeba,” whose meaning is “waters of rest,” now called “Madaba,” about 5 miles southeast of Nebo and 14 miles east of the Sea of Lot. It was so named because it has a pool in the south, 360 feet long and wide, and there are smaller pools in the east and the north.

The prophet says: “On all their heads shall be baldness, and every beard cut off. In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly” [2-3]. All these are signs of extreme grief (Jer 48:37; 2 Sam 3:31; Jer 4:8; 41:5; Lam 2:10). Baldness of the head points to humiliation, for conquerors used to shave the hair of captive men and women as a sign of slavery and ugliness; the cutting off of the beard is a sign of the disgrace of the priesthood and the loss of its spiritual authority and dignity; girding with sackcloth is a sign of utter despair; and weeping until the tears become like a flood means the loss of inward joy.

This is the picture of the soul that withdraws from its God to be taken captive by the evil enemy: it loses its freedom, its beauty, its authority, its dignity and its joy, and becomes like an ugly, humiliated, broken nation, finding no rest in the streets, nor on the housetops (where the pagans place their gods), nor in the squares; wherever it is, it does not feel at rest.

entries.section: 2. The shattering of the great cities:

paragraphs.text: “And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard even unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; her soul shall tremble within her” [4]. It is as though the Moabites fled from city to city, and their cry was heard from afar, from distant cities; the cry of the inhabitants of Heshbon and Elealeh resounds in Jahaz.

“Heshbon”: a Moabite name meaning “reckoning” or “plan.” It is the city of Sihon king of the Amorites; the Moabites took it from the tribe of Levi (Josh 21:29; 1 Chr 6:81). It is now known as “Hesban,” a ruined city on an isolated hill between the Arnon and the Jabbok, lying about seven and a half miles north of Madaba.
“Elealeh”: a Hebrew word which perhaps means “God has gone up,” about two miles north of Heshbon, now called “al-Al,” situated on a hill.
The two cities are considered to be at the far north, and were a place of dispute between Israel and Moab.
As for “Jahaz,” it is a Hebrew word meaning “a trodden place,” called “Yahsah”; it is said to be the village of Umm al-Mawalid or Khirbet Iskandar, about 10 or 12 miles south of Heshbon.

The prophet Isaiah could not bear to see what befell these great cities, and how their people turned to ceaseless crying, until Moab trembled within: “her soul shall tremble within her” [4]; therefore he says, “My heart shall cry out for Moab” [5]. He does not stand gloating over his enemies, but shares their bitterness, longing for their return from their enmity and their enjoyment of salvation. This is the mark of the men of God: sincere inward love and a deep desire for the salvation even of those who oppose them!

* If he were not wicked he would not have become your enemy. So wish him good, and his wickedness will end, and he will no longer be your enemy. He is your enemy not because of his human nature but because of his sin!

St. Augustine * Prayer for friends does not profit us as much as it profits us for enemies... For if we pray for friends we are no better than the tax collectors, but if we love our enemies and pray for them we have become like God in His love for mankind.

entries.section: 2. The shattering of the great cities:

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom. The prophet says: “My heart shall cry out for Moab; her fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, like an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction” [5].

The word “fugitives” came in Hebrew in the singular form; as though the prophet Isaiah pictures for us the fugitives from the far north to Zoar in the south, the little city to which Lot fled at the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, like a single heifer three years old that has fled, as it were, from the heavy yoke to which it was not accustomed. They became like one person, with none to support or comfort him, fleeing to the small places (Zoar) and finding no refuge.
As for Luhith and Horonaim, their location is not known, but most likely they were near Zoar.

6 For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing. 7 Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away over the brook of the willows. 8 For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beerelim. 9 For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, a lion upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.

The matter does not stop at the ruin of cities, the shameful defeat, the flight and the crying, but a famine comes upon Moab as the natural fruit of defeat in war and the destruction of natural and human resources, or perhaps as one of the signs of nature itself rising up against them. The prophet says: “For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing. Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away over the brook of the willows” [6-7].

“Nimrim”: a Semitic name meaning “clear waters”; they are springs in the valley of Nimra on the southeastern shore of the Dead Sea. The meaning here is that the throngs of refugees are so great that the oasis cannot suffice for them and their animals, so they leave their animals and take what wealth and treasures they can carry to complete the journey, hoping that they may not be in want, but they are unable to carry all that they need. Some scholars see that besides the famine that befalls their land, the enemies take possession of their wealth and treasures and carry them to their own land, leaving Moab in ruins.

All Moab is turned into a place of crying and wailing; the cry resounds in all its borders, and is heard in the south in the valley of Nimra as far as Eglaim near Kir, and Beerelim in the north. The waters of Dimon turn to blood [9] because of the great bloodshed on that notable night [Dimon or Dibon, whose meaning is blood, most likely means the waters of the river Arnon], so that no one finds anything to quench his thirst.
The remnant who escape are as though in a state of terror, facing a ravening lion that cannot be resisted [9]!
In short, Moab loses its great cities, its fields, its waters and its peace, to become a complete ruin.

1 Send ye the lambs of the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion. 2 For it shall be, that, as a wandering bird, as scattered fledglings, the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon. 3 Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth. 4 Let the outcasts of Moab dwell with thee; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land. 5 And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness.

We have already seen the heart of the prophet Isaiah moved with deep tenderness toward Moab, so that he cried out for them. Now he offers the Moabites good counsel to set their condition right and to enjoy good relations with the sons of Judah and to taste peace and protection, by offering tribute (lambs) to King Hezekiah; as a symbol of the calling of the nations to submit to the Lord Christ, the Lion who comes out of the tribe of Judah, for there is no peace and no eternal life without receiving Him as King in our inner life.

At the end of the previous chapter it was said: “a lion upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land” (Isa 15:9), and some see that the lion may be Hezekiah, or the Lord Christ, the Lion who comes out of the tribe of Judah to reign spiritually over the nations.

The prophet himself steps forward to declare his readiness to be a mediator or intercessor with Judah on behalf of Moab, calling on the Moabites to pay tribute: “Send ye the lambs of the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion. For it shall be, that, as a wandering bird, as scattered fledglings, the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon” [1-2].

“Sela” Sala is a Hebrew name סֶלַע meaning “rock”; the Greeks called it Petra πέτρα, which has the same meaning, for it is a fortified site in the land of Edom; the Edomites used to flee to it during military sieges as an invincible natural fortress, because it stands on the summit of a mountain (Obad 2). It is now called Umm al-Bayyara.

It is as though the prophet is calling the Moabites who had taken refuge in Edom and fortified themselves in Sela to come forward with the rest of the Moabites who are in the wilderness to Judah, and to offer the lambs in Jerusalem, “the mount of the daughter of Zion.”

It is a call to every person not to think of the human arm or natural resources as a refuge. His peace lies rather in reaching Jerusalem, and offering his life as a sacrifice of love to the Son of David, the Lion who came out of the tribe of Judah. The Lion came as a Lamb to be crucified outside Jerusalem, so that we may come forward as lambs, living sacrifices, sharing His sufferings, and so enter His heavenly Jerusalem.
* “I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1)...

Perhaps it will be asked: How does the body become a sacrifice? Let the eye not look upon evil, and it becomes a sacrifice! Let your tongue not utter defilement, and it becomes a sacrifice! Let your hand not practice a forbidden deed, and it becomes a whole burnt offering...! In this way we need no knife or altar or fire; or rather we need all these, but they are not made with hands; they come to us from above. We need a fire from on high, and a knife like this; our altar is the expanse of heaven.
If, when Elijah offered a visible sacrifice, fire came down from above and consumed all the water and the wood and the stones, how much more will this happen in your case?!
St. John Chrysostom * Bring your offerings... the offerings of your own soul!

St. Jerome. Outside the Lord Christ the prophet sees the daughters of Moab crossing the river Arnon like a wandering bird that has no nest in which to settle, or like scattered fledglings that lack the shade of wings and warmth and protection [2]; but by receiving Him we come under the wings of His Cross, and find our rest and peace and inward satisfaction.

The prophet also offers counsel to the elders of Judah, calling on them to receive the Moabite refugees who take refuge with them and give them shade in the midst of the noonday, so that the time becomes for them like a night of rest from the sun of trials and afflictions; and to hide the outcasts and the fugitives who flee to them without deceit, and not to deliver slaves to the enemies [3-4].

It is fitting for the men of Judah to bear a symbol of the Lord Christ, the true refuge, and open their hearts and their cities to the fugitives, and receive them sincerely; thus they proclaim the kingdom of Christ, established upon the throne of mercy forever: “And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness” [5].

Thus the prophet offers us a Messianic text, declaring that the Church, the tabernacle of David, is the place of deliverance, in which the Messiah reigns to draw the nations to Himself, so that they may find truth in Him and enjoy the divine mercies, singing: “Justice and truth are the foundation of thy throne; mercy and truth go before thy face... for the LORD is our shield, and the Holy One of Israel is our king” (Ps 89:14, 18).
6 We have heard of the pride of Moab, who is very proud: his greatness, his pride, his arrogance, the vanity of his boasting.

The prophet Isaiah offered good counsel to Moab, as the prophet Daniel also offered his counsel to Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 4:27)... and at the same time he disclosed their spiritual weakness, that is, pride, as an obstacle to their accepting counsel. “We have heard of the pride of Moab, who is very proud: his greatness, his pride, his arrogance, the vanity of his boasting” [6]. The prophet had heard of the pride of the Moabites, their excessive haughtiness and their empty (vain) words!
Pride destroys man as it does nations; it deprives its owner of accepting good counsel, and makes him lose the enjoyment of God's grace and mercy.

7 Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl: for the foundations of Kirhareseth shall ye mourn; surely they are stricken. 8 For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah: the lords of the heathen have broken down the principal plants thereof, they are come even unto Jazer, they wandered through the wilderness: her branches are stretched out, they are gone over the sea. 9 Therefore I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah: I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for the shouting for thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen. 10 And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease. 11 Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kirharesh. 12 And it shall come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary on the high place, that he shall come to his sanctuary to pray; but he shall not prevail. 13 This is the word that the LORD hath spoken concerning Moab since that time. 14 But now the LORD hath spoken, saying, “Within three years, as the years of an hireling, the glory of Moab shall be contemned, with all that great multitude; and the remnant shall be few and small, not great.”

The leaders of Moab did not listen to the voice of the prophet Isaiah because of their pride and their conceit in their own opinion, so they fell under bitter punishments and deserved the woes in which the following is to be noticed:
a. A universal wailing: “Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl” [7]; for wailing became a general mark throughout all Moab.

b. The wailing included the greatest cities such as Kirhareseth [7], which was stricken, and also the fields that withered, such as the fields of Heshbon and the vine of Sibmah and Jazer [8-9]; it included cities and villages, the learned and the ignorant, rich and poor, and so on...
Heshbon, Sibmah and Jazer were famous for the richness of their vineyards.
c. The joys of the harvest were turned into weeping and mourning; instead of the joyful shouts of the feast, the bitter cries of battle were heard [10].
d. The Moabites went to the high place to pray in the temple of the god Chemosh, to no avail [12].
e. The time of the punishment was fixed at three years, during which Moab collapses before Sennacherib king of Assyria, and the Moabites are humiliated and their glory shattered [14].

This is the end of the proud man: he becomes like Moab, wailing comes upon his life as a whole, in great matters and small alike; he knows no inward joy nor gladness of heart, his feasts turn into sorrows, his worship is without profit, and he collapses day by day until he loses his glory entirely.

Amid this gloomy picture the prophet Isaiah discloses two cheering aspects. The first is the prophet's sharing the troubles of the sons of Moab, for he says: “Wherefore my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kirharesh” [11]. His inmost being cannot bear to see suffering souls, even if their sufferings are the fruit of their sins.

The second aspect is the existence of a remnant, very small and exceedingly feeble [14]: in ancient times Ruth the Moabitess enjoyed salvation, as she came to take refuge under the shadow of God, and in the New Testament the Gentiles came to faith to enjoy the new life in Christ Jesus.

1 The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap. 2 The cities of Aroer are forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid.

Damascus is considered one of the most ancient cities; it is mentioned in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:15); King David conquered it and set a garrison in it (2 Sam 8:5-6; 1 Chr 18:5-6). Rezon arose and was able to found the Syrian kingdom, and war between it and Israel lasted a long time, but later they allied together against Judah and Assyria. It suffered defeat several times: in 843 BC Shalmaneser attacked Damascus and defeated its king Hazael, and Tiglath-pileser attacked it in 732 BC, killed its king Rezin and led its people into captivity (2 Kgs 16:5-9; Isa 7:1-8; Amos 1:3-5). Afterward it passed from the Assyrians to the Chaldeans, then to the Persians, then to the Macedonian Greeks, then to the Romans at the hands of Metellus in 64 BC, and Syria became a Roman province in 63 BC.

If Damascus allied itself with Ephraim against Judah, the punishment fell upon Damascus and Ephraim together. They represent the evil powers of the world that resist the truth, as it is written in the Book of Revelation: “And the fourth angel poured out his vial upon the sun; and power was given unto him to scorch men with fire. And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory” (Rev 16:19).

“Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap. The cities of Aroer are forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid” [1-2].
Damascus was very prosperous until Tiglath-pileser the Assyrian besieged it, killed its king and took its people captive, and it became like a ruinous heap.

As for Aroer, there are at least 3 cities bearing the same name [Aroer is a Moabite name meaning “naked” or “nakedness”]: a city in Moab, now called Ara'ir, about twelve miles east of the Dead Sea, a little south of Dhiban and north of the river Arnon; a village in the southern part of Judea (1 Sam 30:28), now called Ar'arah, twelve miles southeast of Beersheba; and the third, which is the one meant here, a city in Gilead near Rabbah, which is Rabbah of Ammon (Josh 13:25; Judg 11:33), Amman, the capital of Jordan.

Damascus and Aroer represent the soul that exalts itself against God and allies itself with others against His Church; even though God leaves it for a time to appear strong, successful and prosperous, it returns and collapses in two ways:
a. It is turned from a great city into a ruinous heap, that is, it loses its life, because it withdraws from God Himself, the source of life.

b. Like Aroer it is turned from a dwelling for people (with God) into a pasture for flocks and animals, as though our resistance to the truth causes us to lose our dignity and turns our life into a playground for every beast, so that we bear the animal, carnal nature. Therefore St. Ephrem the Syrian praises the Child of the manger, saying: [Glory to Him who looked upon us, how we had consented to resemble the beasts in our frenzy and greed, and came down to us and became one of us, that we might become heavenly].

3 The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria: they shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, saith the LORD of hosts. 4 And in that day it shall come to pass, that the glory of Jacob shall be humbled, and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean. 5 And it shall be as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as he that gathereth ears in the valley of Rephaim. 6 Yet gleaning shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel. 7 At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel. 8 And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, the poles and the sun-images. 9 In that day shall his strong cities be as a ruin in the forest, and the high places which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation. 10 Because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation, and hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength, therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants, and shalt set it with strange slips: 11 In the day of thy planting thou shalt hedge it in, and in the morning shalt thou make thy seed to flourish: but the harvest shall flee away in the day of the deadly stroke and of hopeless sorrow.

Damascus took the lead in the idea of an alliance against Judah, therefore it deserved to be punished first; and when Israel grew weak and submitted to the counsel, it too deserved harsh discipline, though the door of hope was opened before it and the existence of a faithful and sincere remnant enjoying God's salvation was announced.

The prophecy presents the natural fruit of the evil alliance, in which there is reliance on the human arm and purely human thought while ignoring the divine work; this fruit is a natural punishment under which man falls in his evil:

a. Loss of fortification: “The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim” [3]; “In that day shall his strong cities be as a ruin in the forest, and the high places which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation” [9].

If God, the God of our salvation, is the rock of our fortress [10], then our withdrawing from Him and our rejection of His work is the passing away of the true fortress... Then fortresses cannot protect our inner city, but become like a ruin in the midst of the forest, of no value, and like abandoned high places which have the outward appearance without the power of action!
God is our fortress in which we take refuge, and our depths find rest; then all the powers of darkness cannot creep in upon us.

b. Loss of inward glory: “And in that day it shall come to pass, that the glory of Jacob shall be humbled” [4]. If the king's daughter is all glorious within (Ps 45), then the secret of her glory is her Christ who dwells in her, who establishes His Kingdom within her. In Christ Jesus we are glorified not only before men but also before the Father, as St. Jerome says: [Look upon us, and you will see your Son dwelling in us].
c. Loss of strength: “and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean” [4]; therefore the Lord Christ says: “Without me ye can do nothing” (Jn 15:5).
* We cannot run in the way of God unless we are carried on the wings of the Spirit.
* No one is stronger than he who enjoys heavenly help, and no one is weaker than he who is deprived of it.
* We fear nothing, for in order to overcome Satan we must know that our skill will profit nothing, and that everything is of God's grace.

St. John Chrysostom. d. Loss of fruit: the valley of Rephaim was known for the fertility of its land and the abundance of its fruits and crops, but because of the enemies nothing is left to Ephraim but to gather the ears that fall behind the harvesters and to collect what remains at the top of the olive branches, only two or three berries [5-6], that is, they become like the poor who have nothing to harvest (Deut 24:20).

They hedge in the fields and sow, but at the time of harvest the enemy comes to seize it, leaving them what falls from him on the ground, and the feasts of harvest turn into times of gloom and hopelessness [11]. In other words, they lose the fruit of their labor and forfeit their joy and peace.
Now we ask: why does God permit Ephraim this humiliation?

That he may return to God his Creator, instead of sharing with the Arameans their evil counsels, their idolatrous worship and their unclean abominations, for it says: “At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel. And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, the poles Asherahs and the sun-images hammanum” [7-8].

The poles here mean the statues and images of the goddess of love and beauty (Ishtar), corresponding to Aphrodite, which were set on poles (like pillars of wood). This goddess is counted the wife and companion of the god Baal, so his altar is surrounded by a group of trees or poles bearing statues of the goddess, as a sign of her fertility.

These poles and trees carried licentious sexual meanings, so worship was mixed with uncleanness as an inseparable part of it (Ex 34:13; Deut 16:21; Judg 6:25; 2 Chr 34:4-7; Mic 5:14). God permitted the discipline of His people so that they might not defile their view of sex, but lift their heart and mind toward God, who is above sex and who grants us holiness in married life and in bodily relations.

As for the sun-images, some have translated the Hebrew word as sun-gods, and some have translated it Baal-hamman, the Syrian sun god, while others have translated it “altar of incense,” on which incense was offered to the sun god; so this expression is particular to pagan worship, distinct from the holy incense that is offered in the temple.

12 Ah! the noise of many peoples, which make a noise like the noise of the seas; and the rushing of tribes, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters! 13 The tribes shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but he shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. 14 And behold at eveningtide terror; and before the morning they are not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us.

He likens the enemies to the sea that cannot be resisted... God permitted the many peoples to descend upon Ephraim like many waters to drown it, and yet God has set a limit for the sea. He permits it to drown up to a certain point and for a time, while He keeps the faithful few of His children safe from the sea's raging and tumult.

In a wonderful portrayal he says: “Ah! the noise of many peoples... the tribes shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but he shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. And behold at eveningtide terror; and before the morning they are not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us” [12-14].

God permits the enemies to attack like the waters of mighty seas before which no one can stand, but when He rebukes them they become like chaff in the blast of the wind upon the mountains, with no place to settle and no power to resist, or like a wheel rolling before a whirlwind that cannot be stopped. Our enemy is exceedingly violent: when we leave ourselves in his hands he draws us into his whirlpool to drown us in the depths of his sea; but when we are hidden in the Lord the enemy becomes as nothing before us, withdrawing like chaff before the fiery wind of the Holy Spirit and rolling away before the active word of God.

Therefore he says: “at eveningtide terror” [14], meaning that when the Sun of righteousness is absent from our life, darkness comes upon us and we become as in the evening, so that the enemy finds a place in us and terrifies us; but before the morning, that is, at dawn, when our Christ shines in us, the enemy becomes as nothing and is counted as non-existent. This is his portion: he had plundered our life and robbed us of our glory, but he returns and is shattered before Him who dwells in us.

1 O land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush: 2 That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation tall and bare, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation of power and strength and treading down, whose land the rivers have cut through! 3 All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye. 4 For so the LORD said unto me, I will be still, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. 5 For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the flower becometh a ripe grape, he shall cut off the shoots with sickles, and take away and cast down the branches. 6 They shall be left together unto the fowls of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth: and the fowls shall summer upon them, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon them.
The prophet directs his speech to Cush, saying: “O land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush” [1].
What is meant by the land of the rustling of wings?

a. Some see that it is a reference to the imperial power that spread its wings over all the land of Cush and its surroundings. The Holy Bible has used this figure many times; it is said of the king of Assyria, “and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel” (Isa 8:8). The king of Assyria is also likened to a great eagle with great wings (Ezek 17).

b. Some scholars see that the rustling of wings points to the power and greatness of Egypt, while others see that it is Great Britain, which bore great glories across the seas, and others counted it the United States of America, which takes the eagle as its emblem.

c. The rustling of wings points to insects, so it is a symbol of Cush as a country famous for its flying insects; especially since the Hebrew word here, silsal, was used in Deut 28:42 of insects (crickets).
d. The word sel means “shadow,” so it points to a country near the equator, where the shadow is doubled (or is significant because of the intensity of the heat).

e. Some based their interpretation on what is found in the Septuagint and the Targum, that the rustling of wings points to ships; as though the prophet were saying that the ships of Ethiopia sail with their sails spread like the wings of insects. Sailors used to call the sail a wing.

In any case the king of Ethiopia sent messengers by his ships made of papyrus, and he was in haste, because the enemy was at the gates and represented a danger to the whole world at that time. The Ethiopians were known for their ability to spy on the positions and movements of enemies by means of their small, swift ships, so the king did not hesitate to move in order to call Judah to an alliance against the growing danger of Assyria.

The king's mission was for an alliance, but it was not a mission of peace; rather it was a mission calling to war against Assyria and revolt against Sennacherib, a matter that all the peoples were awaiting, for it was said: “All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign (the banner of war) on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye” [3].

Would that the messengers of the Gospel bore the same zeal as the king of Ethiopia and his messengers, who were called to set out so that all might ally together, not against Assyria but against the enemy of good, when the banner of the Cross is lifted up and the trumpet of the word of God is blown, and the spiritual battle is joined under the leadership of the incarnate, crucified divine Word, who carries us in Himself and hides us in His pierced side, granting us the spirit of conquest and victory. He entered the battle through His temptation on the mountain and was victorious in our name and on our behalf, and He continued to strive for us until He completed His striving by the Cross.
* The Lord gave us by His example how we can be victorious, when He was tempted.
Abba Serapion * Jesus our Leader permitted Himself to be tempted in order to teach His children how to fight.

St. Augustine. The prophet says: “Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation tall and bare, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation of power and strength and treading down, whose land the rivers have cut through” [2].

Some see that the description there applies to the Ethiopians or the Assyrians or the Medes... but the mission was directed to the people of God, who were called “a people terrible,” because their God is a terrible God (Ex 23:27; 34:10; Deut 28:58; Josh 2:9; Ps 139:14). They are a people terrible from their beginning, that is, from the start of their formation, as they came out of Egypt with a mighty hand and a high arm. As for his saying, “whose land the rivers have cut through” [2], it points to the gravity of its position, because the enemy is about to attack it, and he will be like a sweeping river; and its description as “a nation tall (stretched out) and bare (sharp)” [2] is, in the Septuagint, “a nation crushed and torn”... as the enemy draws the people like sheep and they drag them into captivity, so that they are dragged away.
If the prophet asks the people not to accept the mission of the king of Cush to ally together, what then is God's position concerning the attacks of Assyria upon His people?

“For so the LORD said unto me, I will be still, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest” [4]. It seems as though God is calm and still, not concerned with our affairs, and God may leave the tyrannical king of Assyria to destroy and ruin and shatter cities until he reaches the gates of Jerusalem; then God declares His hidden role and turns the king of Assyria back disappointed, his pride and his army shattered.

God, the Governor of all, cares for every small and great matter, but in His longsuffering we think that He has forgotten us or does not care about our condition, so we say with the psalmist: “Do not forsake us utterly (greatly),” for even in what seems as though He has left us, He is ordering the matter for our salvation and edification.

St. John Chrysostom likens God to a nurse who places her hands in the hands of the little child to train him to walk; and suddenly she withdraws her hands from him and he falls, and lifts his eyes to her, reproaching her with his tears, but she returns and holds his hands... In this way he is trained to walk. She leaves him by the hands, but she will not leave him in her thought or her heart.

What we call forsaking is care, for God looks upon us in our affliction and turns the bitter into a heat that gives ripeness to the herbs, or like a cloud in the heat of harvest that gives moisture and shade... outwardly sufferings, inwardly edification and rest!
He also sees in afflictions a kind of “pruning of trees,” that is, removing the superfluous branches so that the tree may bring forth abundant fruit [5].

Finally, after He permitted Sennacherib to be victorious over many cities of Judah, He shattered him and his army before he entered Jerusalem, so that their corpses became food for the beasts and the birds of prey [6], for 185 thousand of the army of Sennacherib died in one day.

entries.section: 2. Cush offers a gift to God:

paragraphs.text: 7 In that day shall a present be brought unto the LORD of hosts of a people tall and bare, and from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation of power and strength and treading down, whose land the rivers have cut through, to the place of the name of the LORD of hosts, the mount Zion.

If Cush or Egypt or other nations think that they are able to protect the people of God from Assyria, all the nations will discover that they need the One who came out of the tribe of Judah to protect them from the devil and all his evil works; then the nations that were stricken with arrogance will come in submission to bring a gift to the LORD of hosts [7] in mount Zion, that is, in His Church.

The prophet Isaiah saw countless numbers of kings, rulers and great men coming to Jerusalem to worship the true King, who bore on His head not a temporal crown but a crown of thorns. He saw the believers as spiritual kings submitting to the King of kings, the Lord of glory Jesus, who came out of the tribe of Judah.

entries.section: 1. The flight of the Holy Family:

paragraphs.text: 1 The burden of Egypt. Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it.

We find no country that the Holy Bible speaks of as much as Egypt, after Canaan. The reason is that Israel, as a nation and a people, dwelt in Egypt, and the Jews lived there about 400 years, and finally went out with a high arm (*). By their going out through the blood of the lambs they became a symbol of the whole world, set free from the bondage of the devil through the blood of Christ, the unique slain Sacrifice. Egypt came to represent the power of the world in general, and the house of bondage from which He saves His people.

Isaiah opened his prophecy concerning Egypt in a way joyful for Egypt, saying: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it" [1].

St. Cyril the Great sees that the light, swift cloud (the Septuagint) is St. Mary, whom the Spirit of the Lord sanctified, so that she became light and uplifted, carrying the Lord of glory Jesus to flee with Him to Egypt from the face of Herod (Mt 2:13-15)... At His entering, the idols trembled and pagan worship was shaken, and the heart of the Egyptians melted with love, to receive Him dwelling among them; for he says: [The shining cloud that carried the Lord Jesus to Egypt is His mother the Virgin Mary, who surpassed the clouds in purity and holiness. And the altar that was set up to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt is the Christian Church, which arose upon the ruins of the pagan temples, after its idols were shaken and its temples collapsed before the face of the Lord Jesus]. For this reason the Church sings on the feast of the entry of the Lord Christ into Egypt: [Rejoice and be glad, O Egypt, with your children and all your borders, for He who loves mankind, who is before all ages, has come to you].

Although Egypt, with its Pharaoh and its pagan worship, represented the ancient pagan world in its violence and abominations, it was also a refuge for many, especially in times of famine. Our father Abraham came to it (Gen 12:10), and it received Joseph, persecuted by his brothers, to become the second man after Pharaoh, supplying from its storehouses all the surrounding lands; and to it came our father Jacob and his sons, where the nucleus of the people of God of old began, and the twelve tribes within it; and there appeared their first leader, Moses, great among the prophets, supported by the first high priest. Among the prophets who came to Egypt was the prophet Jeremiah, who urged the people not to flee to Egypt, but they forced him to accompany them on their journey to it (Jer 41:1; 43:7), and he uttered his last prophecies in Tahpanhes (Tahpanes) in Egypt (Jer 43:8-13). But when the heavenly Lord Christ came to our earth, He established His Church in it, to be colored with the spirit of divine blessing, so that its worship, its rites and its hymns came bearing the melody of heavenly life.

Egypt, which was filled with pagan worship, where it set up the Apis calf, cats, crocodiles and frogs... as gods, received the Lord of glory in it, and He raised up from the hearts of the Egyptians a sanctuary for Himself. Egypt was transformed, in a short period, from being the greatest stronghold of paganism into the greatest center of Christian thought, spiritual worship and evangelical life. The star of the Church of Egypt shone through the School of Alexandria, teacher of theology and of the interpretation of the Holy Bible to the early Christian world, and leader of the movement defending the right faith on an ecumenical level. And from Egypt the movement of Christian monasticism in all its forms set out, to draw the heart of the Church to the wilderness, to practice the inner, angelic life, at the very time when the doors of the imperial court were opened to the men of religion, and danger pursued the Church, where the spiritual, churchly work was mixed with temporal and political authority. The Church of Egypt carried the cross of her Bridegroom through the generations and offered countless numbers of martyrs and confessors; sometimes whole cities were martyred, and many vied with one another to obtain the crowns of martyrdom with joy and gladness of heart...

2 And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians: and they shall fight every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. 3 And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof; and I will destroy the counsel thereof: and they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards. 4 And the Egyptians will I give over into the hand of a cruel lord; and a fierce king shall rule over them, saith the Lord, the LORD of hosts. 5 And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up. 6 And the rivers shall stink, and the brooks of Egypt shall be weakened and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither. 7 The paper reeds by the brooks, by the mouth of the brooks, and every thing sown by the brooks, shall wither, be driven away, and be no more. 8 The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish. 9 Moreover they that work in fine flax, and they that weave white cloth, shall be confounded. 10 And the pillars thereof shall be crushed, and all that work for hire shall be sick in soul. 11 Surely the princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish: how say ye unto Pharaoh, I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? 12 Where are they? where are thy wise men? and let them tell thee now, and let them know what the LORD of hosts hath purposed upon Egypt. 13 The princes of Zoan are become fools, the princes of Noph are deceived; they have also seduced Egypt, even they that are the stay of the tribes thereof. 14 The LORD hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof: and they have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof, as a drunken man staggereth in his vomit. 15 Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do. 16 In that day shall Egypt be like unto women: and it shall be afraid and fear because of the shaking of the hand of the LORD of hosts, which he shaketh over it. 17 And the land of Judah shall be a terror unto Egypt, every one that maketh mention thereof shall be afraid in himself, because of the counsel of the LORD of hosts, which he hath determined against it.

The flight of the Holy Family to Egypt and the setting up of an altar to the Lord there does not mean covering over its evils, but on the contrary, the Lord's revealing its weaknesses and spiritual wounds, so that He may remove from it every weakness (the kingdom of evil) and establish what is new (the Kingdom of God). The Lord's coming to it means the demolition of its idols and the removal of its abominations for the sake of the sanctification of its people.
He has brought out the fruits of the ancient abominations, namely:

First: the rise of civil wars, "And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians: and they shall fight every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof" [2-3]. This is the natural fruit of its withdrawal from God, the Giver of inner peace, love and unity, for wars break out at the level of persons, even between friends, and at the level of cities and kingdoms [for there was a kingdom in Upper Egypt and another in Lower Egypt]. Evil shatters the inner soul and brings it into a state of despair and frustration.

Our withdrawal from God makes us lose our inner harmony, so that our inner life turns into a battlefield, and the body wrestles against the spirit, and the inner energies are not in harmony together... and the heart becomes an unbearable hell. On the contrary, when the Spirit of God takes the lead, man submits to Him wholly and lives in harmony and concord: the body supports the soul in its worship, and the senses and emotions are sanctified to work together with the pure mind, with a holy and good will in the Lord.

Second: the loss of true wisdom. The Egyptians were known as a very intelligent people, and the Holy Bible testifies that Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:20), but their withdrawal from God made them lose everything, so that neither their wisdom nor their knowledge nor their civilization helped them, and they resorted to the idols to seek counsel: "I will destroy the counsel thereof: and they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards" [3].

Third: suffering under fierce rulers [4], who incline to domination and control rather than to serving the people and building the country. For when the hearts of the people grow hard through their distance from God, the Giver of kindness and goodness, He permits them violent leaders, so that as they do, so it is done to them.

When our inner heart grows hard toward others, we should expect nothing but that with the same measure with which we measure to others it will be measured to us; therefore He permits us to fall under violent leaders. This is what happens even in our daily life, in work, in the family and in our personal life... for he who is harsh to his parents will find his body violent in its fleshly warfare against the soul. What we sow for others we reap in our personal life.

Fourth: suffering from a state of drought, "And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up. And the rivers shall stink, and the brooks of Egypt shall be weakened and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither... The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament... Moreover they that work in fine flax, and they that weave white cloth, shall be confounded. And the pillars thereof shall be crushed, and all that work for hire shall be sick in soul" [5-10].

It is as though evil bears the fruit of bitterness even in man's daily life and his essential needs, for the river Nile dries up [in many towns of Upper Egypt it is still called "the sea"], so that people find no water to drink, nor for farming, and the fishermen lose their work and lament in vain; and this affects industry and trade... So the great men, who are the pillars of Egypt, are crushed, and the souls of the slaves who work for the rich are depressed.

Through evil, ruin and corruption creep into the natural resources (the water) and the human energies of all classes! Man loses the water that waters his soul, and the fish that satisfies him inwardly, and the linen garments that cover his depths, and his inner peace; and thus he suffers thirst, hunger, nakedness and shame!

Fifth: the loss of the wise and the counsellors. Man does not suffer only from material deprivation, but from wise helpers who would support him in his distress. Therefore it is said: "Surely the princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish: how say ye unto Pharaoh, I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where are they? where are thy wise men? and let them tell thee now, and let them know what the LORD of hosts hath purposed upon Egypt" [11-12].

In place of the wisdom for which Egypt was known, foolishness has come, even in Zoan, the capital of ancient northern Egypt. It was said: "And Solomon's wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east country, and all the wisdom of Egypt" (1 Kgs 4:30)... But this wisdom passes away when man withdraws from his God, the Source of wisdom; therefore the wise counsellors of Pharaoh give brutish counsel, that is, fleshly thoughts (1 Cor 2). And the sign of their deprivation of wisdom is the inability of the wise men to grasp the plan of God, the LORD of hosts, concerning Egypt [12]; how then can the people of God trust the counsel of Pharaoh concerning an alliance together against Assyria?!

"The princes of Noph are deceived; they have also seduced Egypt, even they that are the stay of the tribes thereof" [13]. This is the calamity of Egypt, that it accepted error as wisdom, for the princes of the capital of Upper Egypt (southern Egypt), Menouf (Memphis), were deceived by the noble wise men, who correspond to the hypocritical false prophets of whom the prophet Jeremiah often spoke.

Sixth: the loss of awareness and the entering into a state of drunkenness; "The LORD hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof: and they have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof, as a drunken man staggereth in his vomit" [14].

Since sin is intoxicating and makes man lose his awareness and his purpose in life, when he drinks its cup God permits a spirit of error to come upon him, so that he staggers like a drunkard, without purpose. He has no serious work for building himself and building others, whether great or despised, branch or rush (reed). And this is the most dangerous point to which man can come, for he thereby loses his human being and lives like one dead, with no taste for life.

Seventh: confusion in a state of fear, "In that day shall Egypt be like unto women: and it shall be afraid and fear because of the shaking of the hand of the LORD of hosts, which he shaketh over it" [16]. Pharaoh, who counts himself in arrogance and pride the rescuer of Israel and Judah from the hand of Assyria, is terrified, he and his men, and they become like women before the LORD of hosts and before Judah [17].

It is as though the Lord encourages Judah not to be terrified by the words of Pharaoh, and not to enter into an alliance with him as Israel and Aram did, for Pharaoh himself is terrified, not before Assyria, but before Judah itself.

entries.section: 3. The setting up of an altar to the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 18 In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of the sun. 19 In that day shall there be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the LORD. 20 And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt: for they shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors, and he shall send them a saviour and a defender, and he shall deliver them. 21 And the LORD shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the LORD in that day, and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the LORD, and perform it. 22 And the LORD shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal it: and they shall return even to the LORD, and he shall be intreated of them, and shall heal them. 23 In that day shall there be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria, and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians. 24 In that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, even a blessing in the midst of the land: 25 Whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.

After God revealed the wounds of Egypt and what sin had done to it, the loss of inner unity and of true wisdom, together with the suffering from the cruelty of the ruler and the cruelty of nature (drought), the confusion of its economy (agriculture and industry), the incapacity of its leading human energies, and even its entering into a state of unconsciousness and drunkenness, with fear and confusion even before Judah, the small kingdom, God intervenes to heal its wounds and save it, giving it the following blessings:

A. A new language: "In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of the sun" [18]. These five cities are none other than the senses of the believer; for when the Gentiles come to faith in the Lord Christ, they hand over the five senses into His hands to be sanctified, to speak the language of the Spirit instead of the language of the flesh, and it is said to them as it was said to the Apostle Peter: "Thy speech bewrayeth thee" (Mt 26:73; Mk 14:70).

The heart of the believer is lifted up to the heavenly Canaan not only during his participation in the sacrament of the Eucharist and all the living liturgies of the Church, but also during his private worship, and even throughout his daily life, even in the moments of his eating, drinking and sleeping. This is the work of the Holy Spirit of God in our life; He carries us to heaven that we may experience it in our depths, and our language becomes Canaanite, that is heavenly, the language of love and inner joy. We share with the heavenly ones their liturgies and their constant joy, and we are not a people "of a strange speech" (Ezek 3:5).
B. Swearing by the name of the LORD of hosts; what does it mean: "swear to the LORD of hosts" [18]?

Swearing was a sign of trust and faith in the one by whose name man swears; so instead of swearing by pagan gods, the Gentiles, headed by Egypt, accept faith in the LORD of hosts, and the Egyptians hold fast to His name, counting this the secret of their strength.

C. The calling of one of the cities "the city of the sun" [8], meaning "Heliopolis," which was a center of sun worship; it turned from the worship of the material sun to the worship of the Sun of Righteousness who rises upon those who sit in darkness.
In the Septuagint it came as "the city of righteousness," for it bears the righteousness of Christ in us.

entries.section: 3. The setting up of an altar to the Lord:

paragraphs.text: D. The setting up of an altar to the Lord: "In that day shall there be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the LORD" [19]. By this is meant the altar of the Church of the New Testament, for the altar of the Old Testament was in Jerusalem and it was not permitted to offer sacrifices to the Lord outside it. The Holy Family crossed into Upper Egypt and hid for about six months in the place where the Monastery of the Virgin, famous as Al-Muharraq, now stands, which is considered to be in the middle of Egypt; in it a church was established to the Lord and the sacrifice of the Eucharist is offered upon it, which is a participation in the very sacrifice of the Cross.

entries.section: 3. The setting up of an altar to the Lord:

paragraphs.text: As for the pillar at its border, it is St. Mark the Apostle, who came to Alexandria (on the border of Egypt) to preach the Gospel and to set up the altar of the Church of the New Testament, that the Egyptians might enjoy salvation from the enemy of good who oppressed them, and the Lord Himself would be their defender, intercessor and deliverer [20].

entries.section: 3. The setting up of an altar to the Lord:

paragraphs.text: E. Spiritual knowledge: "And the LORD shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the LORD in that day" [21]. The Egyptians were concerned with spiritual knowledge, and the School of Alexandria was established for this purpose, to spread the knowledge of the Lord not through abstract rationalistic thoughts, but through a life of devotion and asceticism and the experience of communion with God the Father in His Son Jesus Christ by His Holy Spirit.
Knowledge was mingled with worship, as the prophet continues: "and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the LORD, and perform it" [21].

Perhaps the most wonderful to write on the connection of knowledge with worship, as with evangelical conduct in daily life, is St. Clement of Alexandria, for this thought runs as a golden thread through all his writings. Among his words about knowledge (Gnosis):

[These are the marks that distinguish our Gnosis: first contemplation, then the fulfilling of the commandments, and finally the teaching of the righteous. When these traits are found in a man, he is counted a perfect gnostic. If a man loses one of these traits, his Gnosis is disabled].

entries.section: 3. The setting up of an altar to the Lord:

paragraphs.text: F. Inner healing: "And the LORD shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal it: and they shall return even to the LORD, and he shall be intreated of them, and shall heal them" [22].

God permits its smiting, that is, its chastening for the weakness in it, that it may discover itself and realize its need of the Savior, and return to Him and find Him the Physician who alone is able to heal the wounds of the soul and restore its peace... Our Christ came as Physician and medicine at the same time:
* Blessed is the "Physician" who came down and cut without pain, healed our wounds with a medicine that is not bitter, for He showed His Son as a "medicine" that heals sinners!
St. Ephrem the Syrian. The Lord came to Egypt and struck its idols, that the Egyptians might find in Him the only secret of their healing.

G. Since the world conflict at that time was between Assyria and Egypt, and the other nations, among them Israel, were victims of this conflict, the coming of the Lord of glory Jesus gives peace to all, and all feel - in Christ Jesus - that the earth belongs to the Lord and to His Christ, and is not a center of dispute, and all share together in worship.

entries.section: 3. The setting up of an altar to the Lord:

paragraphs.text: In a wonderful picture of this peace the prophet says: "In that day shall there be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria, and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians. In that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, even a blessing in the midst of the land: whom the LORD of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance" [24].

What does "in that day," which is repeated about five times in verses [18-25], mean, if not the fullness of time in which the Lord Christ came to accomplish these blessings for us? He came as "the Way" in which the Gentiles gather to enjoy the spirit of spiritual unity and the abundance of blessing.

What does the gathering of Egypt, Assyria and Israel together in enjoying the divine blessing and the eternal inheritance mean? It is a symbolic picture of the universal Church, which brought enemies together in the spirit of love and unity. Israel was at that time in conflict between allying with Egypt or Assyria, the two opposing world powers of that time. But the coming of the Lord Christ solved the problem, for all became members of one Church enjoying the divine work, and the Egyptians were called the people of God, and Assyria the work of His hands, and Israel His inheritance.

entries.section: 1. The captivity of Egypt and Cush:

paragraphs.text: 1 In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it; 2 At the same time spake the LORD by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot. 3 And the LORD said, Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia; 4 So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.

Some critics thought that Sargon, king of Assyria, who sent Tartan to Ashdod, was Shalmaneser or Sennacherib. Others denied that a king of this name existed in Assyria; but, as Bultema says, God made the stones speak to put the unbelievers to shame, for it is known today that Sargon was one of the strongest kings of Assyria, and that he was the father of Sennacherib, having usurped the throne from Shalmaneser V and succeeded him.
The word "Sargon" means "appointed by God" or "the righteous king"; he used this name to cover over his usurping of the throne.
"Tartan" is not the name of a person, but most likely a title belonging to the command of the army.
Sargon sent the head of his army to Ashdod, aiming at Sua king of Egypt (2 Kgs 17:4), for Ashdod, which is on the border of the Philistines, was considered the key to entering Egypt.

Modern studies have revealed that Sua is not the name of a Pharaoh, but an abbreviation of the name of a commander of a battalion in the Delta called Siba, or an abbreviation of the name of a city in the western Delta called Sais, which Tefnakhte used as his residence.

Since Assyria had defeated Aram and Ephraim, the time had come to strike Pharaoh; so the king sent his commander to Ashdod and he conquered it, the same commander whom Sennacherib used in the siege of Jerusalem.

entries.section: 1. The captivity of Egypt and Cush:

paragraphs.text: God wished to move the feelings of His people, change their hearts and rebuke them for their reliance on Egypt and Cush; therefore He asked His prophet to walk before the people naked and barefoot for three years, to be himself a prophecy of what would befall Egypt and Cush when Assyria would take them captive and lead their great men into captivity as slaves, naked, barefoot and with their buttocks uncovered... Isaiah himself became a sign and wonder [3], mocked by all who looked at him because of what had come upon him, and this for the salvation of his people and to keep them from relying on Pharaoh of Egypt.

Isaiah, in his sufferings and nakedness, bore a shadow of the sufferings of the Lord Christ, who endured nakedness in order to clothe us with His righteousness, and bore the wounds of His people in His body in order to heal us. Isaiah walked as a slave, wearing no outer garment and no sandals, a picture of his Lord who became as a slave (Phil 2:7) in order to free us from the yoke of bondage.

5 And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory. 6 And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day, Behold, such is our refuge, whither we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?

When Pharaoh of Egypt submits to Assyria, the children of Judah are terrified, their hope is shattered, and Egypt, their glory, is humbled, and they say: "Behold, such is our refuge, whither we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria: and how shall we escape?" [6].
This is the end of everyone who relies on an arm of flesh!

1 The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds in the south pass through; so it cometh from the desert, from a terrible land. 2 A grievous vision is declared unto me; the plunderer plundering, and the destroyer destroying. Go up, O Elam: besiege, O Media; all the sighing thereof have I made to cease. 3 Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it. 4 My heart wandered, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into trembling unto me. 5 They prepare the table, they watch in the watchtower, they eat, they drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield. 6 For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth. 7 And he saw riders, couples of horsemen, riders of asses, riders of camels; and he hearkened diligently with much heed: 8 And he cried like a lion: My lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower in the daytime, and I am set in my ward whole nights: 9 And, behold, here are riders of men, couples of horsemen. And he answered and said, Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground. 10 O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you.

The prophet Isaiah refers to Babylon by a strange symbolic name: "The burden of the desert of the sea" [1]. He called Babylon, the golden city, the glory of the nations, a desert because of its evil, which turned it into a state of wasteland; and it was called "the desert of the sea" because of its location on the river Euphrates, or because it was the capital of more than one nation among the nations, for waters signify the many peoples, so that it became a dry desert in the midst of the peoples.

The Jews believe that the demons dwell in three regions of the world: the barren deserts, the waters, and the air; therefore the Lord Christ fought the devil during His temptation on the mountain in the wilderness and overcame, and fought him in the waters of the Jordan as in his lair and overcame, and also fought him in the air when He was lifted up on the Cross and triumphed. Babylon was called "the desert of the sea" to affirm that it became the place of Satan, who dwells in the desert and also in the sea. St. John the Theologian saw it as a harlot woman sitting upon many waters (Rev 17:1).
The prophet Isaiah saw the army of Cyrus, coming to carry out the plan of God concerning Babylon, like whirlwinds in the south, like a storm coming from the desert, from a terrible land [1].

The whirlwinds or violent winds in the south mean that they are hot, as opposed to those coming from the north, which are cold; as though the army of Cyrus were like hot, violent winds accompanied by a storm from the desert laden with sand, which buries the fields, spoils the crops, damages the houses and roads, and causes diseases, especially of the eyes. In other words, it shatters man's resources, his dwelling and his insight. This is contrary to the hot but gentle southern winds, which cause the crops to ripen; for this reason the bride says: "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 4:16).

The prophet, in his wonderful tenderness even toward enemies, could not bear to see the ruin and plunder that came upon Babylon [2], and so he says: "Therefore are my loins filled with pain: pangs have taken hold upon me, as the pangs of a woman that travaileth: I was bowed down at the hearing of it; I was dismayed at the seeing of it. My heart wandered, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into trembling unto me" [3-4].

It appears that he saw this vision at night [4], for the night of his delight in prayer was turned into trembling... And perhaps he speaks here in the name of the Babylonians, for whom the night of feasting and joy turned into trembling because of Cyrus' storming of the capital; for he saw the royal table prepared and the guards amusing themselves with eating and drinking, though it was fitting for the princes to anoint the shield with oil in order to fight Cyrus.

The prophet could not bear to see Babylon with its great men amusing themselves without concern while the enemy stormed the gates that had become unguarded, so the prophet's heart wandered and was filled with terror and pain. I say, how should we also not groan for the servants who are occupied away from the spiritual struggle with formalities, official matters and feasts, leaving the Church of God and its flock as though without a watchful guard.
The words of St. John Chrysostom concerning pastoral care remain immortal.
[I am a father full of compassion. Hear what Paul asks: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth" (Gal 4:19). Every mother cries out as she travails in the hour of birth; so do I also].

[I wish you could see the fires burning in my heart, that you might know that I burn more than a young woman groaning over her early widowhood; for I do not think she grieves over her husband, nor does a father grieve over his son, as I grieve over this crowd gathered here]...

The divine call came to the prophet: "Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth" [6], for in ancient times the prophet was called a "watchman" or "sentinel," as he was called a "seer." The work of the prophet is to watch from the high tower and guard souls with the word of God, as well as to see with spiritual insight in order to declare the will of God and His plan of salvation.

The prophet Habakkuk stood as a sentinel, for he says: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me" (Hab 2:1); and the prophet Ezekiel was called a sentinel in more than one place (Ezek 3:17; 33:2, 6, 7).

Isaiah saw Persia (riders of asses) and Media (riders of camels) coming to seize Babylon; he saw and heard with great attention [7], for the matter is serious and grave, touching the life of his people. He did not stop at seeing and listening, but began to roar like a lion [8] to declare the plan of God for the fall of Babylon and the salvation of the people of God.

"Babylon is fallen, is fallen; and all the graven images of her gods he hath broken unto the ground. O my threshing, and the corn of my floor: that which I have heard of the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have I declared unto you" [9-10].

The repetition of an expression twice, such as "Babylon is fallen, is fallen," is one of the features of this book (Isa 21:9; 24:4, 16; 28:13; 29:1; 40:1, 9; 43:11; etc.), perhaps because the speech in this book of salvation is addressed to the Gentiles as well as to the Jews, the call to salvation being universal, to accept the God of all and to overcome evil. It is fitting here for every person - whether of Gentile or Jewish origin - to be assured that Babylon, which captured his heart with lusts and gave him violence, collapses before the salvation of God, so that the heavenly Jerusalem may arise in his heart. Let all the idols of Babylon collapse, that the Lord may arise in the heart and declare His Kingdom. Moreover the repetition also means a kind of emphasis. Besides that, the repetition of two carries a symbol of the love that makes the two one, as St. Augustine says. By love the inner Babylon falls and the kingdom of the devil, who cannot bear love, collapses, and through it we enjoy the evangelical life according to the Lord's commandment: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (Jn 13:35).

The prophet sees the world as a threshing floor, on which the crops are trodden and then winnowed to separate the wheat hidden among the straw... It is the wheat of the Lord Himself, which does not perish but is separated from the chaff.
St. Augustine speaks of the Babylonian captivity and the deliverance from it, saying:

[The Apostle says: "Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come" (1 Cor 10:1). We must know our captivity, and then our deliverance; it is fitting for us to know Babylon in which we were taken captive, and Jerusalem to which we groan to return. For these two cities - as to the letter - are two actual cities.
"Babylon" means "confusion" (calamity); and Jerusalem "vision of peace"...!

These two cities were built at a particular time to be a symbol of two cities that remain until the end of the world... when some sit on the right and the others on the left, Jerusalem will be on the right and Babylon on the left...

Two kinds of love found these two cities: the love of God founds Jerusalem, and the love of the world founds Babylon. Therefore let each one ask himself: what is it that he loves? And then he will know which city is his homeland. If he finds Babylon to be his homeland, let him uproot covetousness from himself and plant love; but if he finds Jerusalem to be his homeland, let him endure the captivity, hoping for freedom...
Now, brethren, may we hear about this city of which we are citizens; may we hear about it and sing of it and long for it].

Thus St. Augustine looks to the children of God who are bound by divine love as citizens of the Jerusalem above, the city of eternal love; they live here in struggle against Babylon, which does not cease to spend all its energies to take the children of God captive and deprive them of their heavenly homeland, since they themselves delivered themselves up to captivity when they accepted sin; and the Savior has come to open the door of hope to them, to grant them the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

In a look full of hope St. Augustine comments on the saying of the prophet: "When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted" (Ps 126:1), saying: [Man was a citizen of Jerusalem, but he was sold under sin and became a wanderer (without a city)...

"Babylon" means "confusion"... for the affairs of this present human life are all confusion, as they do not belong to God. In the midst of this confusion, in this Babylonian land, Zion was taken captive, but "the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion," so that we became "like those who are comforted," that is, we rejoiced because we received comfort...

We grieve over what we are now, but we are comforted in hope. The present, which is for our grief, will pass, and eternal joy will come, and there will be no need of comfort where we are not afflicted with any tribulation].

"The burden of Dumah. He calleth to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said, The morning cometh, and also the night: if ye will enquire, enquire ye: return, come" [11-12].

The prophet calls Adam by a secret prophetic name, "Dumah," which is an abbreviation of Idumea. If the name "Edom" means "bloody" or "earthy," since Edom represents the wicked who love shedding blood, bound to the love of earthly, temporal and fleshly things, then the name "Dumah" means "silence" or "the silence of death"...

The prophet stood on the watchtower all the nights [8], for a kind of inner darkness reigned over the world, awaiting the coming of the Sun of Righteousness to remove the darkness of the night and for the morning to come. Now he hears a voice, perhaps from heaven or from the rest of the prophets and men of God: "Watchman, what of the night?"... The fullness of time has come and the light of morning has dawned; let the nations be silent and die to their old man to enjoy the light of life; let them seek now and find their light through their faith in the Lord Christ, let them return to God their Savior and come to Him, and find Him stretching out His hands with practical love to embrace them.

"Watchman, what of the night?" is repeated twice because the speech with the prophet concerns the Jews as well as the Gentiles, and also the believers of the Old and New Testaments, that all may enjoy salvation while they are in stillness contemplating the work of God with them.

13 The burden upon Arabia. In the forest in Arabia shall ye lodge, O ye travelling companies of Dedanim. 14 Bring water to meet the thirsty, O inhabitants of the land of Tema, meet the fugitive with his bread. 15 For they fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war. 16 For thus hath the Lord said unto me, Within a year, according to the years of an hireling, and all the glory of Kedar shall fail: 17 And the residue of the number of archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be diminished: for the LORD God of Israel hath spoken it.
The original reads Ereb and not Arabia, which means "evening," for it speaks of all who dwell in darkness.

Here he addresses the tribes of Dedan and Kedar, who dwell southeast of Edom; these received those fleeing from the sword, who gave themselves up in return for enjoying water to drink or bread to eat..
