Since these tribes lived in the darkness of paganism, they became unable to offer real help to those who fled to them, because a blind man leading a blind man, both fall into a ditch (Mt 15:14; Lk 6:39).

1 The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops? 2 Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. 3 All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far. 4 Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people. 5 For it is a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity by the Lord GOD of hosts in the valley of vision, breaking down the walls, and of crying to the mountains. 6 And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. 7 And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate.
"The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?" [1].
* What is meant by the valley of vision?

A. Jewish scholars see that this title is fitting for Jerusalem because it is the city in which God gave His servants visions and revelations. Perhaps the inspired word used this title to awaken in them the insight that had been blotted out. This Jerusalem, whose siege God permitted, is His city in which He set up His temple to reveal Himself, His kingdom and the glories of His heavens in it, so that it might be a secret of blessing to mankind, but the corruption of its people blotted out its insight.

B. It is called "the valley of vision" although Jerusalem was not built on a valley but on mountains; yet the presence of high mountains around it makes it, in relation to these mountains, like a valley. In any case, God wanted to make of His city a high, firm mountain, but the corruption of its people brought it down to become a valley.
Some ask: what siege is the prophet speaking of here?
Is it the siege carried out by Sennacherib, or the siege of Esarhaddon in the days of Manasseh? Or is it the siege of Nebuchadnezzar, or of Titus?!

Some see that it is the siege of Sennacherib, although from the spiritual side it applies to every siege in which Jerusalem fell, and more so it applies to the siege that comes upon our inner Jerusalem, the heart, the mind and the soul.

* The going up to the housetops [1]: The people did not expect that God, who loves His city and declares His presence especially inside the Holy of Holies, where His glory appeared in the Shekinah (the Ark of the Covenant), would permit the siege of His city by the pagans; therefore they went up to the housetops to see for themselves what had befallen the city from outside.

Perhaps their going up to the roof points to their concern for the outside and not the inside, for appearances and not the depths; instead of entering the house of their inner souls to discover the secret of their weakness, they were concerned with what is on the surface. Therefore the prophet rebukes them, saying:

"Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city" [2]. These are outward marks, for Jerusalem, imitating the capitals of the surrounding countries, boasted and rejoiced in noisy appearances instead of the hidden, silent return to God, the secret of her pride, her strength and her gladness.

* "Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far. Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people" [2-4].

Isaiah saw what had befallen the city of his God, which was very dear to him, and asked that no one comfort him because of the intensity of the bitterness of his soul. He saw the army of Jerusalem going out into the fields under the command of rulers who did not die by the sword, but fled out of fear, and the enemy overtook them, captured them and humbled them.

"Thy slain men are not slain with the sword"... for the people stabbed themselves with the fiery darts of lusts, and isolated themselves from God, the source of their life, and so their souls fell slain before the outward ruin came. The prophet saw what is more dangerous than Sennacherib and his army: surrender to sins and abominations and the practical denial of the faith. For sin "hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her. Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death" (Prov 7:26-27).

The prophet had nothing left but to pour himself out in tears before God; this is what every wise spiritual leader does when he sees the people of God go astray or souls perish, and so he says with the prophet Jeremiah: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!" (Jer 9:1). The Lord of the prophets Himself "beheld the city, and wept over it" (Lk 19:41).
* I do not deny that the first Jerusalem was destroyed because of the evil of its inhabitants, but I ask: is it not fitting for you to weep over your spiritual Jerusalem?!
If anyone sins after receiving the mysteries of the truth, he is wept over, because he was of Jerusalem and no longer is...
Let our Jerusalem be wept over, because on account of sin the enemies (the evil spirits) surround it with a rampart and besiege it and leave in it not one stone upon another.

Origen * He (the Lord) wept over Jerusalem because He wanted blessedness for her - as I said - by her accepting faith in Him and welcoming peace with God. This is what He called them to through Isaiah, saying: "Let us make peace with him" [(Isa 27:5) the Septuagint]... let us make peace with God through faith.
St. Cyril the Great * Our Savior does not cease to weep even until now, through His chosen ones, whenever He sees a person leaving the good life and walking in the evil way.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The people of Jerusalem, especially the civil and religious leaders, lived in luxury and indulgence, spending their nights in parties, eating and drinking, while Isaiah stood warning and cautioning. Now the people stand on the housetops and see the ruin with their own eyes, while Isaiah's heart is broken with grief and bitterness; he enters his chamber and weeps with abundant tears, that perhaps God would have compassion on His people. He lived bold and frank in his directions, and loving and tender in his feelings.

Isaiah describes what befell Jerusalem of trouble, treading down, perplexity and crying [5], for despair came over the whole city; no one knew how to act or where to go. Perhaps some called for strengthening the walls, others called for fleeing to the mountains, and another group preferred to surrender. Jerusalem was transformed from the valley of divine vision, the giver of peace, into a valley that confuses and shatters the soul... And Isaiah called this day "the day of the LORD of hosts" [5], for it is the day of His chastening of His people.

8 And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest. 9 Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool. 10 And ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall. 11 Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago.

What was Judah's attitude to what had happened to Jerusalem? They ignored "the covering of the Most High," which protects and fortifies them, as the psalmist says: "He that dwelleth in the covering of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the God of heaven" (Ps 91:1), "I will trust in the covering of thy wings" (Ps 61:4). By this grace forsook them and they were exposed before the enemy in weakness. "And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest" [8].

Some see that the "covering" here refers to the veil that noble women used to wear to hide their faces. For the prophet looked at Judah as a spiritual bride of God who rejected her Bridegroom and lost her purity and chastity and removed her veil shamelessly, desired by strangers, and gives her body to them. This picture applies to Judah when the walls began to be torn down and Jerusalem became like an uncovered face for which strangers lust.
Judah tried to find a solution to the problem, but instead of returning to God, it used purely human calculations to achieve deliverance; among them:

A. The people rushed to "the house of the forest," which wise Solomon built (1 Kgs 7:2 etc.), in which he placed golden weapons, which Shishak king of Egypt stole, and Rehoboam replaced them with weapons of bronze. The house was full of weapons, but they could not support the people and protect them against the enemies.

B. Concern for the waters of the lower pool and turning the waters from outside the walls into the city, so that the enemies outside the walls would not benefit from them and the besieged people would not be exposed to thirst and lack of water.

C. The walls began to crack, so they thought of tearing down their houses and turning the rubble toward the wall to protect it from collapse. They did not think of God, the true wall, which the enemy cannot approach; God, who sets up His grace to guard our inner walls so that they are not torn down, for it is said: "By my God have I leaped over a wall" (Ps 18:29), "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me" (Isa 49:16).

12 And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth: 13 And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die. 14 And it was revealed in mine ears by the LORD of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord GOD of hosts.

God in His love for us calls us to repentance, that we may weep and mourn over our sins, and so enjoy a surpassing inner peace and an unceasing eternal joy; but man in his short-sightedness wants to enjoy temporary pleasure and worldly luxury, reckoning that he will die tomorrow.

"And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth: and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die" [12-13].

* These wicked ones head toward killing themselves with every kind of lust... Yes, for even when they live they are in shame, since they count their belly their god, and when they die they are tormented.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic

15 Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say, 16 What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock? 17 Behold, the LORD will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee. 18 He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house. 19 And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down.

Opinions differ concerning Shebna's position in the palace of King Hezekiah; here he appears to be in charge of the king's treasury, and in (2 Kgs 18:37) he is called the scribe, and some see that he was a counsellor to the king or the chief chamberlain of the palace or a minister... In any case he had great authority. And it appears that he was of foreign race. He wanted to immortalize his memory, so he hewed out for himself a great tomb in the very rock in which the kings of Judah were buried. He was a wicked man, so Isaiah rebuked him and called him "the shame of the king's house," and prophesied his removal and the setting up of Eliakim in his place, and this was fulfilled around the year 701 BC.

His evil is poured out first in his not believing the words of the prophet Isaiah to the people that they would be taken captive, and his hewing of the tomb was a sign of his unbelief in the prophecies of Isaiah. The other side of the evil is his love of grandeur, for he wanted to be buried with the kings; and finally he was not faithful to the king, for he abused the king's trust in him. For all this the divine judgment was issued to remove him and deprive him of burial in what his hands had built, and instead of his enjoying splendid chariots, he is thrown into a strange city like a ball that a child throws and plays with unhindered.

Many see that Shebna is a symbol of the Antichrist who appears in the last days, or of the man of sin who in his pride wishes not to be buried in the tomb of the kings of Judah, the offspring of David, but to sit enthroned in the temple of the Lord and set himself forth as God (2 Thess 2:4). As for Eliakim, he points to the Lord Christ, who shatters the Antichrist and strips him of his might in order to save the elect.

It is noticed here that the prophet did not say of Shebna that King Hezekiah would remove him. Rather he says: "Behold, the LORD will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee. He will surely violently turn and toss thee (that is, hurl thee with a strong thrust) like a ball into a large country... And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down" [17-19].

entries.section: 5. The setting up of Eliakim in place of Shebna:

paragraphs.text: 20 And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah: 21 And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. 22 And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. 23 And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house. 24 And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons. 25 In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that was upon it shall be cut off: for the LORD hath spoken it.

The speech here [20-25] opens the door of hope before every soul that the enemy of good tries to shatter, for Shebna must necessarily pass away and come to an end and Eliakim take his place. The Antichrist or the false prophet or the man of sin will bear authority and power, but he will certainly collapse, that the Kingdom of Christ may be declared forever.
The prophecy came clearly here that Eliakim is a symbol of the Lord Christ.

entries.section: 5. The setting up of Eliakim in place of Shebna:

paragraphs.text: A. "And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah" [21].

Shebna prided himself on the robe and the girdle along with the authority, commanding and forbidding as the second man, the one the king trusted, acting in a spirit of power and arrogance. But when Eliakim takes his place he takes his robe and girdle, yet he bears a spirit of tender fatherhood toward the people of God. The "Antichrist" has authority with violence and harshness, while "Christ" is love and tenderness and surpassing spiritual fatherhood. What distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil is love full of tenderness as opposed to authority full of violence.

It was said of the Lord Christ: "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the LORD is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself" (Ps 93:1). And the prophet Isaiah saw Him clothed in garments red like him that treadeth in the winefat (Isa 63:1-3). For He clothed Himself with His Church, which He dyed with His precious blood, so that it was sanctified and bore His splendor.
He girded Himself to wash the feet and to serve in a spirit of love and humility.

entries.section: 5. The setting up of Eliakim in place of Shebna:

paragraphs.text: B. "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open" [22]. Who has the key but "he that is holy, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth" (Rev 3:7). It is the Lord Christ, who encourages His Church, saying to her that He alone opens to her the doors of heaven and shuts her in, so that the devil and all his powers cannot approach her. As for the key with which He opens and shuts, it is: "the authority of binding and loosing" which the Lord gave to His Bride through His disciples (Mt 16:19), as St. Cyril the Great and St. Jerome say; and the Cross, by which our Lord Jesus opens His paradise and with it shuts the gates of hell against us, as St. John Chrysostom says; and also the understanding of the Holy Bible, especially the prophecies that were formerly sealed and not understood, as St. Gregory the Wonderworker says. Origen also says: [Every written work needs the Logos who shut it, in order to open it, "he shutteth, and no man openeth," and when He opens, no one can cast doubt on the explanation He gives].

We do not wonder at the saying "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder," for this key is the Cross which the Son of David carried upon His shoulder to accomplish our salvation.

entries.section: 5. The setting up of Eliakim in place of Shebna:

paragraphs.text: C. "And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house. And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons" [23-24].

In poor rural areas a person finds no place in his house for many of his needs and possessions, so he hangs them on nails in the wall: clothes, kitchen utensils, laundry, etc... Now the prophet sees that the Messiah, the Savior, is this nail or peg fastened in a sure place, on which the believer hangs all his possessions and needs, and this in the Church, "his father's house." This is a symbolic picture meaning the believer's reliance on the Lord Christ, who dwells in His Church and bears all our burdens. Upon Him faithful kings place the crowns of their kingdom, and upon Him the poor man places his simple needs. He is the support of the great and the poor without distinction.

Every vessel - whatever its value - that is hung upon Him becomes a vessel of honor. So the believer says with the Apostle Paul: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" (2 Cor 4:7).

entries.section: 5. The setting up of Eliakim in place of Shebna:

paragraphs.text: This is about faith in the Lord Christ, the firm nail in the Church, the house of the Father; so what is meant by the removal of the nail [25]?

Some see that this removal means the Jews' rejection of the crucified Christ, so that those who have the prophecies concerning Him, and the types with them, pass away from their midst and are shattered. And some see that it points here to what the Jews at that time reckoned a sure, firm nail (Shebna or another), comparing faith in the Messiah, the Savior, with reliance on human ways of salvation.

1 The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them. 2 Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle; thou whom the merchants of Zidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished. 3 And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations. 4 Be thou ashamed, O Zidon: for the sea hath spoken, even the strength of the sea, saying, I travail not, nor bring forth children, neither do I nourish up young men, nor bring up virgins. 5 As at the report concerning Egypt, so shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre. 6 Pass ye over to Tarshish; howl, ye inhabitants of the isle. 7 Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn. 8 Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth? 9 The LORD of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth. 10 Pass through thy land as a river, O daughter of Tarshish: there is no more strength. 11 He stretched out his hand over the sea, he shook the kingdoms: the LORD hath given a commandment against the merchant city, to destroy the strong holds thereof. 12 And he said, Thou shalt no more rejoice, O thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon: arise, pass over to Chittim; there also shalt thou have no rest. 13 Behold the land of the Chaldeans; this people was not, till the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness: they set up the towers thereof, they raised up the palaces thereof; and he brought it to ruin. 14 Howl, ye ships of Tarshish: for your strength is laid waste.
We have already spoken about Tyre in our commentary on the Book of Ezekiel [Ezek 26].

The word “Tsor” (tsor) means “rock,” perhaps because the city was built on a rocky island. St. Jerome, however, holds that the word “Tyre” in Hebrew means “trial,” and so he sees its inhabitants as pointing to those who fall under the trial of Satan and his afflictions.
Keith and Urquhart hold that what is said in this chapter about Tyre was fulfilled literally.

Tyre fell under siege several times. Shalmaneser besieged it for five years and was not able to take it; Nebuchadnezzar besieged it for 13 years without success; Alexander the Great besieged it and took it after seven months in 332 B.C., and he destroyed it. Antigonus also besieged it, and in the Middle Ages it was besieged several times by the Crusaders. This Tyre is also counted responsible for the outbreak of the First World War, in which about 40 million people died, for it was kindled by Germany's attempt to build a railway between Berlin and Baghdad in order to develop trade with the countries of the Middle East.
What is stated here does not concern one particular siege of Tyre; rather, it represents what befalls every soul that imitates Tyre in being entangled with wealth and abominations.

The prophet describes the siege of Tyre, saying: “The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them” [1]. Here he brings out the effect of the destruction that befell Tyre upon the sailors of the merchant ships returning from Tarshish. It appears that they had not heard of the collapse of the city, and so they were astounded when they found no entrance to the city, for its walls had been torn down, and they found not a single house. The news, because of its gravity, spread until it reached Chittim, that is, the island of Cyprus, as a sign that all the nations of Europe heard of this event. Some hold that this siege was carried out by the Macedonian army, the army of Alexander the Great, coming from the island of Cyprus.

The prophet calls the neighboring cities to lament the state of Tyre, for she had been a source of good for them through trade, and now she has been utterly destroyed, and some cities lost a great deal of profit.

The merchants of Zidon heard (Zidon means “fishing”; it is about 22 miles north of Tyre and is considered the mother city of Tyre, so she came lamenting the state of her daughter). The merchants who used to go about in her streets came, and they were stunned at what had befallen her; they could not utter a word, but deep grief came upon them. As for the Egyptians, the dwellers of the Nile valley, they grieved because Tyre was an important center for the export of their produce and crops in exchange for the goods of Tyre. The prophet refers to the river Nile by the word “Sihor,” which means “disturbance” (Isa 22:3).

So Zidon grieves over her humbled, indeed collapsed, daughter “Tyre,” who had been like the bride of the Mediterranean Sea, or like a crowned queen who refreshed many lands in Africa and Europe. Now she has become like a spinster who groans in isolation, without husband or sons; she has lost the many lands that were like sons to her [4].

Egypt grieved because it lost an important center for exporting its produce, and perhaps because it feared that what befell Tyre would befall it. This is what happened in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, who plundered the wealth of Pharaoh after besieging Tyre (Ezek 29:17-20).

The prophet asks the remnant that remains in Tyre to depart to Tarshish, an ancient city in Spain and one of the flourishing colonies of Tyre. They departed wailing, because they were fleeing as refugees. Some hold that the prophet said this as a kind of mockery of the inhabitants of Tyre, who had been arrogant since ancient times: here they are, departing in terror and fear to live as strangers and refugees.

The prophet puts a theological question that stirs the hearers to search for the answer: “Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?” In other words, who has passed judgment on Tyre the crowned queen, who made of her colonies princes and rulers, and of her merchants honorable nobles throughout the whole world? She was a rich queen who poured out wealth, luxury and honor, together with pride, upon the nations that dealt with her. Who, then, has judged her thus?

The LORD of hosts is the One who purposed this [9], to bring her pride down to the dust and to bring into contempt all her merchants, men of dignity and worldly honor. This is what the prophet Amos meant when he said: “Shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?” (Amos 3:6). Father Theodoret says: [When divine judgment speaks to human beings, it speaks to them according to their language and their human feelings. The physician cuts or cauterizes those who suffer from sores for the sake of their health, and yet those who cannot bear it see that as an evil.]

God purposed this, but the cause of the ruin is pride and vainglory. It is sin that corrupts man as it does the nations, and God's judgment is only a declaration of what man brings upon himself by himself.

The prophet likens Tyre, fleeing after the destruction, to a woman who has lost everything and crosses the river Nile without a girdle to bind her garments; or he likens her to the waters of the Nile at its mouth, which pour into the sea with no one able to stop them. So the people of Tyre fled from their shattered city, without strength or power, as though the waters were sweeping them toward the sea [10]. Therefore he calls her “thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon” [12].

The Lord stretched out His hand in wrath over the sea, that is, He commanded the kingdoms to rise up against Phoenicia (Canaan) to destroy her strongholds [11] and shatter her pride, so that she no longer rejoices [12]; and instead of being a queen she becomes a disgraced virgin, who flees to Chittim (Cyprus) and finds no rest... What does this mean?

A. The Lord stretched out His hand calling to repentance, but Tyre did not respond to the call, and so the hand was stretched out for punishment. The Lord of glory also spread out His hands on the cross in love; whoever believed found in the cross the power of God unto salvation, and whoever rejected it came under judgment.

B. Tyre was to flee to Chittim... but she found no rest, for man's peace does not depend on the place where he is but on the depths of his inner soul. Man's rest is not in changing his place or his work or his social circumstances, but in returning to God his Savior, who calls: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mt 11:28). As St. John Saba says: [Blessed is he who seeks You within him every hour; from Him life flows to him that he may delight in it.]
Since God knew that Tyre would not listen to this voice, He asked her to take warning from what happened to the Chaldeans at the hand of the king of Assyria, for he turned their palaces into a ruin.

15 And it shall come to pass in that day, that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king: after the end of seventy years shall Tyre sing as an harlot. 16 Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered. 17 And it shall come to pass after the end of seventy years, that the LORD will visit Tyre, and she shall turn to her hire, and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. 18 And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.

In His love for mankind, God does not leave man in his corruption but offers him every possibility of salvation. Therefore, after the prophet portrayed the extent of the ruin that befell Tyre, he returned to speak of her renewal by the Lord the Savior.

She is left enslaved to Babylon for 70 years, which corresponds to the seventy years that the prophet Jeremiah foretold concerning the Babylonian captivity of Israel (Jer 29:10), as though the Gentiles share with Israel in this humiliation, because He has shut up all together in disobedience (Rom 11:32), that all may enjoy the Savior and mercy may be shown to all. Jerusalem was accused of being a harlot (Isa 1:21), and here Tyre bears the same accusation [16].
The period from the first year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar until Cyrus is exactly 70 years, during which the nations served Babylon.

The prophet describes Tyre as a harlot who sings in the public places to draw men to herself. So Tyre acted with her trade, which was bound up with corruption. But after she had gone about the world as though it were one city through which the harlot goes about, she fell under the dominion of Babylon for 70 years, in a humiliation in which she could not carry on her trade or spread corruption among the other nations, until she became forgotten. The world forgot her, but God will not forget her; rather, He turns her humiliation into glory. After her trade had been bound up with corruption, it returns to be bound up with the holy life in the Lord; her merchants become witnesses to the Gospel of salvation, as she enters with the Gentiles into the faith, to live the evangelical life and preach it. After she was in hunger and nakedness, not during the Babylonian captivity but during the bondage of sin, she has come into the presence of the Lord, eating of the bread of life so that she does not hunger, and enjoying the garment of Baptism so that she is not naked, as the Apostle says: “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal 3:27). This is what the prophet meant by saying: “And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the LORD: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the LORD, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing” [18].

1 Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof. 2 And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him. 3 The land shall be utterly emptied, and utterly spoiled: for the LORD hath spoken this word. 4 The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish. 5 The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant. 6 Therefore hath the curse devoured the earth, and they that dwell therein are desolate: therefore the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men left. 7 The new wine mourneth, the vine languisheth, all the merryhearted do sigh. 8 The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth. 9 They shall not drink wine with a song; strong drink shall be bitter to them that drink it. 10 The city of confusion is broken down: every house is shut up, that no man may come in. 11 There is a crying for wine in the streets; all joy is darkened, the mirth of the land is gone. 12 In the city is left desolation, and the gate is smitten with destruction. 13 When thus it shall be in the midst of the land among the people, there shall be as the shaking of an olive tree, and as the gleaning grapes when the vintage is done.

The prophet likens the whole earth to a vessel everything inside which has spoiled, so its owner empties it completely by turning it upside down. He says: “Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof. And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the taker of usury, so with the giver of usury to him” [1-2].

Thus all were shut up in disobedience, all deserved death, and all needed a Savior able to renew their nature. The priest shares in this with the people, the great with the despised, the rich with the poor. This matter calls, as it were, for the emptying of the earth so that it returns to what it was before the creation of the world, void and empty, and the Lord Himself recreates it.

This is the theological foundation of salvation: that creation had become utterly corrupt and needed its Maker to renew its creation. As Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says: [This is like the portrait of a man painted on a panel, which then happens to be disfigured by external stains; it becomes necessary for the one whose portrait it is to come again to renew the image of the face on the same wood (the panel).]

What have sin and disobedience done to mankind? Mankind drew near to the fires of the divine wrath and was burned. The secret of the burning is man's disobedient will, which drags him toward destruction.

The prophet Isaiah offers a comparison that reveals the wretched state to which mankind has come. In the season of the vintage, people used to hold joyful celebrations: they would drink wine, sing with gladness, and make offerings to the poor. But when the time of gathering came, the vineyards proclaimed their mourning, for they bore no grapes; the players of tambourines stopped beating them; there was no one to sing and no one to rejoice, for every pleasure had fled from the face of the earth, and ruin came by the fire of God's wrath, so that everything in the world became ashes [7-12]. Thus he likens the world to a burned city turned to ashes, and to mournful, dry fields that bear no fruit. He likens it to an olive tree that has shed its leaves and become bare, with neither fruit nor leaves [13], and to a vine from which all its clusters have been taken away.
It is fitting for the priest to realize his need of salvation just like the people [2], and as St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [In truth there is no distinction between the people and the priests...]

entries.section: 2. The joy of the believers in the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 14 They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD, they shall cry aloud from the sea. 15 Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the east, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea. 16 From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.
In the midst of this ruin, which deprived mankind of its inner peace and joy, there is a holy remnant that proclaims its gladness and joy in the Lord through praise and psalmody.
“They shall lift up their voice, they shall sing for the majesty of the LORD, they shall cry aloud from the sea.
Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the east, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.
From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous” [14-16].

Here he speaks of the small remnant in the world that accepted the faith and returned to God. These live in the east, that is, they enjoy the Sun of Righteousness shining upon them (Mal 4:3). And lest anyone think that the east here is merely a place, he said: “in the isles of the sea glorify the name of the LORD,” to affirm that those who dwell in the west (the islands of the Mediterranean, west of Jerusalem) enjoy salvation together with those in the east.
The theme of the praise is “Glory to (Christ) the Righteous!”

17 Fear, and the pit, and the snare, are upon thee, O inhabitant of the earth. 18 And it shall come to pass, that he who fleeth from the noise of the fear shall fall into the pit; and he that cometh up out of the midst of the pit shall be taken in the snare: for the windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake. 19 The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly. 20 The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again. 21 And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall punish the host of the high ones that are on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth. 22 And they shall be gathered together, as prisoners are gathered in the pit, and shall be shut up in the prison, and after many days shall they be visited. 23 Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously.
The salvation that God offers to mankind kindles the hearts of the believers with joy and exultation, and it stirs up terror in the unbelieving deniers and also in the demons.

The enemy of good realized that a plundering had been carried out against him, for the cross drew many of the souls that the enemy had enslaved, and the Resurrection shattered all the powers of darkness and opened the gates of Paradise.

The prophet sees the enemy of good as a wild beast that fell into the nets, into a pit, and opened its mouth lamenting its state in despair, with fear and trembling [16-18]. He was terrified when he saw himself descending toward the abyss as into an exceedingly deep pit, while heaven and earth stood witnessing to the cross: “The windows from on high are open, and the foundations of the earth do shake; the earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly” [18-19]; “In that day the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion and in Jerusalem” [23].

Thus nature bears witness to the weight of the sin that the Lord Christ bore for us, as though it were an exceedingly heavy mass thrust down upon the earth, splitting it and shaking it and stirring up earthquakes in it, until the moon was ashamed and the sun confounded at what sin had done. And on the other hand, nature stood, as it were, in shame and humiliation before what man did to his Savior and Redeemer.

By the cross we entered into the spiritual reign (Rev 20), where the LORD of hosts reigns in mount Zion in Jerusalem [23]; He reigns by the cross over the hearts of the believers, binding the devil and all his spiritual hosts as captives until the time of the apostasy comes [22], for He made a public show of them (Col 2:15), granting us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy.
The sight of the cross shattered the enemy, declaring the divine glory before the elders [23], for the Apostles beheld the power of salvation and understood it in their lives as in their preaching.

entries.section: 1. A song of thanksgiving to God:

paragraphs.text: 1 O LORD, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth. 2 For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built. 3 Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee. 4 For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall. 5 Thou shalt bring down the noise of strangers, as the heat in a dry place; even the heat with the shadow of a cloud: the branch of the terrible ones shall be brought low.

The eyes of the prophet Isaiah were opened to the Kingdom of Christ, so his heart overflowed with exultation and his tongue was loosed to praise God for His work of salvation. After prophesying of bitter chastisements, he became a psalmist offering psalms of thanksgiving to God. The secret of his praise and thanksgiving to God is:

A. The fulfillment of God's words and His faithful and true promises: “O LORD, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth” [1]. The prophet realized that the secret of salvation lies in God's faithful promises and the wonderful work of His hands. Therefore St. Irenaeus comments on this song, saying: [We see here that we are not saved by ourselves but by the help of God.]

We praise God and give thanks to Him for His wonderful eternal divine purposes, for from of old He has been concerned for our salvation, before we existed, because we were in His mind, the object of His love.

entries.section: 1. A song of thanksgiving to God:

paragraphs.text: B. The destruction of evil (Babylon): “For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built” [2].

Our salvation by the divine arm is accomplished by doing away with evil, that is, with the city of Babylon, arrogant and full of confusion, which embraces the Antichrist. It is as though the secret of our praise is the rising of the Kingdom of Christ, which is accompanied by the collapse of the kingdom of the devil, the opponent of the truth, the shattering of his city and the demolition of his palace.

Perhaps the city here refers to the enemy of good's dominion over a community, the village refers to his dominion over a smaller group such as the family, and the palace refers to his possession of the heart. For the enemy of good works on every level to reign through the community, the family or the individual... and our Christ also resists him on every level in order to demolish every trace of his kingdom.

As for calling the soul that the enemy dominates a “palace of strangers” or a “palace of foreigners,” it is because the enemy of good and his angels occupy the soul as strangers and foreigners, possessing what is not theirs; it is God's good creation into which they have crept.

Perhaps also the demolition of the city, the village or the palace refers to the demolition of our old man with all his works for the sake of the continual renewal of our inner man in the image of his Creator (2 Cor 4:16).

entries.section: 1. A song of thanksgiving to God:

paragraphs.text: C. Preaching: Among the things that gladden the heart and fill it with praise is that the rising of the inner kingdom of Christ, with the demolition of the kingdom of the enemy of good in us, is accompanied by witness, or preaching, of the work of God and the Gospel of His salvation, so that many souls are drawn and a strong Church arises, strong not in numbers but because of her almighty Christ who dwells in her. The prophet says: “Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee” [3].

Our souls exult in God's strong people, who carry within them the power of His Resurrection that overcomes death, so that they live as “terrible ones” (mighty men of valor) who practice the fear of God. As it is said of them: “and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army” (Ezek 37:10); “terrible as an army with banners” (Song 6:10).

When the city of Babylon collapses in us, the defenced village of the devil is broken down and his palace is laid waste, the Lord reigns in order to raise from us a strong people, terrifying to the enemy... What is this terrifying people but the sanctification of soul and body, thought, words and feelings, even to the shadow of man? Did not diseases flee from the shadow of the Apostle Peter (Acts 5:15)? Did not demons and evil spirits come out at the mere sight of the handkerchiefs of the Apostle Paul?

entries.section: 1. A song of thanksgiving to God:

paragraphs.text: D. Justice for the wronged: “For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall. Thou shalt bring down the noise of strangers, as the heat in a dry place...” [4-5].

Mankind groans under the law of injustice that has prevailed over it since sin entered it. Therefore God Himself comes forward as a practical secret of consolation, upholding every wounded soul, offering Himself as strength and stronghold to the poor and needy in the time of distress, a refuge from the floods (the storms), and a shadow from the heat while the blast of the mighty man is like a storm against a wall. It is as though God, in His surpassing love and fatherly care, presents Himself to His believers according to their needs, becoming everything to them for their peace, their edification and their fulfillment; He is the strength, the stronghold, the refuge, the dark cloud, the bread that came down from heaven, and so on...

entries.section: 2. The feast of the New Covenant:

paragraphs.text: 6 And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined. 7 And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the vail that is spread over all nations. 8 He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it. 9 And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the LORD; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.

The Word of God the Savior comes to every soul to be the One who satisfies its needs and gives it peace and strength against the evil enemy, so that the soul enjoys the new life in Christ as a joyful and perpetual feast. This feast is in truth the satisfying evangelical life offered to all peoples, which he describes here as follows:

A. A universal feast: “And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast...” [6]. The door has been opened wide to all peoples to enjoy the word of God, His covenants, His promises, His laws and His works of salvation, especially communion in the Eucharist (the Body and Blood of the Lord); God's gifts are no longer the monopoly of a particular people or a special race.
The Lord Christ declares the universality of the call by saying: “Go ye therefore into the highways, and as many as ye shall find, bid to the marriage” (Mt 22:9).

B. A rich feast, which he called “a feast of fat things” [6]. What is this rich feast, or rich festival, but the sacrament of the Eucharist, where believers from all peoples join the heavenly beings in praise, and the doors of heaven are opened before them, or rather the Church becomes heaven, so that the believers may enjoy the broken Body of the Lord and His precious Blood for their salvation and fulfillment?
* [“The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want...” (Ps 23)]

Hear about the nature of the sacraments that you have received. Hear what David says to you... How did he begin his psalm, saying that he is no longer in want of anything? Why? Because whoever partakes of the Body of Christ hungers no more.

St. Ambrose * Those who were deprived of earthly blessings because of their young age are given heavenly gifts richly, to the full, so that they have the right to sing with joy, saying: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Ps 23:1).
St. Didymus the Blind * This table is the support of our souls, the bond of our mind, the foundation of our hope, our salvation, our light and our life.
* When you see the table prepared before you, say to yourself:
Because of His Body I shall no longer be dust and ashes, nor a prisoner, but free!
Because of this (Body) I hope for heaven, and I receive the heavenly good things, the immortal life, the portion of the angels, and conversation with Christ.
This Body was nailed with nails and scourged, and death can no longer overpower it!
It is the Body that was stained with blood and pierced, and from it came out the two springs that save the world: the spring of blood and the spring of water.

St. John Chrysostom C. A spiritually joyful feast: “A feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined” [6]. The wine signifies spiritual joy; and its being refined, or pure, means that it does not take away man's consciousness and make him drunk, but gives him spiritual gladness.

* The cup of the Lord makes us drunk in a certain way, as Noah drank a cup of intoxicating wine in the Book of Genesis, but the drunkenness of the cup of the Lord and His blood is not like the drunkenness of the wine of the world... For the cup of the Lord makes those who drink it sober and brings their thoughts back to spiritual wisdom; it moves man from the taste of the world to the understanding of God... It frees the soul and removes its gloom from it... It gives rest to the soul, for it offers it the joy of divine goodness in place of the heart's dark depression under the weight of the burdens of sin.

entries.section: 2. The feast of the New Covenant:

paragraphs.text: The Martyr Cyprian D. A heavenly feast: through it the covering is uncovered and the veil of the letter is removed, so that the partakers enter heaven itself and come to know its mysteries, which were hidden from all the sons of men. “And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the vail that is spread over all nations” [7].

* The people who have been purified and filled with wondrous gifts begin to walk toward the altar, saying: “To the house of God we go, God gladdens our youth...” They hasten toward the heavenly feast.
St. Ambrose * Every time we serve the liturgy of this sacrifice, it is fitting for us to count ourselves as those who are in heaven.

entries.section: 2. The feast of the New Covenant:

paragraphs.text: Father Theodoret E. A life-giving feast: “He will swallow up death in victory” [8].

* Through (this sacrifice) we, who are by nature mortal, await immortality, and we, who are corruptible, incorruption, and in place of the earth and its evils we receive the blessings and joys of heaven.

Father Theodoret * Lest we be puffed up, supposing that life is of ourselves, and become arrogant toward God... we must know by experience that we receive eternal life not from our nature but by the power of this Supreme Being, “the Eucharist.”

St. Irenaeus F. A glorious feast: “And the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it” [8]. For He gives His believers rest in Him through the holy life, or through their enjoyment of the righteousness of Christ. If tears crept into all mankind through its disobedience, our union with God in His Son by the Holy Spirit gives us steadfastness in Christ, who was obedient to the Father; so He removes from us the burden of our disobedience and dries our inner tears, granting the soul glories within, which we experience in our temporal life as a pledge of the eternal heavenly glory.

Our life is a striving and a struggle against the powers of darkness, a continual battle whose field is the inner heart, but our Christ gives us the overcoming and the victory; He binds up every wound and wipes away every tear.
* The sacramental table is the Body of the Lord, who supports us against our lusts and against Satan.
Truly Satan trembles before those who partake of these mysteries with reverence.
St. Cyril of Alexandria

10 For in this mountain shall the hand of the LORD rest, and Moab shall be trodden down under him, even as straw is trodden down for the dunghill. 11 And he shall spread forth his hands in the midst of them, as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim: and he shall bring down their pride together with the spoils of their hands. 12 And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls shall he bring down, lay low, and bring to the ground, even to the dust.

As the believers, who overcome sorrow, bitterness, tears, and even death, exult through the free feast of salvation, they say: “Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us” [9]. Our joy lies in our salvation from our enemies, that is, from the devil and all his hosts and all his evil works. For the glory of the children of God is accompanied by the shame of the powers of darkness, which are symbolized here by Moab. “And Moab shall be trodden down under him, even as straw is trodden down for the dunghill. And he shall spread forth his hands in the midst of them, as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim: and he shall bring down their pride together with the spoils of their hands. And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls shall he bring down, lay low, and bring to the ground, even to the dust” [10-11].

If the powers of darkness have exalted themselves over the children of God and supposed that they were able to humble them, God by the cross demolished their strongholds and brought them down to the abyss, granting us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and all the powers of darkness; we tread them as straw is trodden for use in building materials (in making mud bricks). It is as though those powers that were the cause of our destruction are turned, through the saving work of God, into a despised and humbled instrument under the feet, used for the edification of our souls; for without the devil we would not be crowned.

The secret of the enemy's destruction is his pride, for he counted himself fortified by impregnable walls, but God brings these walls down to the ground, so that the enemy's weakness is exposed and the truth of his helplessness before our God is revealed.

entries.section: 1. A psalm urging trust in God:

paragraphs.text: 1 In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks. 2 Open ye the gates, that the righteous nation which keepeth the truth may enter in. 3 Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee. 4 Trust ye in the LORD for ever: for in the LORD JEHOVAH is the rock of ages.

The psalm begins with the introduction: “In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah” [1]. It is the song of the New Covenant; it was not possible for the men of the Old Covenant to sing it, and so he says “in that day.” The blessings enjoyed by the ancient people, such as the return from captivity, do not bring lasting joy except insofar as they are a type of the joyful salvation accomplished by our return from the captivity of sin through the work of the cross.
This psalm is a song for Jerusalem, the city of God, because of the strength and fortification she enjoyed, with open gates, and righteousness, faithfulness and peace for her inhabitants...
“We have a strong city” [1] means Jerusalem, a type of the heavenly Jerusalem, and also the Church of the New Covenant, as the city of God in which the Lord Himself dwells with His people.

“Salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” [1]; God's saving works are the walls of the city and its instruments of war, so the enemy of good cannot storm it. He may fight against it and try to entice it, but he will not be able to overcome it so long as it is faithful to the Lord.

The Fathers of the Church, especially St. Augustine, often spoke of our inner life as the Church of Christ, the heavenly city of the Lord. In its essence this city is the dwelling of God, who is Love, with men; love is its founder, its treasure, its language and its law... The city of the Lord is the city of love!
* When you attain perfect knowledge and become, through love, the throne of God, you become heaven!
The heaven that we see with our eyes when we look up is not very precious to God; the holy souls are the heaven of God...
Every soul is Zion...

It is clear that Zion is the city of God; and what is the city of God but the holy Church? When men love one another and love God who dwells in them, they become the city of God... For it is plainly written: “God is love” (1 Jn 4:8). Whoever is filled with love is filled with God.
* We have learned that there is a city of God, whose Founder inspired in us the love that makes us desire citizenship in it.

St. Augustine * In love God established every soul to be His fortified city and His holy heavens; He established her as His heavenly bride, united with Him, having the same possibilities as her bridegroom the Savior, who ascended into the heavens, and the everlasting doors were opened before Him that the King of glory might enter in (Ps 24:7-10). She is also His bride who carries His righteousness and faithfulness; the doors of heaven are opened before her, that she may sit at the right hand of her bridegroom the King and in His bosom, and no power can prevent her from passing through the heavenly places until she reaches His throne. She is like Queen Esther, who passed through all the doors of the palace to reach the king, who stretched out to her his golden scepter that she might enter to him, and he caressed her and listened to her petition.

entries.section: 1. A psalm urging trust in God:

paragraphs.text: Isaiah perhaps enjoyed these prophetic feelings when he saw in the Spirit those returning from captivity entering the gates of Jerusalem opened before them, entering as in a procession of victory or a festal procession of joy in the Lord. He said: “Open ye the gates, that the righteous nation which keepeth the truth may enter in” [2].
* “Lift up your gates, O ye princes” (Ps 24:7); let us go straight to heaven.
May the prophet's trumpet sound aloud: “Lift up, O ye rulers of the air, the gates that you have set up in the minds of men...”
St. Augustine St. Ambrose comments on the phrase “Be ye lift up, ye everlasting gates; and the King of glory shall come in” (Ps 24:7), saying:

[They found that a new way must be prepared before the face of this new “Victor,” for He is always, as He was, greater than others; but because the gates of righteousness, which are the gates of the Old and New Testaments, in which the heavens are opened, are everlasting gates, therefore they are truly unchanging, yet they were lifted up, because the One who enters them is not a man but the whole world in the person of the Savior of all...

When (the angels) perceived the approach of the Lord of all, the first conqueror of death and the only Victor, they commanded the (heavenly) hosts to lift up the gates, saying in rapture and devotion... “Be ye lift up, ye everlasting gates; and the King of glory shall come in”].

Thus, as heaven is opened before the believers united with our Lord Jesus, and they are raised with Him to His heavens, they live here in true peace and trust in the Savior. Therefore the prophet says:

entries.section: 1. A psalm urging trust in God:

paragraphs.text: “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee” [3]. A wonderful expression of the sure assurance that God gives to His believers who are faithful to Him, for He gives them peace followed by peace until they reach the final victory because of their reliance on Him.

entries.section: 1. A psalm urging trust in God:

paragraphs.text: By “whose mind is stayed” he means those with a firm purpose, or a balanced, unshakable mind, whom the storms of events do not cause to lose their confidence in God their Savior, Jehovah the rock of ages (Isa 26:4; Ps 18:31): “Trust ye in the LORD for ever: for in the LORD JEHOVAH is the rock of ages” [4].
* Wretched is the people that turns away from God... But our own peace we enjoy now with God by faith, and we shall enjoy it eternally with Him by sight.

St. Augustine * Everyone ought to reform himself, and be at peace with himself, and there should be no division in his conscience. For if a man is reconciled with the whole world while he is divided against himself, his reconciliation is of no benefit. But he who reforms his soul and is at peace with himself is like one who has made peace with the whole world, and he is honored in the eyes of the Master of all.

* Have pity, O Lord, on the soul that has been kindled with Your love, for she is the dwelling of peace; so leave no trace of sin in the conscience, the place of Your dwelling, but burn it with the fire of Your love.
St. John of the Thebaid

5 For he bringeth down them that dwell on high; the lofty city, he layeth it low; he layeth it low, even to the ground; he bringeth it even to the dust. 6 The foot shall tread it down, even the feet of the poor, and the steps of the needy.
“For he bringeth down them that dwell on high” [5-6].

If Babylon has exalted herself and supposed that she is on high, the Lord will bring her down to the dust, to make her trodden by the feet of the poor, whom she had previously trampled with her feet. This is the end of every proud person who opposes the truth, for he drinks of the same cup that he offered to others.

God's constant work is to glorify humble, lowly Jerusalem and establish her as a city of His own, and to bring down proud Babylon. As St. Mary said: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away” (Lk 1:53).
* You taught me the ways of humility, through which men return to life, having fallen because of pride.
St. Augustine * By pride we lean upon the winds, and by it we thrust ourselves into the deep; so do not accept the disease of pride, lest the enemy rob you...
* In the humble man the spirit of wisdom rests.
St. Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 3. The Lord's support for His righteous ones:

paragraphs.text: 7 The way of the just is uprightness: thou, most upright, dost weigh the path of the just. 8 Yea, in the way of thy judgments, O LORD, have we waited for thee; the desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the remembrance of thee. 9 With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early: for when thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. 10 Let favour be shewed to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness: in the land of uprightness will he deal unjustly, and will not behold the majesty of the LORD. 11 LORD, when thy hand is lifted up, they will not see: but they shall see, and be ashamed for their envy at the people; yea, the fire of thine enemies shall devour them. 12 LORD, thou wilt ordain peace for us: for thou also hast wrought all our works for us. 13 O LORD our God, other lords beside thee have had dominion over us: but by thee only will we make mention of thy name. 14 They are dead, they shall not live; they are deceased, they shall not rise: therefore hast thou visited and destroyed them, and made all their memory to perish. 15 Thou hast increased the nation, O LORD, thou hast increased the nation: thou art glorified: thou hast enlarged all the ends of the earth. 16 LORD, in trouble have they visited thee, they poured out a prayer when thy chastening was upon them.

In this psalm the prophet presents to us a wonderful analysis of the life of the righteous man, who finds his delight, his protection and his glory in the Lord; and at the same time he calls us to secret prayer in the closet, with attention to God's judgments and commandments and obedience to Him, to enjoy His free salvation.

entries.section: 3. The Lord's support for His righteous ones:

paragraphs.text: A. God's judgments or commandments are not a burden on the soul of the righteous man; rather they are the cause of his uprightness, so he seeks them and desires them with joy and gladness of heart, saying: “In the way of thy judgments... have we waited for thee” [8]. It is as though the commandment, or the word of God, is the object of the soul's hope, delight and joy. As the psalmist says: “I have rejoiced in the way of thy testimonies, as much as in all riches... I will delight myself in thy statutes... Thy testimonies also are my delight” (Ps 119:14, 16, 24).

Perhaps the secret of the righteous man's joy and gladness in the commandment is that he discovers its depths and finds it to be an encounter with Christ the Word of God and an enjoyment of Him as a mystery of salvation and life. As St. Augustine says: [We understand that there is no way swifter or safer or shorter or higher than Christ with regard to the testimonies of God, He “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3). Therefore he (the psalmist) says that he finds in Him great delight as in all riches. These are the testimonies by which (Christ) assured us how far He loves us...]

B. The secret of the righteous man's joy is his union with God his Savior and his clinging to His holy name and remembrance: “The desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the remembrance of thee. With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early” [8-9]. The soul realizes that in the night of this world she needs the light of the Savior to shine upon her, and indeed within her. She seeks Him in the night because she has tasted what is most bitter throughout the toil of the day and its unceasing pains, so she wants to meet Him within her, to find in Him her rest, her peace and her fulfillment, as the desire of her soul. She asks Him that she may enjoy all His kisses (Song 1:2), and she converses with Him, saying: “His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 5:16).
The soul desires Him that she may cling to Him through all the night of this world, until eternity dawns upon her and she remains with Him in His embrace forever.

She seeks Him within her; she searches for Him and finds Him seeking her; she rises early to Him and finds Him rising early to her. She converses with Him: “Early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is; to see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary” (Ps 63:1-2). And He answers: “I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me. Riches and honour are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness” (Prov 8:17-18).

entries.section: 3. The Lord's support for His righteous ones:

paragraphs.text: C. The end of the righteous man is his enjoyment of the divine glory, which the wicked are deprived of, as the prophet says: “In the land of uprightness will he deal unjustly, and will not behold the majesty of the LORD” [10]. The righteous man enjoys the glory and majesty of the Lord, and the splendor of the Lord is reflected upon him so that he becomes an icon of Him, while the wicked is deprived of the enjoyment of this eternal gift.

* Blessed, thrice blessed, indeed many times blessed are those who are counted worthy to see that glory! Of this the prophet says: “Let the wicked be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord” [10 LXX].

God does not allow any one of us to be taken away or kept from seeing Him. For if we do not enjoy this, a time will come when we say to ourselves: “It would have been better for us never to have been born.” For why do we live? And why do we breathe? What are we if we fail to enjoy the sight of this and are not granted to behold the Lord? If those who do not see the light of the sun count life as more bitter than death, what will be the state of those deprived of such a light?

St. John Chrysostom * It is fitting for us to understand that it is for the sake of this perfection that “we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1 Jn 3:2). This gift is granted when it is said: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you” (Mt 25:34). Then the wicked are taken away so that they do not see the majesty of the Lord, and those on the left go away into everlasting punishment, while those on the right enter into life eternal.

* John says: “Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1 Jn 3:2). This likeness begins to take shape in us from now, while the inner man is renewed day by day after the image of his Creator.

St. Augustine Thus God becomes the secret of the glory of His righteous ones, not only in the world to come, but their glory begins now within them, as they behold the glory and majesty of God as a pledge of meeting Him eternally face to face; and God Himself becomes the cause of the deprivation of the wicked; He is the King of peace to His believers and a consuming fire to those who deny Him. The Apostle says: “To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life” (2 Cor 2:16). Therefore the prophet Isaiah continues, saying:
“LORD, when thy hand is lifted up, they will not see: but they shall see, and be ashamed for their envy at the people; yea, the fire of thine enemies shall devour them.

entries.section: 3. The Lord's support for His righteous ones:

paragraphs.text: LORD, thou wilt ordain peace for us: for thou also hast wrought (rendered) all our works for us” [11-12].

entries.section: 3. The Lord's support for His righteous ones:

paragraphs.text: The Lord lifts up His hand to discipline His children, and gives them peace and growth, since they receive it as discipline for their sins; but for the wicked, the punishment is a consuming fire that destroys them and makes their memory perish [14].

17 Like as a woman with child, that draweth near the time of her delivery, is in pain, and crieth out in her pangs; so have we been in thy sight, O LORD. 18 We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth; neither have the inhabitants of the world fallen. 19 Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust: for thy dew is as the dew of herbs, and the earth shall cast out the dead.

The prophet realizes the blessings of affliction for the people of God, saying: “Thou hast increased the nation, O LORD, thou hast increased the nation: thou art glorified: thou hast enlarged all the ends of the earth. LORD, in trouble have they visited thee, they poured out a prayer when thy chastening was upon them” [15-16]. It is as though discipline causes distress and weariness outwardly, but it leads to continual growth and expansion in glory.

The secret of strength is not in affliction but in the hidden hand of God, able to raise from the dead. The prophet saw his people like a woman writhing with the pains of labor, who bears with effort and then brings forth wind, that is, the pains of labor end in nothing; but if God intervenes, then even if man in his sufferings reaches death, He is able to give him resurrection, to give him a new, risen life full of joy and praise.

The wicked suffer as in the state of childbirth, but they bring forth out of themselves (the ego) wind, or empty pride; but the children of God suffer and bring forth by the work of the Spirit, in likeness to God. It is as though pain apart from the Lord Christ gives birth to wind, but in Christ it brings forth resurrection!

The prophet says: “Like as a woman with child, that draweth near the time of her delivery, is in pain, and crieth out in her pangs; so have we been in thy sight, O LORD. We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind; we have not wrought any deliverance in the earth... Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise. Awake and sing, ye that dwell in dust...” [17-19].

The psalmist says: “For, lo, the kings were assembled... They saw it, and so they marvelled; they were troubled, and hasted away. Fear took hold upon them there, and pain, as of a woman in travail” (Ps 48:4-6). St. Augustine sees that the kings are the company of believers who conceive from the fear of God and enter into labor to bring forth salvation through faith. When we hear of their sufferings we expect a new birth, in which the old man dies with all his works and the new man is born in the image of his Creator.

St. Augustine addresses the virgin soul joined to Christ her Bridegroom, saying: [It is well for you, O virgin soul... By your virginity you keep in your heart what you have borne again (the new man), and keep in your body what you have brought forth, since you conceived by the fear of the Lord and gave birth to the spirit of salvation.]

entries.section: 5. God is the Savior of His people:

paragraphs.text: 20 Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast. 21 For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity: the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain.

If God is angry, it is not to avenge Himself but to discipline, declaring His love for our salvation; therefore He called the period of His anger “a little moment,” which passes quickly, as He waits to reward His believers, while the wicked drink from the cup of their evil what they have filled for themselves.

Our life with all its pains is “a little moment” that passes quickly with us, not to be compared with a glorious eternity without end. Therefore St. Augustine says: [There is a rest in death, of which the prophet speaks, saying: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.”]

How beautiful that the hymn of the Resurrection before us should be concluded with the wonderful phrase: “For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish” [26]. He is a heavenly Father who longs not to punish; if He disciplines, it is as one who has come out of his place, that is, out of mercy full of compassion and tenderness. Our iniquity and disobedience make Him as one who comes out of His place to punish... even in His coming out He seeks to gather us to Himself, to bring us back to the throne of His mercy.
“In that day the LORD with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea.” [1].

Some see in the expression “in that day” a reference to the last day, in which God strikes Satan his final, decisive blow, when the Church enjoys eternal life and the enemy of good perishes, and the followers of the millennial reign try to count it as the day of the thousand-year reign, when the dominion of the devil is shattered; but we see it as the day of the cross, or the day of redemption, in which the Lord reigned from the tree of the cross, and in which He “blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:14-15), for the (spiritual) thousand-year reign began with the crucifixion of the Lord.

As I said before, the tendency of some commentators to apply Isaiah's prophecies of the Messianic age to the thousand-year reign is the natural fruit of present-day Christians not tasting the power of the cross in their lives, not experiencing the divine authority against the devil and his works, and not being in touch with the inner life of victory, full of joy and a peace that surpasses understanding.

What is this sore sword with which the Lord punishes Leviathan but the word of God, the sharp two-edged sword that goes out of His mouth (Rev 1:16; Heb 4:12)? Through the word we meet Christ Himself, “the incarnate, crucified Word of God,” hidden behind the letters and words, always working for our salvation. As Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says: [The Son of God is living and active, working day by day for the salvation of all.]

The punishing of the serpent with the sword and the slaying of the dragon of the sea mean that the incarnate Word of God, our crucified Christ who dwells within us, takes over the leadership of the battle to judge every evil in us until He shatters all darkness, establishing in us the kingdom of light.

* He has overcome the whole world, as we see, beloved... He conquered not by military power but by the foolishness of the cross... His body was lifted up on the cross, and the spirits submitted to Him.

St. Augustine * The Lord despoiled the principalities and powers and triumphed over them by His cross. And this was the reason for our Lord's coming: to cast them out and to recover man, who is His house and His temple.
