"Cometh from far" because He was long-suffering toward Assyria, in case it might turn back from the pride of its heart, and He waited long, for He does not seek punishment but the return of all to Him, and His name still comes from far, being long-suffering toward the wicked, that perhaps they may repent. As the Apostle Paul says: "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?" (Rom 5:4).

"The name of God" dwells in the life of the Church, is declared in the heart of the believer, is near to him, nearer than himself, but to the wicked it seems very far, and even sometimes he thinks it does not exist. This name is a strong tower for the believers (Ps 18:50) and a kindled anger and a great burning for those who resist.
The lips of the Lord drop fatness for His children and are full of indignation for those who deny Him!
His tongue calls all to His heavenly goods and is as a devouring fire to the disobedient.

His breath bestows comfort and a peace which passeth all understanding on the Church, for the Lord breathed on the face of His disciples and gave them His Holy Spirit working in them for the forgiveness of sins (Jn 20:22); but for those who reject the faith, His breath is as an overflowing stream that reaches to their neck.

entries.section: 4. The wrath of God against Assyria:

paragraphs.text: He likens the nations to an empty harvest that is all straw without wheat, or to unruly horses that bridles do not restrain, for he says: "to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity (the sieve of nothingness)" [28], for they sift and the sieve brings up nothing. "And there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err" [28]. Bridles are put in their mouths but they do not walk in the way of truth.

entries.section: 4. The wrath of God against Assyria:

paragraphs.text: B. "Ye shall have a song, as in the night when a holy solemnity is kept; and gladness of heart, as when one goeth with a pipe to come into the mountain of the LORD, to the mighty One of Israel. And the LORD shall cause his glorious voice to be heard, and shall shew the lighting down of his arm, with the indignation of his anger, and with the flame of a devouring fire, with scattering, and tempest, and hailstones" [29-30].

The destruction of the enemy turns into joy for the people, as on a Paschal night... Perhaps what concerns the believers is not the destruction of the enemy (even the devil himself and his angels) but the removal of the obstacles so that they come to the mountain of the Lord, to heaven itself, rejoicing. Our goal is not to gloat over the enemy of good, but our enjoyment of the glory of the Lord and our hearing His voice.

entries.section: 4. The wrath of God against Assyria:

paragraphs.text: C. Isaiah sees in the return of the people from captivity to Jerusalem something like a military procession entering its country with military music proclaiming victory; "And in every place where the grounded staff shall pass, which the LORD shall lay upon him, it shall be with tabrets and harps: and in battles of shaking will he fight with it" [32].

entries.section: 4. The wrath of God against Assyria:

paragraphs.text: D. He presents a final picture of the extent of Assyria's destruction, for he depicts the place of the fire, "Tophet," the place where the remains were burned outside Jerusalem, as prepared to contain the king, "the god Moloch," who will burn with the wrath of the Lord [33].

1 Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD! 2 Yet he also is wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words: but will arise against the house of the evildoers, and against the help of them that work iniquity. 3 Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together.

The prophet Isaiah presents to us a wonderful spiritual thought, for the matter of resorting to Pharaoh is not merely a political and military plan but a theological matter that touches the life of man and his eternal destiny. He who leans on men, however great their number, their resources, or their strength [1], clings to carnal, mortal people and becomes mortal like them, while he who clings to the Savior, the Holy One of Israel, the unchangeable, the eternal, carries immortality with him. Our reliance on men unites us with them and we perish; our reliance on God binds us to Him and we share His eternal glories. This is what he meant when he warned them, saying: "Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together" [3].
Let us then lean on the eternal Creator, not on the weak creature that is unable even to help itself.
* "Put not your trust in princes" (Ps 146:4)...
Now, through a kind of weakness of the human soul, when a man falls into distress he despairs of God, choosing to lean on a man.

Let someone say to a man fallen into distress: "There is a great man who will set you free," and at once he smiles and rejoices and his spirits rise; but if it is said to him, "God will set you free," he falls into a state of discouragement and despair!
You rejoice when you receive help from a mortal; how then do you grieve when you receive help from the Creator?!

You have received a promise that one who himself needs to be set free will set you free, and your spirits rise like one who has received great help. Here you receive a promise from the One (God) who sets free, who needs no one to set Him free, and yet you despair as though you had received a feeble thing.
Woe to such thoughts! They have gone astray; truly a grievous and sorrowful death has come upon them!
* "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish" (Ps 146:4)...
"I have seen the wicked in great power, exalted above the cedars of Lebanon. Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found" (Ps 37:35-36)...
All these are subject to death, quickly passing, perishing.

Then what must we do if we do not hope in the sons of men nor in princes? What must we do? "Blessed is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help" (Ps 146:5), whose help is not this man or that man, nor this angel or that angel, but "blessed is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help." For Jacob had a great helper, who thus raised up Israel from Jacob. What a mighty help! Now he is Israel, "who sees God"! If you also remain here and do not wander away from the vision of God, if the God of Jacob becomes your helper, then you are changed from Jacob into Israel; you see God, and troubles and all sighs come to an end, confusions cease, and happy songs of praise take their place...
Let your hope be in the Lord your God, let your hope be in Him.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 2. God, the protector of His children:

paragraphs.text: 4 For thus hath the LORD spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, he will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the LORD of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof. 5 As birds flying, so will the LORD of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver it; and sparing he will preserve it.

If the enemy of good, the devil, is like a roaring lion who wants to devour in order to eat and be satisfied and destroy his prey (1 Pet 5:8), then "the Holy One of Israel" is the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5), who does not destroy the prey but is able to protect it. He acquires the soul as prey, surrounding it, to give it His royal traits, so He makes His believers "priests and kings" (Rev 1:6), giving them His immortality and a share in His glories.

entries.section: 2. God, the protector of His children:

paragraphs.text: God is a trustworthy refuge, able to protect us and also to shepherd us; therefore He likens Himself to the lion, the king of the beasts, before whom no one can stand, and at the same time to a bird that cares for its young [5].
Our Christ shepherds us on the Cross as a lion who couched and lay down (Gen 49:9), and the enemy was not able to approach Him, nor to approach us.

entries.section: 3. A call to return to God:

paragraphs.text: 6 Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted. 7 For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your own hands have made unto you for a sin. 8 Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man; and the sword, not of a mean man, shall devour him: but he shall flee from the sword, and his chosen ones shall be under tribute. 9 And his rock shall pass away for fear, and his princes shall be afraid of the ensign, saith the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem.

The prophet reveals the purpose of God's work with them, for the Lord shatters Assyria in a way that is neither human nor natural, not to display His divine power but to draw the souls of those who deny Him, for the Lord says: "Turn ye unto him from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted... Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man; and the sword, not of a mean man, shall devour him..." [6, 8].

Is this not a picture of God's salvation accomplished on the Cross, where He brought down the devil not by human thought nor by a material sword but by giving His life as a sin offering for us, and a burnt offering of love on our behalf and in our name, so that the enemy was crushed under our feet and we returned to God with new depths that the men of the Old Testament did not experience as we have?!

entries.section: 1. The blessings of the Kingdom of Christ:

paragraphs.text: 1 Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment. 2 And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land. 3 And the eyes of them that see shall not be dim, and the ears of them that hear shall hearken. 4 The heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. 5 The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the crafty one said to be noble. 6 For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail. 7 The instruments also of the crafty one are evil: he deviseth wicked devices to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right. 8 But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand.

The talk here concerns a flourishing kingdom. Some scholars see that it is the kingdom of Hezekiah, which began with spiritual and social reform, although many reformed only the outward form; others see that the talk here is about the Lord Christ, because the blessings mentioned here were not fulfilled in the days of Hezekiah; but a third group sees that it is about King Hezekiah or other kings as a shadow of the Lord Christ.
What does Christ the King offer us?

A. A constitution of justice and truth: "Behold, a king shall reign in righteousness, and princes shall rule in judgment" [1]. If the Lord reigned on the wood, that is, through the Cross, and paid the price of our sins in fulfillment of justice, then He sets up His disciples and believers as rulers, so that we exercise our spiritual authority not over others but over our souls, our feelings, our emotions, and our faculties, not by suppressing or destroying them but "in judgment," that is, by sanctifying them in Christ the Truth.

B. Instead of troubles and afflictions, this King becomes "an hiding place from the wind," protecting the believers from the winds of trials and bitter pressures; "and a covert from the tempest," that is, like a shelter or covering that protects them from the sweeping waters; "as rivers of water in a dry place," that is, He waters the thirsty souls in the barren wilderness; "as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land," they hide in Christ the Rock, so that no harm touches them.
Thus he presents four similes for the work of the Lord Christ in the life of His believers: a hiding place, a covert, rivers of water, a great rock.

Through these similes the prophet sees us as like a traveler who finds in the Lord Christ all his needs: when violent storms blow upon him he finds in Him the faithful refuge; if sweeping floods overtake him he finds Him a protective covering; if he suffers thirst the Lord becomes for him rivers of living water; and if the whole world is stirred up he takes shelter in Him as a solid rock able to hide him and protect him even from death.

That is, God the Savior offers Himself as everything to His believers so that they lack nothing. He has presented Himself through many names so that we may realize that He is the secret of our true satisfaction, and as St. John Chrysostom says:
[Why is He called the Way? That we may understand that through Him we meet the Father. Why is He called the Rock? That we may understand that He is the keeper and establisher of the faith.
Why is He called the Fountain? That we may understand that He is the source of everything.
Why is He called the Root? That we may understand that in Him is the power of growth.
Why is He called the Shepherd? Because He shepherds us.
Why is He called the Lamb? Because He was offered as a ransom for us and became an offering.
Why is He called the Life? Because He raised us up when we were dead.
Why is He called the Light? Because He rescued us from the darkness.
Why is He called the Arm? Because He is of one essence with the Father.
Why is He called the Word? Because He is begotten of the Father; as my word is begotten of me, so also the Son is begotten of the Father.
Why is He called our Garment? Because I clothed myself with Him when I was baptized.
Why is He called the Table? Because I am nourished on Him when I partake of the Mysteries.
Why is He called the House? Because I dwell in Him.
Why is He called the Bridegroom? Because He received me as His bride.
Why is He called Undefiled? Because He took me as a virgin.
Why is He called the Master? Because I am His servant.
If you hear these things, I beg you not to understand them in a material sense, but soar high with your mind, for they are not to be taken in a bodily sense].

* Blessed is he who has forgotten the talk of the world through his talk with You, for from You all his needs are fulfilled. You are his food and drink! You are his house and his dwelling of rest; to You he enters at all times to take cover! You are his sun and his day; by Your light he sees hidden things. You are the Father who begot him! You gave him the Spirit of Your Son in his heart!

entries.section: 1. The blessings of the Kingdom of Christ:

paragraphs.text: The Spiritual Elder C. The Lord Christ offers His believers spiritual insight to see the unseen things, so that their inner eyes may not be darkened: "the eyes of them that see shall not be dim (darkened)" [3]. He also gives us the ability to listen to His commandment and to hearken to His words with joy: "and the ears of them that hear shall hearken" [3]. He offers wisdom with understanding and knowledge: "the heart also of the rash shall understand knowledge" [4]. He gives the tongue fitting and effective speech: "and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly." And finally He gives us the grace of discernment, so that we do not count the vile person liberal nor the crafty one noble [5].

In short, He gives: inner insight, hearing with obedience, wisdom with understanding and knowledge, the ability to speak constructively, the grace of discernment. All this is accomplished by the Savior, who removes the sin that causes blindness, disobedience, folly, inability to speak the truth, and lack of discernment.
* My God... You are my light! Open my eyes that they may behold Your divine splendor, that I may be able to walk in my way without stumbling in the snares of the enemy...
You are the light for the children of light! Your day knows no sunset! Your day shines for Your children so that they do not stumble!
But those who are outside of You walk in darkness and live in it...!

Yes, outside Your radiance truth flees from me and error draws near to me; conceit fills me, and truth flees from me! I fall into confusion instead of discernment; ignorance becomes mine instead of knowledge, blindness instead of insight; I no longer have a way that leads to life...

entries.section: 1. The blessings of the Kingdom of Christ:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine D. God distinguishes between the vile and the liberal, for He is the searcher of hearts and the knower of hidden things [6-8].

9 Rise up, ye women that are at ease; hear my voice, ye careless daughters; give ear unto my speech. 10 For days beyond a year shall ye tremble, ye careless women: for the vintage shall fail, the gathering shall not come. 11 Tremble, ye women that are at ease; be troubled, ye careless ones: strip you, and make you bare, and gird yourselves upon the loins. 12 They shall smite upon the breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine. 13 Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briers; yea, upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city: 14 Because the palaces shall be forsaken; the multitude of the city shall be left; the forts and towers shall be for dens for ever, a joy of wild asses, a pasture of flocks;

After speaking about the blessings of the Kingdom of Christ, among them the distinction between the vile and the liberal, God knowing how to judge the first and honor the second, he began to speak to us about the judgment of the vile person in the form of an address to the pampered, luxurious women who go out after the harvest to spend periods of play together in temporal joy and in an unseemly, carnal manner. There is no longer a feast of harvest, for the enemy seizes all the crops.
These women represent those who refuse to believe in the Lord Christ, who walk outside His spiritual Kingdom, and they are afflicted with the following:
A. Instead of tranquility and peace they tremble [11]...
* Be all my happiness, O You who are wholly good... By You I stand and without You I perish..! By You I am filled with joy, and without You I perish with sorrow...

Ah! Make haste and make my soul a dwelling for You, and my heart a resting place... Your fragrance restores my strength, and the remembrance of You eases my pains, Your appearing is my satisfaction (Ps 17:10)!

O Life of my soul... my heart runs after You, and melts at the remembrance of Your goodness! When will the time come for my departure to Your Kingdom?! When shall I be granted to behold Your beauty, O Life, the happiness of my heart!
Why do You hide Your face from me, O sole happiness of my soul?!
Where do You hide, O Lord of beauty, O end of all my aspirations...
Draw my heart, for You are my joy!
St. Augustine B. Instead of wearing costly garments they strip and make themselves bare and gird upon the loins [11], a sign of the withdrawal of grace and the loss of spiritual covering.

What are these costly garments that the human soul wears but the person of the Lord Christ, who hides us in Himself and covers us with His blood and gives us His beauty. As St. Paul says: "For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27). In the waters of Baptism we put on the Lord Christ, and so we bear His righteousness and His glory and His splendor in us. As Mar Jacob of Serugh says: [Baptism is the robe of glory given to Adam, which the serpent stole from him among the trees... Come (O soul) and put on majesty, and acquire light through the pure waters. Come, go down, and put on the garments that divinity has woven, and go up and show us your immortal beauty, that we may rejoice with you... You have put on the many-colored garment like the high priest in the house of purification. Fire and the Spirit weave for you the robe that is all light. O daughter of the peoples, betrothed to the light within the waters].
C. Instead of joy they smite upon the breast, lamenting like those who have a dead one [12]; for by their separation from God, the source of life, their souls lost life.

* How wretched I am! My God... when will this corrupt nature leave me, and Your perfect power work in me...?! I am Your creature, and behold, I am dying! I am the work of Your hands, and behold, I am descending toward nothingness...! Shall I command the dead man to come out of the grave...! Ah! O my God! I will cry out before I perish, or at least cry out lest I perish, that I may deserve to dwell in You... Support me, O eternal glory, O my joy, reveal Yourself to me, O my God, that I may love it!
St. Augustine D. Instead of rejoicing in the harvest, the earth brings forth for them thorns and briers (Isa 3:13), a sign of the coming of the curse with spiritual dryness.
E. Their palaces are demolished and the cities are forsaken, and the houses of joy and the joyous city turn into a wilderness with thorns and briers [13-14].
F. The hill and the tower turn into perpetual dens in which wild asses (a symbol of the fierce demons) and flocks (animal thoughts) graze.
These are the marks of the soul outside Christ: trembling, sorrow, dryness, ruin, and destruction come upon it, so it becomes a dwelling for wicked, beastly spirits and for animal thoughts and lusts.

15 Until the spirit be poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness be a fruitful field, and the fruitful field be counted for a forest. 16 Then truth shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field. 17 And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever. 18 And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places; 19 When it shall hail, coming down on the forest; and the city shall be low in a low place. 20 Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth thither the feet of the ox and the ass.

God, in His love, seeks His children for Himself in order to remove from them trembling, bitterness, dryness, and destruction, so He pours out His Holy Spirit upon us that the enemy of good and the thoughts and lusts of the flesh may find no place in us, for it is said: "Until the spirit be poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness be a fruitful field, and the fruitful field be counted for a forest" [15].

Many commentators see that what is mentioned here points to the descent of the Holy Spirit on the Feast of Pentecost, when the barren wilderness of the soul is turned into a garden bearing the fruits of the Holy Spirit that gladden God and men, while those who deny lose even their natural fruit, so that their weak garden becomes a forest.
The prophet depicts for us this Pentecostal work in the life of the Church, saying:

"Then truth shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field" [16], meaning that the Holy Spirit turns our wilderness into a garden or a paradise in which the Lord Christ, who is the Truth and the Righteousness, dwells. If our Christ promised the gift of the Spirit, then the work of the Spirit in the believer is to prepare him for the indwelling of Christ in him, and the establishing of His Kingdom within us.

"And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation" [18]. By the dwelling of the Lord of glory in the midst of His people, peace comes to the midst of the people; our Christ is revealed in us and we dwell in Him, for He is our eternal peace. His peace reigns in our hearts (Col 3:15), so we live in reconciliation with God and men also, and are counted as those who are in heaven itself.

Finally the prophet pronounces blessed those who enjoy the gift of the Spirit through the waters of Baptism: "Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters, that send forth thither the feet of the ox and the ass" [20]. It is as though he who sows by the streams of the waters of the Holy Spirit bears an abundant harvest, so the oxen and the asses do not cease carrying it turn after turn, and the feet of these animals pass freely and repeatedly...

* Blessed is he who sows beside the waters, for this soul is plowed and watered and trodden by the ox and the ass after it had been dry without rain [20] and humbled without cause. Blessed is he who was the "valley (of Shittim)" (Jn 3:18) watered from the house of the Lord, so that it becomes fresh and produces food for man instead of dryness and unfruitfulness... Therefore it is fitting for us to take care not to lose grace.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus

"Woe to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled; and thou that plunderest, and they did not plunder thee. When thou shalt cease to spoil, thou shalt be spoiled; and when thou shalt make an end of plundering, they shall plunder thee." [1].

The woe here is directed against Assyria, and also against Babylon, as against every enemy who exalts himself against God and His people. Though his plan of destruction and plunder is carried out without hindrance, and without any harm touching him, yet this work falls under the woe.

God uses this destroyer as a rod of discipline for His people for a time, then returns to judge him. He leaves him to accomplish the desire for destruction that is in his heart, but as he has done, so it is done to him, so that ruin comes upon him and he is plundered at the appointed time.

Here it is fitting for us to realize that every hand stretched out to destroy has its work come down upon its own head, and drinks from the very cup that it fills for others. But their evil is turned to good for the children of God; even Satan himself cannot crush them, but his opposition to them becomes the cause of their victory and their crown. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The righteous are proved all the more when they are in the midst of those who want to turn them away from the life of righteousness and draw them toward evil, and yet they hold fast to virtue. The (Apostle) says, "For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you" (1 Cor 11:19). For this reason God left the wicked in the world, so that the splendor of the righteous may increase. Do you see the greatness of the gain? But this gain comes from the courage of the righteous, not of the wicked... Let us apply this argument to Satan also, for God left him here so that we may return to a stronger state, so that He may make the wrestler manifest and the struggle great. So when someone asks you, why did God leave Satan here? answer him with these words: that Satan not only does no harm to a man who is watchful and careful, but even benefits him, not by the intention of Satan (the wicked one), but because of the courage of him who makes good use of Satan's evil... Let your intention be good, and no one will ever harm you, but you will receive a great gain, not from the righteous only, but from the wicked also].
Christians have also realized that Satan collapsed completely after the Cross, so that ruin came upon him after he had been a destroyer of souls.

2 O LORD, be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee: be thou their arm every morning, our salvation also in the time of trouble. 3 At the noise of the tumult the people fled; at the lifting up of thyself the nations were scattered. 4 And your spoil shall be gathered like the gathering of the caterpillar: as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them. 5 The LORD is exalted; for he dwelleth on high: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. 6 And wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation: the fear of the LORD is his treasure. 7 Behold, their valiant ones shall cry without: the ambassadors of peace shall weep bitterly. 8 The highways lie waste, the wayfaring man ceaseth: he hath broken the covenant, he hath despised the cities, he regardeth no man. 9 The earth mourneth and languisheth: Lebanon is ashamed and hewn down: Sharon is like a wilderness; and Bashan and Carmel are scattered.

When the prophet sees the ruin that comes upon the people of God, who deserve discipline, and the plundering of them by their enemies, he lifts up a prayer on behalf of the holy remnant, declaring in their name their waiting for the Lord, in which he says:
a. Asking for God's mercies and His salvation: "O LORD, be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee: be thou their arm every morning, our salvation also in the time of trouble" [2].

In the name of the devout people, the prophet lifted up a prayer for the military leaders who had fallen into distress and affliction because of Sennacherib and his army. "Be thou their arm every morning"; the literal translation is "be their arm every morning," a wonderful expression that reveals God's saving role in people's lives. He does not disregard their arms, even though they are as nothing and utterly unable to work; rather, He works by them as though they were His own arm. He takes them as His own, sanctifies them by His Holy Spirit, and supports them with heavenly power so as to save. He is the One who works in the lives of His believers, yet without disregarding them or destroying their energies, but through their sanctification.
* God wants the servant to appear as though he had contributed something, lest he fall into shame.

* Grace is always ready! It seeks those who receive it with all welcome. So when our Lord sees a soul that is watchful and burning with love, He pours out His riches upon it in abundance and plenty that surpass all its requests.
* God asks of us a small cause, so that He Himself may do the whole work.
St. John Chrysostom. This divine arm is a continual daily work in the life of the Church, as in the life of every member, "for his compassions fail not. They are new every morning" (Lam 3:22-23).

b. Asking for divine intervention, for it is enough for God to speak, and the Assyrians or others cannot bear the divine voice, so they flee. "At the noise of the tumult (roaring) the people fled; at the lifting up of thyself the nations were scattered" [3]. By the mere utterance of a divine word the wicked tremble and flee; the mere appearance of God in the battle scattered the hostile nations.

How much we need the word of God to be proclaimed in the heart, so that evil flees and the powers of darkness are scattered, and the Crucified One to be revealed within us, so that sins and all evil spirits flee, and the Lord alone reigns in our depths.

Before the appearing of the Lord on the field and His uttering a word, the invaders became like the caterpillar (the larvae of the butterfly) and the locust, fleeing in shame and disgrace, while the people of God gather them [4]. Perhaps by the caterpillar he meant the dead and wounded of the Assyrian army, whom the people gather so that they may not cause a plague, and by the locust those who flee, so they run after them to catch them without any need of weapons. It is shame and disgrace for the enemy who destroyed and plundered with cruelty and arrogance!

c. The sanctifying of the city so that it becomes the righteous city of God, or the city of righteousness, in which God Himself dwells as "judgment and righteousness" [5]. It is filled with peace, security and salvation, with wisdom and knowledge. Its true treasure is "the fear of the LORD" [6]. This is a fear that springs from love, the fear of wounding the feelings of the Father, and not the fear of a slave toward his master, nor of a hired servant toward the owner of the house or of the work.

Now, after the prophet has asked God, in the name of the people, to intervene to crush the enemy and save the people, he sets out before God what has befallen the city, perhaps to move His divine compassion [7-9].
a. The heroes of war had no way to move, but stopped at crying out in helplessness and fear [7].

b. The ambassadors of peace wept bitterly [7] because Sennacherib broke the covenant. Hezekiah had paid a large sum so that he would leave the land, and yet he sent his army to storm it (2 Kgs 18:4, 17).

c. The highways lay waste [8] because everyone feared that the enemy would meet them on the road; for the reports of the messengers had come declaring the gravity of the situation, and the enemy had surrounded all the cities.
d. They entered into humiliation, so the cities became despised [8].

e. Barrenness occurred even in the most fertile and delightful regions, so that they became like the desert... Fruitlessness and barrenness are considered a disgrace, a sign of God's anger. Among these regions are Sharon, Bashan and Carmel.

When the prophet, in the name of the devout, took refuge in God, lifting up prayer for His divine intervention and confessing the ruin and devastation that had befallen the land, God intervened to condemn the enemy, Assyria. It is as though God longs to support us against the enemy, the devil, and is able to save us, but He waits for us to take refuge in Him and ask for His work with us, for He does not compel us even to our own salvation. He sanctifies the freedom of our will, longing that we ask by our own choice. As St. John Chrysostom says: [God does not force us, nor does the grace of the Spirit compel our will, but God calls us and waits for us to come to Him in our full freedom, and if we draw near He grants us all His help].

10 "Now will I rise, saith the LORD; now will I be exalted; now will I lift up myself. 11 Ye shall conceive chaff, ye shall bring forth stubble: your breath, as fire, shall devour you. 12 And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire." 13 Hear, ye that are far off, what I have done; and, ye that are near, acknowledge my might. 14 The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites: "Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?"
Though God is patient with the wicked, yet when the measure is full He judges them:

a. God Himself leads the battle: "Now will I rise, saith the LORD; now will I be exalted; now will I lift up myself" [10]. What man is unable to do, the Lord Himself does, out of His jealousy for the weak and the oppressed, counting their enemies as His enemies, as it is said, "Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him. As smoke is driven away, so drive them away... But let the righteous be glad; let them rejoice before God: yea, let them exceedingly rejoice" (Ps 68:1-3).

b. The judgment that comes upon them is the natural fruit of their deeds, for since they conceive chaff they bring forth not wheat but stubble [11], which is offered to the devouring fire. And since they breathe out violence like fire, they burn themselves [11].

Their works are chaff and thorns, good for nothing, and your threats are a blazing fire; therefore they carry within them the chaff and the thorns together with the fire, to become a blazing furnace not for others but for themselves!
If their evils, especially hypocrisy, are a devouring fire [1], then by this they practice, of their own will, the pledge of the everlasting burnings (fires) [1].

Just as righteousness carries its reward within it, and so brings the human soul into a pledge of eternal glory, so evil carries its reward within it, and so brings the soul into a pledge of the eternal fire of Gehenna.

Many of the Fathers of the Church see that virtue needs no reward because it carries its reward within it. As the martyr Justin says: [Does not virtue lead to the fulfillment of happiness? And St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [For virtue to be virtue, it must have no reward]. Perhaps the secret of this is that the Fathers looked at virtue as an enjoyment of unity with Christ, as Origen says: [Virtue is for us to be one with Christ, for He is the virtues that fill Him], He is justice, wisdom and truth; so whoever practices virtue partakes in the divine nature, and this is the fullness of reward.

Vice is an imitation of the enemy of good and a sharing with him in his traits, together with a deprivation of the enjoyment of the Savior and of being like Him... and in this are the fruit of sin and its recompense.

15 He that walketh in truth, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil; 16 He shall dwell on high: his place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure. 17 Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off. 18 Thine heart shall meditate terror: "Where is the scribe? where is the receiver? where is he that counted the towers?" 19 Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand. 20 Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken. 21 But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby. 22 For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us. 23 Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail: then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey. 24 And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick: the people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity.

If God in His justice is a devouring fire that consumes the evil that carries corruption within it, and glorifies the believers who carry within them the righteousness of Christ, then He judges the wicked who persist in their evil and protects His righteous ones from their hands.
The prophet presents to us the traits of the righteous man, which are:
a. He walks in truth and righteousness, that is, he walks in Christ Jesus, the Way and the Truth, who is our righteousness.
b. He speaks uprightly [15]; his words declare his Gospel hidden in his heart.
c. He despises the gain of oppressions.
d. With disdain he shakes his hands from accepting a bribe.
e. He stops his ears from listening to plans that drive to the shedding of blood.
f. He shuts his eyes from looking upon evil.
g. He lifts up his heart to the heights to dwell with his Savior in the heavenly places [16].
h. He always takes refuge in his Christ as in the munitions of rocks that protect him from evil.
i. He is generous in giving, even out of his own needs: bread and water.

Such a man, who is sanctified by the Lord Christ to live pure with all his senses, whose depths are lifted to the heights, and who practices a life of fellowship with God and continual giving, deserves to enjoy the sight of the Lord Christ in His glories, for it is said, "Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty" [17]. This is the greatest gift to the righteous: to behold the Messiah in His splendor!

Some think that the talk here is about King Hezekiah, who enjoyed a special splendor when his heart rejoiced at seeing the destruction of Sennacherib's army, but the text is clear here that it speaks rather about the Lord Christ, who was glorified on the Cross, drawing the Gentiles to Himself and granting them a new nature: in place of enmity they bore love and friendship, in place of fierceness they became gentle, and in place of the strange language of evil they began to speak with a heavenly accent, for it is said: they became gentle, and in place of the strange language of evil they began to speak with a heavenly accent, for it is said:

"Where is the scribe? where is the receiver? where is he that counted the towers?" [18]. Where is the scribe who counts the army and records the names of the soldiers? And where is the receiver who determines the tribute that is paid to the enemy? Where is he who counted the towers in order to set guards over them and watchmen who observe the enemy and warn of the battle? All these energies have been turned from working for war and resistance into calm, peaceful energies working for the sake of the Kingdom of God, through their acceptance of faith in the Lord Christ.

"Thou shalt not see a fierce people" [19], for the works of the old, violent man have been removed so that we may bear the traits of our Creator through our enjoyment of the new man who is renewed every day.

"A people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive, dull of a tongue that is not understood" [19]; they received a new tongue, the language of the Spirit, the tongue of love and unity with understanding and wisdom.
And now, what is the work of the King, the Messiah, in the life of the Gentiles who come to Him by faith in Him?

a. "Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities" [20]. In place of the old terror of the scribe who records the army and the receiver, Zion becomes a city of joyful feasts, in which the people gather with constant gladness for common worship and for meeting with God Himself, our unceasing feast.

b. "A tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken" [20], that is, firm and established, which not even death can destroy, for it remains eternal.
c. Surrounded by rivers and streams on every side [21], which makes it fruitful in the Spirit.
d. It cannot be approached or fought against; for there sail in the waters surrounding it no small ships to spy on it and no great warships [21].

e. Christ the Lord Himself is the judge, the lawgiver, the king and the Savior [22]; He gave the constitution of the Gospel, reigned on the Cross and saved us, and still intercedes for us as our propitiation by His precious Blood.
f. Its enemy becomes like a broken ship in the midst of the waters, so that the enemy cannot raise its mast or spread its sail [23].
g. They defeat the enemy with power, so that even the lame are able to plunder him [23].
h. There is no sick person in it [24].
i. Its inhabitants receive the forgiveness of sins [24].

This is the picture of the soul that is joined to the Lord Christ: it becomes Zion, the joyful city of God, filled with gladness and peace, firm in the Lord, surrounded by the Spirit of God, the Holy One, who turns it into a fruitful paradise. Satan cannot defeat it, nor can the enemy of good destroy it. The Lord Christ declares His Kingdom in it, being its King, its judge, its lawgiver and its Savior. It overcomes the enemy of good and crushes him; no spiritual sickness can strike it; and finally it enjoys the forgiveness of sins through constant repentance.

1 Come near, ye nations, to hear; and hearken, ye peoples: let the earth hear, and all that is therein; the world, and all things that come forth of it. 2 For the LORD hath indignation against all nations, and fury against all their army: he hath devoted them to destruction, he hath delivered them to the slaughter. 3 Their slain also shall be cast out, and the stench of their carcases shall come up, and the mountains shall flow with their blood. 4 And all the host of heaven shall perish, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.

The prophet presents a general call to all the nations, that the world may listen, see and be silent, because the Lord has spoken. He proclaims God's judgment upon the nations that hold fast to evil, that perhaps they may return and heed His judgments, after God has been long-suffering toward them for a time.

It is like a call directed against the whole world, in which the Lord Himself enters as a party to the battle, declaring His indignation and the heat of His wrath upon all their armies [2]; for on account of evil they were exposed to slaughter and to the casting out of corpses until they stink; the blood runs on the mountains like water.

The prophet returns to affirm that God does not mean the sons of men; rather, the battle is between God and His angels and the devil and his angels. Therefore he says: "And all the host of heaven shall perish" [the hosts of evil in the heavens (Eph 6:12; Rev 12:7-9; 20:1-8)].

What does he mean by his saying: "And all the host of heaven shall perish, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree" [3].
a. Some millennialist interpreters try to see in this a reference to the passing away of the old heaven, so that in the millennial reign a new earth and a new heaven may come into being.

b. St. Augustine sees that the heavens which are rolled together here as a scroll (a book) are the Holy Scripture, for he says: [The books of the two Testaments are called "the heavens"... I perceive and understand the Holy Scriptures which Thy servants wrote by the work of the Holy Spirit]. It is as though one of God's disciplines for the wicked who persist in their evil is their loss of the possibility of enjoying the host of heaven, that is, the power of the Holy Scripture, so that it becomes for them a closed book whose secrets they do not grasp in their lives, or it is for them like the leaves of a vine that have fallen and scattered, and like a falling fig from a fig tree. But for the children of God, the Holy Spirit opens their minds and their hearts and all their energies, so that they may grasp the power of the Word working in their depths as in their conduct.

Origen says: [The Holy Scriptures were written by the Spirit of God; and they have meanings not as they appear at first sight but other meanings which many do not grasp. For these (words) that are written are forms of certain mysteries and images of divine things. Therefore there is one opinion in the whole Church, that the entire matter is truly spiritual, and that the spiritual meaning contained in the Law is not known by all, but is known only by those to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit has been given in the word of wisdom and knowledge].

c. We can say that the earth and the heaven are a type of the body of man and his soul. The wicked lose the holiness and soundness of their bodies as well as of their souls. Their bodies become like mighty mountains, but blood flows from them [3]; they have the appearance of bodily strength, and perhaps bodily beauty and outward splendor, but they are like bodies stained with blood that bear the smell of death and stench. And their souls become like heavens that have lost all their energies (their host), closed like a sealed book... They have the appearance of courage, and perhaps of nobility and strength of personality, but when you come into close contact with them you find them narrow souls, broken by despair and corrupted by inner gloom, with a sense of isolation and deprivation.

This is the picture of the wicked man: he has a strong appearance outwardly but carries every weakness in his depths. As the psalmist says: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb" (Ps 37:1-2).

5 For my sword is bathed in heaven: behold, it shall come down upon Edom, and upon the people I have devoted to judgment. 6 The sword of the LORD is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. 7 And the wild oxen shall fall with them, and the bullocks with the bulls; and their land shall be soaked with blood, and their dust made fat with fatness. 8 For it is the day of the LORD's vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion. 9 And the rivers thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. 10 It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it for ever and ever. 11 But the owl and the hedgehog shall possess it; the crane and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of desolation, and the plummet of emptiness. 12 As for her nobles, there is none there to call to the kingdom, and all her princes shall be nothing. 13 And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of wolves, and a court for the daughters of the ostrich. 14 The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the jackals, and the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; there shall the night settle, and find for itself a place of rest. 15 There shall the arrow snake make her den, and lay, and hatch, and rear under her shadow: and there shall the falcons gather, one with another.

It was the custom to smear swords with fat before the battle, so that they would not need cleaning after the killing of each of the enemies, since the grease keeps the blood from sticking to them. But the symbolic sword of the Lord is smeared, as it were, with heavenly wrath: "For my sword is bathed in heaven" [5].

The coming of the sword of the Lord upon Edom is like the knife of a priest slaughtering a flock unable to resist; it worked in the capital "Bozrah" [6] as in the rest of Edom, to offer sacrifices not for reconciliation but burnt offerings of judgment [5], upon which the divine curse has fallen.

This sword passed through all: the wild oxen and the bullocks with the bulls... that is, the violent men of war (the wild oxen) as well as the common people; the great with the small, for it is a general judgment, because all shared together in iniquity.

"Their land shall be soaked with blood, and their dust made fat with fatness" [7]; if the name "Edom" means "dust" (Adam) and also "blood," so their shed blood is mingled with their dust. They lived as dust, lovers of earthly and temporal things, and they perished by their blood.
God does all this for the sake of His Zion, His beloved people, whom Edom hates.
Finally he affirms that the destruction of Edom is complete [9-15].

"And the rivers thereof shall be turned into pitch, and the dust thereof into brimstone, and the land thereof shall become burning pitch. It shall not be quenched night nor day; the smoke thereof shall go up for ever: from generation to generation it shall lie waste..." [9-10], meaning that it turns into a furnace of fire that needs no fuel from outside, for its rivers turn into tar and its dust into brimstone, so that its land becomes a blazing fire that is not quenched by day or by night; its smoke goes up as a defiling odor like dark smoke, and its ruin continues throughout the generations.
It turns from a dwelling for men into a dwelling for animals and birds of prey [10, 11, 13, 14].
Instead of building, the line of desolation and the plummet of emptiness are stretched out [11].
Its leaders are lost; there are in it neither nobles nor princes.
Instead of fruits, thorns grow up even in its palaces, and nettles and brambles in its fortresses [13], a sign of the abandonment of the palaces and the disuse of the fortresses for a long time.

"There shall the arrow snake make her den, and lay, and hatch, and rear under her shadow" [15]. The nakkazah (arrow snake) is a serpent, one of the most malicious kinds of snakes, small in size but poisonous, living in regions of Africa and Arabia. However, what is stated here suits a bird rather than a snake, so some scholars see that what is stated here is a poetic description referring to the dwelling of deadly evil spirits in souls that resist God.
"There shall the falcons gather, one with another" [15], birds of prey that inspire terror..

Edom, then, refers to the soul that denies the faith and resists the truth; it falls under the divine wrath and becomes a furnace for itself, with no one to quench its inner flame and no one to grant it rest or comfort. It turns into ruin and loses its balanced thinking. It becomes a haunt for defiled thoughts and perverted emotions; sins make sport of it and demons play with it. Its life becomes dry as thorns and barren without fruit; it loses its beauty and its fortification, and turns into the darkness of a perpetual night without day or light [13].

16 Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail, none shall miss its mate: for his mouth hath commanded, and his spirit hath gathered them. 17 And he hath cast the lot for them, and his hand hath divided it unto them by line: they shall possess it for ever, from generation to generation shall they dwell therein.
"Seek ye out of the book of the LORD, and read: no one of these shall fail" [16].

He does not mean here the book of life or the book of judgment (Ezek 32:32; Ps 56:8; 69:28; Dan 7:10; Mal 3:16; Rev 3:5; 20:12; 21:27), but the prophecies which he proclaimed concerning Edom about its destruction.

Some observe that the prophet rarely issues a command, but here he commands, "Seek... and read," because the matter in his days seemed impossible and unreasonable. This prophecy was fulfilled in part after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar... and it is still being fulfilled every day with respect to those who resist the truth, until it is fulfilled in perfection at the last coming of the Lord, when the devil and all his hosts will perish.

entries.section: 1. Turning the wilderness into a paradise:

paragraphs.text: 1 The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the narcissus. 2 It shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice even with joy and singing: the glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it, the excellency of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the excellency of our God. 3 Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees. 4 Say to them that are of a fearful heart: "Be strong, fear not: behold your God. Vengeance cometh, the recompence of God. He will come and save you."

Some scholars see that what is stated here concerns the state of the children of Israel after their return from the Babylonian captivity, but many see in it a description of the state of the Church of the New Testament, which enjoys the Lord Christ as her Head, who pours out His glory and splendor upon her. This is the opinion of most scholars among the Orthodox, the Catholics and the Protestants, although the followers of the millennial reign reckon this chapter a prophecy about it that has not yet been fulfilled.
The true believer who experiences the new life in Christ Jesus can experience the glory of the Church declared in his inner life, which is:

a. The turning of the wilderness and the dry land into a fruitful garden; for by the Lord's entering the heart and the Holy Spirit's dwelling in it, the inner barrenness is removed and the Lord's fruitful garden is planted, which gladdens the heart of God [1-2].

* It is clear that he is not speaking here about places outside the soul and the senses, but is announcing joyful good news for the thirsty soul, unadorned, through the symbol of the wilderness. As David says: "My soul has become toward thee as a dry land" [(Ps 143:6) Septuagint]. My soul thirsts for the Almighty, for He is the living God (Ps 42:2).

St. Gregory of Nyssa b. Perhaps the most important trait of the Church of the New Testament is "the joy of the Lord," for she lives exultant and inwardly rejoicing because of God's work in her. This line is clear in the whole book of the prophet Isaiah: the Messianic age is an age of joy, whereas there is no peace and no joy for the wicked who reject God's saving work.

"The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the narcissus. It shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice even with joy and singing" [1-2]. Joy, gladness and singing!
* He who has looked within himself to our Lord, and whose soul has been mingled with His light, let his heart boil over with joy.

The Spiritual Elder * Just as trees cannot grow if they do not drink water, so the soul, if it does not receive heavenly joy, cannot grow and ascend to the heights. But the souls that have received the Spirit and heavenly joy are those that are able to rise to the heights... for the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven have been uncovered to them while they are still in the body, and they have found boldness before God in everything, and all their requests have been fulfilled.
* The soul is always nourished by this joy and made happy by it, and by it ascends to heaven, for like the body it has its spiritual food.

entries.section: 1. Turning the wilderness into a paradise:

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great b. The glory and splendor of the Lord shine forth in the heart as a pledge of the eternal heavenly glory. "The glory of Lebanon shall be given unto it... they shall see the glory of the LORD, the excellency of our God" [2].
St. Macarius the Great speaks of this hidden glory that fills the life of the believer, to be revealed on the great day of the Lord, saying:

[By the renewing of the mind (Rom 12:3), the peace of the thoughts (Phil 4:7) and the heavenly love of the Lord (Eph 3:19), the new creation of Christians (2 Cor 5:17) is distinguished from the rest of mankind... Each one, in proportion as he is counted worthy of fellowship with the Holy Spirit by faith and diligence, in that measure his body will be glorified on that day, for everything the soul has stored up within it in this present life will be revealed on that day, and made manifest in the body... everything that belongs to the soul now will appear in the body on that day].
The Apostle says: "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Cor 3:7-18).

entries.section: 1. Turning the wilderness into a paradise:

paragraphs.text: c. A man becomes a support to his weak brethren: "Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees. Say to them that are of a fearful heart: Be strong, fear not: behold your God. Vengeance cometh, the recompence of God. He will come and save you" [3-4].

Though life with God represents a personal, hidden relationship between God and the believer, it is not in isolated individuality, but through the life of fellowship between God and His one Church; each member supports his brother in the Lord so that all may be strengthened together as one bride. Every support you give your brother is a support for you personally, because he represents your hands and your knees.

* There is nothing that makes men so quickly defeated in trials and so collapsed as isolation. Tell me; scatter a company in war, and the enemy is not troubled in capturing and enslaving them one by one.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. Meeting the needs of the believers:

paragraphs.text: 5 Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. 6 Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert. 7 And the mirage shall become a thicket, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of wolves, in their resting place, shall be a home for reeds and papyrus. 8 And a highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called "The Holy Way." The unclean shall not pass over it, but it shall be for them. Whoever walks in the way, even the foolish, shall not err. 9 No lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon, it shall not be found there; but the redeemed shall walk there.

a. When he says: "He will come and save you. Then..." [4-5]; that is, when the Lord Christ the Savior comes, extraordinary things are accomplished, marvelous miracles and signs: "Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert" [5-6].

Those who proclaim the millennial reign try to attribute this to the millennial reign, although the Lord Christ Himself used this text when He answered the disciples of John the Baptist, affirming that He is the expected Messiah (Mt 11:4-6). St. Augustine comments on this, saying: [It is as though He said to them: You have seen me, so know me! You have seen my works, so know their Maker... and blessed is he who is not offended in me].

God, who made everything good, came Himself into the world to renew His creation, mending what had been corrupted, and to restore to man his peace, health and joy. He opens his inner sight to behold the divine mysteries, and the ears so that they may delight in the divine voice and respond to His commandments; He gives the lame the ability to walk in the heavenly way, and makes the dumb speak inward praises... All this is by the action of the Holy Spirit (the waters and the streams), whom the Lord Christ sent from the Father...

* The prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled not only in bodily matters but in spiritual ones also... for those who were formerly lame now leap by the power of Jesus like the hart. They were compared to the hart not without purpose, for it is a clean animal, an enemy of snakes, which cannot harm it with their poison. And so also with regard to the dumb, for they speak...

entries.section: 2. Meeting the needs of the believers:

paragraphs.text: Origen b. "And the mirage shall become a thicket, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of wolves, in their resting place, shall be a home for reeds and papyrus" [7]. By this he means that instead of dryness there will be an abundance of water; for the dry land (the mirage) becomes a pool of water and the thirsty land springs of gushing water; in the habitation of wolves, where there is wilderness, there is water, so grasses grow and papyrus appears, which is found only in places where there is plenty of water.

The prophets often speak to us of the Messianic age as an age of waters (Isa 41:17-20; 43:18-20; 44:3-4; Ezek 47:1-12). The psalmist says: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved" (Ps 46:4-5).

* What is this river of streams? It is the overflow of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Lord said: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:37-38). These rivers overflowed from the bosom of Paul and Peter and John and the rest of the Apostles, and from the believing Evangelists. And since these rivers overflowed from one river, therefore "the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God"....
It is clear that the courses of the river are understood to mean the Holy Spirit, by whom every devout soul that believes in Christ is sanctified to become a citizen of the city of God.

entries.section: 2. Meeting the needs of the believers:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine c. "And a highway shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called The Holy Way. The unclean shall not pass over it, but it shall be for them. Whoever walks in the way, even the foolish, shall not err. No lion shall be there... but the redeemed shall walk there" [8-9]. What is this "way" but the Lord Christ Himself, who offered Himself to His believers as a safe way in which no unclean one passes, but all in it are saints; even the foolish receive understanding and wisdom so that they do not err, and the enemy of good (the ravenous lion) cannot come near those who walk in it.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem speaks to us of our faith in the Lord Christ as a shield against the enemy of good, the devil, saying:

[Is there anything more terrifying than Satan? And yet we find no armor against him except faith, for it is an invisible shield against an invisible enemy, who aims various arrows in the middle of the night at those who are not on guard.

But since he is an invisible enemy, we have faith as a strong weapon, as the Apostle says: "Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked" (Eph 6:16).
So when Satan throws a burning spark of base lust, faith shows the image of judgment and so quenches the wicked mind].

entries.section: 3. A kingdom of joy and gladness:

paragraphs.text: 10 And the redeemed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: gladness and joy shall overtake them, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.

All the peoples of the nations who come to Him are anointed with the oil of gladness, and become a holy nation crowned with crowns of joy springing from victory. Sorrow and sighing cannot find a place in their hearts, but only outside.

This is the anointing of the Church of the New Testament, being the icon of heaven exulting in the Lord. Therefore it is said: "And the redeemed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: gladness and joy shall overtake them, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away" [10].

* There is truly rest where there is no pain or sorrow or sighing, where there are no confusions or troubles or struggles or fear of the soul's bewilderment and disturbance, but there is the fear of God, full of joy.

St. John Chrysostom * Let us grieve here, meditating on the matter, so that we may not grieve there in punishment, but enjoy the eternal blessings... Let us delight in the things that surpass the mind in Christ Jesus our Lord (so that we are not troubled by grief).
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 1. Sennacherib seizes the cities of Judah:

paragraphs.text: "Now it came to pass in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, that Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah, and took them." [1].
The invasion of Judah by Sennacherib is recorded here in (Isa 36) and also in (2 Kgs 18:13-20), and by comparing the two texts the following is observed:

a. It is stated in (2 Kgs 18) that Hezekiah sent to the king of Assyria apologizing to him and saying: "I have offended; return from me: that which thou puttest on me will I bear," and indeed he imposed on him a tribute of three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, which Hezekiah paid out of the house of the LORD and out of the treasures of the king's house... But Sennacherib broke the covenant and again sent an army to storm Jerusalem. The history of Assyria confirms this, for Hezekiah is counted as a bird in a cage who was unable to go out of Jerusalem, and that he paid the tribute, and that 200,000 persons of his people fell captive.

The prophet Isaiah did not mention the matter of the tribute, because he did not aim at the history of the life of Hezekiah, but wanted to bring out God's dealings with him, to confirm God's ability to save when the matter seems impossible.
b. Some scholars see that Sennacherib made two campaigns of invasion against Judah, the first in 701 B.C. and the other in 688 B.C., in the days of Tirhakah king of Egypt and Cush (Isa 37:9).
c. It is stated in (2 Kgs 18:17) that Sennacherib sent with Rabshakeh two commanders, Tartan and Rabsaris; the mission included three commanders, and Rabshakeh was the only speaker among them.

Some see that Rabshakeh is not the name of a person but a title equivalent to "chief cupbearer," who tastes the wine before the king drinks of it so that the king may not be poisoned, and who also performed other principal roles in the royal palace.

God allowed this distress in the days of Hezekiah, who carried out many reforms among the people, although many, especially among the religious and civil leaders, cared for outward reform without the inward, so they cared for formalities without the holy life. God wanted to prove Hezekiah and turn the distress into His glorification. On the other hand, He wanted to reveal Hezekiah's weakness to himself, for his courage failed him and his reliance on God was not complete... By trial he confessed his weakness, and his faith in God and his trust in Him increased.

entries.section: 2. His sending of Rabshakeh to Jerusalem:

paragraphs.text: 2 And the king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem unto king Hezekiah with a great army. And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field. 3 Then came forth unto him Eliakim, Hilkiah's son, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, Asaph's son, the recorder. 4 And Rabshakeh said unto them, "Say ye now to Hezekiah, Thus saith the great king, the king of Assyria, What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? 5 I say, mere words of the lips are counsel and strength for war. Now on whom dost thou trust, that thou rebellest against me? 6 Lo, thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all that trust in him. 7 But if thou say to me, We trust in the LORD our God: is it not he, whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before this altar? 8 Now therefore give pledges, I pray thee, to my master the king of Assyria, and I will give thee two thousand horses, if thou be able on thy part to set riders upon them. 9 How then wilt thou turn away the face of one captain of the least of my master's servants, and put thy trust on Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? 10 And am I now come up without the LORD against this land to destroy it? The LORD said unto me, Go up against this land, and destroy it."

Sennacherib sent Rabshakeh from Lachish (Lakhish), a fortified city lying in the plains of Judah (Josh 15:33, 39), formerly known as Tell el-Hesi, which is 16 miles northeast of Gaza and eleven miles southwest of the city of Jibrin; it is now thought more likely to lie at Tell ed-Duweir, five miles southwest of Beit Jibrin. Sennacherib besieged it, and from the camp in front of it he sent Rabshakeh to Jerusalem so that the king and his men might surrender it.

Rabshakeh stood with a great army by the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field [2], that is, the field of the bleacher of cloth, outside Jerusalem and very near it, where those on the wall of the city could hear whoever spoke in the fuller's field. Some think it was in the Kidron Valley, and that the conduit referred to is the tunnel connecting the Virgin's Spring with the Pool of Siloam, although others see that it was north of the city, since the north was the natural side from which attack came.

Eliakim, who succeeded Shebna, came out to him, being in charge of the king's house (Isa 22:15-20), something like the head of the ministry; and Shebna the scribe, who records for the king the most important events as a reminder and plays the role of historian of the king's life; and also Joah the recorder.

entries.section: 2. His sending of Rabshakeh to Jerusalem:

paragraphs.text: Rabshakeh mocked King Hezekiah before his great men, for he called Sennacherib "the great king, the king of Assyria," while he gave no title to Hezekiah [4]. He derided him because he trusted in Pharaoh of Egypt, saying: "Lo, thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it" [6]. In this he spoke the truth, that whoever trusts in an arm of flesh leans on a broken reed that cannot support him but even pierces his hand. He also mocked him because he trusted in God his God, saying: "Is it not he, whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before this altar?... Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD, saying, The LORD will surely deliver us: this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria... Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?... Who are they among all the gods of these lands, that have delivered their land out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?" [7, 15, 20].

In the very same place where Ahaz mocked the Lord, refusing to deal with God and relying on the human arm (Isa 7), Rabshakeh came to mock God, as though the sons of Judah were drinking from the cup that Ahaz their king had offered them before! In the very same place where Isaiah came to Ahaz asking him to ask a sign of the Lord to confirm God's ability to save, and he refused, Rabshakeh came to mock Judah and their king and their God!

entries.section: 2. His sending of Rabshakeh to Jerusalem:

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah also had relied on human treaties with Pharaoh, and God rebuked him for it on the tongue of a pagan man, calling them mere words of the lips, verbal counsel [5] that has no power or effectiveness. Now he wagers with him that he will give him two thousand horses if he brings two thousand horsemen from his people able to use them. It is as though he were saying to him: Why do you rely on the horses of Egypt and its horsemen? Here we offer you the horses; offer us your men!

11 Then said Eliakim and Shebna and Joah unto Rabshakeh, "Speak, I pray thee, unto thy servants in the Aramaic language; for we understand it: and speak not to us in the Jews' language, in the ears of the people that are on the wall." 12 But Rabshakeh said, "Hath my master sent me to thy master and to thee to speak these words? hath he not sent me to the men that sit upon the wall, that they may eat their own dung, and drink their own piss with you?" 13 Then Rabshakeh stood, and cried with a loud voice in the Jews' language, and said, "Hear ye the words of the great king, the king of Assyria. 14 Thus saith the king, Let not Hezekiah deceive you: for he shall not be able to deliver you. 15 Neither let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD, saying, The LORD will surely deliver us: this city shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria. 16 Hearken not to Hezekiah: for thus saith the king of Assyria, Make peace with me, and come out to me: and eat ye every one of his vine, and every one of his fig tree, and drink ye every one the waters of his own cistern; 17 Until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of corn and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. 18 Beware lest Hezekiah persuade you, saying, The LORD will deliver us. Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? 19 Where are the gods of Hamath and Arphad? where are the gods of Sepharvaim? and have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? 20 Who are they among all the gods of these lands, that have delivered their land out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?" 21 But they held their peace, and answered not a word: for the king's commandment was, saying, "Answer him not."

Since Rabshakeh used a war of nerves to stir up the people against the king and his men, and to drive them to despair and destroy their faith in the saving God, Hezekiah's men asked Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, the Syriac, which was spoken by the inhabitants of the north and east of Palestine and was understood by the Assyrians since it belongs to the same family as their languages, and which the common people of the Jews did not understand. But Rabshakeh insisted on speaking in Hebrew, to stir up the people and cause a kind of division, hoping he might ignite a civil war among the people and the leaders.
This is the work of the enemy of good: he uses the language that stirs up our weakness, and that causes division and splits.

Rabshakeh wanted to stir up the people, so he reminded them of the destruction that would come upon them instead of their enjoying the good things in Assyria, to show that Hezekiah was deceiving them and that their God would not deliver them. He uses the same method that the enemy of good has used through all generations, for today we see the followers of the "Church of Satan" in America proclaiming that they worship him because he answers them and gives them their requests, which God does not give them.

The principal work of the enemy of good is to stir up terror in a person's life and to make him doubt the power of faith. On one side he crushes their spirit with intimidation and terror, and on the other side he wants to isolate them from God, their King and Savior, so as to have them to himself. Therefore the prophet David cries out, saying: "Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God" (Ps 3:2); "All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him" (Ps 22:7-8); "For mine enemies speak against me; and they that lay wait for my soul take counsel together, saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him" (Ps 71:10-11). This is the picture of the war of the enemy of good, who mocks the believers and insults them, crushing their souls until they lose their hope in the Lord their God, so that he may overtake them and bring them down with him to the pit. The enemy wanted to practice the same war on the Representative of mankind and their Savior, for it was said to Him: "He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him" (Mt 27:42).

"But they held their peace, and answered not a word: for the king's commandment was, saying, Answer him not" [21] (2 Kgs 18:36). It was expected that they would declare their revolt and rebellion against the king, but they kept silent as a sign of obedience and trust, awaiting the king's command and instructions. They obeyed the king who asked them not to answer him, that is, not to enter into dialogue with him lest they fall into weakness as Eve fell by her dialogue with the old serpent. As St. John Chrysostom says: [She ought to have kept silent; she needed not to exchange talk with him, but in foolishness she disclosed the Master's saying, and so gave Satan a great opportunity... See what an evil this is, to deliver ourselves into the hands of our enemies and of those who plot against us]. He also says: [Since Satan was not able to offer anything in practice, he offered rather promises in words. Such is the character of deceivers]. And St. Augustine says: [God is our Leader and Satan is our destroyer; the Leader presents His commandment, while the destroyer suggests a deception.
