Shall we listen to the commandment or to the deception?!].

22 Then came Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, that was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, the son of Asaph, the recorder, to Hezekiah with their clothes rent, and told him the words of Rabshakeh.
The men came to Hezekiah with their clothes rent and told him the words of Rabshakeh [22]... they came in sorrow and bitterness to the king.

Would that we too, when we feel bitterness, would not rend our garments but rend our hearts with repentance, taking refuge in Christ the King, who alone is able to give us good counsel and who works in us by His Holy Spirit.

entries.section: 1. Hezekiah takes refuge in God and in His prophet:

paragraphs.text: 1 And it came to pass, when king Hezekiah heard it, that he rent his clothes, and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the LORD. 2 And he sent Eliakim, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth, unto Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz. 3 And they said unto him, "Thus saith Hezekiah, This day is a day of trouble, and of chastening, and of insult: for the unborn children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth. 4 It may be the LORD thy God will hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of Assyria his master hath sent to reproach the living God, and will reprove the words which the LORD thy God hath heard: wherefore lift up thy prayer for the remnant that is left."

entries.section: 1. Hezekiah takes refuge in God and in His prophet:

paragraphs.text: Opinions differ about the assessment of Hezekiah's conduct. Some saw in him the pious, devout and humble man, who therefore wrested God's mercies, although afterward he fell into pride and perished; and some see that what Hezekiah did was not from devotion or from faith, because shortly afterward he gave the treasures of the temple to Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:14-16) and said to him, "I have offended." Terror and fear also overtook the king, and in his speech he repeated the phrase "the LORD thy God" [4], and not "the LORD our God" or "my God."

We return to the king to see him, on hearing the words of Rabshakeh, "rent his clothes, and covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the LORD" [1]. That was a sign of his sorrow together with his humbling before God.

Hezekiah sent Eliakim and Shebna and the elders of the priests covered with sackcloth to Isaiah the prophet [2]. The situation had changed: whereas the civil and religious leaders had mocked Isaiah when he went barefoot and naked warning them that Pharaoh and his men would not be able to rescue them (Isa 21), now here they come to him wearing sackcloth in bitterness, declaring their need of his prayers and his counsel. They realized that it was "a day of trouble, and of chastening, and of insult" [3], so let it be a day of repentance and prayer. They felt "that the unborn children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth" [3]; who can help but God through prayer?! Pharaoh with all his resources cannot give a pregnant woman strength to give birth even when the time of labor has come... Prayer is the "midwife" of mercy that brings about the birth.

St. John Chrysostom says: [Nothing equals prayer! It makes the impossible possible, and the difficult easy. A man who prays cannot fall into sin]. And Fr. Theophan the Recluse says: [Prayer is everything; it is the summary of everything: faith, life according to faith, salvation, etc...] He also says that prayer is [the breath of the spirit], it is [the measure of the spiritual life], and the whole Church [breathes through prayer].

Rabshakeh exalted himself and reproached the living God, therefore the matter requires the intervention of this God to declare His glory and His power, and for the salvation of the remnant faithful to Him. The psalmist says: "O God, how long shall the adversary reproach?" (Ps 74:10).

5 So the servants of king Hezekiah came to Isaiah. 6 And Isaiah said unto them, "Thus shall ye say unto your master, Thus saith the LORD, Be not afraid of the words that thou hast heard, wherewith the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me. 7 Behold, I will put a spirit in him, and he shall hear tidings, and return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land."
Isaiah mocked the king of Assyria and his men, for he counted his men of war and his commanders as boys, having neither understanding nor power; so it is not fitting for Hezekiah to fear them [6].

What Sennacherib did through his men is done to him; for his men tried to fill the ears of the people with words of blasphemy and also threatened them with death, therefore the ears of the king of Assyria were filled with news that troubles him [7] and he falls by the sword in his land. He uttered harsh words and threatened death, so the words rebounded upon him and he was killed. As for His saying, "Behold, I will put a spirit in him" [7], it means that God leaves him to the spirit of evil which he accepted of his own free choice, delivers him to it, and so he practices his evil, which rebounds upon him.

entries.section: 3. The king of Assyria reproaches the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 8 So Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria warring against Libnah: for he had heard that he was departed from Lachish. 9 And he heard say concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "He is come forth to make war with thee." And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, 10 "Thus shall ye speak to Hezekiah king of Judah, saying, Let not thy God, in whom thou trustest, deceive thee, saying, Jerusalem shall not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. 11 Behold, thou hast heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands by destroying them utterly; and shalt thou be delivered? 12 Have the gods of the nations delivered them which my fathers have destroyed, as Gozan, and Haran, and Rezeph, and the children of Eden which were in Telassar? 13 Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arphad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah?"
Rabshakeh returned to Sennacherib to find that he had left Lachish and gone to Libnah to fight against it.

"Libnah" is a name meaning "whiteness," a city between Lachish and Makkedah (Josh 10:39; 12:15), in the portion of Judah, assigned to the sons of Aaron (Josh 21:13). It is thought likely to be at the place called Tell Burnat, at a distance of two miles northwest of Beit Jibrin, and it is supposed to be Tell es-Safi or es-Safiya.

entries.section: 3. The king of Assyria reproaches the Lord:

paragraphs.text: The king heard that Tirhakah king of Egypt and Cush [9] had come out to fight him, so he sent to Hezekiah once more, threatening him, demanding the submission of Jerusalem and its surrender to him, blaspheming God, on whom Hezekiah relies.

Some ask why Sennacherib repeated his threat. Perhaps because he was surrounded by hostile nations and feared Tirhakah, the strong king of Egypt and Cush, so he wanted to take Jerusalem without bloodshed to be a support for him.

Despite the blasphemy against God that the message carried, it is shorter than the first and much milder in its tone, perhaps because he wanted to win Hezekiah and persuade him without provoking him. He showed him that there is no personal enmity against him, but that it is a battle between the god of Sennacherib, who has overcome all the gods of the other nations, and the God of Hezekiah...

Our spiritual battle is in truth a battle between God and the devil; we are not a party to it, and cannot be a party. If we hide in God we gain the victory by Him and in Him, however much the enemy tries to reproach us! This is what the prophet David realized when he saw Goliath the giant opposing his people, for he said: "For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" (1 Sam 17:26), "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts..." (1 Sam 17:45).

14 And Hezekiah received the letters from the hand of the messengers, and read them: and Hezekiah went up unto the house of the LORD, and spread them before the LORD. 15 And Hezekiah prayed unto the LORD, saying, 16 "O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, that sittest above the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth: thou hast made heaven and earth. 17 Incline thine ear, O LORD, and hear; open thine eyes, O LORD, and see: and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he hath sent to reproach the living God. 18 Of a truth, LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations, and their countries, 19 And have cast their gods into the fire: for they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone: therefore they have destroyed them. 20 Now therefore, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the LORD, even thou only."
Hezekiah took Sennacherib's written letter from the hand of the messengers and read it, then went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD, then prayed [14-15].

If Sennacherib reckoned that he bore no personal enmity toward Hezekiah but that it was a battle between gods, Hezekiah set out to his God to lay the matter before Him in His holy house. Perhaps among the most beautiful traits of Hezekiah is that he was a man of prayer, for on five occasions we hear of him that he enjoys power through prayer.
The following is observed in his prayer:

a. The openness of his heart in prayer together with his reverence and humility... He did not justify himself in anything, but disappeared completely, setting the matter in full frankness in God's hands.
b. He calls God "LORD of hosts," as the mighty Commander of the battle, whose hosts are heavenly, able to give victory and triumph over the enemy.

St. Jerome tells us of an Egyptian monk called Abba Aban: [One of those working in the fields beside the river asked him to drive away from them the "Behemoth" (a kind of Egyptian crocodile), which was harming them by its violence, and he, in a gentle voice, commanded the animal: "I adjure you in the name of Jesus Christ to depart," and the animal began to withdraw as though by an angel, and no longer appeared in that region].

In Christ Jesus our Lord we enjoy sure victory. Origen asked: [If Satan and his powers have truly been crushed, how do we believe that he still has such authority against the servants of God? And he answers, saying: The violent activity of Satan has its effect on the wicked alone, but he no longer has authority over those who are in Christ.

c. He calls God the One who sits above the cherubim, for He has no need of a temporal throne, but His throne is heavenly... Therefore in His work He seeks not what is for Himself but what is for the edification of His people and His believers.
d. He calls God "God of all the kingdoms of the earth," and not only the God of Israel; all the nations are in His hand, and He moves the whole world by His holy will.
e. Truly Sennacherib overcame the neighboring nations and cast their gods into the fire to burn and perish... but what can he do to the Creator?!

f. He offered a wonderful conclusion to the prayer: "Now therefore, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that thou art the LORD, even thou only" [20]. It is as though the victory You give us is a witness in the world to the sincerity of our faith in You, and that You, You alone are God, and there is no other besides You.

21 Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent unto Hezekiah, saying, "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Whereas thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria: 22 This is the word which the LORD hath spoken concerning him; She hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn, the virgin, the daughter of Zion; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee. 23 Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? even against the Holy One of Israel. 24 By the hand of thy servants hast thou reproached the Lord, and hast said, By the multitude of my chariots am I come up to the height of the mountains, to the sides of Lebanon; and I will cut down the tall cedars thereof, and the choice fir trees thereof: and I will enter into the height of his border, the forest of his Carmel. 25 I have digged, and drunk water; and with the sole of my feet will I dry up all the streams of Egypt. 26 Hast thou not heard long ago, how I have done it; and of ancient times, that I have formed it? Now have I brought it to pass, that thou shouldest be to lay waste defenced cities into ruinous heaps. 27 Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded: they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up. 28 But I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me. 29 Because thy rage against me, and thy pride, is come up into mine ears, therefore will I put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest. 30 And this shall be a sign unto thee: Ye shall eat this year such as groweth of itself; and the second year that which springeth of the same; and in the third year sow ye, and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat the fruit thereof. 31 And the remnant that is escaped of the house of Judah shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward. 32 For out of Jerusalem shall go forth a remnant, and they that escape out of mount Zion: the zeal of the LORD of hosts shall do this. 33 Therefore thus saith the LORD concerning the king of Assyria, He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shields, nor cast a bank against it. 34 By the way that he came, by the same shall he return, and shall not come into this city, saith the LORD. 35 For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake."
Hezekiah prayed to God, and the answer came quickly by way of Isaiah the prophet, the content of which is as follows:

a. If Sennacherib blasphemed God and mocked Him, the Lord directed His speech to Sennacherib, mocking him, saying: "She hath despised thee, the daughter of Zion hath laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee..." [22] and so on... It is as though He were saying to him: If you have raged against Me like a ravenous beast, I know how to restrain you and mock you through the virgin, the daughter of Zion, the daughter of Jerusalem... or as though He were saying to him: You come to Me with your massive army, and I crush you by a virgin girl who despises you. You boast of the multitude of your chariots, for you went up to the high mountains and cut down the cedars of Lebanon and its fir trees and went deep into the wild thicket of Carmel, and you did not perceive My power, for when I dig in the mountains with My hand I send forth water to drink, and when I tread the rivers with My feet I dry them up; in My hand are the keys of nature... Remember what I did to Pharaoh in the days of the prophet Moses [24-26]. Remember what I did to the nations when I gave the Promised Land to My people! Learn from history through practical events so that you may not be crushed!

God declares to Sennacherib that He is the Controller of all and the Knower of secrets, and He has no need for him to send letters blaspheming Him, for He knows his sitting down and his going out and his coming in and his raging against Him... and He is able to bridle him like animals, putting a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips, and to turn him about like a led animal to return from where he came.

In other words, God mocked him in several ways: He can humiliate him through a virgin girl who despises him; He stirs up nature against him, controls his movements and leads him where he does not wish! In other words, God humbles the enemy of good through His virgin, chaste Church, making nature serve on behalf of His queen, and crushing all the resources and plans of the enemy of good.

It is told in the life of St. Melania that the enemy of good realized that all his struggles against her had failed; he felt defeated and surrendered, and was no longer able to resist her. And Origen sees that it is fitting for us to blame ourselves when we sin, and not to reckon that Satan is the cause of our error, as the simple common people think. We have been given in Christ Jesus the power to crush the enemy if we wish.

b. God gave Hezekiah a glorious sign to remove from him the terror of the hardships that came upon him because of Sennacherib's invasion [30-32]. If the enemy had seized the harvest so that no seed remained for sowing, which leads to the occurrence of famine or at least to a shortage of food, then the crop comes up that year without need of seed (perhaps from the remnants that fell by chance); and so in the following year, and in the third year, when the people recover their strength, life returns to normal. It is as though God works wonders for them as long as they are helpless and their resources are exhausted, until, when they are in their normal state, He works by them through the natural life and through the laws of nature.

This sign was a symbol of the remnant that escaped from Judah, for their deliverance is a gift from God despite the resistance and violence of the enemies, as He says: "They shall again take root downward, and bear fruit upward" [31], as though the enemy had uprooted them completely, so that they became like those without roots, but God raises them up and gives them fruit, as He did with the crop in the first and second years of Sennacherib's invasion... "The zeal of the LORD of hosts shall do this" [32]. That is, this salvation is not accomplished by human merit but out of God's love for His people and His jealousy over them, being the heavenly Bridegroom jealous over His bride, that she may be holy to Him and that no other may seize her.
"Thus saith the LORD of hosts; I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy" (Zech 1:14).
"For the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God" (Ex 34:14).
Through this sign God declares blessings toward His people, which are:
First: the deliverance of the people from judgment, so that famine does not come upon them but they enjoy abundant fruit [30].
Second: the remnant is planted anew in Jerusalem [32], a reference to the renewal of human nature and God's care for His Church.
Third: they bear fruit upward [31], that is, they carry a heavenly, exalted nature.
Fourth: the spread of the preaching from Jerusalem [32].
Fifth: the secret of this saving work is the fire of God's love and His burning zeal [32].

c. God's assurance that Sennacherib will not enter Jerusalem [33-35]; he will not shoot one arrow toward it nor come before it with a shield, nor cast a bank against it... but will return in shame to where he came from. So God, in His love for His children, uses every means to remove anxiety from them, assuring them of His protection, His care and His practical love toward them.

d. The secret of His protection of His people is not their own righteousness but His jealousy for His glory and for His covenants with His beloved children such as David. It is not for the sake of Judah, nor for the sake of Hezekiah's moving prayers, that God intervenes, but as He said: "For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake" [35].
David died, but his life continues through his lifted-up prayers, for the sake of which God defends the city of Jerusalem.

entries.section: 6. The smiting of the Assyrian army:

paragraphs.text: "Then the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote of the army of Assyria a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses." [36].
By the angel of the LORD is most often meant the Word of God before the Incarnation, and this was fulfilled on the very night that followed the prophet Isaiah's talk with Hezekiah (2 Kgs 19:35).

Sennacherib was defeated this time although he had previously besieged Hezekiah and humiliated him, for in one of the excavations found in the ruins of Nineveh there are words on the tongue of Sennacherib that he attacked Hezekiah and took 46 horses and small cities, and also carried captive 150 and 200 persons, great and small, male and female, and a great number of animals; and that he shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage and set up ramparts before his city and imposed on him a doubled tribute, etc...

entries.section: 7. The death of Sennacherib and his son Sharezer:

paragraphs.text: 37 So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh. 38 And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Ararat: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.

Sennacherib was killed, and his son with him, while he was bowing down in the house of Nisroch his god, whom he thought able to protect him and the secret of his victory over all the nations and their gods...

entries.section: 1. Set your house in order, for you shall die:

paragraphs.text: 1 In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said unto him, “Thus saith the LORD, Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live.” 2 Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the LORD, 3 and said, “Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight.” And Hezekiah wept sore. 4 Then came the word of the LORD to Isaiah, saying, 5 “Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years. 6 And I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria: and I will defend this city. 7 And this shall be a sign unto thee from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he hath spoken; 8 Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward.” So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down.

“In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death” [1]. It is clear from this phrase and from verse [6] that Hezekiah’s illness came in the days of Sennacherib’s invasion. Some scholars think it was because of a plague that struck the city on account of the siege, while others think it was a psychological and physical collapse because of what had befallen his country.
Isaiah came to him, taking away from him every hope of remaining in this world, saying to him, “Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live” [1].
The news of his death was a shock to him, perhaps for one of the following reasons:
a. Like our teacher the Apostle Paul, he longed to depart, but he felt an obligation toward serving others.
b. Perhaps, like other men of the Old Testament who feared death, because in their minds it was bound up with sin and the wrath of God upon man.

entries.section: 1. Set your house in order, for you shall die:

paragraphs.text: c. Perhaps he expected to see in his days the Christ of the Lord, the Second Adam, the representative of all humanity, as is stated in his psalm [11].

d. Perhaps the main reason was that Manasseh had not yet been born (2 Kgs 21:1), so there was no one to succeed him on the throne. This troubled him, for how would the promise to the house of David be fulfilled, that it would remain forever? In this Hezekiah was very weak, unlike Abraham, who offered his son as a sacrifice without fear, trusting that God’s promise would surely be fulfilled, believing in God, who is able to raise him from the dead. Afterward Hezekiah begot “Manasseh,” a lover of idol worship, who provoked God’s wrath against Judah (2 Kgs 23:26).

In any case, Hezekiah was a man of prayer. The news did not rob him of his hope in the Lord; he knew how to pray and to wrestle. He turned his face toward the wall, perhaps facing the Temple as was the custom of the Jews, to pray to the Lord, saying, “Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect (complete) heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight” [3]. Hezekiah looked upon his life as a journey in which he walked with God (Gen 5:24; 1 Kgs 9:4) with sincerity, not in absolute perfection but aiming toward perfection (Mt 5:45), with a single mind, neither hesitant nor deviating.
Hezekiah wept sore [3].

The divine command was issued to Isaiah to go to the king and tell him, “Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years” [5]. The answer came very quickly (2 Kgs 20:4); perhaps God spoke with Isaiah mouth to mouth before he left the royal palace, while he was giving spiritual counsel to the men of the palace to prepare the atmosphere for after the king’s death.

God heard Hezekiah’s prayer, looked upon his tears, and remembered His promise to David his father, since God remembers His covenant with the father in the case of his sons (Ex 20:5; Ps 89:28-29). He gave him the request of his heart, what he uttered with his tongue and what he spoke in his heart: He granted him length of days, deliverance from the king of Assyria, and protection for his city, or the capital of his kingdom, Jerusalem.

entries.section: 1. Set your house in order, for you shall die:

paragraphs.text: The Lord gave him a sign as he requested [22]; Hezekiah differed from his wicked father, who refused to ask a sign from God (Isa 7:10).

The divine sign came to confirm the fulfillment of the divine promise in this way: the sun returned ten degrees [8]. Some think it was merely a retreat of the shadow on the steps leading to a “balcony” in the palace or leading to the upper chamber. Others think it was an eclipse of the sun that occurred on January 11, 689 B.C. The sun is the true measure of time, and in God’s hand it is the mover of history, of events and of time itself. He used it as a sign in the days of Joshua (Josh 10:12), and also in the days of Hezekiah, and at the crucifixion of the Lord of glory, and before His final coming, when the sun shall be darkened...
God, the Father of lights, moves the sun and directs it for our edification.
Perhaps some will ask: Did God change His mind by lengthening Hezekiah’s life?

St. Augustine holds that Hezekiah ought to have died through natural causes such as illness, but that he added fifteen years to his life; this addition God knew before the foundation of the world, keeping it in His will. What He did by way of addition accomplished what was in God’s plan, since He knows what Hezekiah would do and what God would give him.

What should occupy our minds is not to inquire whether God had previously fixed Hezekiah’s age and then retracted it by adding fifteen years to it, but rather to realize the power of prayer in our lives, for it gave him life after he ought to have died according to the laws of nature. Prayer, as a clinging to God, the Giver of life, is able to do all things, and is victorious over death, the death of sin.
St. John Chrysostom says: [When we pray for the forgiveness of sins, we fulfill God’s will, and so we are assured that our prayer is answered.]

* Through prayer offerings were accepted; prayer is what turned the flood away from Noah; prayer healed barrenness and routed armies; prayer revealed mysteries; prayer divided the sea and made a way in the Jordan; prayer turned the sun back and stayed the moon, destroyed the defiled, and brought down fire.
Prayer shut the heaven, brought (men) out of the pit, rescued from the fire, and delivered from the sea. The power of prayer, like the power of pure fasting, is exceedingly great...
* Hezekiah prayed, and his prayer overcame 185,000 men, by means of an angel who acted as the commander of the army (2 Kgs 19:15, 35)...
* Daniel prayed, and his prayer stopped the mouths of the lions...
* Each one of our righteous fathers took up the weapon of prayer when sorrows met them, and they were delivered from them.
Father Aphrahat * Blessed is the man who agrees to be an intimate friend of faith and prayer, for he lives with a single mind...
* The prayer that rises in a man’s heart opens for us the door of heaven...
* Prayer establishes peace with the wrath of God...

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * Prayer is able to press upon Satan, who presses upon the human race. It is able to deliver from his hand and to free from every temptation in the world. For this reason our Lord rightly commanded us to watch and pray, lest we enter into temptation (Mt 26:41).
Father Martyrius

9 The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick, and was recovered of his sickness: 10 “I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years. 11 I said, I shall not see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world. 12 Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd’s tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off from the loom: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me. 13 I cried until the morning; as a lion, so will he break all my bones: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me. 14 Like a swallow chirping, so did I cry: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me. 15 What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul. 16 O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these things is the life of my spirit: so wilt thou recover me, and make me to live. 17 Behold, for peace my bitterness was turned for me, and thou hast held my soul back from the pit of destruction: for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back. 18 For the grave cannot praise thee, death cannot celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. 19 The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth. 20 The LORD is for my salvation: therefore we will play on our stringed instruments all the days of our life in the house of the LORD.”

a. We often remember God in time of distress and hardship but forget Him in time of relief and joy. Hezekiah, however, showed himself a man of prayer and tears in the midst of suffering, and a man of praise at the time of relief, who knew how to thank God for His benefits.
In this psalm he showed himself to be a man of prayer, a man of praise, a poet and psalmist, a stranger in the world, full of hope in the Lord who saves from death and gives joyful life.

b. It was good that Hezekiah offered this psalm as a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, the Giver of life, and it would have been better for him to offer his very life as a sacrifice of thanksgiving to Him; but sadly he offered a song of thanksgiving without a life of thanksgiving, for it is said: “But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem” (2 Chr 32:25).

It befits us to praise God not only with our tongues, uttering psalms of thanksgiving to Him, but also with all the members of our body, our feelings and our senses, as well as our practical conduct, so that our whole life is turned into a harp of varied strings playing a symphony of love to God, our Creator and Savior.

c. Hezekiah’s psalm shows how he suffered at the beginning from a spirit of despair, for he said: “I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years” [10]. Hezekiah was about thirty-nine years old; he felt that in the prime of his youth his happy days had been cut off and that he was deprived of serving God and His people, which he had set in his heart to complete throughout the years of his life. It is as if he were repeating the words of King David: “For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes” (Ps 31:22).

d. Perhaps Hezekiah expected to see the Christ of the Lord in his days, or hoped for His coming incarnate from his seed, and here he was dying without offspring. Therefore he cried out in despair: “I said, I shall not see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world” [11]. Thus he was awaiting to see the Christ of the Lord here, or to enjoy the glory of the Lord in the other life, but despair shattered him.

“I said, I shall not see the LORD”... What hope have we in this world or in the world to come unless we enjoy the sight of the Lord, here through the eyes of the heart by faith, and there face to face!

* Blessed, thrice blessed, indeed many times blessed are those who are counted worthy to behold that glory. Of this the prophet says: “Let the wicked be taken away, that he behold not the glory of the LORD” [(Isa 36:10) LXX]. May God grant that none of us be taken away or excluded from beholding (the Lord)... For why do we live? Why do we breathe? What will become of us if we fail to behold our Lord and are not granted this? If those who cannot behold the light of the sun count life harsher than death, what will be the state of those who are deprived of that Light?

St. John Chrysostom * Before I show you our God, show me your man; and give me proof that the eyes of your soul can see and the ears of your heart can hear. On the contrary, those whose eyes are afflicted with the cloud of sin cannot behold God...

When you are removed from your corruptible nature and put on incorruption, you will see God, since you will be made worthy of it. For God will give life to your body and make it, with your immortal soul, deathless; then you will see the One who alone is immortal, if you believe in Him now.
St. Theophilus of Antioch e. He presents several similes by which he expresses his temporal life:

The first simile: the shepherd’s tent, quickly moved [12]. This creates the sense of being a stranger; we have no place in the world in which to settle, so that we are like our father Abraham, who did not cease to walk on the journey of his life... We remain in this moving tent until we pass over to an eternal dwelling not made with human hands. Our teacher the Apostle Paul used this simile (2 Cor 5:1), and also St. Peter (2 Pet 1:14).

The second simile: weaving, “I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off from the loom: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me” [12]. Thus God weaves our life like a garment cut from the loom, woven according to the size of each one’s body; it does not last long but only for a while, like one who wears it for a single day and night and then it is taken off. As Eliphaz the Temanite says: “They are destroyed from morning to evening” (Job 4:19-20).
The third simile: the prey whose bones the lion breaks, all of them, between one day and night [13].

The fourth simile: like a swallow chirping, he cries out in weakness, for his voice grew faint because of illness, or rather because of his despair of recovery; his voice became like the moaning of a dove [14], and his eyes became unable to look upward [14].

f. We find a swift transition from the feeling of the bitterness of the despairing soul [15] to the experience of new life, for he says without preface: “O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these things is the life of my spirit: so wilt thou recover me, and make me to live” [16]... He passes from death to life and from bitterness to peace [17]; the secret of this is the intervention of the Lord Christ, and the discovery of His divine work of salvation, for he says: “For thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back... The LORD is for my salvation: therefore we will play on our stringed instruments all the days of our life in the house of the LORD” [17, 20].
What did he find in his Savior?
First: his life was changed from an exceedingly terrifying journey, bitter to the soul, into a calm life filled with peace, in which the believer fears not even the pit [17].
Second: his soul rejoices not because of his healing from the illness and the length of his life, but because of the forgiveness of all his sins [17].
Third: he came to long to hand on to the coming generations this new life, or the truth of God [19].

Fourth: all the rest of his life was turned into a psalm of unceasing joy [20], which he sings as in the house of the Lord. For this reason St. Athanasius the Apostolic speaks to us of the feast (or joy) as being “Christ” Himself, the secret of our constant gladness. As he said: [Only those who live in Christ are able to glorify God and bless Him; by this they go up to the feast.]
In any case, the believer who lives in Christ enjoys a life of constant joy and also constant thanksgiving, in the midst of his sufferings and his joys.

* There is no time more fitting for a man to hold feelings of thanksgiving toward God than when he is in trials and troubles. And there is no better time for offering thanks than when he comes to rest after struggles and trials.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic * Prayer is a joy that expresses itself in thanksgiving.
Father Evagrius * Through spiritual prayer and utterances of thanksgiving we rise from the earth to the heights.
Father Martyrius

entries.section: 3. His healing by a lump of figs:

paragraphs.text: 21 For Isaiah had said, “Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover.” 22 Hezekiah also had said, “What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?”

Isaiah the prophet asked Hezekiah to place a lump of figs [a cake of pressed figs] on the inflamed part of his body so that he would be healed... Why? So that God might declare that although He is the Physician who heals, He uses the medicines and material means that He created to meet our needs; and at that time they used to place a lump of pressed figs on inflamed places of the body as a treatment. On the other hand, healing is a free divine gift that God gives of His own accord.

entries.section: 3. His healing by a lump of figs:

paragraphs.text: The lump of figs, like the cluster of grapes, both point to the living life of the Church. For the fig holds countless very fine seeds; a single seed has no value or taste unless it is joined with the rest of the seeds under one covering that gathers them together, as if in the sweetness of love and unity. This is the secret of the Church’s sweetness. And this is the cause of our healing: with the personal, hidden relationship each of us has with God, we gather together like a sweet fig in the mouth of God. Therefore Hezekiah said of the sign of his healing, “that I shall go up to the house of the LORD” [22], to gather with the people of God through the Lord Himself.

1 At that time Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present to Hezekiah: for he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered. 2 And Hezekiah was glad of them, and shewed them the house of his precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices, and the precious ointment, and all the house of his armour, and all that was found in his treasures: there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not.

Hezekiah’s star rose because of the defeat of Sennacherib king of Assyria, and Hezekiah offered a psalm of thanksgiving to God, especially after God gave him fifteen years more of his life; but he did not practice thanksgiving in his life, for his heart was lifted up and he became haughty (2 Chr 32:26), and he had “exceeding much riches and honour, and he made himself treasuries for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones, and for spices, and for shields, and for all manner of pleasant vessels... and he made himself towers, and possessions of flocks and herds in abundance: for God had given him substance very much” (2 Chr 32:27-29).

God left him in the midst of this wealth and glory for a time, and wanted to discover what was in his heart (2 Chr 32:31), so He allowed Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, to send letters and a present after his healing. It was fitting for Hezekiah to glorify God and to show forth the grace of God, not to reveal his treasures. He fell into self-reliance and the display of his own glory, as Samson had fallen before, who disclosed the secret of his strength to the harlot and so collapsed.

“Merodach” is a title borne by many persons; it is the name of the king of the gods, mentioned together with Bel (Jer 50:2), and is symbolized by the planet Mars. His name is often part of the name of one of the kings of Babylon. As for “Baladan,” its meaning is: “a son has been given.”

St. Hippolytus says: [Merodach the Chaldean, king of Babylon at that time, was astonished when he studied astronomy and measured these bodies and learned the cause, so he sent a letter and gifts, as the Magi from the East did with Christ.]

Hezekiah was carried away by the pride of his heart and his love of vain worldly glory, so as to reveal everything he had to the messengers of Merodach-baladan: “there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not” [2]. Hezekiah had not experienced the words of David his father: “The glory of the king’s son is from within” (Ps 45).
* Vainglory has the power to blind the minds of those who are captive to it, even to plain truths, and to lead them to dispute even matters that are generally agreed upon...

* Those who are enslaved by zeal for the glory of this present world cannot obtain the glory that is from God. For this reason the Lord rebukes them: “How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from the (only) God?” (cf. Jn 5:44).

This passion is a kind of intense drunkenness, and whoever submits to it is hard to cure. It separates the souls of its captives from heavenly things and nails them to the earth; it does not let them look to the true light but urges them to wallow in the mud; it sets over them harsh masters who dominate them, needing only to give orders.
Whoever is struck by this disease acts according to his own whim...
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. The divine command to take away the treasures:

paragraphs.text: 3 Then came Isaiah the prophet unto king Hezekiah, and said unto him, “What said these men? and from whence came they unto thee?” And Hezekiah said, “They are come from a far country unto me, even from Babylon.” 4 Then said he, “What have they seen in thine house?” And Hezekiah answered, “All that is in mine house have they seen: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them.” 5 Then said Isaiah to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: 6 Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD. 7 And of thy sons that shall issue from thee, which thou shalt beget, shall they take away; and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
God sent His prophet Isaiah to Hezekiah to discipline him, and he asked him:
* What said these men?
* And from whence came they unto thee?
* What have they seen in thine house?
He did not answer the most important question: “What said these men?”
He thought that they had come from a far country, from Babylon [3], and so there was no danger to him from them; therefore the divine sentence of punishment was issued through Babylon.

entries.section: 2. The divine command to take away the treasures:

paragraphs.text: The punishment came severe, because pride is an exceedingly dangerous disease, meaning fellowship in the nature of Satan. Hezekiah would not only lose the treasures he had revealed, but would also lose the freedom of his children, who would become eunuchs in the house of the king of Babylon [7].

Origen holds that pride is the chief sin of Satan. St. John Chrysostom says: [Satan would not have fallen and become Satan had he not been struck by this disease. It cast him out of confidence (in God) and brought him to the pit of fire, and it is the cause of all woes. It is able to destroy every good thing of the soul, whether there is giving (the offering of alms) or prayer or fasting or anything else... Nothing is more foolish than the proud man, even if wealth surrounds him, or he has gained much of the wisdom of this world, or is found in a royal palace...]
“Then said Hezekiah to Isaiah, Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken. He said moreover, For there shall be peace and truth in my days.” [8].

Outwardly the king uttered words that carry submission, but we do not know what his attitudes and motives were; perhaps it was a surrender without repentance and without trust in God, who is able to forgive sins.

He confessed that he had sinned, but he did not offer repentance. The proof of this is that instead of crying out to God with tears in order to return to Him, he felt reassured that the discipline would come after his death, in the days of his children. He carried a kind of selfishness, for he was concerned to spend his days in peace, with no concern for what would befall the people and his descendants afterward.

entries.section: 1. Comfort ye, comfort ye my people:

paragraphs.text: 1 Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God. 2 Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD’s hand double for all her sins.

God was accustomed to ascribe the people to Himself when He was pleased with them, calling them “My people”; but in the case of their disobedience He sometimes ascribes them to Moses (Ex 32:7) or calls them “the people” (Ex 32:9), and more plainly He says, “not my people” (Hos 1:9), in order to provoke them so that they would return to Him, and then He returns to ascribing them to Himself (Hos 2:23). But here, as He opens before them, indeed before believing humanity, the door of salvation, He calls them “My people.”

The prophet was accustomed to repeat some words twice, as here, “Comfort ye, comfort ye” (Isa 51:9, 17; 5:1), because he is speaking of the Church of the New Testament that comes from two groups, the Jews and the Gentiles; for it is the Church of love, which unites and binds together, since the number 2 points to love. Love makes the two one.

entries.section: 1. Comfort ye, comfort ye my people:

paragraphs.text: It is the Church of love, by which God binds her to Himself as a bridegroom to his bride, and which binds the members coming from all the nations as one body to the one Head. Through this love He addresses her, saying, “Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem” [2]; the literal translation is “speak to the heart of Jerusalem,” an expression repeated eight times in the Old Testament (Gen 34:3; 50:21; Judg 19:3; Ruth 2:13; 2 Sam 19:7; 2 Chr 20:22; Hos 2:14) and directed to a beloved man or woman. The Church here is the bride of Christ, beloved of Him, and He speaks to her in the language of love, which only the heart understands. It is the language in which He spoke most plainly and profoundly through the Cross, to acquire humanity as His bride (Rev 19:7; 21:2, 9).

It is an invitation that the Bridegroom offers to His suffering bride, that in the midst of her sufferings she may look to the joyful end, and so bear suffering in hope and with joy, like her Bridegroom, who suffered for the joy that was set before Him (Heb 12:2), since He saw our salvation and glorification in His bearing of the Cross. As the Apostle says: “For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ” (2 Cor 5:1).

What is the secret of our comfort? God says: “I, even I, am he that comforteth you” (Isa 51:14). This is the secret of our comfort: the Father comes forward to receive us to Himself as His children, through our union with Christ, the Only-Begotten Son, who offers His life as an atonement for our sins as the secret of our comfort: “our consolation also aboundeth by Christ” (2 Cor 1:5). Our Christ, who has received us to Himself by His blood, gives us His Holy Spirit, “the Comforter,” who fills our hearts with Him, establishing the kingdom of joy in our hearts. For this reason He gives a speech directed to the heart, saying, “Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD’s hand double for all her sins” [2].

From the literal side, the prophet looks at the captivity that befalls the people not as a political disaster that happened by chance or as the fruit of military weakness, but as a divine permission for the sake of discipline. She received the discipline twofold, for on the one hand she committed sins unbecoming to her, and on the other hand she did not practice the righteousness of God or do good. The divine commandment requires us to cease from evil and to do good.

From the prophetic side, as she looks to her crucified Bridegroom she finds that He has paid the debt for her in the fullest form, not merely to relieve her of the debt but to justify her by His blood and sanctify her, so that she enjoys fellowship in His glories. It is as though the supplications of humanity, which David the prophet expressed, had been fulfilled when he said: “Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins” (Ps 25:18).

Now the prophet looks at the procession of the people returning to Jerusalem as a symbol of the procession of those redeemed by the blood of the Lord of glory, Jesus, and St. John the Baptist came to prepare the way for this heavenly Messianic procession.

entries.section: 2. Preparing the way for the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 3 The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, “Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. 4 Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: 5 And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.” 6 The voice said, “Cry.” And he said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: 7 The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. 8 The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.”

Perhaps the prophet Isaiah heard a heavenly voice calling the heavenly ones to prepare the procession of the return from captivity to Jerusalem. For the prophet Ezekiel had previously seen the glory of the Lord departing from the city (Ezek 11:22-25), and now the procession returns with the return of the captives, as though it were a royal procession led by God Himself, the liberator of His children!

But the greater procession is the preparation of the way for the entrance of the Messiah the Savior into the life of humanity, which was accomplished by St. John the Baptist, the angel of the Lord, through preaching repentance and proclaiming the need for a Savior (Mk 1:3; Mt 3:3; Lk 3:4-6; Jn 1:22).

entries.section: 2. Preparing the way for the Lord:

paragraphs.text: St. John was the voice that resounds in the wilderness to prepare the way for the divine Word, proclaiming that every arrogant and haughty soul is brought down [4], and every crooked heart becomes straight, and all obstacles vanish, because the glory of the Lord is revealed through the Messiah the Savior, and all flesh sees it together, both Jews and Gentiles. Therefore the prophet says: “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain: and the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it” [3-5].

John was called a “voice,” while Christ was called the “Word,” and how great the difference between the voice and the word! For the Fathers say that the voice is what is heard by the ear, while the word is what is grasped by the mind. So John came as a witness to Christ, the divine Word:

* Perhaps this explains how Zechariah lost his voice at the birth of the “voice” who points toward the Word of God, and was not healed of this until after the birth of the “voice” who precedes the Word. The voice must be perceived by the ear so that the mind receives the Word toward whom the “voice” points. John points toward Christ, because the speech (the word) is made known by means of the voice.

Origen * From our speech you know that the “voice” comes first when the “word” is heard; therefore John declares of himself that he is a “voice,” since he goes before the “Word.” By his coming before the Lord he was called a “voice,” and by his ministry men heard “the word of the Lord.” He cries out, proclaiming: “make his paths straight”... The way of the Lord to the heart is straight when it receives with humility His words of truth; it is straight if we conduct our lives in agreement with His commandments. Therefore it is said: “If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him” (Jn 14:23).

Father Gregory the Great * Isaiah was aware of John’s work of evangelism, for while Isaiah calls Christ God and Lord (Isa 9:6), he points to John as a messenger and servant, and a lamp that shines before the appearing of the true Light. He is the morning star that announces the rising of the sun from beyond the horizon, whose brilliant rays then dispel the dense curtains of darkness. John was a voice, not the Word, going before Christ as the voice goes before the word.

St. Cyril the Great With what does this voice cry out? With the Gospel of the New Testament, which is the way of the Lord, which lifts the humble souls up to the heavenly life, and breaks down the pride of the haughty; it renews the creation that had become crooked so that it walks uprightly, and removes the obstacles from before it, so that the Lord is glorified in believing humanity [3-5].

* May you walk in the royal way, not turning from it to the right or to the left, but may the Spirit lead you through the narrow gate; then all your affairs will prosper when you are examined there in Christ Jesus our Lord.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness” [3] resounds in the wilderness of this barren life, since it does not bear within it the tree of life as in the first Paradise; he came to proclaim the Lord Christ, the tree of life, who is planted in the wilderness of our nature to make of it a fruitful Paradise by His dwelling in us. In this sense St. Ambrose says: [Before the Son of God raised up the members of the Church, He began His work in His servant John; for this reason St. Luke (Lk 3:2) informs us that the word of God came at once upon John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness... This was accomplished in the desolate wilderness, for “the children of the desolate are more than the children of her which hath a husband” (Isa 54:1), and it was said to her, “Rejoice, O barren one that didst not bear” (Isa 54:1)... for she had not yet been planted among the foreign peoples... and He had not yet come who said, “But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God” (Ps 52:8), and the heavenly Vinedresser had not yet given fruit to the branches (Jn 15:1). So the voice rang out in order that the wilderness might bring forth fruit.]

* Let the way of the Lord be prepared in our heart, for the heart of man is great and wide, as if it were the world. Look at its greatness not in bodily size, but in the power of the mind, which gives it the ability to embrace a very great knowledge of the truth.

Therefore let the way of the Lord be prepared in your heart through a worthy life and through good and perfect works, so that this way may keep your life upright, and the words of the Lord may enter you without hindrance.

entries.section: 2. Preparing the way for the Lord:

paragraphs.text: Origen St. Augustine observed that the prophet used the word “flesh” in the phrase “And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all mankind (flesh) shall see it together” [5], and that by this he does not mean the flesh without the soul but the whole man, for Holy Scripture often uses the word “flesh” or “soul” to mean the man. For the one who beholds the glory of the Lord is the whole man [for the flesh alone without the soul sees nothing].

When the Evangelist said, “the Word was made flesh” (Jn 1:14), he did not mean that the Word of God took flesh without a human soul, as Apollinaris claimed, which led Pope Athanasius the Apostolic to write a book against his friend Apollinaris, in which he refutes his opinions.

entries.section: 2. Preparing the way for the Lord:

paragraphs.text: The prophet Isaiah heard another heavenly voice affirming that all flesh (man) is like the grass of the earth (Ps 90:5; 103:15), “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” [8]. Whoever clings to the dust of the earth or to the love of temporal things becomes passing grass, and whoever clings to the Lord Christ, “the Word of God,” rises with Him to live in His glory forever. This is the way that Holy Scripture has prepared for receiving the Savior: our commitment to fellowship with the One who transforms us from the passing grass of the earth into fellowship with Him and abiding in Him eternally in His glories. As St. Augustine says: [If a man longs for true rest and true happiness, he must lift his hope above mortal, passing things and fix it on the word of the Lord, so that, clinging to it, it remains forever and he remains with it eternally.]

Origen comments on the saying that “all flesh is grass,” saying: [The Lord Christ commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass (Mt 14:21) in order to feed them, meaning that if a man subdues his body (sitting on the grass) and places all temporal things under the leadership of the soul, so that he walks wholly in the Holy Spirit, then he enjoys the blessings of the Lord Christ and the true satisfaction. We cannot meet our Christ or receive His divine gifts through the disciples, that is, the Church, as long as we live according to the flesh. Therefore let us subject the body to our souls by the Holy Spirit and let us recline on the grass, so that the body may be an obedient servant working in harmony with the soul without resisting it; then we shall enjoy spiritual things.

The following are some comments of the Fathers on the phrase “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: the grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it” [6-7].

Look, for whatever your soul clings to, it clings to forever. If you cling to the grass and the flower of the grass, you bind your soul to the grass that withers and the flower that falls, and God will destroy these in the end.

* Since God, as a Father, knows our formation, that we are nothing but dust that can flourish only for a time, He sent us His Word, and this Word of His remains forever. He made Him a brother to the grass that does not last.
Do not marvel, for you have become a partaker with Him in His eternity, since He first shared with you in the grass.

* So Moses did with the head of the calf [(Ex 32:20) he burned it with fire], for the head of the calf represents a great mystery, in that it represents the flesh of the wicked, because it eats grass and seeks temporal things; for all flesh is grass...

St. Augustine * Why do you fear temporal things that pass like the course of a river?! For this is the nature of present things, whether joyful or painful. Another prophet compares human prosperity to grass.
St. John Chrysostom * We hear this and the like every day, and yet we remain nailed to the earth.

St. John Chrysostom * I know that some try to show that these words (all flesh is grass) refer to the condition of barbarous people of different nations and different customs, who came to faith (in the word of the Lord) and so came into the harmony of the righteous.
St. Irenaeus

9 O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain; O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings, lift up thy voice with strength; lift it up, be not afraid; say unto the cities of Judah, “Behold your God! 10 Behold, the Lord GOD will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him: behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. 11 He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.” 12 Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance? 13 Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him? 14 With whom took he counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the way of truth, and taught him knowledge, and shewed to him the way of understanding? 15 Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing. 16 And Lebanon is not sufficient to burn, nor the beasts thereof sufficient for a burnt offering. 17 All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity. 18 To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him? 19 The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains. 20 He that is so impoverished that he hath no oblation chooseth a tree that will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman to prepare a graven image, that shall not be moved. 21 Have ye not known? have ye not heard? hath it not been told you from the beginning? have ye not understood from the foundations of the earth? 22 It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in: 23 That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity. 24 Yea, they shall not be planted; yea, they shall not be sown: yea, their stock shall not take root in the earth: and he shall also blow upon them, and they shall wither, and the whirlwind shall take them away as stubble. 25 “To whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal?” saith the Holy One. 26 Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names by the greatness of his might, for that he is strong in power; not one faileth.

Now, after showing that whoever is attached to perishable temporal things becomes like the grass of the earth that withers, while whoever clings to the eternal Word of God remains with Him forever, he declares the meaning of attachment to the word of the Lord.

a. Receiving the joyful evangelical message: “O Zion, that bringest good tidings, get thee up into the high mountain; O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings, lift up thy voice with strength; lift it up, be not afraid; say unto the cities of Judah, Behold your God! Behold, the Lord GOD will come with strong hand, and his arm shall rule for him” [9-10].

Who is she that lifts up her voice but the Church of the New Testament, which ascends with humanity as upon the mountain of the Word of God through the preaching of the disciples and the apostles, indeed through the witness of all the people; she ascends with souls to the heavenly life, or the new life that has become ours in Christ Jesus, to meet God our Savior as a source of joy and exultation. She sees Him coming to her to rule in her depths and to establish His kingdom by His lofty arm.

b. Perceiving the reality of God; for as we are lifted up to the new life we meet the Lord on a personal level, and we do not find Him a hidden, unknown power but a Being who deals with us: “He comes and rules and rewards and cares, etc... As St. Gregory of Nyssa says in his reply to Eunomius: [Is God, then, an energy and not a person?]
St. John Cassian says: [It befits us, when we hear the word “His arm” or the like, not to understand it in a bodily, material sense.
c. Discovering God’s care for us, as He is the Shepherd who is concerned for His flock [11], and He is unique in His person as in His care:

* He is the almighty Creator in His care: “Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?” He is the Creator of the waters and the heavens, as of the dust and the solid mountains. He who created is able to renew creation.

The waters point to the peoples, the heavens to the soul, the earth to the body, and the mountains and hills to man’s abilities and gifts; as if God in His care is almighty, renewing the Church as a whole by joining the peoples to her, and renewing every soul together with the body, with its energies, senses, feelings and capacities.
He measures and weighs everything, for He is all-powerful.

Perhaps he wanted to affirm that God cares for His lifeless creation, from the waters and the firmament of heaven to the dust and the mountains and hills; so how would He not care for us, who are in His image and likeness, and for whose sake He created the whole world?

* If you doubt God’s providence, ask the earth and the heaven and the sun and the moon. Ask the irrational beings and the crops... Ask the rocks and the mountains and the sand dunes and the hills. Ask the night and the day; for God’s providence is clearer than the sun and its rays, in every place: in the wilderness and the cities and the inhabited world, on the earth and in the seas... Wherever you go you hear a speaking testimony to this crying providence.

St. John Chrysostom * All-wise: “Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him? With whom took he counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the way of truth, and taught him knowledge, and shewed to him the way of understanding?” [13-14].

Though He is the almighty Creator who brought nature into being for our sake and cares for it and looks after it, He is also all-wise, who knows what is for our salvation and edification; His plan is not our plan, and His ordinances are higher than ours (Rom 11:34).

* He (the Apostle Paul, Rom 11) did not say only that His judgments are past finding out, but also that they are beyond searching out. Not only can man not understand them, he cannot even begin to search them out. It is impossible for him to grasp their end or even to discover how their planning began.
* He wants to say that He is the fountain and source of all good things, and has no need of a partner or counsellor.

St. John Chrysostom * The Almighty: nothing escapes His hand: “Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a rudder...” [15].

He is the Almighty... So if the nations want to rule the world and dominate it through violence and force, they are exceedingly weak; God sees them as a drop of water in a bucket and the dust of a balance... But God, in the weakness and foolishness of the Cross, rules and reigns with power and authority over the depths.

The earth with all its peoples is very small to the Savior; He carries it like dust on a small scale; and the inhabitants of the isles, who boast of their merchant and war ships, all of them together are like a rudder that the Lord holds in His hand!
* He (God) comprehends in Himself all rational creation so that all things remain in existence, held together by His power, which embraces all.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * His concern for the nations: “And Lebanon is not sufficient to burn, nor the beasts thereof sufficient for a burnt offering. All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity” [16-17]. A poetic picture of the nations’ acceptance of faith in God, so that all the trees of Lebanon (the cedars) do not suffice to kindle the altar of the Lord and all its beasts do not suffice to offer burnt offerings... The need has become for the wood of the Cross, which towers above all the cedars of Lebanon, and the sacrifice of Christ, which cannot be compared with all the animal sacrifices. Through this altar (the Cross) and this sacrifice the Gentiles enjoy salvation.
* The living divine Lamb reached the place of sacrifice, and the crucifiers stood like high priests offering Him as a victim...!

* Our Lord was crucified and bore the sins of the world, and nailed sin with nails so that it might not reign. When they crucified Him, He crucified it with Him on Golgotha, lest it kill other generations.
Mar Jacob of Serugh * The greatness of the Lord Christ, the Savior and the Sacrifice:

“To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?” [18]; the cost of idols is heavy, requiring gold and silver or wood that will not rot, together with the cost of the cunning workman who makes them [20], and set against this is the thieves’ longing to steal them; but our Christ offers a free salvation, and proclaims His kingdom in the heart, where no one can steal it from our depths.

* “He that sitteth upon the sphere of the earth” [22]. The prevailing belief was that the earth is flat and not a sphere, but Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon the sphere of the earth like a king sitting on his throne, establishing His kingdom in the hearts of men.

* “The inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in” [22]. He does not reign out of need for the service of earthly or heavenly beings, but out of love and fatherly care. The earthly beings are to Him like the grasshopper (locust), and the heaven is like a piece of cloth or a tent. The great ones are as nothing to Him, and the judges, like vanity, dissolve.
Earth and heaven are as nothing compared with His power; but in His love He reigns over and leads the earthly and the heavenly as King and Savior..

The astrologers were occupied with the calculations of the heavens and their systems, but God knows all their details as their Creator, and calls them by names [26]; so how would He not know every man and care for his salvation?!

27 Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, “My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God”? 28 Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding. 29 He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. 30 Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: 31 But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

Those who deny the faith often think that God, in His own realm, is far from the circle of men: He is in His heavens while man lives in his world... This is the essence of contemporary atheistic thought, and it is an ancient thought with which the enemy strikes man in order to make him lose his meeting with his Creator and union with Him and fellowship. As it is stated here in this book: “Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God” [27].

This is what man repeats in the midst of his spiritual weariness... He counts himself alone, isolated even from God, who does not care about man’s way and his life. Perhaps this is what the captives said, as they thought that God had forgotten them completely; months and years passed as though He had broken His covenant with their fathers and no longer thought of them or cared for their return. He does not care about their cause or concern Himself with their way; He left them in Babylon and remained in His heavens, not moving to remove their disgrace and lift humiliation and bondage from them.
The prophet replies to this as follows:

a. The continuity of God’s work: God in His love may be patient, but He continues in His care for man, “fainteth not, neither is weary” [28]. He is “the everlasting God,” His love never passes away and His covenant is eternal and unchanging.
b. His judgments cannot be searched out [28]... He saves in an unexpected way.

c. Because of our sins we grow weak in our faith, but He “giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength” [29]; therefore we need to place the matter in His hands, and He will sustain us even in our faith.

d. He gives us His Holy Spirit, who renews our nature and lifts us up on the wings of the Spirit as to heaven itself, and we rise without anxiety... “But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” [31].
* By the Holy Spirit we are freed from slavery and called to freedom!
By Him we have become children of God by His adoption of us!
And above all this, if I may say so, we have been renewed, putting off from us the hateful weight of sins...!

Through Him we receive the forgiveness of sins, and by Him we are cleansed from every stain, and through His gift we are changed from human beings into angels, who share with us in the enjoyment of His grace; yet we do not become so at once, but, what is marvelous, while we are still in human nature we show a conduct in life that befits angels!
Such then is the power of the Spirit...
St. John Chrysostom

1 “Listen unto me, O islands; and let the tribes renew their strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment. 2 Who raised up from the east him whom victory meets at his feet? He gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings: he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow. 3 He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet. 4 Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he.” 5 The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came. 6 They helped every one his neighbour; and every one said to his brother, “Be of good courage.” 7 So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying of the soldering, “It is good”: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.
The prophet Isaiah presents a wonderful poetic picture of the victory that Israel gains through Cyrus, who allows them to return from captivity.
The prophet affirms that what will happen by means of Cyrus is not of his own accord but by divine ordering.

“Listen unto me, O islands; and let the tribes renew their strength: let them come near (let them keep silent); then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment” [1]. He addresses the distant islands, which the waters surround on every side. This is an allusion to Israel in captivity in Babylon, far from his country, surrounded by the waters of trials to drown him... He asks him to listen first, then to be silent, and then to speak and converse with God, as in a trial between two equals or two parties.

Listening and silence do not mean passivity, but mean lifting the heart to God and meditating on His wonderful works, awaiting His continual salvation of His people and His Church. Silent prayer moves heaven itself; God hears it and answers it, as happened with Moses crying out in his heart (Ex 14:15) and with Hannah in the Temple (1 Sam 1:13).
* Let us now come to the silent prayer of Hannah, the mother of Samuel, how it was a delight before God: it opened the barren womb and removed her reproach, for she bore a Nazirite and a priest.

Father Aphrahat * Jonah prayed a prayer without a voice (Jn 2); the shepherd was silent in the belly of the fish, and from within the dumb creature his prayer crept upward and God heard it in the heights, for his silence was a cry.
Mar Ephrem the Syrian * If your mouth is quietly silent, your heart is always aflame with the warmth of the Spirit!
If you speak with your tongue while your heart is not moved to prayer, your speech is a loss!
Silence your tongue so that your heart may speak... and silence your heart so that God may speak!
The Spiritual Elder * Stillness makes you shine like the sun and purifies you from ignorance.
* If you want to know a man of God, tell it from the constancy of his stillness.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * Those who stand in the presence of Christ, who pour all their attention into divine things and are freed from all the distractions of the world, keep always the hidden prayer of the heart and the spiritual thoughts of the mind, rejecting every temporal thought that darkens the soul and driving it away, so that it does not distract them from thinking about God...

* Would that we, beloved, put off the burden of temporal care and spend all our time in thoughts of God; by this our soul is purified and soars in the heavenly realms toward God. For the divine words remove the rust from the mind and take away from it the weight of temporal things, and lift it to the vision of divinity...
* Let us pray in a hidden way with humility of heart, without any desire to be puffed up in pride concerning the outward show of prayer, which makes us lose the reward.

Father Martyrius Silence must be accompanied by the inner dialogue of love between God and the soul. At the beginning of this book God asks us to enter with Him into a dialogue so that we may seize the forgiveness of our sins (Isa 1:18), but here He wants us to draw near to Him and speak with Him closely through the language of stillness; we hear Him with our inner ears and converse with Him with our tongue of the heart, and our spiritual insight is opened so that we may perceive closely the saving mysteries of God... This is what He meant by His saying, “Let them come near; then let them speak” [1].

Father Martyrius says: [Let us imitate Mary, the sister of Lazarus, who sat at our Lord’s feet and heard His words (Lk 10:39; Jn 11:1); by her love her soul was lifted up to heaven at His words. For this reason our Lord gave a good testimony about her: “Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Lk 10:42).
