Let us imitate this blessed woman in the good part that she chose, for our Lord is even now near to us...]
What did the prophet Isaiah see and what did he hear as he drew near to God in stillness?

“Who raised up (the righteous one) from the east, him whom victory meets at his feet? He gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings: he gave them as the dust to his sword, and as driven stubble to his bow” [2]. From the literal side he means Cyrus, whom the Lord raised up from the east, granting him victory at his feet, meaning that He gives him swiftness of movement; wherever he settled with his army, victory was achieved for him. Most scholars hold that Cyrus, the destroyer of Babylon, was known for justice, even though his army and his men were known for violence and ferocity. He became a symbol of the Lord Christ in His salvation, not from the captivity of Babylon or any other, but from the captivity of the devil and sin.

In some translations, such as the Septuagint, he is called “righteous,” and some Jewish rabbis thought that the discourse here is about Abraham, the father of the fathers, who came from the east to possess, through his seed, the land of Canaan. But the Fathers of the Church throughout the ages, such as St. Jerome, St. Cyril, Eusebius of Caesarea, Theodoret and Procopius, hold that the discourse here concerns the Messiah.

The Hebrew word for victory here is “Sedek,” which means “righteousness or divine judgment or victory, etc...” For the Lord Christ, who is without sin, the only Righteous One, came and meets us with a righteousness that is His own, to bestow it on us. His victory is not through wars and physical resistance, but through establishing us in His righteousness.

The sword of Christ and His holiness are His evangelical word, which turns evil into dust and stubble, while souls are purified from every blemish; by this He reigned over the Gentiles, shattering all evil in them.

“He pursued them, and passed safely; even by the way that he had not gone with his feet” [3], as though Cyrus had come so swiftly that he seemed not to touch the ground with his feet. This also pointed to the swift spread of the preaching of the Gospel of salvation, or the saving work of Christ.
This salvation is accomplished through God Himself, who is “the first”; He worked, and remains working in the life of His people from the beginning to the end [4].

The Lord put a question in the judgment of the peoples, and since no one answered, He answered: “Who hath wrought and done it, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he” [4]... It is He who called the generations from the beginning to draw near to Him and enjoy His salvation, and He remains, even with the others (the appearance of pagan gods), the same, unchanging in His love through the generations.

He called humanity from the beginning to live with Him, but it rejected the Creator and made for itself gods unable even to protect themselves, made by the carpenter and the goldsmith and the one who smooths with the hammer and the soldering... each encourages the other so that the statue may come out perfect, and the nails hold it fast “that it should not be moved” [7].

There is no basis of comparison between idols that need someone to make them and someone to guard them and someone to repair them lest they fall into ruin, and a Creator Christ who moves with practical love to renew our unstable, corrupt nature.
By exposing the falsity of the idols He declares the weakness of the nations, in order to call them to the greatness of Christ, who alone is able to save!

entries.section: 2. My servant whom I have chosen:

paragraphs.text: 8 “But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend. 9 Thou whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and called from the corners thereof, and said unto thee, Thou art my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away. 10 Fear thou not; for I am with thee: look not around; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. 11 Behold, all they that were incensed against thee shall be ashamed and confounded: they shall be as nothing; and they that strive with thee shall perish. 12 Thou shalt seek them, and shalt not find them, even them that contended with thee: they that war against thee shall be as nothing, and as a thing of nought.”

He exposes the weakness and disorder of the nations, and declares that they are dust and stubble [2], and calls them to enter the new Israel to enjoy, through the saving work of Christ, the divine friendship that Abraham, the father of the believers, experienced, for He says:

“But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend” [8]. God chose Abraham as His friend, called him from a pagan nation that did not know God, to become righteous, raising him up from the east, with victory meeting him at his feet [2]. God has not changed; He still seeks to justify and befriend sons of His, calling them from among unbelieving people to accept faith in Him and become His beloved.
* Abraham, who was called the Friend, was found faithful, because he obeyed the words of God.

St. Clement of Rome Who is the chosen servant but the Lord Christ, who took the position of a servant to represent weak humanity, and so establishes a covenant in its name before the Father, sealing it with the precious blood. As St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [He was called a servant to serve many in truth... He came as a servant in the flesh and by birth for the sake of our life, that He might free us, saving us from the bondage of sin.]
The incarnate Word of God became a servant so that, as we who are servants abide in Him, we may hear the divine voice calling to us:
“O Israel my servant”: you who were strangers and far off have become the new Israel, a holy Church and a justified people, good servants united with the Only-Begotten Son who became a servant.
“Jacob whom I have chosen,” as the Lord Christ said to His disciples: “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you.”
“The seed of Abraham my friend”: you have become the sons of Abraham spiritually, his sons in faith, so you are counted beloved to Me as your father was a friend to Me.

entries.section: 2. My servant whom I have chosen:

paragraphs.text: “Whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and from the corners thereof I called him” [9]: I brought you from the farthest parts of the inhabited world and called you from among the nations...
“Fear thou not; for I am with thee”: this is the subject of My calling, and the secret of My choosing you, and the aim of My salvation, that I may be with you...

entries.section: 2. My servant whom I have chosen:

paragraphs.text: “I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” [10]: I will be a help and support to you, because I have justified you by My blood, so that you have become righteous in Me, worthy of every help and support against your opponents who perish, and against your adversaries whom you seek and do not find, since they have become as nothing [11, 2].

In former times you sought nails to hold the plates of gold and silver on the wooden idols so that they would not fall [7], to gain for them outward beauty and give them precious value; but now I hold your right hand so that you are not shaken, I pour My glory into you and give you My righteousness, and you are glorified: “For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee” [3].

The phrase “Fear not” is often repeated in this book... for God knows the true disease of human nature, or its dangerous germ, namely fear, which shatters our peace, our joy and our inner glory. The secret of this fear is our feeling of isolation and loneliness: no companion, no helper, no one who grasps the reality of our feelings, no one who shares the depths of our inner emotions. Therefore the Savior comes forward Himself to accompany us, not from outside but by dwelling in our depths, filling the inner emptiness, and being the companion and helper and the One who satisfies all our inner needs, who shares our hidden feelings.

In brief, what does God our Savior offer? He offers Himself to us and so gives us: being with Him, help, strength, and He lifts us up to Himself! In other words, He comes down to us so that we may receive Him into our life, and so He supports us with His grace and is our hidden helper, and carries us to Himself so that we share with Him His eternal heavenly glories.

entries.section: 3. The weak worm becomes a new threshing instrument:

paragraphs.text: 13 For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee. 14 “Fear not, thou worm Jacob, thou remnant of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. 15 Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff. 16 Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel.”

The two words “Fear not” are repeated three times in verses [10-14]; this was necessary for poor souls shattered by despair during the captivity and the sense of humiliation and slavery. But God reassures by every means His faithful believers who agree to enter with Him into a covenant, so that they do not fear or tremble. The secret of their hope and strength is their enjoyment of Him as their King, who gives Himself to them that they may enjoy Him, saying: “For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee” [13].

Thus God ascribes Himself to them: “I the LORD thy God,” that they may take refuge in Him not as a stranger to them but as their own “God,” who longs to receive them to Himself and keep them in Him. It befits them not to be slow in seeking His help, for He holds their right hand, longing for their salvation more than they themselves long for the salvation of their souls; therefore He does not cease to say: “Fear not; I will help thee.”

It is noted that God calls Himself “I the LORD thy God.” If He called Himself “Jehovah” (Ex 3:14; 15; 6:2) when He called Moses to save the people from the bondage of Pharaoh, He made clear to him the secret of His name, which is: “I AM THAT I AM” (Ex 3:14), affirming that He is ever existing, dwelling among His people without His love or care changing. Thus God presents His name with many titles to reassure His believers, among them:
“Jehovah-jireh” (Gen 22:14), which means “the LORD is seen,” for Abraham saw with the eyes of faith the unique sacrifice of Christ, which gives the power of the Resurrection.

“Jehovah-shalom” (Judg 6:24), which means “God is peace,” for Christ, the Word of God, is our peace (Eph 2:14); by Him we enjoy reconciliation with God as the secret of our inner peace and our peace with others.
“The LORD that healeth thee” Jehovah ropheka (Ex 15:26): He longs to heal our souls and our bodies as the true Physician of humanity.
“The LORD our righteousness” Jehovah-Zidkenu (Jer 23:6); in Christ we have become righteous (1 Cor 1:30), since we bear fellowship in His nature and enjoy His righteousness in us.

“Jehovah-nissi” Jehovah- nissi (Ex 17:15) (the LORD is my banner); God has become my banner, going before my steps in the spiritual battle; He is the secret of my victory and the sign of my triumph over the enemy of good.
“Jah Jehovah” Jehovah-yah (Isa 12:2), which means “I AM THAT I AM,” “I am who I am,” as One present among His believers whose love for them does not change.

“Jehovah-shammah” Jehovah- Shammah (Ezek 48:35), that is, “the LORD is there,” which points to the declaration of the presence of the Lord in the Church of the New Testament, in the midst of the new Israel, since she has become the icon of heaven, which is “the tabernacle of God with men” (Rev 21:3).

entries.section: 3. The weak worm becomes a new threshing instrument:

paragraphs.text: God declares His love for His people, whom He called “the worm of Israel,” in order to raise up from it a new sharp threshing instrument able to thresh the mountains and crush them and fan them so that the storms scatter them, for He says: “Fear not, thou worm Jacob, thou remnant of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat them small, and shalt make the hills as chaff. Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel” [14-16].

This is the work of God the Savior in our lives, for He transforms us from a despised worm living in the mire of this world, trodden as under foot, to raise from us a threshing instrument with sharp teeth able to thresh the mountains and crush them, or like a winnowing fork that separates the wheat from the straw... Thus God wants to befriend the despised worm in order to make it an instrument of discernment and of separating the useful wheat from the worthless straw.

God called His people “the worm Jacob,” for it lives in the clay, despised, without strength or beauty or glory, trodden by feet without care or concern. Pharaoh trod upon the people as upon a worm, but Pharaoh died, while the people enjoyed the promises of God and His salvation. Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar also trod upon this worm, and the whole kingdom of Assyria came to an end, and Babylon also collapsed with its mighty kings, and the worm remained alive and glorious. Thus mighty men arose through the ages such as Nero and Diocletian, and also heretics such as Arius and Nestorius... and all died and the worm remained alive, growing and being glorified. The secret of its life is that the Word of God, who became flesh, also became a worm for our sake, as the psalmist says, “But I am a worm, and no man” (Ps 22:6), that is, He condescends to become a despised man until He was counted as a worm, and so lifts us by His humility to His glory.
* “But I am a worm, and no man” (Ps 22:6).

But I speak now not in the person of Adam, but I speak originally of Myself, I, Jesus Christ. I was born without the seed of man according to the flesh, so that I, as man, might be behind every man, that human pride might imitate My humility. “A reproach of men, and despised of the people” (Ps 22:6). By humility I became a reproach among men, so that it is said mockingly, “Thou art his disciple” (Jn 9:28), and the people despise Me.

St. Augustine By our clinging to the Lord He transforms us from a weak worm, incapable of work, into a threshing instrument able to crush the mountains, which represent the works of the old man, that he may enjoy the blessings of the new life.

If our old man has become like mountains by his hard evil works, and like hills that no one can move, it is God alone who touches the mountains and they smoke (Ps 104:32). He makes us, in Christ Jesus our Lord, a new sharp threshing instrument, to thresh the mountains and crush them and fan the hills like chaff, without age touching us, and we do not lose our strength or have our abilities weaken with time. This is what delights our souls in the Lord, the Renewer of our life, and we glory in the new Holy One of Israel.

17 “When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue faileth for thirst, I the LORD will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them. 18 I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. 19 I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the cypress, and the oak, and the box tree together: 20 That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.”

As the prophet Isaiah looks to the Messianic age as the age of the waters of the Holy Spirit, he sees the wilderness turned into an oasis overflowing with water, changed from a desert into a fruitful divine garden.
This figure is repeated several times (Isa 35:1-10; 43:18-21; 49:9-11; 48:21; 55:13).

In former times God brought water out of the rock for His thirsty people (Ex 17:1-7; Num 20:1-13; Isa 48:21). And in the second Exodus He does what is greater: He causes rivers to burst forth on the high barren heights and springs in the valleys; for the Lord Christ gives a new water that changes the face of the earth, turning the desert of our hearts into His spiritual Paradise, and our inner wilderness into a divine oasis, so that spiritual trees grow in us that bear delicious spiritual fruit: “I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree...” [19].

How beautiful is the phrase: “That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it” [20]... We behold the work of the Lord in us, and we come to know its secrets, and we contemplate the surpassing things and understand what cannot be grasped, because all this is from the hand of the holy Savior and from His creation.
St. John Chrysostom speaks in the person of the Savior, saying:
[Who can equal Me in generosity? I am Father and brother and bridegroom and home and food and clothing and root of all that you desire; I will not leave you in need of anything.
I will also be a servant to you, for I came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.
I am also friend and member and head and brother and sister and mother; I am everything, only be a friend to Me!
For your sake I became poor, and for your sake I was a beggar.
For your sake I prayed, and for your sake I was buried.
In heaven I ask the Father about you.
You are everything to Me: brother and co-heir and friend and member.
What more do you want than this?
Why do you turn away from the One who loves you, and toil for the world?]

21 “Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong reasons, saith the King of Jacob. 22 Let them bring them forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they be, that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come. 23 Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye are gods: yea, do good, or do evil, that we may look and behold it together. 24 Behold, ye are of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination is he that chooseth you. 25 I have raised him up from the north, and he is come: from the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name: and he shall come upon rulers as upon mortar, and as the potter treadeth clay. 26 Who hath declared from the beginning, that we may know? and beforetime, that we may say, He is righteous? yea, there is none that sheweth, yea, there is none that declareth, yea, there is none that heareth your words. 27 I first said to Zion, Behold, behold them: and to Jerusalem I gave one that bringeth good tidings. 28 For I beheld, and there was no man; even among them, and there was no counsellor, that, when I asked of them, could answer a word. 29 Behold, they are all vanity; their works are nothing: their molten images are wind and confusion.”

In order that the Lord may give reassurance to His people and give them trust in Him, He affirms to them that the whole future is in His hands, apart from all the gods of the nations. He asked them to ask the idols whether they are able to tell of future matters, with the aim of prophesying concerning the rise of Cyrus, since that was unexpected.
God declares of Himself that He is the first to bring good tidings to His people of the rise of Cyrus [27].

Cyrus, on his father’s side, was a Mede, and on his mother’s side a Persian, and his army included men from Media who came from the north [25] and men from Persia who came from the east [25]. The Lord Christ also came from Nazareth in the north, and He is the Sun of righteousness rising from the east.

Cyrus knew God (Ezra 1) and respected all religions, including the worship of the living God; therefore it is said: “From the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name” [25]. Perhaps he also called upon the name of the Lord Christ as being a type of Him, accomplishing salvation for the whole world. Cyrus was likened to the sheep who tread the clay, an allusion to the Lord Christ as Judge to whom all nations submit like clay in the hands of the potter... (Cyrus came upon the rulers of Babylon as upon mortar) [25].

entries.section: 1. The chosen servant of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 1 “Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth; I have put my spirit upon him: he shall bring forth judgment to the Gentiles. 2 He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. 3 A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth. 4 He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law.”
The song here presents to us the person of the chosen Servant, who is the Lord Christ Himself, for it says in it:

First: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delighteth” [1]. It is not strange that the Messiah is called “the servant of Jehovah” or “the servant of the Lord,” though He is His Word, begotten eternally and one with Him in the same divine essence. Rather, by His divine love He longed to descend to our servitude in order to carry us to His glories, and as a representative of us He obeyed the Father unto death, even the death of the cross, so that He might accomplish our salvation and establish us in Him, that we may be counted obedient and become the object of the Father’s good pleasure (Eph 1:3-5).

If the Father chose His only-begotten Son to accomplish salvation, declaring the perfection of divine love, then when we enter into Him and enjoy membership in His body, we too become chosen by the Son, the object of His love and delight!

The word “my chosen” does not mean the choosing of one from among many; rather it points to the greatness of the Father toward the Messiah. As the Lord Christ Himself says: “As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love” (Jn 15:9); “that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them” (Jn 17:26). This love is portrayed by the words: “in whom my soul delighteth” [1]. For all the Father’s delight in Him is eternal, and was declared at the Lord’s baptism and transfiguration and throughout the stages of His saving works.
The Evangelist Matthew quoted what is stated here in [1-3] as an explicit prophecy about the Lord Christ (Mt 12:17-21), affirming the following points:
a. The one chosen to accomplish salvation.
b. In Him is the Father’s delight in us.
c. The desire and hope of the Gentiles.
d. By meekness He grants victory.
e. He deals tenderly with every weak one.

St. Augustine comments on this text, saying: [The expression “my servant” refers to the form of a servant, in which the Most High emptied Himself... The Holy Spirit was given to Him, and this was declared in the form of a dove, as the Evangelist testified (Jn 1:32). He brought forth judgment (truth) to the Gentiles, for He declared to them what was hidden from them. In His humility He does not cry out, without ceasing to proclaim the truth. His voice was not heard; those who are outside do not hear it, for those who are outside His body did not obey Him. He did not break the Jews themselves who persecuted Him, though they were a bruised reed that had lost its balance, nor did He quench them, though they were a smoking flax, for He forgave them. He came to be judged, not to judge.]

Our Christ, of whom it was said: “my chosen, in whom my soul delighteth,” came that we may realize that in Him we are chosen by the Father, the object of His delight and love, as the Apostle Paul says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ: according as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love: having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will” (Eph 1:3-5).

Second: “I have put my spirit upon him” [1]. The Messiah is the Word of the Father, one with Him and equal to Him in the same essence; therefore the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of the Father, is also the Spirit of the Son. The Holy Spirit is not a stranger to the Son; He enjoys Him without measure and without separation. The Holy Spirit is He who sanctified the womb of the Virgin Mary to accomplish the divine Incarnation, and He never departed from the Son; He led the Lord Christ up to the mountain to enter the decisive battle with the devil on the mountain of temptation... He is the Spirit whom He gave to His disciples for the pastoral work in Christ Jesus, and the Spirit whom He gave to the whole Church on the day of Pentecost, that He might sustain it in witness to Him, in worship and in daily life. Thereby He fulfilled what He promised in His farewell discourses (Jn 14:16-18, 26; 15:26; 16:7-8, 13, 14). And as St. Clement of Alexandria says: [The Instructor creates man from dust, renews him with water, and makes him grow by the Spirit].

St. Basil tells us about the work of the Holy Spirit in us, saying: [Through the Holy Spirit we regained our dwelling in Paradise, our ascent to the Kingdom of Heaven, our return to divine adoption, our boldness to call God “our Father,” our participation in the grace of Christ, our being called children of light, our right to eternal glory, and in one word, our obtaining the fullness of blessing in this age and in the age to come].

Third: “He shall bring forth truth to the Gentiles” [1]. Though the Lord disciplined the Gentiles, He came to them as “the Truth,” that they might receive Him into their lives as a mystery of eternal salvation, for He says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Jn 14:6).
* Christ dwells in the inner man, as the Apostle says (Eph 3:16-17), and to the inner man belongs the vision of the truth, for He said: “I am the truth” (Jn 14:6).
* He Himself is the life, and He Himself is the truth. Let Him come and save us... to separate the wheat from the tares!

St. Augustine * I cry out with a calm and quiet voice, saying: O You who are hidden within me and concealed, reveal within me Your hidden mystery, disclose to me Your beauty that is within me. O You who built me a temple for Your dwelling, overshadow me with the cloud of Your glory within Your temple.

entries.section: 1. The chosen servant of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: The Spiritual Elder Fourth: “He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street” [2]. For He came to proclaim the voice of practical, quiet love through self-giving unto the cross; His pulpit is the cross, and His words are the wounds of His body that speak of love.

The Word of God came to us to teach us the life of true action that springs from love, with the quietness and calm of the soul in it, instead of being occupied with many glittering words and deceiving outward appearances. The divine Word taught us how to speak through love and practical life, so that He Himself may shine forth in us!
* If you are silent, you will have peace wherever you live.
Father Piamun * I have often spoken and regretted it, but of silence I have never once regretted.

entries.section: 1. The chosen servant of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: St. Arsenius Fifth: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth” [3].

Our Christ came to the broken souls to awaken hope in them; He does not wound the feelings of sinners, nor flatter them. He speaks the truth with love so as to bind up every inflamed wound and to support every weary soul.

* Jesus had compassion on us, so as not to frighten us away from Him but to call us to Him; He came in meekness and in humility... and thereby He said: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mt 11:28). Thereby the Lord refreshed us and did not shut us in or drive us away...
* We must know that God is a God of mercy, inclined to pardon rather than to severity; therefore it was said: “I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6)...

* When you refuse to accept repentance, you are in effect saying: “No wounded man shall enter our inn, and no one shall be healed in our Church. We do not care for the sick, for we are all healthy, and we have no need of a physician, because He Himself said: ‘They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.’”

* Send, O Lord, to the streets of the city, and gather the good and the bad, and bring into Your Church the weak, the blind and the lame (Lk 14:21). Command, O Lord, that Your house be filled, bringing them (the sinners) to Your banquet, for You create those who follow You when You call them...

* May no one fear perishing, whatever his condition and however great his fall, for the good Samaritan of the Gospel will pass by, and we find him going down from Jerusalem to Jericho... This good Samaritan is a symbol of the Lord Christ, the keeper of souls; He will not leave you but will have compassion on you and heal you. The good Samaritan (= keeper) did not leave the one who was lying between living and dead, for he saw in him breaths of life, and hoped for his healing.

entries.section: 1. The chosen servant of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: St. Cyprian Sixth: “He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law” [4].

Our Christ was marked by practical love and meekness; in His love He opens the doors of hope before sinners, however great their evils. This is unlike the man who is harsh with his brother and counts himself more righteous than he, and closes the door before many. This meek divine love is accompanied by divine work without ceasing unto death, even the death of the cross, and in this He was not broken but was glorified by the Resurrection, and declared the truth by accomplishing salvation.
Some scholars try to interpret the word “isles” here as Europe, the United States of America or Australia.

entries.section: 2. The call of the servant of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: 5 Thus saith God the LORD, he that created the heavens, and stretched them out; he that spread forth the earth, and that which cometh out of it; he that giveth breath unto the people upon it, and spirit to them that walk therein: 6 “I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles; 7 To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house. 8 “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images. 9 Behold, the former things are come to pass, and new things do I declare: before they spring forth I tell you of them.”

In His love God created the heavens and the earth for the sake of man [5], and here He calls the Son who became man to establish Him as a covenant of the people and a light of the Gentiles [6], to open the inner insight to behold the Kingdom of God, and to free the captives in the prison of eternal darkness to live in the freedom of the glory of the children of God [7].

What does the calling of the servant of the Lord “a covenant” mean? As the Son of God who became the Son of Man, He was able to reconcile the Father with humanity in the body of His humanity; in Him the Father saw humanity sanctified and qualified for sonship to Him, so He declared His eternal fatherhood toward it in His only-begotten Son, and in Him humanity saw the love of the Father who gave His only Son for its salvation, that it might find a portion for itself in the Father’s bosom. This is the covenant that was established in Christ Jesus, which He sealed with His precious blood on the wood of the cross. Therefore He was called “the messenger of the covenant” (Mal 3:1).

Trypho the Jew tried to interpret what is stated here about the covenant and the light of the Gentiles as pertaining to the Mosaic Law, and St. Justin the Martyr replied to him, saying: [that if the Law were able to give enlightenment to the Gentiles and to those who received it, what need would there be to speak of a new covenant? But since God had declared beforehand that He would bring a new covenant and an everlasting law and an everlasting commandment, this is not to be understood of the old Law but of Christ and those who believe in Him, that is, of us who were of the Gentiles and have enjoyed enlightenment. The Lord says: “In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages” (Isa 49:8). What is the inheritance (possession) of Christ? Are they not the Gentiles? What is the covenant of God but the Lord Christ? As it is said in another place: “Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee. Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and thy dominion (thy possessions) unto the uttermost parts of the earth” (Ps 2:7).]

entries.section: 2. The call of the servant of the Lord:

paragraphs.text: Again St. Justin the Martyr comments on the divine saying: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” [8] thus: [I say (to the Jews): Do you not realize, my friends, that God gives glory to the one whom He has set as a light to the Gentiles, and does not give it to another?]. Thus whatever glories the Son the Savior receives, the Holy Trinity receives, being the one God in essence and divinity.
“And give thee for a covenant of the people” [6].

We have previously studied the role of the “covenant” among primitive tribes and in the Old Testament and finally in the New Testament, where the Lord Christ gave His mystical blood in the cup as a new covenant for His believers to partake of. This blood, being the sacrifice of Christ, is able to establish a compact between the Father and man, to grant us a heavenly spiritual kinship, so that we are truly counted as sons firmly established in the only-begotten Son; through it we enjoy the life-giving heavenly banquet.
Father Theodoret says: [In our partaking of the elements of the Bridegroom and drinking His blood we enter with Him into a conjugal union].

“And give thee... for a light of the Gentiles” [6]; for Christ is the divine Light who opens our inner insight that we may behold the light. Therefore the Psalmist says: “In thy light, O Lord, shall we see light,” and the Evangelist says:
“That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world” (Jn 1:9).
* “O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles” (Ps 43:3).
“Light” and “truth” are in reality two names expressing one (God). For what is the divine light but the divine truth? And the divine truth but the divine light? And the Hypostasis of Christ is both.

“I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness” (Jn 8:12); “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Jn 14:6). He Himself is the light, and He is also the truth. Let Him come, then, and save us....
* My God... You are my light; open my eyes so that they may behold Your divine splendor, that I may be able to walk in my way without stumbling in the snares of the enemy.
Truly, how can I avoid his snares unless I see them?!
And how can I see them unless I am enlightened by Your light...?!
You are the light for the children of light! Your day knows no sunset! Your day shines for Your children so that they do not stumble!
But those who are outside of You walk in darkness and live in it!..

St. Augustine * I behold one lamp, and by its light I am illumined, and now I am in amazement, rejoicing spiritually, for within me is the fountain of life, that which is the goal of the world that is not perceived by the senses!
The Spiritual Elder

10 Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof. 11 Let the wilderness and the cities thereof lift up their voice, the villages that Kedar doth inhabit: let the inhabitants of Sela sing, let them shout from the top of the mountains. 12 Let them give glory unto the LORD, and declare his praise in the islands. 13 The LORD shall go forth as a mighty man, he shall stir up jealousy like a man of war: he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies.

“Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth” [10]. What is this song, marked by newness, that men utter from the end of the earth, but the song of the redeemed who come from all nations, kindreds, peoples and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb... “And they cry with a loud voice, saying, Salvation to our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb” (Rev 7:10). A new song because it grants unceasing renewal through “the new life which is in Christ.”
The following is noted in this song:

a. A new song that never grows old or aged, for it expresses the enjoyment of the life of heavenly joy that does not grow old. Thus the sighs of creation are turned into fellowship in the praise of the heavenly ones.

b. A universal song that includes members from the end of the earth, revealing the joy of the dwellers of the earth, the seas, and the inhabitants of the isles [10]. It springs from the depths of the inner heart and not from outward circumstances; therefore the believer practices it wherever he may be, on land or sea, in the wilderness or in a city or a village or a cave on a mountaintop [10-11].

c. The secret of the joy is the Lord Christ going before the ranks as the leader of the spiritual battle, “he shall cry, yea, roar; he shall prevail against his enemies” [13]. It is the song of victory and triumph in Christ, who cries out in victory over the devil and all his evil powers.

14 “I have been silent from of old; I have kept still; I have restrained myself. Like a woman giving birth I cry out; I blow and snort together. 15 I lay waste the mountains and hills, and dry up all their herbs; and I make the rivers dry land, and dry up the pools. 16 And I lead the blind in a way that they knew not; in paths that they have not known I make them walk. I make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things I do, and I do not forsake them. 17 They are turned back; they shall be greatly ashamed that trust in graven images, that say to the molten images, Ye are our gods!

The secret of our praise is the emptying out of the works of the old man from our depths through our receiving the works of the new man in Christ Jesus... a matter so exceedingly astonishing that it was said, “I have been silent from of old; I have kept still; I have restrained myself” [14].

He likens the leaving of the old man and the enjoyment of the new man to the woman who gives birth: she cries out from pain but brings forth a new human being; so we enjoy, through the Lord Christ, as it were the bringing forth of a new world within us: “Like a woman giving birth I cry out; I blow and snort together” [14].

He also likens the great and small nations to the mountains and hills whose herbage He dries up [15], drying up their love for earthly things, which are like the perishing grass. He also likens them to rivers that He makes dry [15]... Thus He removes their old waters to give them the living water.

Again He likens them to the blind who walk in darkness; they need the removal of blindness and darkness so as to enjoy the light and walk in the new, true spiritual way instead of walking in crooked paths, for He says: “And I lead the blind in a way that they knew not; in paths that they have not known I make them walk; I make darkness light before them and crooked things straight” [16].

entries.section: 5. A call to the deaf and blind people:

paragraphs.text: 18 “Hear, ye deaf; and look, ye blind, that ye may see. 19 Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD’S servant? 20 Seeing many things, but thou observest not; opening the ears, but he heareth not.” 21 The LORD is well pleased for his righteousness’ sake; he will magnify the law, and make it honourable. 22 But this is a people robbed and spoiled; they are all of them snared in holes, and they are hid in prison houses: they are for a prey, and none delivereth; for a spoil, and none saith, “Restore.” 23 Who among you will give ear to this? who will hearken and hear for the time to come? 24 Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? did not the LORD, he against whom we have sinned? for they would not walk in his ways, neither were they obedient unto his law. 25 Therefore he hath poured upon him the fury of his anger, and the strength of battle: and it hath set him on fire round about, yet he knew not; and it burned him, yet he laid it not to heart.

Many of the Fathers see that the deaf and blind people are the Jews who did not heed the voice of the prophets concerning the Lord Christ, and their eyes were blinded from perceiving Him, so they glorified Him... The Lord chose them as His servant, but only a very few accepted faith in the Savior while the others denied Him; therefore He rebukes them, saying:
“Hear, ye deaf; and look, ye blind, that ye may see.
Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent?!
Who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD’S servant?!” [18-19].

He calls them His servant because He chose them as His people devoted to Him; and also His messenger because He chose them to accept the faith and preach it as messengers proclaiming salvation and witnessing to the Gospel life; He called them “perfect” because He expected holiness in them, since He gave them every possibility for the perfect life, and indeed even for preaching the Lord Christ, the Giver of perfection.
He rebukes them, saying:

entries.section: 5. A call to the deaf and blind people:

paragraphs.text: “Seeing many things, but thou observest not” [20], for the Lord Christ came in their midst and did wonders and they saw what other peoples did not see, yet they did not observe that He is the Savior of the world, but crucified Him out of envy! They saw Him in the flesh and did not realize His true nature.

“Opening the ears, but he heareth not” [20]; they heard the prophecies as they heard the voice of the Lord Christ, yet they did not respond either to the voice of the prophets pointing toward Christ or to the voice of the Lord Himself at His coming.

entries.section: 5. A call to the deaf and blind people:

paragraphs.text: The fault is in them and not in the Mosaic Law, for God magnifies the Law and makes it honourable [21]; but the enemy of good robbed the people of the depths of the Law and plundered from them the spiritual prophetic understanding, so they fell into the pit of denial and were imprisoned in the rejection of faith. The enemy of good robbed them of the enjoyment of Him to whom the Law pointed and plundered from them what the books of the Old Testament had given, and there is none to restore to them what they had lost [21-22], because they fell under the divine wrath.
The Jews hold that what is stated in this section [18-25] does not apply to them but to the idolaters or to some individuals.

entries.section: 1. Fear not, for I am with you:

paragraphs.text: 1 And now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel: “Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine. 2 When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be scorched; neither shall the flame burn thee. 3 For I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee. 4 Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life. 5 Fear not: for I am with thee: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west; 6 I will say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back: bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth; 7 Even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him.”

He begins His speech thus: “And now thus” [1]; as though God wants to change the previous picture, the picture of the bitter captivity of sin, which robbed us of inner insight and of the ears of the soul, by presenting the riches of His saving promises and the abundance of His surpassing grace.

God wants us to turn our eyes away from our wretched state or from thinking about what sin has done in us, looking instead to the Redeemer and Savior, so that despair may not crush us but we may be filled with hope.
Now what is the role of the Redeemer who frees us from the captivity of sin?
a. God the Creator alone is able to renew creation: “And now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee” [1].

When Arius denied the divinity of the Lord Christ, St. Athanasius the Apostolic concentrated in his reply to him on the fact that the divinity of the Lord is not a theoretical, philosophical doctrine but a matter that touches our very salvation. Our human nature had become utterly corrupt and needed the Creator to save our fallen nature and restore it to its origin, granting it His image and reforming it from corruption to incorruption; in Him humanity overcomes death and is re-created. There was urgent need for the Son of God, one with the Father and equal to Him in essence, to offer Himself as a sacrifice able to pay the debt of our sins and to fulfill divine justice and mercy at the same time. He is God, who overcomes Satan, not for His own sake but in the name of humanity and on its behalf. Finally, being true God, He restored to us our dignity, granting us sonship to the Father in Him by the Holy Spirit. Pope Athanasius says: [He became man that we might become gods], [and though there is one Son by nature, a true, only-begotten Son, we have become sons not by nature and truth but by His grace that calls us, and though we are men on earth, yet we have been called gods].

St. John Chrysostom says: [Because of love He took our flesh and had compassion on us; there is no other reason for His Incarnation]. God did not repay us for our many transgressions that we committed against Him despite His benefactions to us, but gave us His Son. He made Him sin for our sake... He let Him be condemned and die as one accursed. He who knew no sin He made as a sinner and as sin... He is like a king who sees a thief about to be executed, and sends his beloved only son, transferring upon him the very death and even the criminal’s fault! All this for the salvation of the guilty one, to raise him to great honor], [The Lord Christ paid more than we deserve, by as much as the ocean exceeds a drop of water].
By this we understand the prophetic words: “Thus saith the LORD that created thee... Fear not: for I have redeemed thee” [1].

b. Personal care on the part of the Savior toward man; God did not create man as one being among billions of beings that He brought into existence, but gave him special care as a creature beloved to Him; He knows man by name, and calls him and redeems him to be His, that is, that man may enjoy union with Him.
How beautiful is the voice of the Redeemer when He speaks intimately to every man, saying:
“Fear not: for I have redeemed thee.
I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine” [1].

The secret of redemption lies in God’s surpassing love: He wants me for Himself, and He is mine... He knows me by name and calls me to enter with Him into a unique relationship of love. He asks nothing of me but asks my being and my heart and my love, and I do not ask His gifts but His person and His Holy Spirit and His love! It is as though God here comes forward as Creator and Savior and a personal Bridegroom to me.

* My God... when I contemplate in my conscience, I see You always looking toward me, and attending to me day and night with great effort, as though there were no creature in heaven or on earth but me.
* Your eyes are drawn toward the steps of men...
Since You care for all Your creation, You deprive none of the work of Your hands of the abundance of Your love!

You Yourself care for my steps and my ways night and day, You watch over my care, You observe all my paths, You do not cease to care for me, so that I could say that You forget heaven and earth and what is in them, concentrating Your care on me, so that You seem as one who cares for no creature but me!
* You watch over me as though You had forgotten all creation! You give me Your gifts as though I alone were the object of Your love!
* There is never anything that You do not know... my thoughts, my purposes, my joys and my works... none of this is not laid before Your eternal care!

entries.section: 1. Fear not, for I am with you:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine c. God the Savior is the secret of our victory; as long as He is with us the waters of this world do not overwhelm us nor do the fires of lusts burn us: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be scorched; neither shall the flame burn thee” [2].

A wonderful picture of the Savior’s work: He gives us Himself, so death with all its means and ways cannot swallow us... We bear our Christ, “the Resurrection” (Jn 11:25), within us, and we live the risen life that overcomes death.

If we face the waters of the love of the world that drown the soul and kill it, and the flame of the fire of lust that destroys it, the Savior has given us His Holy Spirit through the waters of Baptism, in which we renounce Satan and all his hosts and all his works and bruise his head under our feet; He gave us His Holy, fiery Spirit as on the day of Pentecost, who burns up sin and scatters its deadly flame.

Perhaps the prophet Isaiah here reminds his people of God’s work with their fathers at their exodus from Egypt. By the cross He gave them victory over the waters of the Sea of Suph (by means of the rod), and also victory over the fiery serpents (by the bronze serpent). God who worked in ancient times works in the second exodus from the Babylonian captivity, and these two exoduses are a type of the greatest exodus that the Savior accomplishes by His cross in the lives of His believers.
* Can you resist Satan, O you unfaithful ones, unless you have the shield of faith? For by it you are able to quench his darts...!
Do you perhaps justify yourself since sin has reigned over your body? And how can you glorify God in your body, when He is the One who redeemed you with His pure blood?!

entries.section: 1. Fear not, for I am with you:

paragraphs.text: St. Anba Shenouda, Archimandrite d. The Savior pays the price: the early Church looked to the cross as the payment of the debt that we owed to the Father, and as an acquiring of us from the hand of the devil, who bought us as slaves to himself, so the Lord paid His blood as the price for this for our freedom. This is the work of the holy Savior, who wants to sanctify us by His blood and free us from the slavery of the devil; therefore He says: “For I am the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour: I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee” [3].

Egypt with its Pharaoh, which represented one of the two great powers at that time (Egypt and Assyria; then Egypt and Babylon...), does not support God’s people nor protect them but occupies a position of weakness... As for Cush and Seba, they were known for their wealth. It is as though God is the One who redeems and saves, being the Holy One, and not Pharaoh with his might nor Cush and Seba with their riches and resources.
The Lord bought us not with gold or silver but with His precious blood, to make us kings and priests:
“For thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation; and hast made us unto our God kings and priests” (Rev 5:9-10).
“For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your bodies and in your spirits, which are God’s” (1 Cor 6:20).
“Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men” (1 Cor 7:23).

“Knowing that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, even the blood of Christ” (1 Pet 1:18-19).
* You were bought with a price, that is, with blood. You have been removed from the empire of the flesh so that you may glorify the Lord in your bodies.

Tertullian * Let no one think that a different price was paid for him because of his wealth; for wealth in the Church is wealth in faith; for the believer has the whole world of wealth. What wonder is this if the believer possesses the inheritance of Christ, which is more precious than the world.

entries.section: 1. Fear not, for I am with you:

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose e. The Savior restores to us our glory and our unity: often many despaired during the captivity of the possibility of returning to their land because of the length of their stay in it, but God the Savior reassures His children, saying: “Fear not: for I am with thee: I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west; I will say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back: bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth; even every one that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him” [5-7].

It is noticed in this chapter that God speaks of Himself as “I” no fewer than 36 times, so that it has been called the chapter of “the divine Self” or “the divine I,” and the same occurs in the forty-fifth chapter 31 times... What does this mean? If the work of sin is man’s encapsulation in the “I,” so that he finds in himself a center for the world and for others, wanting to enjoy bodily pleasures or honor for his own account in pride and selfishness, then our Christ on the contrary offers His Self, which is “Love,” that we may possess Him. When He calls to us not to fear, and when He calls us by name, and affirms His care for us wherever we are and whatever trials come upon us, and when He offers us His promises to gather us from the ends of the inhabited world to embrace us to Himself... in all this He seeks not what is for Himself but what is ours. He grants us His presence that we may possess Him. Therefore from time to time He says “I am with thee,” and that He is ours, our eternal portion.
The glory of God’s name and His honor are declared in His practical, self-giving love, in the giving of Himself to His creation.

8 Bring forth the blind people that have eyes, and the deaf that have ears. 9 “Gather together, O all ye nations, and let the tribes be assembled: who among them can declare this, and shew us former things? let them bring forth their witnesses, that they may be justified: or let them hear, and say, It is truth. 10 Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. 11 I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour. 12 I have declared, and have saved, and I have shewed, and there is no stranger among you: and ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and I am God. 13 Also from this day I am he; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand: I will work, and who shall turn it back?”
What does God offer us?

He offers Himself as light to us, opening our senses to see His glories in us and His heavenly Kingdom revealed within us, and opens our ears to hear His divine voice and to understand the aim of His commandment, so that we have the ears of children who know their father’s voice and even the movement of his feet... This is what He meant by saying: “Bring forth the blind people that have eyes, and the deaf that have ears” [8].
This is the role of God our Savior in our inner life, where He renews our nature in the waters of Baptism by His Holy Spirit to grant us the new man able to enjoy divine fellowship.

Through this experience we bear witness to others, and the Church calls for a general assembly of the nations [9-13] to get to know the Savior and to confirm the fulfillment of what He had promised before through His prophets across the generations before His coming.

“Gather together, O all ye nations, and let the tribes be assembled: who among them can declare this, and shew us former things? let them bring forth their witnesses, that they may be justified: or let them hear, and say, It is truth. Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me. I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour...” [9-11].

God requires those who have enjoyed the new insight and the new spiritual ears to call the nations and tribes to enter with them into a practical dialogue through what they live. In this dialogue they declare the following:

a. Let them ask the nations whether they have earlier clear and sure prophecies concerning the future (Isa 41:22); but as for us, we have received prophecies not about the victory of Cush over Babylon to rescue the ancient people of God, but about the Messiah, the chosen Servant. We received prophecies about His person and His works and His mission; we knew that He would be born of a virgin, and we knew the time of His birth and its place, and about His works with His people and the offering of Himself as a unique sacrifice of love, etc... So what the prophets uttered concerned the unique, eternal Lord before whom no god was formed and after whom there shall be none... and as He says: “I am the first, and I am the last” (Isa 44:6).
St. John Chrysostom sees that Satan is able to imitate miracles [but prophecy is the special work of God, which the demons cannot imitate, though they struggle mightily for it].

In His love for mankind God gave the prophets these prophecies, and spoke through the tongue of His holy men and inspired the divine Word, and He still works in us by granting us the knowledge of these divine mysteries. And as Irenaeus says: [It is impossible for us, without God, to come to the knowledge of God, who teaches men through His Word].

b. Besides the prophecy that centered on the coming of the Savior... Holy Scripture affirms that God alone is the Savior: “I, even I, am the LORD; and beside me there is no saviour” [11]. God the Creator, in His jealousy for His beloved man, entrusts his salvation to no one but shepherds His people Himself and lays down His life for them: “the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Jn 10:11). He created, and He is the One who renews creation and saves it!
In His repetition of “I, even I, am the LORD” is an affirmation that the One who offers salvation is the Lord Himself, the First and the Last, declaring His divine love through His saving knowledge!
* Being “the Life,” He died that we might live; being “the Word,” He became flesh that He might teach the flesh in the Word.

* He is the Word of God and His power and His wisdom, as Solomon testifies concerning wisdom that it is “the One, she can do all things, and remaining in herself, she maketh all things new, and passing into holy souls, she formeth friends of God, and prophets” (Wis 7:27).
St. Athanasius the Apostolic

14 Thus saith the LORD, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: “For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and have cast down all the bars, and the Chaldeans in the ships of their singing. 15 I am the LORD, your Holy One, the creator of Israel, your King.

God, who allowed the discipline of His people by the Babylonian captivity, now, out of His love for His people, allows the fall of Babylon. He speaks in the past tense to assure His hearers that what will happen is an actual fact that must be accomplished.
The text has come differently from one translation to another while the meaning remains constant:

“Thus saith the LORD, your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I have sent to Babylon, and cast the bars upon it (brought down its nobles), and the Chaldeans in the ships of their singing (their cry in their ships)” [14].
Here God appears as the commander of the hostile armies, sending Media and Persia to Babylon, and there He casts terror into the hearts of its inhabitants so that they flee quickly.
The Hebrew word barichim was translated “nobles,” and in Arabic “bars,” and the English has used “nobles” because they protect the city like bars for it.

Many of the rich fled to their ships that were moored in the Euphrates and the Tigris. Babylon had no seagoing ships, but the rich went out to their pleasure boats, therefore it was said “ships of their singing,” because they were accustomed to use them during their trips full of mirth. And when they found in them no possibility of salvation, their songs turned into cries and bitterness.

In [15] God is called by three titles: Jehovah, your Savior, the Holy One of Israel, through which He reveals the role of God as leader of His people or His Church; He is the God unchanging in His love and His power, able to grant victory over the enemy of good; He is the Savior who in His love offers the unique sacrifice of salvation; and He is the Holy One who renews the creation of His believers and sanctifies them to reign with Him eternally.
Perhaps by these three titles He intended that salvation and sanctification are at the very heart of the work of God as One who loves His weak creation and longs to renew it in Himself.

16 Thus saith the LORD, which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters; 17 Which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow. 18 “Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. 19 Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert. 20 The beast of the field shall honour me, the wolves and the daughters of the ostrich: because I have made waters in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen. 21 This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise.

God, who saves His people, had previously given them salvation by the hands of Moses to free them from the slavery of Pharaoh; and here He brings them out of the Babylonian captivity as in a new exodus, and He remains continually bringing them out from the captivity of sin to the freedom of the glory of the children of God, setting them forth, as it were, from the works of the old man to the continual enjoyment of the works of the new, inner man.

“Thus saith the LORD, which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters; which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow” [16-17].

He saved them from the power of Pharaoh by their crossing the Sea of Suph, cutting off every possibility of Pharaoh’s rising against them again. He likened Pharaoh’s sudden and swift destruction to a wick that was quenched and does not blaze again; with the same power God saves them from the hand of Babylon also.

This salvation that was accomplished against Pharaoh and also against Babylon must be accomplished against the works of the old man (Col 3:9), so the prophet continues his speech, saying: “Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old; behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?! I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert” [18-19]. He wants us not only to put off the old man with his works but to forget him completely and no longer remember him or ponder him, lest we despair and be shattered, but rather be occupied with the new life that springs forth in us. He makes a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. What is this way but the Lord Christ Himself, who says: “I am the way” (Jn 14:6), who arose in the midst of us, the barren wilderness, and dwells in our hearts to enter with us into His Kingdom?! And what are these rivers but the springs of the Holy Spirit bursting forth within us, the desert without inhabitant, so that our desolate heart is turned into a dwelling of the Holy God?! It is as though the secret of our renewal is the indwelling of the Lord Christ in us and the coming of His Holy Spirit in our inner depths.

God affirms the opening of the door of faith before the Gentiles to acquire a new people, who know inner joy and praise, saying: “The beast of the field shall honour me, the wolves and the daughters of the ostrich: because I have made waters in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen. This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise” [20-21]. He likens the Gentiles to the wild beasts that live in the wilderness, because of the extreme violence that marked them, and because they lived as in a wilderness with no promises among them, no covenants, no divine law, etc... in a state of extreme desolation. They were likened also to the daughters of the ostrich, a symbol of folly and lack of understanding because of their worship of idols and their practicing of abominations as a pious religious act. These, who were known for cruelty and folly, who lived in a barren wilderness, have come to enjoy the water of the rivers of the Holy Spirit to drink and be satisfied, and to receive membership in the chosen people of God. Thus their nature is changed through the work of the Holy Trinity in them, and their heart is opened to joy and their tongue to praise.
How beautiful is the divine phrase: “This people have I formed for myself!” [21] We have become His, the Lord’s portion, as He is ours, our portion!

22 “And thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob, that thou shouldest weary thyself for me, O Israel. 23 Thou hast not brought me the sheep of thy burnt offerings; neither hast thou honoured me with thy sacrifices. I have not caused thee to serve with an offering, nor wearied thee with incense. 24 Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with silver, neither hast thou satisfied me with the fat of thy sacrifices: but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities. 25 I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and I will not remember thy sins.” 26 “Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified. 27 Thy first father hath sinned, and thy mediators have transgressed against me. 28 Therefore I have profaned the princes of the sanctuary, and have given Jacob to the curse, and Israel to reproaches.”
God offers His saving works freely to humanity, but there are some obstacles that hindered God’s purposes with the ancient people who refused to believe in the Savior; these obstacles are:

a. Not praying: “And thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob, that thou shouldest weary thyself for me, O Israel” [22]. For prayer is the secret of our enjoyment of God’s work, and as Father Martyrius says: [Prayer does what it wishes as God can! It issues commands on earth that they may have their effect in heaven].

b. Ignoring God even in small matters: “Thou hast not brought me the sheep of thy burnt offerings; neither hast thou honoured me with thy sacrifices. I have not caused thee to serve with an offering, nor wearied thee with incense. Thou hast bought me no sweet cane with silver, neither hast thou satisfied me with the fat of thy sacrifices” [23-24].

When God brought His people out of Egypt He was not in need of their offerings and animal sacrifices, but sought their hearts, longing to draw them near to Himself as His own people, while the sacrifices were types of the sacrifice of Christ and a sign of love for Him... He was waiting for them to offer their hearts with their burnt offerings and sacrifices and incense, etc...

* When He indicates that He did not lead them out of Egypt that they might offer Him sacrifice but that they might forget the worship of idols of the Egyptians so that they might hear the voice of the Lord, which was for them salvation and glory (Jer 7:21).

St. Irenaeus c. Preoccupation with bodily pleasures and worldly lusts: “but thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities” [24]. Instead of honoring the Lord by offering the heart as a burnt sacrifice together with practicing worship, the people turned to selfishness and entanglement with temporal things, so they exploited God’s love and care and gifts for the sake of the “I.”
We often misuse the gifts of God, such as emotions, impulses and talents; we use them not for the sake of the Kingdom of God and the edification of the community but to practice evil.

Despite the evil we have reached, God remains waiting for our repentance and our confession of our sins that He may forgive them for us for the sake of His holy name and His surpassing love, assuring us: “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and I will not remember thy sins; put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified” [25-26].
* The first way of repentance is our condemnation of sins.
* He asks this of us (the confession of our sins) that we may intensify our love toward Him.
* He who practices repentance after he sins deserves not grief over him but congratulation, as he passes over to the choir of the righteous.

* Let nothing confuse you but rise up to the highest heavens themselves. Sigh bitterly and offer a sacrifice of confession, for it was said, “Declare thou first thy transgressions, that thou mayest be justified” [26] (the Septuagint); offer the sacrifice of a contrite heart. For these sacrifices are not turned into ashes, nor become smoke, nor are dissipated in the air. They need no wood and fire but a heart repentant within. This is the wood and the fire that burn without destroying, for he who prays fervently is burned but not consumed, but becomes like gold tried by fire that it may increase in splendor.

St. John Chrysostom Thus it befits us to remember our sins and confess them so that they may be forgiven... Then we ought to remember God’s work with us and glorify Him instead of thinking of the sins...
* How do we forget the evil that is coming upon us? By the remembrance of good things, and by remembering God. For if we remember God continually we cannot remember these things also.

St. John Chrysostom We must not be ashamed of confessing sins, for our first fathers sinned before us, foremost among them Adam the first: “Thy first father hath sinned, and thy mediators have transgressed against me” [27]. The majority of the Fathers of the Church, and also the rabbis, see that it means all humanity represented in Adam our first father, and some interpret it in the light of what is stated in (Ezek 16:3) “thy father was an Amorite.” Some saw that it is the chief father Urijah as the high priest who led the people to the worship of idols in the days of Ahaz (2 Kgs 16:10-16), and some saw that it means the kings and high priests, that is, the civil and religious leaders together leading the people to disobedience.
The fruit of sins and disobedience is “the curse” and the loss of honor, for it was said: “I have given Jacob to the curse, and Israel to reproaches” [28].

1 “And now hear, O Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen: 2 Thus saith the LORD that made thee, and formed thee from the womb, which will help thee: Fear not, O Jacob, my servant; and thou, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. 3 For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring: 4 And they shall spring up as among the grass, as willows by the water courses. 5 One shall say, I am the LORD’S; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD, and surname himself by the name of Israel.”

God fulfills His calling and choosing of the new Israel by the outpouring of His Holy Spirit upon the believers to establish the Church of the New Testament, for He says: “And now hear, O Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen: Thus saith the LORD that made thee, and formed thee from the womb, which will help thee: Fear not, O Jacob, my servant; and thou, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring: and they shall spring up as among the grass, as willows by the water courses. One shall say, I am the LORD’S; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD, and surname himself by the name of Israel” [1-5].
In this great gift the following is noted:

a. God longs to give not only His outward blessings and gifts but to give Himself to man: “I will pour my spirit upon thy seed”; the Giver of gifts and the Bestower of blessing gives Himself as a gift and a present...
* He who is washed for salvation receives the water and the Holy Spirit.
Origen * (The baptized) receives the Holy Spirit within him and truly bears the title of temple of God.
St. Cyril the Great * O Only-begotten One, who gave us His Spirit in Baptism, give me a word that I may chant to You with love.
* The only-begotten Son came down and raised you from the dunghill and gave you His Spirit in Baptism and made you His brother.
* We were naturalized into His divinity within the waters, and became sons in truth, and from that time it has been ours to call Him our Father, that hidden One who gave us His Spirit in Baptism.

Mar Jacob of Serugh considers this gift of God to be the greatest, for it is He who in His love formed us, and from the womb helped us, and here He demands of us not to fear because He chose us, and to accomplish this choosing He gave us this gift.

b. He calls His Church “Jeshurun,” and this name appeared four times in the Old Testament (Deut 32:15; 33:5-6), its meaning being “upright,” derived from yashar. It is as though He calls His Church, which has included sinners, “upright,” and that by the work of His Holy Spirit. It is as though He encourages His people to respond to the gift of His Holy Spirit so that they leave their deviation and disobedience and sing of the splendor of the Lord and His spiritual beauty.

For in the Song of Songs, while the Church confesses that trials have darkened her (Song 1:6), yet God the Bridegroom and Savior never hinted at any fault in her, but on the contrary brings out all the beauty in her: “Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes” (Song 1:15), “Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee” (Song 4:7).

The Lord Christ sees in His Church a surpassing beauty whose secret is the two dove eyes, for the Holy Spirit, who appears in the form of a dove, has come down upon her, granting her spiritual enlightenment. Origen says: [Her eyes are compared to doves surely because she has now come to understand the Holy Scriptures according to the Spirit and not according to the letter. She has come to perceive the spiritual mysteries in the Holy Scriptures, for the dove is a symbol of the Holy Spirit. When we understand the Law and the Prophets in a spiritual way we have the two dove eyes. Therefore in the Book of Psalms her soul longed to have the wings of a dove (Ps 55:6), that she might be able to fly to the understanding of the spiritual mysteries and rest in the courts of wisdom]. As for St. Gregory of Nyssa, he sees that the secret of the Church’s beauty is her dove eyes, for they are pure, and in them appears the image of the Holy Spirit, upon whom the Bride gazes continually, so that His image is imprinted on the pupil of the eye.

St. Jerome sees that the secret of the Church’s beauty is her union with the only-begotten Son of God, so that she bears His glory within her, for he says: [What is more beautiful than the soul that is called a daughter of God (Ps 45:10), that does not seek outward adorning (1 Pet 3:3)?! She believes in Christ, and since His Spirit is given to her she takes her way toward Christ, who is at the same time her Bridegroom and her Lord, with great hope].

c. He presents to us the gift of His Holy Spirit, who works in us according to our need; for whoever is thirsty, He pours water for him to quench his thirst, and whoever is like dry ground, He pours out upon him floods so that dryness and desert are turned into a garden. He is generous in giving, giving us according to our need and the measure of our response to Him. He says: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps 81:10).
* Whatever flame the Spirit kindles within us we can, if we wish, make blaze more and more, and if we do not wish we lose it at once (by our slackness and our lack of response to Him).
St. John Chrysostom * Those who receive Him (the Holy Spirit) enjoy Him according to their capacity, not according to what He is able.

St. Basil the Great * You are receiving military equipment against the power of the enemy (Satan)... Behold the weapon is prepared: the sword of the Spirit (Eph 6:17). It is ready, so it befits you to stretch out your right hand in a good way, that you may fight the battle of the Lord and overcome the opposing powers and become an impregnable (fortress) that repels every attempt of the heretics...
* Do not despise grace because it is free, but receive it and treasure it with piety.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem d. What does it mean: “they shall spring up as among the grass, as willows by the water courses”? Perhaps He meant that he who enjoys the gift of the Holy Spirit grows like a huge tree among perishing grass.

e.
