He who enjoys the Spirit writes on his hand: “For the Lord”; for the ancient custom was that a man would write the name of his god or master on his hand as a tattoo, and God forbade His people from doing so, lest they write the name of the idol on their hands when they deviated, so that it would be difficult, indeed impossible, to remove.

“And surname himself by the name of Israel,” for the Church of the New Testament, which enjoys the gift of the Spirit, bore the title “the new Israel”; she inherited from the old Israel the Holy Scriptures with what they contain of divine law and commandments and prophecies and covenants and promises... She understood all that by the Spirit and not the letter and perceived divine mysteries and enjoyed surpassing things.

6 Thus saith the LORD the King of Israel, and his redeemer the LORD of hosts: “I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God. 7 And who is like me? Let him call, and let him declare it and set it before me, since I appointed the ancient people. And the things that are coming, and shall come, let them shew unto them. 8 Fear ye not, neither be afraid: have not I told thee from that time, and have declared it? ye are even my witnesses. Is there a God beside me? Nor any rock that I know not of?”

The speaker here is the Lord Christ, the Rock that poured forth water for the people (1 Cor 10:4), therefore He says “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty” [3]; and here He calls Himself “the King of Israel, and his redeemer” [6], and He confessed before Pilate that He is a king.

He calls Himself here “the LORD of hosts,” “I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God” [6]. And in the Book of Revelation the Lord Christ says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending” (Rev 1:8), “I am the first and the last” (Rev 1:17; 22:13). It is clear that the Redeemer, the LORD of hosts, the only God beside whom there is no other God, is Christ the Savior... This is the testimony of those who enjoy His salvation: “Ye are even my witnesses. Is there a God beside me?!” [8].

What we enjoy in the New Testament is an extension of the continuing work of God; the God who worked with the ancient people [7] had declared to them beforehand the things to come, that is, what He had planned for the sake of the New Testament [7].
Perhaps He presented Himself here as “the first and the last” to declare that He Himself who worked in the old is still the same One who works in the New Testament.

God the Savior is the first and the last: He goes before all the ranks to lead His flock and comes behind them to support every slow or weak sheep... He embraces all and has compassion on all. He is also the first as the Head of the Church and the last as He became the servant of all. We find Him the first and the last in our lives, satisfying all our needs, so that we lack nothing!

9 They that fashion an idol are all of them vanity, and their delectable things shall not profit; and their witnesses are they; it seeth not, nor knoweth; that they may be ashamed. 10 Who hath formed a god, or molten a graven image that is profitable for nothing? 11 Behold, all his fellows shall be ashamed: and the workmen, they are of men. They are all gathered together, they stand up; they fear, and they shall be ashamed together. 12 The smith hath wrought iron into an axe, and worketh in the coals, and with hammers he fashioneth it, and worketh it with the strength of his arm: yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth: he hath drunk no water, and is faint. 13 The carpenter hath hewn wood; he stretcheth out the line; he marketh it out with an awl, he maketh it with chisels, and he marketh it out with the compass, and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man; that it may remain in the house! 14 He hath hewn him down cedars, and taken the cypress and the oak, and chosen for himself among the trees of the forest. He planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish it. 15 Then it becometh for a man to burn: for he taketh thereof, and warmeth himself; yea, he kindleth it, and baketh bread; then he maketh a god, and worshippeth it! He hath made it a graven image, and falleth down thereto. 16 He burneth part thereof in the fire; with part thereof he eateth flesh; he roasteth roast, and is satisfied! yea, he warmeth himself, and saith, “Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire.” 17 And the residue thereof he hath made a god, a graven image for himself! He falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, “Deliver me; for thou art my god.” 18 They know not, nor understand: for their eyes are smeared, that they cannot see; and their hearts, that they cannot understand. 19 And none considereth in his heart, neither is there knowledge nor understanding to say, “I have burned part of it in the fire; yea, I have baked bread also upon the coals thereof; I have roasted flesh, and eaten it: and shall I make the residue thereof an abomination? shall I fall down to the stock of a tree?” 20 He feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath led him astray, that he cannot deliver his soul, nor say, “Is there not a lie in my right hand?”

After speaking of the great gift of the Spirit, which presented us as witnesses for the truth, we declare our enjoyment of God our Savior as the LORD of hosts, the leader of the spiritual battle, and the One who satisfies all as the First and the Last, the support of the men of the Old Testament and also of the believers of the New Testament... Now He compares the testimony of the believers with the testimony of the idol-worshippers:

a. Witness to the Savior grants satisfaction and quenching of thirst and fruitfulness: “For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground... and they shall spring up as among the grass, as willows” [3, 4], while witness to idols offers vanity and emptiness and hunger with blindness and ignorance: “They that fashion an idol are all of them vanity, and their delectable things shall not profit; and their witnesses are they; it seeth not, nor knoweth; that they may be ashamed” [9].

Our Christ satisfies the depths, in Him is all sufficiency; those who have experienced Him have felt satisfied and lacked nothing at all; but outside Him is the loss of all inner satisfaction and the deprivation of enjoyment of fellowship with God, the source of life and satisfaction.

b. Witness to the Savior grants peace: “Fear not” [2]; “Fear ye not, neither be afraid” [8], but outside Him is fear and trembling: “They are all gathered together, they stand up; they fear, and they shall be ashamed together” [11]. All the energies were gathered together against Him: chief priests and scribes and Pharisees and Sadducees and Roman governors, etc... yet they carried terror and fear even in the moments of the crucifixion and the mocking of the Crucified One! Their inner evil terrified them and the emptiness of their hearts of divine grace, and nature rose up against them, so the sun was darkened and the moon was eclipsed and earthquakes occurred and the rocks were rent and many of the dead arose!

c. The Lord’s witnesses enjoy honor, being counted “the new Israel,” and they engrave the name of the Savior on their inner hands, as though they do nothing except in His name [5]; but the witnesses of those outside Him carry shame and disgrace [11].

He presents to us a wonderful portrayal of the corruption of idol worship, showing that the idols and their makers and those who worship them all carry shame and vanity. The makers of idols are earnest, not caring for hunger or thirst or weariness [12] in order to make the axe of iron and to beat out plates to set up images. So also the carpenters who spend every effort to carve wooden images... All of them labor and do not tire to set up images of metal or wood unable to offer salvation, while the children of God are lax in their spiritual striving despite their enjoyment of divine possibilities able to bring them to enjoy eternal salvation. It is as though these workers of vanity condemn the lax children of God, as the Lord of glory Jesus said that the sons of this generation are wiser than the sons of the Kingdom (Lk 16:8).

On the other hand, the making of metal images exhausts the energy of the makers, while the making of wooden images is accompanied by amusement with the remaining wood, as it is used in the hearth for warmth or for cooking food, at the same time that they soothe their conscience by worshipping the wood carved as an image.
Finally, what does idol worship (= withdrawal from God) offer:
a. Blindness of inner insight and inner darkness [18], while Christ is the Sun of righteousness (Mal 4:2).
b. Ignorance and lack of knowledge [9], while Christ is our righteousness.
c. Hunger, so that man eats ashes [20], while the Lord Christ is the heavenly Bread.
d. Falsehood, deceit and misleading [20], while the Lord Christ is the way and the truth.

In other words, we find in our Christ inner enlightenment and knowledge and satisfaction and truth and all our needs, but outside Him there is nothing but inner emptiness and a sense of isolation and the loss of inner insight.

21 “Remember these, O Jacob and Israel; for thou art my servant: I have formed thee; thou art my servant: O Israel, thou shalt not be forgotten of me. 22 I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed thee.” 23 Sing, O ye heavens; for the LORD hath done it: shout, ye lower parts of the earth: break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein: for the LORD hath redeemed Jacob, and glorified himself in Israel. 24 Thus saith the LORD, thy redeemer, and he that formed thee from the womb: “I am the LORD that maketh all things; that stretcheth forth the heavens alone; that spreadeth abroad the earth. Who is with me? 25 That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish; 26 That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith of Jerusalem, She shall be inhabited; and of the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof.”

He highlighted the vanity of idol worship or withdrawal from God, not for abstract rational criticism, but to stir the soul and urge it to accept the saving work of God, which centers on the following:
a. The establishment of God’s people: “Remember these, O Jacob and Israel; for thou art my servant” [21]... We have become the new Israel who worship God.
b. Our belonging to Him: “thou art mine” [21]; we are not only His creation and His people, but God takes pride in us as His children, belonging to Him.
c. Not being forgotten by Him [21].
d. We enjoy forgiveness of sins however dense they may be: “I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed thee” [22].
e. He grants the soul (the heavens) praise, and the body (the earth) a shout of joy, and our energies (the mountains) singing, and everything within us becomes like trees glorifying God [23].

27 That saith to the deep, Be dry, and I will dry up thy rivers: 28 That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: and saith of Jerusalem, She shall be built; and to the temple, Thou shalt be founded.

About 220 years before, God declared what would be accomplished by the hand of Cyrus the pagan for the building of Jerusalem and the founding of the temple according to God’s good pleasure: “That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: and saith of Jerusalem, She shall be built; and to the temple, Thou shalt be founded” [28]. Here for the first time the name “Cyrus” is mentioned explicitly; its meaning in Persian is “sun”; and in Aramaic “shepherd”; some see that “my shepherd” was a title of some kings of the Middle East anciently.
The Jewish historian Josephus mentions that Cyrus read his name in Isaiah 220 years before and wanted to fulfill what was stated about him (see Ezra 1:2; 2 Chr 36:23).
What does He mean by saying: “That saith to the deep, Be dry, and I will dry up thy rivers” [27]?

a. He portrays Jerusalem as a deep of water and a river in which the temple cannot yet be established, according to human thought, because the Jews had lost their hope completely during the Babylonian captivity, but God, the Almighty and Caring, dries up the deeps and rivers, fulfilling His promises to us.
b. Perhaps He points here to the crossing of the Sea of Suph and the river Jordan to affirm that He is able to bring them across from captivity and return them to the land of promise.
c. Perhaps He pointed to Cyrus, who crossed the Euphrates and stormed the kingdom of Babylon.

1 “Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut; 2 I will go before thee, and make the crooked places straight: I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron: 3 And I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I, the LORD, which call thee by thy name, am the God of Israel. 4 For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me. 5 I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me: 6 That they may know from the rising of the sun, and from the west, that there is none beside me. I am the LORD, and there is none else. 7 I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things. 8 Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the LORD have created it.”

It appears from the Babylonian writings that this Cyrus was the son of Cambyses and the grandson of another Cyrus, and that all of them, with their forefathers, reigned in the east of Elam, where Shushan was the capital of their kingdom from about the year 550 B.C.

Cyrus is considered the founder of the Persian kingdom. It is said that he began his life as the commander of an obscure troop in Persia, and succeeded in becoming the commander of two troops of mountain soldiers. He was extremely ambitious, so he began his conquests of the small neighboring kingdoms. Babylon, however, mocked him and made light of his abilities, until he entered Babylon in 539 B.C., in the days of Belshazzar its king, having gathered in his person the strength of the two kingdoms of Persia and Media. Thus the prophecy of Daniel was fulfilled (Dan 5:28), and Daniel was also in the court of Cyrus (Dan 6:28).

Herodotus and Xenophon (the young Greek) praised the person of Cyrus. The latter spoke of him, about 100 years after his death, as a supreme example of strength joined with simplicity, purity and self-control.
Now God addresses Cyrus about two centuries before his coming, declaring in it how He regards him, His divine work in his life, and God’s purpose for him. The following is observed in this address:

a. The word “I” of the Lord appears 16 times in God’s address to Cyrus [1-7], and 31 times in the whole chapter. It is as though God wants to affirm that the rise of Cyrus is by divine permission, and that his victory and that of his army, and the shattering of Babylon like an earthen vessel that cannot be mended, is from God Himself.

b. The Lord calls Cyrus “His anointed” [1], although he does not know the Lord [4-5]; perhaps because he worshiped the one unknown God while respecting religions as a whole, or because he fulfilled God’s plan for the deliverance of His people from the Babylonian captivity, and because he was a symbol of the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world.

c. Concerning God’s work with him, He says, “whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings” [1]. God takes the role of the father who holds Cyrus as His child so that he may walk, as though God were his guide and the secret of his strength, upholding him to destroy evil. He gives him victory in the war against the nations so that he treads them down, since it was the custom for the victor to tread on the necks of the great men who were taken captive, and to loose the loins of kings, that is, to make them lose their strength and greatness, for kings used to wear exceedingly precious girdles as a sign of their greatness and might. This was fulfilled literally when King Belshazzar saw the fingers of a man’s hand writing on the wall of the palace: “the king’s countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another” (Dan 5:6).

In any case, Cyrus was a symbol of the Lord Christ in this matter, of whom it is said, “The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath” (Ps 110:5). It is said of Cyrus that the Lord held his right hand, and here it is said of the Son, the Word, “The Lord at thy right hand”; and, wonderfully, it is said in the same psalm on the tongue of the Father, “Sit thou at my right hand” (Ps 110:1). It is as though the Son is at the right hand of the Father (Ps 110:1) and the Father at the right hand of the Son (Ps 110:5)... For the right hand does not signify a position in place or a particular direction, but is a symbol of divine power and a sign of union and inseparability, since the two are one in divinity and one in power.

And as Cush broke kings in pieces, so the Lord Christ broke the kings who were ungrateful and who resisted the truth, for it is said: “shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath” (Ps 110:5). St. Augustine comments on this, saying: [These kings were wounded by His glory, and He made them weak by the weight of His name, so that they no longer had power to accomplish what they wished... They wished to blot out the Christian name from the face of the earth, but they could not, for whoever falls on this stone will be broken. The kings fell on this stone of stumbling and were wounded when they said: Who is Christ?!].

Perhaps by the kings He meant especially those who did not receive the Lord Christ (Jn 1:11), for it was fitting that they should unite with Him as the King of kings and so become kings, preachers and witnesses for Him. This is a matter that astonished the prophets when they prophesied about it, for Isaiah says in the same chapter, “Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour” [15]; and the Apostle Paul was also astonished at it (Rom 10:20; 11:7; 9:30).

d. “To open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut” [1]. Thus God goes before Cyrus His anointed to open the closed gates before him, and the fortresses made by human hands collapse before him; even nature moves to support him: “I will go before thee, and make the crooked places straight: I will break in pieces the gates of brass, and cut in sunder the bars of iron” [2].

When we are joined to our victorious Christ, we walk in the royal way and rise toward heavenly things as though without hindrance, because the Lord goes before us, and the gates of eternity are opened before Him on our behalf. Cyrus stormed the walls of Babylon with their huge bronze gates, which numbered a hundred gates according to Herodotus.
e. God gives Cyrus the hidden treasures of Babylon, for it was the custom of kings to hide their treasures in places that no one knew, so that the enemy could not seize them.

“And I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I, the LORD, which call thee by thy name, am the God of Israel” [3]. Since God is the “One who forms the light” [7], He reveals the hidden things to His children and grants them the treasures of His grace that cannot be comprehended.

f. God reveals to Cyrus His purpose for him: “For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me” [5]. What He gives him is given on behalf of His believers and for the sake of His people... Thus it is fitting for us, as anointed ones of the Lord, to cling to our unique Lord Jesus Christ, and to recognize our mission, which is the building up of the congregation and its growth in the Lord.

g. Since the Persian religions were known for the Gnosticism that focused on the “duality of God,” meaning the existence of a god of good and a god of evil, God wanted to remove this thought from Cyrus, saying to him: “I am the LORD, and there is none else; I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things” [7].

The word “evil ra” has come not in the sense of sin, but the fruit of sin or its punishment, of sorrow and distress. St. John Chrysostom says: [There is an evil that is truly evil: adultery, debauchery, covetousness, and countless other hidden things that deserve severe rebuke and punishment. And there is also an evil that is in truth not evil, but is so called, such as famine, disaster, death, sickness and the like; for these are not evils, but are so called. Why? Because if they were evils they would not become a source of our good, since they discipline our pride and our sloth, lead us to zeal, and make us more watchful]. In the same sense Abba Theodore says in the Conferences of St. John Cassian: [Holy Scripture is accustomed to use the expressions “evils” and “sorrows” in improper senses, for they are not evil in their nature, but are so called because they are thought to be evils by those to whom they have not brought good].

entries.section: 2. Murmuring against the choice of Cyrus:

paragraphs.text: 9 “Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands? 10 Woe unto him that saith unto his father, What begettest thou? or to the woman, What hast thou brought forth? 11 Thus saith the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and his Maker, Ask me of things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me. 12 I have made the earth, and created man upon it: I, even my hands, have stretched out the heavens, and all their host have I commanded. 13 I have raised him up in righteousness, and I will direct all his ways: he shall build my city, and he shall let go my captives, not for price nor reward, saith the LORD of hosts.”

It appears that murmuring arose among the Jews and also among the Gentiles. The Jews murmured against God because He accomplishes salvation by a pagan man, for his choice shatters their pride and their zeal for their own kind. This was on the part of the Jews; as for the Gentiles, the soul of some of them was embittered that one of them should take this role, accomplishing for the Jews deliverance from captivity and helping to establish the rites in Jerusalem.

In the face of this situation Isaiah lifted his heart toward God to offer a liturgical prayer, declaring in it that what takes place through Cyrus is a symbol of what is accomplished by the Lord Christ. It is as though he were asking the Jews as well as the Gentiles to turn from their murmuring to the experience of the free salvation offered to all. This is what moved Isaiah to turn in his address from Cyrus to Christ, our righteousness and salvation, saying: “Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness: let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together; I the LORD have created it” [8]. It is as though he were repeating what is in the Book of Psalms: “Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land. Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other. Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven, etc....” (Ps 85:9-13); “Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us” (Ps 67:6); “The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness” (Ps 72:3)...

It is as though the prophet were repeating that salvation is accomplished not because of Cyrus, but through the salvation of the Lord Christ and His righteousness... In Him our peace is accomplished through the meeting of mercy with truth, or mercy with divine justice, for on the Cross He paid the price in full through His infinite righteousness.

St. Augustine sees that in Christ the Jews met with the Gentiles through the meeting of truth with mercy; for the Jews knew the truth through the Law and the prophecies, and the Gentiles received mercy after they left their idolatrous worship, and these met with those as one people, righteous and holy to the Lord.

In the Lord Christ heaven met with earth, for He, the heavenly Son of God, became the Son of man, and was born as a human being on our earth... Therefore the prophet says: “Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness” [8], as though he were saying: “He bowed the heavens also, and came down” (Ps 18:9); the Righteous and Holy One came down as from His heavens to accomplish our salvation. As for his saying, “let the earth open, and let them bring forth salvation, and let righteousness spring up together” [8], it means: “Truth shall spring out of the earth” (Ps 85). And as St. Augustine says: [Christ was born of a woman; the Son of God became flesh. What is the truth? The Son of God! What is the earth? The flesh... But the Truth that sprang out of the earth was before the earth, for by Him the heavens and the earth were made; yet that righteousness might look down from heaven, that is, that human beings might be justified by divine grace, the Truth was born of the Virgin Mary, that He might offer a sacrifice that justifies them, the sacrifice of suffering, the sacrifice of the Cross].

After the prophet turned our eyes from Cyrus to Christ the Savior, through His unique sacrifice that is able to justify, he rebuked the Jews and the Gentiles for their murmuring against the Lord, presenting two woes:

a. The first woe: the potsherd entering into strife with the potter, and the clay with him who fashions it; for it is not the right of a piece of pottery to demand of its maker a particular form, as to say to him, “thy work, He hath no hands” [9]... that is, you made the pottery without hands.

b. The second woe: the child’s protest against his father and mother, “What begettest thou?” or “What hast thou brought forth?”... I wished that you had borne me an angel and not a human being who carries human weakness and comes under the burdens of earthly life and its troubles.
It is fitting for us, as pottery or as children, to thank our Maker and Father, not to murmur against Him!

14 “Thus saith the LORD, The labour of Egypt, and merchandise of Ethiopia and of the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over unto thee, and they shall be thine: they shall come after thee; in chains they shall come over, and they shall fall down unto thee, they shall make supplication unto thee, saying, Surely God is in thee; and there is none else, there is no God. 15 Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour. 16 They shall be ashamed, and also confounded, all of them: they shall go to confusion together that are makers of idols. 17 But Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end. 18 For thus saith the LORD that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the LORD; and there is none else. 19 I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth: I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain: I the LORD speak righteousness, I declare things that are right.”

The Jews, like the Gentiles, were occupied with the story of Cyrus in its letter and in his temporal works, although it was fitting for all to pierce through the letter and meet the hidden God who works behind history for the salvation of all. So in a fatherly rebuke the Lord says: “Ask me of things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me” [11].

I would have you be occupied only with the things to come, that is, with the eternal future, where it is fitting for you to seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. And that you pray for His sons, that is, that in our prayers we be occupied with His believers and the work of His hands, for it is fitting for us to realize our standing and our wonderful boldness before Him. In other words, our eternal Kingdom, our witness to others and our longing for the salvation of every human being, all these are matters more important than murmuring at Cyrus’s taking this role in their deliverance from the Babylonian captivity.
Once again He affirms to them that they must be occupied with Him and not with Cyrus, for He is “a God that hidest thyself... the Saviour” [15]; He is the One who works in secret.
The characteristics of this divine salvation are:

a. A free salvation: “I have raised him up in righteousness, and I will direct all his ways: he shall build my city, and he shall let go my captives, not for price nor reward, saith the LORD of hosts” [13]. Cyrus fulfilled God’s plan for His people without awaiting a reward from the people; they did not pay Cyrus a price for making the ways easy for them, building the city and freeing them from captivity. That was a symbol of the free salvation of the Lord Christ, as the Apostle Paul says: “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God” (Rom 3:24-25).

b. A collective salvation: He turns the Egyptians, the Ethiopians and the Sabeans to faith, so that they enter the new Israel in a spirit of humility and worship [14]. Our Lord Jesus Christ stretched out His hands on the Cross to gather with one the old people and with the other the company of the Gentiles; He gathered the whole world into His embrace to raise humanity to sonship to the Father by His Holy Spirit.
c. An eternal salvation: “But Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end” [17].
d. A public salvation: “I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth” [19]. The Lord of glory was crucified openly on the hill of Golgotha.

entries.section: 4. A call to salvation in Christ:

paragraphs.text: 20 “Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, ye that are escaped of the nations: they have no knowledge that set up the wood of their graven image, and pray unto a god that cannot save. 21 Tell ye, and bring them near; yea, let them take counsel together: who hath declared this from ancient time? who hath told it from that time? have not I the LORD? and there is no God else beside me; a just God and a Saviour; there is none beside me. 22 Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else. 23 I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear. 24 Surely, shall one say, in the LORD have I righteousness and strength: even to him shall men come; and all that are incensed against him shall be ashamed. 25 In the LORD shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.”

The Lord Christ speaks to the Gentiles to call them to enjoy Him as a Savior able to justify them. “Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, ye that are escaped of the nations... Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else. I have sworn by myself, the word is gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return, That unto me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear. Surely, shall one say, in the LORD have I righteousness and strength: even to him shall men come; and all that are incensed against him shall be ashamed. In the LORD shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory” [20-24].
It is observed in this call:
a. A collective call, in which He asks the Gentiles to gather together as one holy Church, coming forward in the spirit of the community to receive His work of salvation.

b. God is the Savior and there is no other, as the Apostle Paul says: “For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings” (Heb 2:10). And as Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says: [By these words he means that it was not the place of anyone else to bring human beings back from what they had begun, except the Word of God, who also made them from the beginning... For by the sacrifice of His body He put an end to the decree that was against us, for just as death reigned over human beings through a man, so also through the Word of God, when He became man, death was destroyed and the resurrection of life began].
c. A call full of hope, which achieves its aim in that every knee shall bow to Him.
d. A call whose foundation is faith: “Look unto me,” as the old people believed before and looked at the bronze serpent and were healed.
e. The enjoyment of the righteousness and power of the Savior.
f. The Savior is the secret of the glory of His believers and the shame of those who oppose Him.

entries.section: 1. God, the bearer of our burdens:

paragraphs.text: 1 “Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast. 2 They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity. 3 Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb: 4 And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you. 5 To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like? 6 They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship. 7 They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove: yea, one shall cry unto him, yet can he not answer, nor save him out of his trouble.”
God compares the gods of Babylon with Himself: the former need someone to carry them, but He is the bearer of our lives with all their troubles, for He says:

“Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast. They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity” [1-2].

The two chief gods of Babylon were shaken before Cyrus and bowed down to him, so the two objects of worship became slaves, carried with all their statues on animals without power, since all were unable to walk, indeed unable even to move. All the jewels that adorn the statues were taken by... and Cyrus came and all were taken into captivity... Can these two objects of worship deliver anyone, as long as they are unable even to save themselves?!

“Bel”: an Akkadian name corresponding to the Hebrew name “Baal,” meaning “lord”; perhaps he is the very god Marduk (Jer 50:2; 51:44); he is the god of the sun and the god of spring. He has the form of a great man with a crown on his head and seven bull horns. Food and drink were offered to him in large quantities every evening, and they believed that he ate and drank them, until the prophet Daniel disclosed to the king the existence of a secret door in the temple through which the priests entered with their families at night to eat the food and drink in secret, as is recorded in the story of Bel in the additions to Daniel.

“Nebo”: a Babylonian name meaning “announcer,” the god of science and knowledge; Borsippa, near Babylon, was the center of his worship. The kings of Babylon sought blessing by him and bore his name together with their original names, such as Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan and Nebushasban.

entries.section: 1. God, the bearer of our burdens:

paragraphs.text: These two gods were exposed, and their inability to move or to protect their adornment was disgraced before Cyrus. But the living God is the Savior of His people; He bears our burdens when we have not yet been formed in our mothers’ wombs, until we reach old age, for He affirms to us, “I am he... I will bear” [4]. It is as though He says: I have myriads of angels and the heavenly creation and many prophets, priests and servants... but I place Myself in the hands of My people to bear their troubles Myself, and to take their sins away from them, and to support them in all their responsibilities... I bear them Myself as upon My shoulders.

This is what God affirms throughout the generations, saying: “Behold, I will inquire after my sheep and visit them... I will feed my flock, and I will cause them to lie down, saith the Lord GOD. I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment... Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle” (Ezek 34:11-22). Thus He affirms: “I am he... I will bear.”

God our Savior does not cease to call us to Himself that He may bear our burdens, saying: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mt 11:28). Therefore it is said of Him: “Surely he hath borne our griefs” (Isa 53:4); “he bare the sin of many” (Isa 53:12); “the God of our salvation bears us” (Ps 68:19).

Our Lord Jesus came as a Savior not only to bear our burdens and our sins, atoning for them, but to bear us in Himself; He captivates us by His love to lift us up with Him to His glory. He came down to us to bear us in Himself, that we may ascend in Him and by Him to His Kingdom.
We return to His address in the Book of Isaiah: “I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you” [4].
“I have made,” that is, I allowed the Babylonian captivity in order to expose your weaknesses.
“And I will bear” (I lift up): I remove this shame from you and arrange your release from captivity.
“And I will carry”: I Myself take up the bearing of your troubles... I am the hidden God.
“And I will deliver you”: I bring you into freedom, and return you to the land of promise, and save you.

This is the work of God the Savior: He makes, He lifts up, He bears, and He saves. He allows our sins to be exposed so that we may realize that we are captives, not in the captivity of Babylon, but under the captivity of the devil and his evil works; and He lifts up as He removes this shame from us by His divine plan for our salvation; and He bears as He took away the debt Himself on our behalf and did not entrust our salvation to an angel or an archangel or a prophet; and finally He saves when He carries us to His heavens and grants us fellowship in His divine glories.

The Apostle Paul says: “Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28). The Lord Christ bowed His back to bear the sins of the whole world, for He died for all, but He is counted a Savior for the believers alone, those who accepted that the weight of their sins be lifted from them, so that they are borne as righteous in Him and He enters with them into the bosom of His Father.
* He died for all, that is on His part, for this death was the counterpart against the perishing of all humanity, but He did not bear the sins of all people because they did not wish it.

* The lamb of Moses (the Passover) did not bear at once the sins of anyone, but this Lamb bore the sins of the whole world, for since the world was in danger of perishing, He hastened and saved it from the wrath of God.

* They heard that He bears the sins of the world (Jn 1:36), and at once they ran to Him, saying: If it is possible for Him to remove the accusations directed against us, why do we delay? Here is the One who saves without toil on our part.
St. John Chrysostom * By the Cross He gave salvation to the world.

No human being in history attained the greatness that qualifies him to take away the sin of the whole world, neither Enoch nor Abraham nor Isaac, even though he offered himself to death, but he was spared, since he was not able to remove the stain of sin.

Who, then, is this great Man by whose death sin dies?! This cannot be one of human beings... But God chose the Son, the Son of God who is over all, and He is the One who can be offered for the sins of all!
It was necessary for Him to die, because by His victory over death He is able to rescue the others who are like slain men lying in the graves.
He broke the bondage of the passions, and the chains of death were not able to hold Him!
St. Ambrose * Loose my pains by Your pains; heal my wounds by Your wounds; cleanse my blood with Your blood, and mingle in my body the fragrance of life that belongs to Your holy Body!

The Spiritual Elder The Lord bore our sins with all their weight in His body in order to grant us His righteousness in us, and we ourselves became borne in Him by His Holy Spirit so that He might lift us up to His heavens. He is the One who earlier bore His old people out of the land of bondage with all its weight and bitterness, to bring them into the land of promise, indeed to bring them to Himself. “I bare you on eagles’ wings, and brought you unto myself” (Ex 19:4); “thou hast seen how that the LORD thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son, in all the way that ye went, until ye came into this place” (Deut 1:31).

God has affirmed His surpassing love for us: He bears us while we are in the womb and remains bearing us until old age [3-4]. This surpasses the love of a mother who is able to carry her child in the womb, or the infant, and to some extent when he becomes a little child in the first few years of his life... She carries him bodily and bears some of his troubles, but she is unable to grasp all his hidden secrets in order to share his troubles. But God bears us until old age; He bears all our troubles, visible and hidden, and as the psalmist says: “My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord embraces me” (Ps 27:10).

entries.section: 1. God, the bearer of our burdens:

paragraphs.text: In His love God has no like, neither the parents nor the other gods who need someone to make them, and lift them on the shoulder, and set them in a place, and guard them lest they be stolen; their worshipers cry out to them, but they do not answer them in the time of distress [5-7].

entries.section: 2. The calling of Cyrus from the east:

paragraphs.text: 8 “Remember this, and shew yourselves men: bring it again to mind, O ye transgressors. 9 Remember the former things of old: for I am God, and there is none else; I am God, and there is none like me, 10 Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure: 11 Calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country: yea, I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it. 12 Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness: 13 I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry: and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory.”

entries.section: 2. The calling of Cyrus from the east:

paragraphs.text: This is the pleasure of God [10]: that He worked in the past and still works and remains working for the salvation of His people. He bore their burdens in the days of Moses when they came out of Egypt, and He bears them during their return from the Babylonian captivity, and He still bears them through the standing sacrifice of the Cross.

entries.section: 2. The calling of Cyrus from the east:

paragraphs.text: Cyrus, a symbol of the Lord Christ, was called the ravenous bird [11] because he is swift in movement and strong, swooping down on Babylon to seize it like prey, seizing its gods and its treasures... He is a symbol of the Lord Christ, who swooped down on the enemy of good and shattered his kingdom to restore to man his dignity, his freedom and his spiritual wealth.

“The man that executeth my counsel from a far country” [11], a symbol of the Lord Christ who came from heaven to become the “Son of Man” (the man of My counsel), who fulfills the will of the Father in Himself with pleasure.

entries.section: 2. The calling of Cyrus from the east:

paragraphs.text: The prophet Isaiah sees the Savior coming from afar, so he calls the distant Gentiles to draw near to Him and enjoy His righteousness and salvation: “Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness: I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry” [12-13].

Perhaps here he directs his address to the hard-hearted Babylonians, announcing to them that their resistance to God’s righteousness and salvation will not last, for the time of salvation has drawn near.
And perhaps he is speaking to the hard-hearted Gentiles so that they may accept the righteousness of the Lord and His salvation without resistance.

1 “Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate. 2 Take the millstones, and grind meal: uncover thy locks, make bare the leg, uncover the thigh, pass over the rivers. 3 Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and I will not meet thee as a man. 4 As for our redeemer, the LORD of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel. 5 Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms.”
“Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: there is no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate” [1].

Babylon was called “the virgin”; this comparison is used in the Holy Bible concerning cities (Isa 1:8; 37:22; Jer 31:21; 46:11; Lam 1:15). This virgin is either betrothed to God as a holy bride to Him, like Jerusalem, or betrothed to the enemy of good and becomes his bride, united to him, bearing his kingdom of darkness.
Since Babylon represents the soul that has fallen through pride, together with luxury and temporal joy and the seeking of earthly passions, what befell her reveals what happens to man because of sin.
What befell Babylon? Or what are the fruits of sin?

a. Being the capital of the greatest state of that time, she inclined to care for the show of splendor while practicing corruption; she had the appearance of outward joy, so intense grief befell her and she came down to the dust [1], as though she had lost her husband or one of her loved ones (Josh 7:6; Job 2:12; 10:9; Ps 22:15; Lam 3:29).
The first work of sin is the loss of inner joy and the peace that passes understanding, so the soul is filled with bitterness and despair, with a feeling of isolation and deprivation.
* Yes, my God... in the absence of Your light there is an appearance of death, or rather a coming of nothingness....
Woe is me... many wounds have befallen me, and although You are the Comforter, the Giver of peace, I have gone far from You.
Woe is me... many follies have overtaken me, and although You are the Truth, I did not seek counsel from You...
My evils caused me deep wounds, for I did not walk in the narrow way; although You are the Life, I was not with You.
St. Augustine b. Instead of the throne, the “chair,” and authority, Babylon sits on the ground in humiliation as a captive [1]

God created man as lord over the earth and granted him dignity and authority, but pride brought him down to the abyss. Man became in the humiliation of slaves, bowing to sin and led after the lusts of the flesh like a slave, after he had been a king who knew how to direct his feelings and his senses and all his energies for the sake of the Kingdom of God. Therefore it is said: “he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city” (Prov 16:32).

The Holy Bible warns us of pride: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Prov 16:18-19).
* Temporal glory is like a hidden rock in the sea, unknown to the sailor until a ship strikes it and its bottom is torn and fills with water.

St. Isaac the Syrian c. After Babylon had been the lady of the haughty kingdoms, she became one who performs the hard works of slaves for the sake of her masters. Here the prophet Isaiah depicts her as a woman grinding with the millstone, a work that needs two women working together; and the great millstone is turned by animals; yet here she is commanded to do this violent work without help from anyone [2]. She becomes like Samson when sin humbled him and he began to turn the mill in place of the animals, so that all laughed at him and mocked him.

When St. John Chrysostom speaks of our ascent to the heavens in Christ Jesus who ascended, he reveals to us how our life and nature descended until we became lower than the animals, but our Christ lifted us out of this humiliation by His ascension and granted us the enjoyment of His heavens, for he says: [Look at our nature, how it was lowered and then raised. For it was not possible to descend further than man descended, nor possible to ascend higher than Christ was raised... Paul makes this clear when he says: “He that descended is the same also that ascended.” Where did He descend? “Into the lower parts of the earth”; and He ascended “far above all heavens” (Eph 4:9-10)... We were nothing but dust and ashes... We became more foolish than the irrational animals, for man came to be compared with them and became like them (Ps 49:20; Isa 1:3)... See how we became more foolish than the ass and the ox (Isa 1:3), and than the birds of the heaven, the turtle and the swallow (Jer 8:7)... We became disciples of the ants (Prov 6:6)... more rigid than stones (Isa 6:2), we are likened to serpents (Ps 58:5)... we are called children of the devil (Jn 8:44)... Such became our lowliness and unworthiness... But today our nature has been raised above every creature. Today the angels have recovered those whom they lost long ago! Today the archangels have seen those whom they have long desired to see! Today they have seen our nature on the divine throne, shining in eternal beauty and everlasting glory!].
e. “Uncover thy locks, make bare the leg” [2]; this is a thing unbecoming for young noble girls at that time, to uncover their faces or to gather up the hem of their garments.

After she had been sailing with her commercial or war ships, adorned and of great price, as the queen of the world, it is said to her: “make bare the leg, pass over the rivers. Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and I will not meet thee as a man” [3]. She shattered many and wronged many nations, so she deserved that her work should return upon her and she should bear the same shame. It is as though sin brings man into shame and disgrace.
Sin caused us to lose the garments of divine grace, so we became naked; but our Christ, who bears our sins, was stripped for our sake, to offer Himself as a garment covering our shame.
* Those who crucified Him stripped Him of His garments like butchers, but He was silent like a sheep before the butcher!
He left His garment when He rejoiced (at the wedding of the Cross), that those who went out of Paradise naked might put it on!
He clothes them with His garments and remains Himself in mockery, because He knew that they were fitting for exposed Adam!
They stripped off His garments and put on Him a scarlet robe, the color of blood, so that the slain (sacrificed) Bridegroom might be adorned with it!

St. Jacob of Serug f. She enters a state of bewilderment and gloom because of the disaster that befalls her, and becomes unable to speak, living in darkness: “Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms” [5].

6 “I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst shew them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke. 7 And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: so that thou didst not lay these things to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it. 8 Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall not sit as a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: 9 But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, and for the great abundance of thine enchantments. 10 For thou hast trusted in thy wickedness: thou hast said, None seeth me. Thy wisdom and thy knowledge, it hath perverted thee; and thou hast said in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me. 11 Therefore shall evil come upon thee; thou shalt not know from whence it riseth: and mischief shall fall upon thee; thou shalt not be able to put it off: and desolation shall come upon thee suddenly, which thou shalt not know. 12 Stand now with thine enchantments, and with the multitude of thy sorceries, wherein thou hast laboured from thy youth; if so be thou shalt be able to profit, if so be thou mayest prevail. 13 Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee. 14 Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them; they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame: there shall not be a coal to warm at, nor fire to sit before it. 15 Thus shall they be unto thee with whom thou hast laboured, even thy merchants, from thy youth: they shall wander every one to his quarter; none shall save thee.”

The decree for the collapse of Babylon was issued, but not without grounds for this judgment, for God in His love always declares to those who fall under judgment the reasons for the verdict, so that others may take warning and not fall into the same sins. As for the sins of Babylon, they are:

a. Violence and lack of mercy. God allowed His people to be handed over to Babylon for discipline, but Babylon exploited the situation and practiced violence even on the elders, with no regard for their helplessness because of their old age [6]. God was expecting from her gentleness toward His people, whom He loves even in the moments of handing them over to discipline.

b. She thought she was above the law; in her use of violence she did not realize that what she does to others will come upon her, and with the measure she measures it will be measured to her. She thought she was lady of all and did not remember her latter end [7].

c. Her clinging to deceptive security or false peace [8], which is not based on the soul’s meeting with God, the source of peace, but on man’s belief that nothing will befall him because of his vain greatness or his position or his wealth. She reckoned that she would not become a widow nor bereaved of children, relying on sorcery and enchantments, so she was deceived, and widowhood and bereavement came upon her suddenly in one day [9]. She became a widow because she lost the kingship, and she became bereaved by the slaughter of her inhabitants, who were as sons and daughters to her.
d. Her ignoring that God sees her and knows her secrets: “For thou hast trusted in thy wickedness: thou hast said, None seeth me” [10].

e. Her reliance on mere human wisdom [10], together with resorting to sorcery and enchantments, for she reckoned that the stargazers could save her in the time of distress by their counsel and their knowledge of the unseen, but they themselves burn like stubble and do not escape from the flame [11-15]. There was no state in the world known for sorcerers and astrologers like her (see the Book of Daniel), and here the prophet mocks them.

1 “Hear ye this, O house of Jacob, which are called by the name of Israel, and are come forth out of the waters of Judah, which swear by the name of the LORD, and make mention of the God of Israel, but not in truth, nor in righteousness. 2 For they call themselves of the holy city, and stay themselves upon the God of Israel; The LORD of hosts is his name. 3 I have declared the former things from the beginning; and they went forth out of my mouth, and I shewed them; I did them suddenly, and they came to pass. 4 Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass; 5 I have even from the beginning declared it to thee; before it came to pass I shewed it thee: lest thou shouldest say, Mine idol hath done them, and my graven image, and my molten image, hath commanded them. 6 Thou hast heard, see all this; and will not ye declare it? I have shewed thee new things from this time, even hidden things, and thou didst not know them. 7 They are created now, and not from the beginning; even before the day when thou heardest them not; lest thou shouldest say, Behold, I knew them. 8 Yea, thou heardest not; yea, thou knewest not; yea, from that time that thine ear was not opened: for I knew that thou wouldest deal very treacherously, and wast called a transgressor from the womb.”

In the previous chapter God exposed Babylon, the virgin, the lady of kingdoms, who was swept away into a life of revelry with haughtiness and violence, and so collapsed completely. Now, before announcing the departure of His people or their release from captivity, He speaks in a fatherly rebuke, frank, revealing their weaknesses and sins and also His purposes in allowing their captivity, so that they might not return to their sins again.

Perhaps the most dangerous sin facing believers who have spiritual knowledge is hypocrisy together with formalism in worship. God does not want to humiliate them, but to raise them to a lofty position, and He gave them spiritual possibilities for life with Him, the most important of which are:
a. He called them “Israel” [1], as they are His chosen people.
b. A royal people, “come forth out of the waters of Judah” [1].

c. The name of God was called upon them: “which swear by the name of the LORD, and make mention of the God of Israel,” but they do this “not in truth, nor in righteousness” [1], although they realize that He is the one true God whom they worship, but in formalism and literalism without spirit.
d. They enjoyed the city of Jerusalem [2] as the holy city of God, which contains His temple.
e. “[They] stay themselves upon the God of Israel” [2]: they boast in His promises, confess His covenant and lean upon Him (Mic 3:11)..

f. They enjoyed the divine prophecies, for God used to tell them of the things to come, that is, of the things that were about to happen [3]. The secret of giving these prophecies was to establish them in faith in Him and in believing His words and promises. He knew that they were hard of heart, their necks iron and their brows brass, so that it was difficult for them to believe the prophetic words; therefore He gave them prophecies that were fulfilled in the near future so that they might believe the prophecies, and also to distinguish between God and the idols [5].

With all that God gave His people of these possibilities, they lived in formalism of worship with a Pharisaic spirit full of hypocrisy; they also mixed the worship of God with idols, and ignored the prophetic words and despised them and did not understand their mysteries. Therefore He rebukes them, saying: “Yea, thou heardest not; yea, thou knewest not; yea, from that time that thine ear was not opened: for I knew that thou wouldest deal very treacherously, and wast called a transgressor from the womb” [8].
The prophet Isaiah was occupied with speaking of spiritual insight and the holy inner ear, for his talk about the Savior seemed to many in his time, indeed to the majority, almost impossible.

The Savior has come, and yet many reject Him in spite of the fulfillment of the prophecies that came in the Old Testament in His person and through His saving works; therefore the world still needs true insight and the holy ear. Even those who have believed in Him and received Him need this, to enjoy deeper mysteries and to perceive the hidden inner heavenly glories.

We all need the Lord of glory to accompany us and speak with us so as to sanctify our depths, so that we may say with the two disciples of Emmaus: “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Lk 24:32).
* My God... You are my light, open my eyes that they may behold Your divine splendor, so that I may walk in my way without stumbling in the snares of the enemy.
* You are the light who enlightened the mind of Jacob, so he revealed to his children the various matters.
St. Augustine

9 “For my name’s sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off. 10 Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction. 11 For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it: for how should my name be polluted? and I will not give my glory unto another. 12 Hearken unto me, O Jacob and Israel, my called; I am he; I am the first, I also am the last. 13 Mine hand also hath laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand hath spanned the heavens: when I call unto them, they stand up together. 14 All ye, assemble yourselves, and hear; which among them hath declared these things? The LORD hath loved him: he will do his pleasure on Babylon, and his arm shall be on the Chaldeans. 15 I, even I, have spoken; yea, I have called him: I have brought him, and he shall make his way prosperous. 16 Come ye near unto me, hear ye this; I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time that it was, there am I: and now the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me. 17 Thus saith the LORD, thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; I am the LORD thy God which teacheth thee to profit, which leadeth thee by the way that thou shouldest go. 18 O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea: 19 Thy seed also had been as the sand, and the offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before me.”
God presents to His people the reasons for allowing their captivity:

a. “For my name’s sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off” [9]... In other words, this people should have perished completely and been cut off, but God in His jealousy for His name and glory gave them over to discipline, that perhaps they might return to Him and not perish. It is as though the captivity were a “gift,” being a divine discipline offered to the beloved, despite their unworthiness of this fatherly disciplinary love.

This is a wonderful spiritual view of discipline, through which the believer realizes that he is not worthy of this discipline, as it is a sign of fatherly love. The Apostle says: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons” (Heb 12:6-7).
* If the absence of discipline is a sign peculiar to bastards (Heb 12:8), then it is fitting for us to rejoice in discipline as a sign of the legitimacy of our sonship!

St. John Chrysostom * A father does not discipline his son if he does not love him, and a teacher does not correct his pupil unless he sees in him signs of obtaining the promise. When a physician withdraws his care from a patient, this is a sign that he despairs of his recovery.
St. Jerome * “Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes” (Ps 89:32).

It is mercy (of God) not only to call them but also to discipline them and scourge them. Let your father’s hand be upon you; if you are a good son, do not murmur at discipline... Let him discipline him as long as he has not taken away his mercy from him; let him strike him when he sins as long as he does not prevent him from inheriting.
If you rightly understand your father’s promises, do not fear his scourgings, but fear lest you do not inherit...
May the pious children not say: “If You come to us with a rod, do not come at all. For it is better to learn by the Father’s rod than to perish by the thief’s care for you.
* The Lord, the Preserver of the little ones (Ps 116:6), scourges those whom, when they become mature, He seeks to be (His) heirs...
He helped me when I was in distress, for the pain that the physician causes with his scalpel is not for punishment but for honor.

St. Augustine b. For purification: “Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction” [10]. We are the silver and gold of the Lord; He cares for refining us in the furnaces of toil and pain.
* Blessed is the man who is disciplined in this life twice, for the Lord does not punish for anything twice (Nah 1:9) LXX.

St. Jerome c. God, who allows discipline to purify us, lifts it from us when He accomplishes His aim. He has called the heavens and the earth, that all creation may gather and see the marvelous salvation of God. He loved Cyrus to accomplish His aim, and that his arm be on the Chaldeans [14].

What Cyrus accomplishes is not of his own, but from God, the Savior of His people: “I, even I, have spoken; yea, I have called him: I have brought him, and he shall make his way prosperous” [15]... “from the time that it was, there am I: and now the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me” [6].
Cyrus was sent by the Lord and by the Holy Spirit of God, as a symbol of the Lord Christ, who came of His own will and at the same time was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit... How?
Here is the unity of the work of the Holy Trinity; the Holy Trinity, as inseparable hypostases of one divine essence, works for the salvation of humanity.

The Father loves humanity, and in His love He sent His Word, who is not separated from Him, reckoning the sacrifice of Christ a gift on the part of the Father, as the Lord Christ Himself said: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (Jn 3:16). The Father, the Lover of mankind, sent His Son as a sacrifice of love.
The Son on His part offered Himself to be given in obedience to the Father, and also of His full will, for the Apostle says: “who loved me, and gave himself for me” (Gal 2:20).

As for the Holy Spirit, He did not stand in a passive role but had His positive role in the whole work of salvation; by Him the divine Incarnation was accomplished in the womb of the Virgin (Lk 1:35), and it is He who led Jesus up to be tempted, and He who bears witness to the Lord Christ (Jn 15:26).

g. To practice obedience to God, for the captivity did not happen by chance nor by fate and destiny, but is the natural fruit of disobedience; without it they would not have fallen into captivity. Therefore they ought, on their return, to practice obedience, so that they may enjoy the righteousness of God and His good things. “O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea: Thy seed also had been as the sand, and the offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before me” [18-19].
Had they obeyed God, not only would they not have fallen into the Babylonian captivity, but the peace of God would have overflowed like a wide, deep and ever-flowing river, watering many.

20 “Go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans, with a voice of singing declare ye, tell this, utter it even to the end of the earth; say ye, The LORD hath redeemed his servant Jacob. 21 And they thirsted not when he led them through the deserts: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out. 22 There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked.”
God presents a call to depart: “Go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans” [20].

Although God sent Cyrus for their deliverance, He does not compel them to depart against their will, but calls them and urges them to do so... And indeed 40,000 persons went out under Zerubbabel (Neh 7:66-67).

It is a continual call for us to depart, under the leadership of our Savior, from every place of stumbling, so that we may be freed by the Spirit of God from its yoke, as Lot and his family were called to leave Sodom and Gomorrah.
Fleeing from evil is not weakness nor passivity, but a bold act in which man, by the Spirit of God, declares his victory over his depths that long for or find pleasant the places of stumbling.
This call is accompanied by joy and rejoicing in the saving work of God: “with a voice of singing declare ye, tell this” [20].

As the prophet Isaiah looks at the release from captivity as a second exodus resembling the people’s departure from the bondage of Pharaoh by the hand of Moses, when He brought forth water for them from the rock in the wilderness that they might not thirst, so in this new exodus they enjoy the same gift: “And they thirsted not when he led them through the deserts: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out” [21]. This was fulfilled when the salvation of the Lord Christ was joined with the gift of the Holy Spirit on the feast of Pentecost, as a spring of living water that overflowed in the Church of Christ.
Finally, this salvation is optional; whoever does not accept it is deprived of the surpassing peace of God, for it is said: “There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked” [22].
* It is said to us: “I will cause the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness to cease from their mouths” (Jer 7:34). Yes, for the feasts of the wicked are woes.
* When the ungrateful withdraw from prayer and thanksgiving, they deprive themselves of the fruit of joy.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic The Septuagint reads: “There is no joy, saith the Lord, to the wicked.” St. Augustine distinguished between the temporary joy of the wicked, bound to temporal things and passing away with them, and the righteous, who rejoice even in their chains. The martyr Crispina rejoiced when she was bound and when she was led away to trial, as when she was imprisoned and when the sentence was passed against her... Her joy was before the angels, as the psalmist says: “Before the angels I will sing praise unto thee” (Ps 138:1).

entries.section: 1. The humility and glorification of the Savior:

paragraphs.text: 1 “Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far; The LORD hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name. 2 And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me; 3 And said unto me, Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified. 4 Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the LORD, and my work with my God. 5 And now, saith the LORD that formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob again to him, Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious in the eyes of the LORD, and my God shall be my strength. 6 And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth. 7 Thus saith the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers, Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the LORD that is faithful, and the Holy One of Israel, and he shall choose thee.”

In the previous chapter the address was directed to the house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel (Isa 48:1), but the address here is directed to the Gentiles, for He says: “Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far” [1]. The Gentiles were called “the isles of the Gentiles” (Gen 10:5), since they looked to the islands of the Mediterranean as the distant western regions, foreign to Israel; and He called the Gentiles “from far” because they had not entered into fellowship with Israel.
The Lord Christ the Savior speaks to the Gentiles, declaring the following:

a. Called from the womb: “The LORD hath called me from the womb” [1]. Some scholars think that the speaker here is in the name of Israel, since God chose His people before they existed, while they were in the loins of Abraham and in the womb of Sarah; and some thought it was Cyrus, whom God chose to accomplish his mission before he existed; but it is clear that the address here is in the name of the Lord Christ, the incarnate Word of God; for the archangel Gabriel preached to the Virgin His birth before she conceived Him, and He was called Jesus because He saves His people from their sins (Mt 1:21); therefore it is said, “from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name” [1].

entries.section: 1. The humility and glorification of the Savior:

paragraphs.text: b. Possessing authority: “And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword” [2]. And it is said of the Lord Christ:

“out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword” (Rev 1:16), and it is said of Him that He spoke as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees (Mt 7:29). He entered the battle against the enemy of good, the devil, with His word, which is like a twoedged sword (Heb 4:12).

c. The hiding of the mystery of Christ, His saving Gospel work and His call of the Gentiles to faith, behind the shadows of the Mosaic Law and the prophecies, for He says, “in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me” [2]. Perhaps by this saying He also meant what happened in His childhood, when Herod rose against Him and wanted to kill Him, so the Father sent an angel to Joseph commanding him to flee to Egypt. The Word became flesh, the Son of God became the Son of man; therefore in His humility He walked in our way as one of us, guarded by the Father with His protection as in the shadow of His hand, though He is able to command nature to destroy Herod and all who oppose Him.

“And made me a polished shaft (that does not rust); in his quiver hath he hid me” [2]. As the Word of God, He is an arrow that does not rust; He was hidden behind the shadows and symbols until the fullness of time came, and He declared Himself through the Cross as an arrow aimed against the devil and his hosts, stripping them of their authority and making a public show of them, triumphing over them (Col 2:15). He is the arrow that kills evil, and the giver of the wounds of divine love to the believing souls who cry out, “I am sick with love” (Song 2:5; 5:8).
* Holy Scripture teaches us that God is love (1 Jn 4:8); He aimed His only-begotten Son, “the chosen arrow” [2], toward the chosen, planting its threefold point in the spirit of life.

The head of the arrow is faith, which joins the one who shoots the arrow (Christ) with those who are struck by it, as though the soul were raised by divine ascents, and sees within itself the arrow of sweet love wounding it, adorned with the wounds....
It is a good wound, and a sweet pain, by which “Life” pierces the soul.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * Can anyone see the many wounds of divine love like those in the Song of Songs, she who complains that she is wounded: “I am wounded with love” (Song 2:5)?! And can he see the arrow that wounds many souls with the love of God except in Him who said: “He made me like a chosen spear”?!

* If anyone was ever inflamed with sincere love for the Word of God, if anyone received the sweet wounds of this “chosen arrow,” as the prophet calls it, if anyone was wounded by the spear of His knowledge, worthy of all love, so that he yearns and longs for Him night and day, and cannot speak except of Him, nor listen except to Him, nor think except of Him, nor incline to any desire or hope for anything else, when the matter becomes so, the soul rightly says: “I am wounded with love.” She receives her wound from the One of whom it was said: “He made me a chosen arrow, and in His quiver He hides me” [2].
It is fitting for God to strike our souls with such a wound, to wound them with such arrows and spears, to strike them with such healing wounds.
Origen * The words of the Lord are arrows that kindle love, not pain... Therefore we ought to understand “thine arrows stick fast in me” (Ps 38:2) thus: Your words have stuck fast in my heart.

* May the unhealthy be wounded, for when they are rightly wounded they become healthy. Let these, having become dwellers in the Church, the Body of Christ, say with the Church: “I am wounded with love” (Song 2:5) LXX.

entries.section: 1. The humility and glorification of the Savior:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine d. By the Cross the Son submitted in obedience to the Father; He became a servant for our sake that the Father might be glorified in Him, and that He might also be glorified in the weakness of the Cross. “And said unto me, Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified. Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the LORD, and my work with my God” [4].

Some ask: Who is His servant Israel? He is the Lord Christ, who came from the Jews, and accepted servitude by His own will although He is equal to the Father in essence (Phil 2:7). He came as a servant to raise the servants in Him to sonship to God; by this He glorified the Father and was glorified Himself through weakness, for the Apostle says: “And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
