Like a child He cried in speechless infancy, He who is the “Word” without whom all the eloquence of men is unable to speak!
Behold, O man, what God became for your sake...?!
Though you were a man, you wished to be God and went astray! And He, though He is God, wished to be man in order to bring back the one who had gone astray!
Human pride brought you down, so that only by divine humility might you be raised up!
St. Augustine * No one has been able to speak of Your eternity, so let me speak of Your coming, O my Teacher, with amazement...
Love drew You to come to our country for our sake... You became with us and of us, and You are our Lord!
Behold, Immanuel is with us, beside us, and for this reason tongues unworthy of You have spoken...

St. James of Serugh By saying “and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?!” [1] he means the appearing of the Lord Christ, not only in history, which amazes the whole creation, but also His appearing in our personal life, or His continual manifestation in the heart as a source of inner satisfaction.
* The arm of the Lord is Christ, so do not forget Him! Do not let (the spiritual enemies) rejoice, saying: Christians exist only for a time!
* “And to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?!”
By giving you His Christ He gives you His arm, and by giving you His arm He gives you His Christ.
He leads (man) to the way by leading him to His Christ, and He leads him to His Christ by leading him to the way, and Christ is the truth.
* “Thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good” (Ps 104:28).

What does it mean, O Lord, that You open Your hand? Christ is Your hand. “To whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?!” It is opened when it is revealed, for revelation is an opening. “Thou openest thine hand, they are filled with good”; when You reveal Your Christ, they are filled with good.

St. Augustine Our Christ, the arm of the Father, has been revealed to us that we may enjoy Him as the mystery of our life, saying: “For the life was manifested, and we have seen it, and bear witness, and shew unto you that eternal life, which was with the Father, and was manifested unto us” (1 Jn 1:2).

entries.section: 2. The Cross is shame and disgrace:

paragraphs.text: 2 For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. 3 He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
The Lord, the Savior, came like a branch growing up before Israel and like a root out of a dry ground; therefore the people made light of Him, and His own received Him not.

“He shall grow up before him as a tender plant” [2], for He came from the seed of David as a small shoot, as a branch, though He is the Creator of the vine and the One who brought it into being. He came hidden, in humility, and so He was symbolized by the bush burning with fire, which appears a weak plant with no strength, yet in His divinity He is a blazing fire!
He came “before” Israel as the Shepherd who goes ahead of His flock!

“And as a root out of a dry ground” [2]; His appearing came in an unexpected way, for the Jews thought they would see the Messiah as a great king with authority, able to shatter the Roman Empire and to establish a state that would rule the world; but He came as a hidden root in dry ground, from which no one expects that it will sprout and bear fruit. He came from a dry ground, for He was born of St. Mary, who was betrothed to Joseph the carpenter, and both of them were poor; “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich” (2 Cor 8:9).

The Lord Christ came as a root out of a dry ground, for the Jews at that time were in a state of severe dryness; He came in the midst of the dryness to make a paradise out of the wilderness. The bride said of Him: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song 2:3).

“He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not” [2-3].

Here the prophet moves from the scene of the Incarnation to the scene of the Cross. In the Incarnation he saw Him as a small shoot from the seed of David, and a root out of a dry ground; He came as a son of men when all humanity, including the people of God, was in complete dryness, and He came from a poor family, so that Nathanael said: Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?! Now the prophet looks upon the scene of the Cross and sees it without form, without comeliness, without appearance, despised, so that no one dares to approach it, a man of sorrows, from whose sight we hide and cover our faces because of the intense grief.

* He has no form nor comeliness in the eyes of the Jews, but to David He is fairer than the children of men (Ps 45:2). On the mountain (at the Transfiguration) He was radiant and shone more than the sun (Mt 17:2), pointing us to His future mystery.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * He who is fairer than the children of men was seen by men on the Cross without form or comeliness; His face was bowed down, and His position unseemly. Yet this lack of comeliness in your Savior poured out the price of your inner beauty, for the glory of the king’s son is from within (Ps 45:2).
St. Augustine

entries.section: 3. The Cross is redemption and salvation:

paragraphs.text: 4 Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. 5 But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. 6 All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. 7 He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth. 8 He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. 9 And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth. 10 Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. 11 He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities. 12 Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
After speaking of the Cross from the outside, he leads us into its depths that we may discover its mystery and its power as a sin offering and an atonement for our sins, saying:

“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted” [4]. What He bore was not His own griefs nor His own sorrows, but our griefs and our cares and our wounds...
What He bears is the weight of our sins, which He willingly bowed down to carry in His body for us, out of His love.

* He bore our sins and carried our diseases, and yet He suffered nothing that needed a cure, for He was tempted in all things like as we are, yet without sin. He who persecutes the light that shines in the darkness cannot overcome it.
* He was bruised and wounded, yet He healed every disease and every weakness.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Be not ashamed of the Crucified One, but rather boast of Him, saying: He bore our sins, He carried our sorrows, and with His stripes we are healed.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem The Lord Christ bore our sorrows, as we saw Him in the Garden of Gethsemane drinking our cup to the end, in all its bitterness, when He prayed to His Father, saying: “O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done” (Mt 26:42). He took Peter and the two sons of Zebedee so that they might see Him begin to be sorrowful and very heavy, saying to them: “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death” (Mt 26:38).

entries.section: 3. The Cross is redemption and salvation:

paragraphs.text: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin” (2 Cor 5:21), for He offered Himself as a sin offering, bearing our sins and our iniquities and making atonement for them. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him [had He not endured the chastisement for us, we would not have enjoyed peace]; and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” [5-6].
* The Lord delivered His body to death that we might be sanctified through the forgiveness of sins, which is accomplished by the sprinkling of His blood...

We must thank the Lord from the depths, for He told us of the things that are past, and gave us wisdom concerning the things that are present, and did not leave us without understanding concerning the things to come.
The Epistle of Barnabas * We are cleansed by His precious blood, which purifies us from every sin, His blood which does not cry out for vengeance like the blood of Abel (Heb 12:24).

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * Let us remind ourselves of the benefit of the true faith. For it is useful for me to know that Christ bore my weaknesses for me, and submitted to the sufferings of my body; so that for my sake, that is, for the sake of each one, He became sin and a curse (2 Cor 5:21; Gal 3:13).
For my sake He humbled Himself and submitted...!
He became a curse, not in respect of His divinity but in respect of His humanity, for it is written: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” (Gal 3:13).
In the flesh He was hanged, and therefore He became a curse, He who bore our curse!
He wept so that you, O man, would not weep much!
What a glorious remedy! That we should have the consolation of Christ.
He endured these things with wondrous patience for our sake... and we truly cannot endure ordinary patience for His name’s sake.
Behold, His tears wash us and His weeping cleanses us!
St. Ambrose * By death He raised the dead from death, for He bore the curse, saving us from it.
St. John Chrysostom * By the death of the Righteous One, which was accomplished of His own free choice, He removed the death of sinners, which occurred of necessity as a judgment we deserve.

entries.section: 3. The Cross is redemption and salvation:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” [7].
The prophet speaks here in the past tense, and as St. John Chrysostom says: [This was the custom of the prophets of old, to speak of the future as of the past].
* Surely the prophecy speaks most plainly of the Lord Jesus when it is said, “as a lamb to the slaughter” [7] (as being our Passover).
Your forehead has been anointed with the sign (of His blood) and also the doorposts, since all Christians bear the same sign.

St. Augustine * When (Pilate and the religious leaders) entered into dialogue with one another, He was in peace, fulfilling the saying of the prophet: “He opened not his mouth; in his humiliation his judgment was taken away” [7-8] (the Septuagint).
St. John Chrysostom * It was fitting for Him to be silent during His sufferings, but He will not be silent in the judgment.
He who afterwards comes as Judge came to be judged; therefore He will come with authority to judge, He who in great humility was judged.
* He bore evil patiently, since He would afterwards bring righteousness.
* When He was led as a sacrifice, “before her shearers he opened not his mouth,” and when He was crucified and buried He was always the hidden God of gods.

St. Augustine * When He was scourged, He was silent! And when He was crucified, He prayed for those who crucified Him! “What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the LORD” (Ps 116:12-13).

St. Jerome St. Augustine sees that the Lord Christ was silent during His trial and mockery because He hid His divinity so that they might accomplish what they wanted; but in His final coming to judge, “he doth send out his voice, and that a mighty voice” (Ps 68:33), “shall not keep silence” (Ps 50:3), for He reveals His divinity.

entries.section: 3. The Cross is redemption and salvation:

paragraphs.text: “And who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken” [8].
* “Who shall declare his generation?” [8]. He was born eternally... He was born of the Father without time, and He was born of the Virgin in the fullness of times.

entries.section: 3. The Cross is redemption and salvation:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine “And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth” [9].
* They crucified Him with thieves, fulfilling the prophecy involuntarily. What they did to dishonor Him was counted for truth, that you may perceive the great power of the prophecy...

Satan tried to throw a veil over what happened but he failed, because the three were crucified, yet Jesus alone was glorified, that we may perceive His authority over all. Miracles took place when the three were nailed to the crosses, but no one ascribed what happened to the other two, but to Jesus alone. Thus the plan of Satan was completely frustrated and everything turned back upon his own head, for one of the two thieves was saved, one who did not offend against the glory of the Cross but contributed to it not a little. For the changing of a thief while on the cross and drawing him into Paradise is no less than the shaking of the rocks.

St. John Chrysostom St. Augustine sees that the prophecy “And he made his grave with the wicked” was fulfilled by the setting of wicked guards at the tomb of the Lord Christ, who accepted a bribe to lie, saying, “His disciples came by night, and stole him away while we slept” (Mt 28:13). They spoke falsely and so bore witness to His resurrection, for if they were asleep, how did they know that His disciples stole Him?! They testified that His body was not in the tomb, while their accusation of the theft of the body is a matter that reason does not accept.

entries.section: 3. The Cross is redemption and salvation:

paragraphs.text: “Because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors” [12].

* If for your sake and for the sake of your sins He was numbered with the transgressors, then be a keeper of the Law for His sake. Worship Him who was hanged for your sake, even if you yourself are hanged... Buy your salvation with your death, and enter with Jesus into Paradise, that you may know from whence you are fallen (Rev 2:5).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * He intercedes for us every day, washing our feet, and we too need to have our feet washed daily by walking in truth with spiritual steps, so that we may know the Lord’s Prayer, saying:
“And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Mt 6:12).
St. Augustine

1 “Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith the LORD. 2 Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes; 3 For thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles, and make the desolate cities to be inhabited.

“Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith the LORD” [1].

Origen sees that the husband here is the Law, to which the ancient people were bound as to a husband, and it was fitting for her to bring forth abundant fruit, while the Gentiles were deprived of it; yet when they were united with the Lord Christ through faith in Him, they bore children holy to the Lord.

St. Augustine compares the Church of the Old Testament with the Church of the New Testament: the first was married to the Law, so that she and her children were in bondage, because she sought temporal blessings; but the second worships God for His own sake, that He may be all in all, and her service is free, belonging to the children of the free woman, not of the bondwoman. The latter was formerly barren and had no children, but now she has many children, more than the first had... This gives her joy and singing.

What we say of the Church of the New Testament as a whole we say of every soul that is joined to her, for however barren and dry our past life may have been, the Lord’s wide mercies are able to grant us spiritual fruits of the soul (sons) and of the body (daughters), by our accepting the Cross and enjoying the resurrection with Him.

* The Law came to work to make men righteous, but it could not; so (Christ) came and opened the way of righteousness by faith, and in this He accomplished what the Law desired. What the Law could not accomplish by the letter, He accomplished by faith.
St. John Chrysostom * The Church extends to the right and to the left, and no longer remembers the shame of her widowhood.

* Jerusalem was called, but the first Jerusalem refused to listen, so it was said to her: “Behold, your house is left unto you desolate” (Mt 23:38). But she of whom it is written: “Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear”... did not despise Him who called her. He sends her rain and gives her fruit...
After His resurrection He called the Church from all the world, so that she is no longer weak on the Cross but strong in heaven.

* That prophecy is fulfilled in which Isaiah speaks through Your tongue to Your Church, Your holy city, the barren one who has children and who is desolate more than she who has a husband. For it was truly said to her: “Rejoice, O barren, thou that didst not bear”... more than the Jewish nation, which has a husband in having received the Law, and more than she who has a visible king. For Your King is hidden, and you have many children from the hidden Bridegroom.
St. Augustine What is the result of this fruitfulness?

a. “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes; for thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles, and make the desolate cities to be inhabited” [2-3].

The prophet looked upon the Church of the New Testament as a tent of meeting with the Lord, to which innumerable multitudes would come from the right (the Jews) and from the left (the Gentiles) in an unceasing flood, until the place became very narrow, so he asked for the place of the tent to be enlarged, the curtains made for it to be stretched forth and its cords to be lengthened... For she extends so that the earth may become the Lord’s and His Christ’s; she turns pagan nations into sanctuaries for the Lord, and makes desolate cities into holy dwellings for the people of God.

This is the image of the soul that meets the Cross: it truly becomes the tent of the Lord, whose heart widens day by day to bear the image of the Savior, the Lover of mankind. It opens its depths to the good (those on the right) and to the bad (those on the left), so as to embrace in love every soul into a life of fellowship with God in His Son by the Holy Spirit. It is as though the fruitful work of the Cross is the pouring out of the Spirit of love in us, that we may share the love of the Crucified One; we spread the arms of our hearts to embrace all, that His divine saying may be fulfilled in us: “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Jn 13:35).

If the Cross has opened the doors of hope before all nations by divine love, our witness to the Crucified One will not be realized so long as the tent of our hearts is narrow, its doors closed, its cords short and its stakes loose... Let us give our hearts to the Crucified One, and He will establish them as the kingdom of His love, wide enough for all humanity and ever growing!
Often we judge others as desolate cities, when it was fitting for us to judge ourselves, because we have not borne in us the love of the Crucified One, which inhabits the desolate cities!

* It is not fitting for a man to care for himself only; he must care for others also... For what use is a lamp that does not shine for those sitting in darkness?! And what profit is a Christian who benefits no one else and brings no one back to virtue?!
St. John Chrysostom

4 Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed: neither be thou confounded; for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood any more. 5 For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called. 6 For the LORD hath called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit, and a wife of youth, when thou wast refused, saith thy God. 7 For a small moment have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I gather thee. 8 In a little wrath I hid my face from thee for a moment; but with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee, saith the LORD thy Redeemer. 9 For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth; so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee. 10 For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee.

If the Cross is a shame, a stumblingblock to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor 1:23), yet we bear its fruit and so perceive it as “the power of God, and the wisdom of God,” and we are not ashamed of it (Gal 6:14). Therefore the prophet says: “Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed: neither be thou confounded; for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood any more” [4]. At the Cross the soul meets her Bridegroom, the Giver of life, the Conqueror of death, and she forgets her former widowhood and the shame of her youth, for she lived a long time as one alone and forsaken, with no one to fill the void of her heart. Her gazing upon the crucified Bridegroom satisfies all her inner depths, so she cares nothing for the mockery of the daughters of Jerusalem who reject salvation, but in the power of love she says: “I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please” (Song 3:5).
St. John Chrysostom relates to us a dialogue between the heavenly Bridegroom and the human soul, in which he says:
[Great is my dowry...! He came and took me, and appointed a dowry for me, saying: I give you my riches!
Have you lost Paradise? I restore it to you...
And yet He did not give me the whole dowry here; why?
So that I may give it to you when you enter the royal place.

Did you come to Me? No, it is I who came to you... not that you should remain in your place, but that I might take you with Me and return with you. So do not ask Me for the dowry while you are here in this life, but be full of hope and faith.]

This is the secret of our joy, and this is the place of our unceasing praise. The Cross has turned our widowhood into a unique wedding in which we are united with the Lord Himself, “For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called. For the LORD hath called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit, and a wife of youth, when thou wast refused, saith thy God” [5-6].

We were in shame like a woman whose husband had forsaken her, so that her spirit was broken with shame and disgrace; he refused her because of her adultery and her abominations, and behold, she becomes a bride of the LORD of hosts, the Holy One of Israel, the God of the whole earth, Jesus Christ.

When she meets her Bridegroom and enjoys His glories, she forgets the period of her widowhood with all its bitterness, and reckons the whole past as less than a moment or the twinkling of an eye. The grace of the Lord of glory and His kindnesses, which make us one with Him and unite us with His Father, make us perceive with joy His words to us: “For a small moment have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I gather thee. In a little wrath I hid my face from thee for a moment; but with everlasting kindness will I have mercy on thee, saith the LORD thy Redeemer” [7-8].

Before the eternal mercies of God we count all the days of our affliction as like a small moment that passed so that we might enter the heavenly glories. As for His saying “I will gather thee,” it means the gathering of the holy Church together from all nations, peoples and tongues as one body to the Head, or as one bride to her heavenly Bridegroom. Also in her the believers are gathered together, all the men of the Old Testament with the men of the New Testament; in her the heavenly are gathered with the earthly, and the priests with the people, and so on... All this will not be accomplished unless man is gathered together with himself as a whole, where the soul is subject together with the body with all its senses and feelings, and the mind with the heart and the gifts, and so on... so that he becomes wholly holy to the Lord.

This marital love between Christ and the human soul is eternal and does not pass away; for just as God gave Noah a promise that He would not drown the world with a flood in His wrath against mankind [9], so the Lord gives us a promise that He will never leave us or take away His mercy from us, saying: “For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee” [10].

In short, He chose us as a bride for Himself, taking away the shame of our widowhood, confirming His love for us and His mercy upon us, giving us sure promises, ever renewed and eternal. He raised us up from the house of adultery, and washed us and sanctified us as a bride for Himself, to bring us into His heavens as a queen sitting at His right hand. And as St. John Chrysostom says: [God desires the adulteress, so what does He do? He does not lead her on high while she is an adulteress, for He does not want to bring her into heaven in this condition, but He came down to her. He came down to earth since she was unable to go up on high. He came to the adulteress and was not ashamed to take hold of her while she was in her drunkenness...].

11 “O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. 12 And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones. 13 And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; and great shall be the peace of thy children.

The secret of our praise is that we were like a barren woman to whom God gave a multitude of children, and like a desolate, forsaken woman who found the Lord Himself as a bridegroom for her, and also like a ruined city which the Lord renewed and rebuilt.

“O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones” [11-12].

What a wonderful picture it is that reveals the degradation to which humanity had sunk and the surpassing glory, beyond utterance, that has come upon it! It was like a ruined, demolished city, counted in humiliation, and disturbance came upon it through the enemy who took its people captive and made them lose all hope, so that they were without comfort. Now the Lord builds it up in this way:

a. He builds its stones with antimony, a sign of strength and firmness. These stones are the souls that accepted faith in the Savior and became living stones in the temple of the Lord, which the enemy of good cannot shatter or snatch away!
b. The foundation is of blue sapphire. The foundation is our heavenly (blue) Lord Jesus, the cornerstone who gathers all together in Him.
c. The pinnacles of translucent ruby are a reference to the believer’s inner glory, which rests on the righteousness of Christ and the holy life in Him, and is reflected on the outer pinnacles.
d. The gates of carbuncle stones point to the sanctification of the senses and our care for them, without shattering them or making light of them.
e. All the borders of precious stones point to the complete sanctification of the soul together with the body.

f. All her inhabitants are counted disciples of the Lord, and her children are full of peace [13], for the faithful members of the Church are made disciples at the hands of the Lord Himself through her, and every priest or teacher disappears before them, that they may see the Lord Himself working in all. And as St. John Chrysostom says: [Behold the honor of faith: it is not from men nor from man, but by God that they learn this...! The sonship here does not mean “all” (all thy children shall be taught of the LORD) in an absolute way, but means all who have the will. For the teacher sits ready to give what he has to all and to pour out his teaching for all]. And St. Augustine says of the grace of being taught by God: [This grace is called “teaching,” for God teaches those whom He calls according to His purpose, giving them to know what they ought to do, and at the same time to do what they know]. It is as though being taught by God, as a divine gift, has two complementary sides: true spiritual knowledge, and the enjoyment of working and practicing this knowledge in our daily life. He grants us to know the truth and to live it in Him!
Through this discipleship the children of the Church enjoy a surpassing peace: “and great shall be the peace of thy children” [13].
By sitting at the feet of the Savior we hear His voice and enjoy His resources so as to practice the truth in Him; He grants us the inner peace of the Spirit as a special gift for His children.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic described St. Anthony after he had spent a period in his severe asceticism, saying: [His body did not change... the disposition of his soul also was blameless, for his soul was not constrained as by grief, nor sunk in pleasure, nor affected by laughter or despair].

* Peace is the inheritance that the Lord promised His disciples before His crucifixion... saying: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you.” Whoever wishes to be an heir of the Lord Christ, let him reign over the peace of Christ and dwell in it.

St. Augustine g. The secret of the Church’s abundant peace, her edification and her strength is the righteousness of Christ, for He says: “In righteousness shalt thou be established: thou shalt be far from oppression; for thou shalt not fear: and from terror; for it shall not come near thee” [14]. The Apostle says: “Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification” (Rom 4:25).

14 In righteousness shalt thou be established: thou shalt be far from oppression; for thou shalt not fear: and from terror; for it shall not come near thee. 15 Behold, they shall surely gather together, but not by me: whosoever shall gather together against thee shall fall for thy sake. 16 Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy. 17 No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD.

How it gladdens the heart of the Church which the Lord Himself built and chose as a bride for Himself and a heavenly queen, making her children His disciples at His hands, granting them His surpassing peace, giving them His righteousness and working in them that they may live in righteousness and reject all evil and injustice; yet at the same time she is resisted by the powers of darkness gathered together, and the Lord gives her victory over them and triumph even over death.

a. The union of the powers of darkness against her: “Behold, they shall surely gather together, but not by me” [15]... They take counsel and work together against the Church of Christ, as the powers of evil gathered before seeking the crucifixion of her Bridegroom, so that their injustice was turned into salvation for the world, and God brought forth out of the eater meat, and out of the strong sweetness.
b. Their being united together makes them fall under the feet of the Church: “whosoever shall gather together against thee shall fall for thy sake” [15].

c. Their gathering is by divine permission: “I have created the waster to destroy” [16]; therefore we do not fear him nor are we disturbed by the severity of his violence, for he is held in the hand of the Creator.

d. Every resistance will surely come to an end, and the Church will be crowned to receive an eternal inheritance of righteousness: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD” [17].

1 “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. 2 Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. 3 Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David. 4 Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people. 5 Behold, thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not, and nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee because of the LORD thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he hath glorified thee.”
The divine call to enjoy the free salvation of the Lord carries the following items:

a. A general call to the thirsty: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” [1]. It is a general call to all; the doors of the Church are open before everyone, and whoever feels need, that is, “the thirsty,” listens to it. As the Lord said: “Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled” (Mt 5:6).
As we have repeated before, water in the Holy Bible sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit who works in the waters of Baptism; as though the call here is addressed to all to enjoy Baptism freely.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of the gift of Baptism, saying: [Do not hesitate however long the journey may be, whether by sea or by land, so long as the gift is offered to you, however many or few the obstacles, for Isaiah calls you: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye...” How swift are the mercies of God, how easy is the covenant! You receive this blessing as soon as you desire it. He accepts your very desire as a great price. He thirsts for your thirst, and satisfies all who desire the mystery. He offers kindness to all who ask kindness. He is ready to give generously, and rejoices in giving more than those who receive rejoice.]

b. A satisfying giving to all. This free gift, which is not bought with silver or with a price, offers every person his needs; so the mature find wine that gladdens them and the little ones find milk that sustains them.

The spiritual wine enjoyed by the mature signifies the state of joy enjoyed by those who have reached spiritual stature, so that their souls delight in the fatness of the Lord [2]. As the Spiritual Elder says: [Blessed is he who carries Your remembrance in his heart at all times, for his soul is always made drunk with Your sweetness.]

The spiritual milk offered to the little ones signifies God’s gentleness toward beginners, giving them what suits their spiritual stomach until they grow and mature; He knows how to offer each one what is for his edification, peace, satisfaction and refreshment.
Thus no one feels deprived, but as it is said: “eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness” [2].
* Do you not want to be satisfied? And how can that be?
The body longs to be satisfied, but hunger returns to it again after digestion; therefore the Lord Christ says: “Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again” (Lk 4:13)...
Then let us hunger and thirst after righteousness, that we may be satisfied from it..
May our inner man hunger and thirst, that he may have the food and drink suited to him.
He (the Lord) has said: “I am the bread which came down from heaven” (Jn 6:41). This is the bread of the hungry.
Let us also long to drink like the thirsty, “For with thee is the fountain of life” (Ps 36:9).
* Blessed is he who has forgotten the talk of the world through his talk with You, for from You all his needs are fulfilled.
You are his food and his drink...!

You gave the Spirit of Your Son in his heart, and the Spirit gave him boldness to ask of You all that is Yours, as a son asks of his father! His talk is with You at all times, for he knows no father but You!.
The Spiritual Elder * Ah! I shall not be satisfied until Your glory is revealed before me...!
He who possesses You has all his desires satisfied!

But how hideous is my wretchedness! Woe is me, O my God, for my heart tends to flee from You; to flee from You, the true Rich One and true joy, in order to follow the world in which there is nothing but sorrow and pain.
St. Augustine * Let them be all the more in need that they may deserve to be satisfied, lest while they show an arrogant fullness they be deprived of the bread that gives healthy life.
“Seek ye the LORD,” O needy, hungry and thirsty, for He is the living bread which came down from heaven (Jn 6:33, 51).
“Seek ye the LORD, and ye shall live.” You seek bread that your body may live, and the Lord seeks you that your souls may live.
St. Augustine * [“His eyes shall be red with wine, and his teeth white with milk” (Gen 49:12)].

His eyes are red with wine; these are His spiritual people who are made drunk with His cup; and His teeth are whiter than milk, which is the words with which are nursed the babes who are not yet fit for strong meat, as the Apostle says (1 Cor 3:2; 1 Pet 2:2).

St. Augustine * Be drunk, but be careful of the source. If you drink abundantly from the wonderful cup of the Lord, your drunkenness will be seen in your works, and will appear in your holy love of righteousness, and finally in the estrangement of your mind from earthly things to heavenly things.
St. Augustine Let us then draw near to our Christ and buy His wine and milk freely, according to His promise and His call.

c. Entering into an everlasting covenant to establish the fallen kingdom of David according to the sure divine promise: “and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, even the sure mercies of David” [3]. Through this covenant we become kings (Rev 5:10) belonging to the King of kings, of whom it is said: “Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people” [4]. He is the King who lays down the law of the New Testament and the new commandment, not for a particular people but for all peoples.

d. The acceptance of the pagan Gentiles who return to God by faith: “Behold, thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not, and nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee because of the LORD thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he hath glorified thee” [5].

This matter was not acceptable to the ancient people, and even after the door was opened before the Gentiles, the Church throughout the world remained for centuries in amazement before God’s love for all mankind, as He draws them from paganism and its abominations to proclaim the glory of God. In wonder St. Augustine says: [How have the Gentiles entered into the faith so swiftly...?! We ask them: What do you want? They answer: “To know the glory of God.”]

6 “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near: 7 Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. 8 For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. 9 For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts. 10 For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: 11 So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it. 12 For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands. 13 Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the LORD for a name, for an everlasting sign that shall not be cut off.”
Before this general, free and holy call to the thirsty, it is fitting for man to declare his response to it and his acceptance of it in practice by the following means:
a. Prayer, or seeking God in order to meet Him: “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near” [6].

If God loved us first, and came down to us to declare that He is not far from us but at the doors of our hearts, knocking that we may open to Him and He may enter (Rev 3:20), then it is fitting for us to seek Him, asking Him to take the keys of our hearts, that He may open and enter and shut, so that no one else shares with Him in our hearts, since He “openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth.”
The declaration of our acceptance of God’s love through prayer is a response of love to love, and the soul’s declaration of her desire for her unique Bridegroom, who asks for her hand forever.

b. Repentance: “Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon” [7].
What does repentance mean but the declaration of accepting light rather than darkness, and Christ rather than Belial (2 Cor 6:14)?!
Repentance is the way that St. John the Baptist prepared for the Lord Christ, and which the disciples preached to prepare mankind to receive His Kingdom within them!

c. Relying on God’s wisdom and trusting in His plan and His dispensations toward us, for He says: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” [8-9].

Our faith in the heavenly Bridegroom requires relying on Him with confidence in His abilities as the Almighty, all-wise and all-loving, who knows how to plan for His bride, for her edification and salvation, even if His plan appears harsh and His dispensations bitter.

d. Being watered by the word of the Lord that gives fruit: “For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” [10-11].

The Word of God came down incarnate to water human nature with His blood as a unique rain able to re-create it and renew it, turning it from a barren wilderness inhabited by fierce beasts into a fruitful paradise inhabited by the Holy Trinity, in which the heavenly and also the earthly rejoice. So it is fitting for us also to receive the written word of God, not for purely intellectual study, but as a life lived out that bears divine fruit.

e. Constant praise is a sign of accepting the Bridegroom in the heart and responding to Him inwardly: “For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands” [12].

Going out with joy means the soul’s going out from the “ego,” and her widening in love on behalf of her Bridegroom and all His beloved, her widening to the heavenly and the earthly... She goes out in order to return with all in peace and reconciliation with God, the angels and men. This wide love creates an atmosphere of joy through which the mountains and the hills sing, that is, the company of believers around you, as they see an eternal wedding taking place within you. As for the trees of the field clapping their hands, it means that joy is not in the tongue only but is declared by deed (by the hands)...

f. Abundant positive fruit. It is not enough to pull up the thorn and the brier, but the fir tree and the myrtle tree must appear as a sign of our being sealed with the name of the Lord, the Giver of spiritual fruit. In other words, our acceptance of His call does not mean only our leaving evil, but our doing the righteousness of Christ and practicing His holy, fruitful life by the work of His Holy Spirit in us.

entries.section: 1. A house of prayer for all peoples:

paragraphs.text: 1 Thus saith the LORD, “Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. 2 Blessed is the man that doeth this, and the son of man that layeth hold on it; that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and keepeth his hand from doing any evil.” 3 Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, “The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people”: neither let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.” 4 For thus saith the LORD unto the eunuchs that keep my sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and take hold of my covenant; 5 “Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off. 6 Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant; 7 Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.” 8 The Lord GOD which gathereth the outcasts of Israel saith, “Yet will I gather others to him, beside those that are gathered unto him.”

In the previous chapter the call was to all the thirsty (Isa 55:1); to Jews and Gentiles, to the thirsty and the hungry, to the blind and the deaf, and so on... that they might drink from the springs of the Gospel of free salvation and the gift of the Spirit offered to the Church of the New Testament. Now, fearing that someone might draw back from the gift, counting himself a stranger, the son of a stranger because he was born of a pagan family that denied the faith, or because he is barren by nature as a eunuch or a dry tree, he began to encourage all to enter through the doors of God’s wide mercies:

a. The salvation of the Lord is not far off, “for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed” [1]. As to time, there remained only seven centuries until the coming of the Lord Christ, the Savior of the world, that is, about 700 years, and a thousand years in the sight of the Lord are as one day (Ps 90:4). But what is more important is that the salvation of the Lord is near to everyone, because the Word is inside the heart, and the Cross of the Lord can be revealed in every soul. As St. Augustine said: [In my folly I was seeking You outside... and You were within me, deeper than my depths and higher than my heights.]

The way of our salvation is in our depths, because He has given us the Holy Spirit of God and our membership in one body, the Lord Christ, through Baptism... so we have become a dwelling for God and a temple for Him; therefore the Apostle says: “The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart” (Rom 10:8).
When St. Ephrem the Syrian speaks of the birth of the Lord of glory Jesus, he directs our eyes inward, where the Lord drew near to us and came to dwell by faith in our hearts (Eph 3:17).
* Let every man adorn the doors of his heart on this feast, for the Holy Spirit longs to enter and dwell in the heart and sanctify it. He goes about to all the doors to see where He may enter!

Let the doors of the heart rejoice on this feast together with the doors of the churches, so that the holy God may rejoice in the holy temple, the mouths of children may exult in praise, and Christ may rejoice on His feast as a mighty one.

St. Ephrem the Syrian b. By saying “Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed” [1] he reveals the concept of virtue. For we are bound to keep judgment and to practice justice, that is, to walk according to the divine commandment, which is judgment and justice, and this is difficult, indeed impossible, for human nature in itself. But if salvation is declared in the heart and the righteousness of Christ is manifested, the commandment becomes easy and possible, indeed natural and sweet, because the One who fulfills it is God who dwells in us and works by His Spirit in us.
Virtue according to St. John Cassian is [that through which we offer the kingdom of the heart to Christ].

We deliver the heart to Him that He may work in it and transform us into His likeness and image. Origen says: [We were created in the image of Christ, therefore virtues in his view are that we become one with Him, for He Himself is the virtues that we acquire]. [He is justice, wisdom and truth at the same time. Therefore whoever truly practices these virtues is a true partaker of the divine nature].
St. Gregory of Nazianzus says: [God is called love and peace; by these names He urges us to be formed according to these virtues, which are His marks].
Virtue is the work of God in His believers who accept His call and respond to His love:
* Do we not notice that there is nothing we do without Christ.
* We cannot run in the way of God except when carried on the wings of the Spirit.
* There is none stronger than he who enjoys heavenly help, as there is none weaker than he who is deprived of it.
St. John Chrysostom * God is holy and sanctifies, God is righteous and justifies.

entries.section: 1. A house of prayer for all peoples:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine c. This divine gift is free, but it is not given by compulsion nor to the slack, but to those who respond to it in practice. “Blessed is the man that doeth this, and the son of man that layeth hold on it; that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and keepeth his hand from doing any evil” [2]. For if God has given us His resurrection, or His risen life, as a “sabbath,” that is, rest for our souls, then it is fitting for us to live this life and keep it, and not to live in the misery and corruption of death. Let us keep our hand from the practice of every evil work, lest we be subject to the death of sin, but remain in the Lord, our true “sabbath.”

Our true sabbath is our Lord Jesus, the Sacrifice risen from the dead; in Him the Father finds His rest (His sabbath) concerning us, as we are justified in Him and counted His children; and in Him we find our rest, as we find in Him a place in the bosom of the Father.
* We ourselves become the seventh day (the sabbath) when we are filled with the blessings of God and His sanctification and are overflowing with them.

entries.section: 1. A house of prayer for all peoples:

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine d. The turning of strangers into sons of the house of God: “Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people” [3]. Rather they enjoy the divine covenant, and have the right to worship and to serve the house of the Lord. “Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the LORD, to serve him, and to love the name of the LORD, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant” [6].

What does the acceptance of strangers as sons of the house of the Lord and their taking hold of the divine covenant mean? It is the enjoyment of union with the Lord Christ, to enter the heavenly sanctuaries without hindrance, as holy sons in Him and as members of His body, having the right to union with the Father by the Holy Spirit through the blood of the covenant, the atoning blood of the Lord Christ.
The opening of the door of salvation before strangers that they may become sons of God, with the right to worship as well as to serve, gives hope to all, and as St. Hippolytus says:
[The “Word” shows His tenderness while showing no partiality...
He loves to teach the ignorant, and to bring the erring back to the true way.
Those who live in faith find Him easily, those who have the pure eye and the holy heart, who desire to knock at the door; for He opens the door quickly.
He drives away none of His servants as unworthy of the divine mysteries.
He does not honor the rich more than the poor, nor does He despise the poor because of his poverty.
He does not scorn the barbarian nor reject the eunuch as one who is not a man [3-4].
He does not hate females because of the disobedience of the woman at the beginning (Eve), nor reject males because of the disobedience of the man.
He seeks all, and desires the salvation of all, longing to make all sons of God, calling all the saints as one perfect man.]

e. He gives the eunuchs sons: “Neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree” [3]. Physical eunuchs were not permitted to be admitted to the priesthood (Lev 21:20) nor to join the people in the assemblies... (Deut 23:1).

Now that the doors of God’s mercies have been opened, there is no spiritual eunuch in the Church of God, for there is none barren among them, but all bear twins (Song 4:2)... All bear witness to God and bring forth sons for Him. It is as though our meeting with the Lord does not stop at our right to enter His house and enjoy His covenant, but gives us the power to witness to Him and to bear fruit.
God promised His people, if they obeyed, “Thou shalt be blessed above all people: there shall not be male or female barren among you, or among your cattle” (Deut 7:14).

entries.section: 1. A house of prayer for all peoples:

paragraphs.text: f. He raises the believers up as heroes, and their memory remains immortal forever, even in heaven. “Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off” [5]. How wonderful! The Lord came to us incarnate that He might die on our earth and rise to lift us up to His heavenly house, immortal, death unable to shatter us, but our names will be engraved in the book of God and on the palm of His hand forever.

The secret of the immortality of our name in the heavenly divine house is our union with the Lord Christ, as we are the living stones resting on the cornerstone. “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ. Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded” (1 Pet 2:5-6).

entries.section: 1. A house of prayer for all peoples:

paragraphs.text: g. Enjoying a worship that is joyful to us and a source of the Father’s pleasure: “Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” [7].

What does this mean but our enjoying worship not as a duty we are bound to or as formalities, but as a joyful ascent on the holy mountain of the Lord and rejoicing in the heavenly house of the Lord, as a house of prayer in which we offer our life as a burnt offering of love and a holy sacrifice united with the sacrifice of the holy Christ; we exult, and the Father accepts it as bearing the sweet fragrance of Christ, the source of His pleasure. Tertullian says: [This sacrifice comes out of every heart, is nourished on faith, and observes the truth. It enters in innocence and purity, in chastity, and is adorned with love. We must guard it with the greatness of good works, offering psalms and hymns on the altar of God that we may receive all things from Him].

h. The opening of the house of the Lord before all peoples, among them the outcasts of Israel. Perhaps the outcasts here are meant to include the return of Christians who have fallen (the new Israel), for the doors of the house of the Lord are open to all, even to the believers who have fallen or gone astray, since some heretics refused to accept them. St. Cyprian wrote two wonderful (works) on this matter under the title Repentance.

Thus this chapter presents to us a living picture of the Church of the New Testament, whose marks are these: she is a house of prayer, that is, the place of God’s meeting with men, where we enjoy a living fellowship with God who is near us, who makes His dwelling in us [1]. She is the dwelling of truth and justice, since we are united with our Christ, the Righteous One, who is able to justify the ungodly, offering them Himself as truth, justice, righteousness and love [1]. The mark of this house is the sanctification of free will: its doors are open to all without exception, but without compulsion or constraint [2-3]; whoever enters it has estrangement from God removed from him and becomes one of the household of God, but whoever wishes to remain outside, there is none who compels him to enter. Inside this house all become like fruitful trees that know no dryness [3], because it is the house of the Lord and His fruitful paradise. Whoever dwells in it lives with his Savior in His glories forever, so his name is engraved in heaven and a memorial that is never shattered is set up for him [5]. Inside is unceasing eternal joy and holy, heavenly, angelic worship (Isa 57:7). Finally, it is the house of mercy: whoever leaves it, the doors are not shut in his face, but the arms of the Lord remain waiting for his return.

entries.section: 2. The rejection of those who deny the faith:

paragraphs.text: 9 “All ye beasts of the field, come to devour, yea, all ye beasts in the forest. 10 His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber. 11 Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter. 12 Come ye, say they, I will fetch wine, and we will fill ourselves with strong drink; and to morrow shall be as this day, and much more abundant.”
Though the house of the Lord is open to all, even to fallen believers, whatever their fall, entering it is through “repentance.”
Whoever remains in his denial remains outside the house of the Lord, under no shepherding, inevitably exposed to the beasts of prey in the outer wilderness that he has chosen.

entries.section: 2. The rejection of those who deny the faith:

paragraphs.text: The prophet looks at those who reject the faith and sees their watchmen all blind, without spiritual knowledge [10], since they do not enjoy the gift of the Holy Spirit, the Giver of enlightenment; they have become like dogs unable to bark, unable to utter even a word for edification for the salvation of the flock, negligent and slack: “sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber” [10]. Their shepherds are like dogs that eat and do not bark, concerned with shameful gain, not with the benefit of the people, that is, greedy, who do not understand self-giving pastoral love [11]. They get drunk and make merry, and even invite others to share their drunkenness and luxury, reckoning that the life of revelry and luxury will last until tomorrow, and even expecting more luxury than they now have.
This is the picture of a pastoral care that lacks true divine love.

Whereas at the beginning of this chapter the Lord opens His spiritual house to all peoples without distinction, calling strangers to enjoy drawing near to Him and uniting with Him to receive fellowship in His eternal glories, and seeks even the fallen to return to Him that they may enjoy His love, He here contrasts that with the selfishness of some shepherds who have curled up around the “ego,” closing the doors of God’s mercies in the faces of people, seeking what is for their temporary pleasure at the expense of the salvation of others.

"The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil. He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness." [1-2].

Here the prophet speaks of what befalls the children of God throughout the generations, as they fall under many afflictions without cause, wounded like their Savior even in the houses of their loved ones (Zech 13:6), finding enmity even from their own household (Mt 10:36). But the prophet speaks here rather of the age of King Manasseh, who shed much innocent blood (2 Kgs 21; 2 Chr 33), so that the righteous desired death and counted it a rest from what they saw with their own eyes. This applies even more clearly in the days of the Antichrist, when the man of sin reigns in the temple of the Lord and persecutes the Church (2 Thess 2:4 etc.), until it is said: "Who is like unto the beast? who is able to make war with him?" (Rev 13:4), "And it was given unto him to make war with the saints, and to overcome them: and power was given him over all kindreds, and tongues, and nations... Here is the patience and the faith of the saints" (Rev 13:7, 10). Before this bitterness it is said: "the righteous is taken away from the evil" [2].

When the righteous are destroyed, or persecuted and killed, no one gives thought to it, for the wicked live in amusement like little children without understanding, while their parents and the loving ones who serve them die and they do not know it. But the righteous rejoice in death, counting it a release of their souls from the atmosphere that kills the soul, the atmosphere of hateful evil.
* "In his letter to a young widow."

Truly, if he had perished altogether, or if his affair had come to a complete end, that would have been a great calamity, and the matter would have been grievous. But if all that has happened is that he has sailed to a calm harbor and made a journey to God, who is in truth his King, then we must not grieve but rejoice. For this death is not death; it is rather a kind of emigration and a passing from the worse to the better, from earth to heaven, from among men to the angels and archangels, and indeed to be with God, the Lord of the angels and archangels... Now he is in great safety and calm.

* If your husband had walked like those who live a shameful life that does not please God, it would have been better for you to lament and weep, not only at his departure, but even while he was alive here. But inasmuch as he is one of the friends of God, we must rejoice in him, not only while he is alive here but also when he falls asleep in rest... Listen to what the Apostle says: "Having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Phil 1:23).
St. John Chrysostom * What a benefit we gain by departing from this world!

When the disciples grieved because Christ, the Teacher of our salvation and the Teacher of our good works, announced to them that He would depart, He said to them: "If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father" (Jn 14:28); teaching us to rejoice, and not to grieve, when one of our loved ones departs from this world, truly remembering the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Phil 1:21); counting death the greatest gain... For by death we leave behind painful toils and are delivered from the poisonous fangs of Satan, to go to the calling of Christ for us, rejoicing in eternal salvation.
The martyr Cyprian * He fears death who awaits another death after death.
* By death the children escape the afflictions that exceed their strength, obtaining the happiness that is the reward of their patience and innocence.

The martyr Cyprian St. Augustine sees that what is stated here about the death of the righteous, with no one taking it to heart, points to the Lord Christ, whom the wicked wanted to destroy by crucifixion, and they did not realize that He had permitted this in order to save what had been lost and destroyed. As the Apostle Paul says: "for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:8).

3 "But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the whore. 4 Against whom do ye sport yourselves? against whom make ye a wide mouth, and draw out the tongue? are ye not children of transgression, a seed of falsehood, 5 Enflaming yourselves with idols under every green tree, slaying the children in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks? 6 Among the smooth stones of the stream is thy portion; they, they are thy lot: even to them hast thou poured a drink offering, thou hast offered a meat offering. Should I receive comfort in these? 7 Upon a lofty and high mountain hast thou set thy bed: even thither wentest thou up to offer sacrifice. 8 Behind the doors also and the posts hast thou set up thy remembrance: for thou hast discovered thyself to another than me, and art gone up; thou hast enlarged thy bed, and made thee a covenant with them; thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it. 9 And thou wentest to the king with ointment, and didst increase thy perfumes, and didst send thy messengers far off, and didst debase thyself even unto hell. 10 Thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way; yet saidst thou not, There is no hope: thou hast found the life of thine hand; therefore thou wast not grieved. 11 And of whom hast thou been afraid or feared, that thou hast lied, and hast not remembered me, nor laid it to thy heart? have not I held my peace even of old, and thou fearest me not? 12 I will declare thy righteousness, and thy works; for they shall not profit thee. 13 When thou criest, let thy companies deliver thee; but the wind shall carry them all away; vanity shall take them: but he that putteth his trust in me shall possess the land, and shall inherit my holy mountain."

The righteous suffer from the wicked, but what can the wicked do to them? For even death the righteous count a divine gift, through which they pass from the gloomy atmosphere to enjoy the joyful meeting with the Bridegroom of their souls. But the wicked the Lord summons to judgment, in which the following takes place:
a. The wicked bear several titles, among them:

* Sons of the sorceress: the whole nation rejected the true words of the prophets and resorted to sorcery and divination to know the future and to seek counsel. This is counted a rejection of belonging to God and an acceptance of sonship to the devil and his evil works, so the wicked were counted sons of the sorceress who mocks God [4].

* The seed of the adulterer and the whore [3]: they have no relation to the righteous life, neither on the father's side nor on the mother's; the father is an adulterer and the mother a whore. Thus corruption has come upon all, men and women.

They boasted that God was their Father and Zion their mother, but their abominations revealed their true condition: they forsook belonging to God and His Church in order to belong to the evil one and his kingdom. The Evangelist says: "They said to him, We be not born of fornication; we have one Father, even God. Jesus said unto them, If God were your Father, ye would love me: for I proceeded forth and came from God... Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning... for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 8:41-44).
* Children of transgression [4], because they refused to obey God and to respond to His prophetic declarations and commandments.
* A seed of falsehood [5]; they deal with their faults by lying and deceit, instead of frankness and clarity.

b. Their immersion in idol worship with intense impulsiveness, setting up idols, enflaming themselves under every green tree, and offering their children as human sacrifices, burning them for the sake of Baal and Ashtaroth [5]. This hideous picture, in which men declared their ingratitude toward God and toward their children, still exists in one form or another today. Instead of thanking Him for His gifts (the green tree), we sometimes offer our hearts, inflamed with evil, for the sake of the devil and his kingdom, as unclean standards set up in the hearts; and instead of caring for our inner life so that we may enjoy spiritual fruits for soul and body, that is, begetting sons and daughters in our hearts who praise God, we offer the powers of soul and body as human sacrifices for the sake of the enemy of good.

c. Their practice of evil in the valleys [6] as on the high mountains [7] and in the houses [8]... as though evil were not tied to place or circumstances, but to the heart that has turned away from its Creator and wanted independence from Him.
Perhaps he also wanted to stress that the wicked, in their shamelessness, do evil openly and in secret, in public places as well as inside houses.

d. The wicked are likened to an adulterous woman who is not satisfied with evil but enlarges her bed [8] to accept entering into a covenant with anyone and uniting with any man, instead of uniting with God as the sole Bridegroom of her soul and making an everlasting covenant with Him. She loved the wicked not for their persons, but for the sake of lying with them as an opportunity to satisfy the lusts of the body [8].

e. She set up remembrances -drawings or statues- for those with whom she commits evil; instead of repenting she boasts of evil. Perhaps by remembrances he meant the setting up of pagan statues as spiritual adultery, and attachment to strange gods instead of God her husband, or because adultery was joined to idolatry in her life.

f. She adorned herself and anointed herself with perfumes and sent messengers to the king to commit evil with her, and so descends to hell [9]. Perhaps by the king here he meant Pharaoh, to whom they sent that he might rescue them from Assyria, and God counted this deed spiritual adultery, being reliance on the arm of man instead of trust in God.

Her sending to the king points to her union with authority, as will happen in the days of the Antichrist, when perverted religious work will be joined to worldly power, so that opposition to the Church will come through blasphemy together with the use of violence against her.
g. She seeks evil diligently in many journeys until weariness overtakes her without her despairing; because of the desire for evil she neither weakens nor tires [10].

h. She commits evil without fear of God; she did not respond either to His threats, since she did not bear the fear of the Lord [11], nor to His encouragement of her by pointing out her good works [12].

i. Her reliance on her lovers and those who desire her, as crowds who admire her; yet all of them are carried away together with her as by the wind, or are blown away with a breath, and are not found.

Perhaps by her lovers he meant the pagan gods, since she cried to them without finding any response from them, for they are unable to offer salvation; the Lord scatters her together with them like wind and like a swift breath.

entries.section: 3. The blessings of returning to God:

paragraphs.text: 14 "And shall say, Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people. 15 For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones. 16 For I will not contend for ever, neither will I be always wroth: for the spirit should fail before me, and the souls which I have made. 17 For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth, and smote him: I hid me, and was wroth, and he went on frowardly in the way of his heart. 18 I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners. 19 I create the fruit of the lips; Peace, peace to him that is far off, and to him that is near, saith the LORD; and I will heal him. 20 But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt. 21 There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked."
Despite the corruption and spiritual adultery they have committed, God awaits their return to Him in repentance, to grant them the following blessings:

a. They inherit the land as a way by which they pass to the eternal inheritance. As the Lord says: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth" (Mt 5:5), and it is written in the Psalm: "For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth" (Ps 37:9). "But he that putteth his trust in me shall possess the land, and shall inherit my holy mountain. And shall say, Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way" [13-14].
If the land here points to Canaan and the holy mountain of the Lord points to Zion, then repentance grants man enjoyment of the divine blessings in this world as a pledge of the heavenly Jerusalem.

St. John Chrysostom sees that God has promised us a heavenly dowry: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man" (1 Cor 2:9) [He appointed these as a dowry, namely: immortality, the praise of the angels, deliverance from death, freedom from sin, the inheritance of the Kingdom, whose wealth is so great, righteousness, sanctification, deliverance from present evils, the discovery of the blessings to come. Great is my dowry...! The betrothal gifts are the present blessings that make us long for the blessings to come, but the dowry in its fullness is given in the other life].

If the "land" points to the body, then the pledge we receive here is to possess the body, that is, to hold authority over it, so that we may live holy in the body by the Spirit of God who dwells in us.
By saying "Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way" [14], He means our receiving Christ our Savior as "the Way", by whom and in whom we enjoy the eternal inheritance.
b. The removal of the stumblingblock, as it is said: "take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people" [14].

entries.section: 3. The blessings of returning to God:

paragraphs.text: c. God's dwelling in their midst, as they are counted the high and holy mountain of God [15]. To the degree that they humble themselves in their own eyes, God exalts them and counts them worthy of His dwelling, as it is said: "I dwell... with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones" [15].

* He is far from the proud, near to the humble; "Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly" (Ps 138:6). The proud do not think of themselves that they are unseen, "but the proud he knoweth afar off" (Ps 138:6). He saw the Pharisee from afar, since he boasted of himself, but the tax collector was near to Him that He might help him, because he confessed (his sins) (Lk 18:9-14).

St. Augustine * Pride, even if righteousness, fasting and the paying of tithes accompany it, sees its chariot driven backward; but humility of spirit, even if sin accompanies it, outstrips the horse of the Pharisee, even if the one who leads it is poor!

St. John Chrysostom d. Even if God, as a chastener, is angry with the wicked, yet He is the Creator of souls who desires their salvation and their return to Him; therefore He does not contend for ever, nor is He always wroth, but wants everyone to return to Him, that He may heal every weakness and lead the people Himself and restore to them His comforts, as He says:

entries.section: 3. The blessings of returning to God:

paragraphs.text: "For I will not contend for ever, neither will I be always wroth" [16]. As St. Augustine says, the troubles we endure here are because of God's wrath (against our sins) so that we may repent.

He continues the discourse thus: "for the spirit should fail before me, and the souls which I have made" [16]... God, who created human souls, will not abandon them, but longs for their salvation and works for it.

entries.section: 3. The blessings of returning to God:

paragraphs.text: "For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth, and smote him: I hid me, and was wroth, and he went on frowardly in the way of his heart. I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners" [17-18].

The blows that befall him are divine wrath, for God in His love hides and is wroth in order to strike His children for a time.
